en: [1. The Perfection of Giving] The *Śikṣāsamuccaya*;
the first chapter, titled "The Perfection of Giving."
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

By listening to which, you have experienced the intense, repeated, and endless sufferings of the great precipices of hell and the like with unpeaceful minds; therefore, apply yourselves with the most noble diligence to hearing it once again.
Having heard this, one whose mind is not agitated exhausts entirely the vast evil previously accumulated;
they attain a happiness never before reached and never suffer any decline from that happiness.
They attain the supreme, inexhaustible bliss of the bodhisattvas, as well as incomparable perfection;
for they have obtained the opportunity to hear with reverence this most rare jewel of the Dharma being spoken, even though it was previously unobtained.
And may the gods, nāgas, and beings, with serene minds, come to hear the words of the one who is the sole benefactor of the three worlds;
and may the lords of the gandharvas, yakṣas, garuḍas, asuras, and kinnaras, along with the pretas and others, come with joy, their thirst for hearing [the Dharma] having been aroused.

Having respectfully prostrated to all the Sugatas together with their Sons and their Dharma-bodies, as well as to all those worthy of veneration, I shall explain the entry into the vows of the sons of the Sugatas through words that condense the essential meaning.
There is nothing unprecedented here to be said, nor do I possess skill in composition;
for this very reason, I have no effort for the sake of others, but this is intended by me to cultivate my own mind.
For my part, by this means the force of my serene confidence increases as I cultivate virtue;
if another who possesses a nature similar to mine should also behold it, then for that reason too, this [act] becomes meaningful.
This perfection of the opportune moment, so difficult to obtain, has been acquired; it is the means for accomplishing the goals of human life.
If one does not contemplate what is beneficial now, how will such an encounter occur again?
As it is said in the noble Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra,
in the noble Vimokṣa of Jayoṣmāyatana:

The cessation of the eight inopportune states is difficult to obtain; the attainment of human birth is difficult to obtain; the purity of the endowment of opportune conditions is difficult to obtain; the arising of a Buddha is difficult to obtain;
the possession of unimpaired faculties is difficult to obtain;
and the hearing of the Buddha’s Dharma is difficult to obtain.
Encountering a true person is difficult to find;
genuine spiritual friends are difficult to find;
and the imparting of instruction according to the true method is difficult to find.
A right livelihood is difficult to obtain;
likewise, an effort conducive to the true Dharma is difficult to find in the world of humans.

Thus, having encountered such a gathering, for that Great Being who— through the power of the Buddha-lineage— has well understood the suffering of saṃsāra from both the conventional and ultimate perspectives and desires the bliss of its pacification, this very reflection arises:
"When fear and suffering are not dear to me and are likewise not dear to others,
what is the distinction of my own self such that I protect it and not another?"—
thus [he reflected] regarding himself and the realm of sentient beings.
By one desiring to bring an end to suffering and wishing to reach the pinnacle of happiness,
the root of faith must be made firm, and the mind should be established steadfastly in awakening.
For it is said in the *Ratnolkā-dhāraṇī*:
Having faith in the Victors and the teachings of the Victors, and having faith in the conduct of the sons of the Buddha;
having faith in unexcelled awakening, the mind of great beings is born.
Faith is the precursor, the mother, the leader, the protector, and the increaser of all virtues;
it dispels longing, carries one across the flood, reveals faith, and points the way to the city of security.
Faith is the clarity of an undisturbed mind, rooted in reverence free from pride;
faith is a treasure-store and the foremost wealth, like a hand that is the root for gathering all that is auspicious.
Faith brings joy in renunciation;
faith brings delight in the Dharma of the Jinas;
faith brings excellence in the knowledge of virtues.
The guides have attained the state of a Buddha.
The power of faith is for the sake of the sharp radiance of the faculties, for the sake of being uncrushable,
and for the sake of not being overcome by the afflictions that serve as a basis.
Faith is the seeker of the qualities of the Self-existent One.

Faith finds delight in the joy of unattached attachment; it is devoid of the inopportune moments and is supreme in a single moment. Faith transcends the path of Māra and reveals the supreme path to liberation.
Faith is the seed of the qualities of causes, free from decay; it is the sprout of the tree of awakening,
and the nourisher of the excellence of knowledge and bliss.
The one who demonstrates faith in all the Victors.
Those who always possess faith and a mind of reverence do not abandon their ethical discipline or their training;
and those who do not abandon their ethical discipline or their training—
Those who possess qualities are worthy of praise for their virtues.
Those who always possess faith and reverence for the Dharma listen insatiably to the teachings of the Jina.
Those who listen insatiably to the qualities of the Victors develop resolute faith in those inconceivable dharmas.
Those who always possess faith and reverence for the Saṅgha are irreversible and have clear confidence in the Saṅgha.
Those who are irreversible because they have clear faith in the Saṅgha are irreversible by virtue of the power of faith;
for those who are irreversible by virtue of the power of faith,
their faculties are sharp and radiant.
Those whose faculties are sharp and radiant have avoided evil friends;
those who have avoided evil friends are embraced by virtuous friends.
Those who are embraced by spiritual friends accumulate vast merit;
those who accumulate vast merit become great-souled ones through the power of their causes.
The Great Beings have attained the power of causes; their superior aspirations are sublime. Those whose superior aspirations are sublime are always sustained by all the Victors.
Those who are always sustained by all the Victors give rise to the mind of awakening;
those in whom the mind of awakening arises apply themselves to the qualities of the Great Sages.
Those who are devoted to the qualities of the great seers, born into the family of the Buddhas and truly reborn therein—
being thus born into the family of the Buddhas and truly reborn— they possess perfect union, liberated from all lack of union.
Those who are liberated through the yoga of non-union—
their intention is pure with serene faith.
Those whose intention is pure through serene faith possess a supreme and most excellent resolute intent;
those whose resolute intent is supreme and most excellent always practice the perfections.
Those who always practice the perfections are those who have set out here in the Mahāyāna;
those who have set out here in the Mahāyāna honor the Buddhas through their practice.
Those who worship the Buddhas through their practice possess an indestructible mindfulness of the Buddhas;
those who possess this indestructible mindfulness of the Buddhas shall always see and contemplate the Buddhas.
For those who always see and contemplate the Buddhas,
there is never a time when a Buddha does not stand before them.
"For those for whom the Buddha never fails to appear, the Dharma never fails them;
for those for whom the Dharma never fails them, they are always sustained by all the Victors.
Thus, an infinite expansion of qualities rooted in faith has been taught therein.
Having concluded that, he spoke again in brief:
"Rare are the bodies of ordinary beings who will have faith in such teachings as these."
But those who have accumulated merit and performed virtuous deeds, they shall have faith in this through the power of their causes.

One might serve beings as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields with every kind of happiness for an entire eon; yet such a distinction of merit does not exist as that which belongs to one who has faith in these teachings.
Thus it is taught also in the noble Daśadharmasūtra.
For faith is the supreme vehicle by which the Leaders depart;
therefore, a wise person should cultivate obedience to the Buddha's instructions.
In a person who lacks faith, the pure dharma does not grow,
just as a green sprout does not emerge from seeds scorched by fire.
Thus it is said; for this very reason, it is proclaimed in the *Ārya-lalitavistara-sūtra*: "Ānanda, one should apply oneself to faith; this is what the Tathāgata makes known."
Likewise, in the *Siṃhaparipṛcchā*, it is said:
"By means of faith,
one avoids the opportune moments and the non-opportune moments."

Thus, having firmly established the root of faith, one should make the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) firm, because it comprises all merit; as it is said in the *Āryasiṃhaparipṛcchā*, where the Blessed One was questioned by Prince Siṃha:
By what action is the inclusion of all phenomena produced,
such that one becomes beloved by sentient beings wherever one is reborn?
The Blessed One said:
"One should direct the mind toward awakening for the sake of the liberation of all sentient beings;
this is the summary of all dharmas, and by it one becomes beloved."
Thus it is said; likewise, it is also described in the noble Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra:
"O son of good family, the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is indeed the seed of all the qualities of a Buddha;
it is the field, because it causes the growth of the pure qualities of the entire world."
It is like the earth because it is the refuge for all the world, and so on, up to being like a father because it protects all bodhisattvas.
... [and so on] ... (peyālam) ...
He is like Vaiśravaṇa because he cuts off all poverty; he is like the king of wish-fulfilling jewels because he accomplishes all aims;
he is like the auspicious vase because he fulfills all intentions.
It is like a spear for the sake of conquering the enemy of the afflictions;
it is like a sword for the sake of cutting off improper mental attention; it is like a scimitar for the sake of felling the heads of the afflictions.
It is like an axe, by virtue of cutting down the tree of suffering;
it is like a weapon, by virtue of protecting against all calamities;
it is like a hook, by virtue of pulling out those who are like aquatic creatures in the ocean of saṃsāra.
It is like a whirlwind, in that it scatters all the grass of the hindrances and obstructions;
it is like a summary, in that it encompasses all the practices and vows of the bodhisattvas;
and it is like a shrine for the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Thus, noble son, the thought of awakening is endowed with these and other immeasurable, distinguished qualities.
How, then, is it known that the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) arises even in an ordinary person (pṛthagjana),
and that this is not merely words?
Because it is seen in many sūtras.
As it is taught in the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa*:
"Having first generated a view of a self-existent body as large as Mount Sumeru, the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) arises;
and from that, the qualities of a Buddha grow."
And from the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra*, it is known that even an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is a bodhisattva.
As it has been said: "Mañjuśrī, it is just as if, for example, a young kalaviṅka bird were placed inside an eggshell;
even though its egg is unbroken and it has not emerged from the shell, it utters the very cry of a kalaviṅka."
In the same way, Mañjuśrī, even though a bodhisattva is enclosed within the shell of the egg of ignorance,
because his view of a self is unbroken, he does not depart from the triple world, yet he utters only the cry of the Buddha—
namely, the cry of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
It is also stated in the *Sarvadharmapravṛttinirdeśa* that the earth split open for the bodhisattva Jayamati,
and having passed away, he fell into the Great Hell.
For he had no faith in emptiness and had harbored resentment toward the proponent of emptiness.
It is also declared in the *Niyatāniyatāvatāramudrā-sūtra*:
What is the bodhisattva who proceeds like one on a beast-drawn chariot?
It is as follows: suppose there were a certain man who desired to travel across world-systems as numerous as the atoms in five buddha-fields.

Having mounted that animal chariot, he sets out upon the road; after traveling a hundred yojanas over a long and distant path, he is then pulled back and turned away by a great whirlwind from behind by eighty thousand yojanas. Would that man be able to traverse those world-systems on that animal chariot?
"Even in as many as unspeakably unspeakable numbers of eons, it would not be possible to traverse even a single world-system.
He replied,
"Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"In the very same way, Mañjuśrī, whoever, having generated the thought of awakening, does not uphold the Mahāyāna..."
He does not study;
he associates with those belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle and cultivates intimacy with them.
He studies, recites, investigates, and understands the Śrāvakayāna, and he teaches its meanings to others, even up to awakening them.
Because of that, his wisdom becomes dull; he is drawn away from and turned back from the path of unsurpassed knowledge.
Even that faculty of wisdom and that eye of wisdom which belong to that bodhisattva through the cultivation of awakening are rendered blunt and obstructed for him.
"This Bodhisattva is one who proceeds by means of cattle and chariots."
Thus, this lack of conviction in emptiness and lack of delight in the Mahāyāna is generally not seen even in one whose practice of the mind of conviction is incomplete,
let alone in a bodhisattva whose practice of conviction is superior;
for it is said in the *Ratnamegha*:

He is described as having completely transcended the misfortunes of all the conduct of fools; he sports with incalculable samādhis, dhāraṇīs, liberations, superknowledges, and sciences; he has attained the light of the force of non-conceptual joy, which is effortless and directed toward the garden of the infinite Dharma and free from worldly desire for tens of millions of kalpas until the end of time; and he is perfected in the various meditations of the supreme Great Vehicle throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of immeasurable kalpas.

It is taught that there is the departure through the practice for the sake of others, the accomplishment of the production of the accumulations of merit and wisdom, and the fulfillment of hundreds of thousands of previous yogas.
Now, if this were of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*),
why would other producers of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) not be accepted on this stage?
And here, no specific mark can be found by means of one's own preference to establish [the text] as being of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Furthermore, it is understood from the statement regarding the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) of the practice of superior resolve (*adhimātrādhimukti-caryā*) that there is indeed a practice of resolve even in the middling and weak categories.
Furthermore, what is the intended meaning of this *Tathāgataguhya-sūtra*, wherein it is asked:
"Bhagavān, for whom is there the arising of the thought of awakening?"
He said:
"It is he, Great King, whose resolute intention is unshakable.
He said:
"Blessed One, whose higher aspiration is unshakable?
He replied,
"O Great King, it is that of one who gives rise to great compassion."
He asked: "Blessed One, for whom does the arising of great compassion occur?
He replied:
"O Great King, [it is the state] of one who does not abandon any sentient being.
He asked, "Blessed One, how is it that sentient beings are not abandoned?"
He said:
"O Great King, when one's own happiness is relinquished"—
this was said for the purpose of generating a longing for compassion in those who are satisfied with merely the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
Just as it is said that those who lack renunciation have not truly gone forth in the teaching of the Tathāgata,
so too here, one should understand this as a censure of other [inferior] forms of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), and not that the thought of awakening cannot arise in any other way at all.

As it is taught in the *Daśadharmaka-sūtra*: "In this case, noble son, a bodhisattva who is established in the lineage but has not yet generated the thought of awakening, being exhorted, inspired, and encouraged by a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata, generates the thought of awakening toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
This is the first cause for the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

Hearing the praise being spoken of either perfect enlightenment or the thought of awakening, one generates the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is the second cause.

Seeing sentient beings who are without refuge and without an island, one establishes a mind of compassion and generates the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is the third cause for the generation of the thought of awakening.

Having seen the Tathāgata’s perfection in all aspects and having generated joy, he resolves his mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; this is the fourth cause. Furthermore, that bodhicitta is twofold: the mind of aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhipraṇidhicitta*) and the mind of setting out for enlightenment (*bodhiprasthānacitta*), as it is stated in the *Āryagaṇḍavyūhasūtra*.

"Noble son, those beings in all the worlds who direct their resolve toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment are rare. Even rarer than they are those beings who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In this context, there is the mind of the vow for enlightenment (*bodhipraṇidhicitta*).

The thought "I must become a Buddha" arises from a formal vow (*praṇidhāna*). This is because even in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, it is stated that the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), even if produced through deceit, serves as the cause for Buddhahood.
How much more so, then, for having performed even some slight wholesome deed?
As it is said in the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra*:
"The Tathāgata named Ghoṣadatta was where the Tathāgata Nakṣatrarāja first generated the mind of awakening by giving him a betel leaf while he was acting as a cowherd."
Thus, it was under the Tathāgata named Vidyutpradīpa that the Tathāgata Yaśas first generated the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), having given a skein of thread while serving as a weaver.
Likewise, it was under the Tathāgata named Anantaprabha that the Tathāgata Arciṣmān first generated the thought of awakening, having given a torch of grass while serving as a city scavenger.

In this way, it was before the Tathāgata named Dṛḍhavikrama that the Tathāgata Duṣpradharṣa first generated the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), having given a piece of wood while acting as a wood-gatherer,
and so forth.
Furthermore, one must not despise the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) even when it is deficient in practice,
because it too gives birth to the happiness of infinite saṃsāra;
as it is described in the *Āryamaitreyavimokṣa*.
It is just as if, noble son, even a single diamond jewel surpasses all superior golden ornaments;
it does not relinquish its name as a "diamond jewel," and it dispels all poverty.

In the same way, noble sons, even when separated from the practice of its underlying intention, the diamond-jewel of the arousal of the mind for omniscience outshines all the golden ornaments of the qualities of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; it does not abandon the name "bodhisattva," and it brings to an end all the poverty of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is beneficial even without [extensive] conduct,
because it is stated in the *Apararājāvavādaka-sūtra*:
"Since you, O Great King, have many duties and much to be done..."

It is impossible for anyone, in any way, in every respect, entirely, and at all times, to train in the perfection of generosity, and likewise up to training in the perfection of wisdom. Therefore, O Great King, you should thus maintain the aspiration for perfect enlightenment, faith, [and]... the vow, whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or awake.
Even while eating,
even while drinking,
you should constantly and continuously keep [this] in mind.
Attend to this and cultivate it: having condensed, weighed,

and gathered together all the roots of merit— past, future, and present— of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, noble Śrāvakas, ordinary beings, and yourself, rejoice with the most supreme rejoicing, and so forth.

Rejoice with the equality of space and the equality of nirvāṇa; having rejoiced, offer it for the purpose of making offerings to all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and noble śrāvakas. Having offered it, make it common to all sentient beings.

Therefore, for the sake of all sentient beings, until the attainment of omniscience and the fulfillment of all Buddha-qualities, you should daily dedicate [your merit] three times a day toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. In this way, O Great King,
while practicing such conduct, you shall govern your kingdom and yet not neglect your royal duties or the accumulations for awakening.
And you shall fulfill it.
And right here its maturation has been explained:
"Furthermore, O Great King, by the maturation of that wholesome root of action consisting of the thought of perfect awakening, you have indeed been reborn many hundreds of times among the gods,
and you have been reborn many hundreds of times among human beings."
And in all rebirths among gods and humans, you exercise sovereignty;
yet, O Great King, no deficiency or incompleteness is perceived in that virtuous karma of the thought of perfect enlightenment (samyaksaṃbodhicitta).

Moreover, O Great King, even a single thought of perfect enlightenment, because it has the rescue of all sentient beings as its objective and the liberation of all sentient beings as its objective, [is inexhaustible].

Because it has as its objective the consolation of all sentient beings and as its objective the parinirvāṇa of all sentient beings, there is an accumulation of immeasurable and incalculable roots of merit;
what need is there to mention one who practices this extensively?
And this bodhicitta arises from the sight of the form-body (rūpakāya).
Regarding this, it is recited in a previous avadāna:
"In this way, the bodhicitta of aspiration (praṇidhāna-bodhicitta) is to be understood."
However, this must be addressed: does one who has not yet entered the stages (bhūmi) also have the qualification for the bodhisattva vow, or not?
It should be understood that they do; for in the *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra*, a root downfall is mentioned for the sake of gain and honor.
Yet, in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, it is shown to occur on the first stage.
Nor does he expect any honor from anyone else, thinking instead: "I myself must provide all these sentient beings with an abundance of every kind of requisite.
And so it is said:
"On the Bodhisattva stage of the Joyous (Pramuditā), he becomes well-established in the yoga of immovability..."
Furthermore, it is said:
"He becomes fixed in the lineage of the Tathāgatas and has full enlightenment as his ultimate goal.
However, the Ākāśagarbha-sūtra states:
"For him, even the Śrāvaka vehicle does not exist, let alone the Mahāyāna.
Likewise, in the *Āryograparipṛcchā*, training rules are prescribed even for one who is completely bound by stinginess;
however, in the *Pramuditā* [bhūmi], it is recited as follows:
And because the notion of a self has departed for him, attachment to a self does not arise; how much less, then,
attachment to any material requisites?
Likewise, the giving of his head and so forth is also mentioned here in this context.

In such passages as these in the sūtras, the prescription of training is seen even for one who has entered the stages (*bhūmi*). Where, however, there is an instruction concerning a bodhisattva in general, if it is through the capacity for practice or by means of a prohibitive statement, then this should not be practiced by a beginner bodhisattva (*ādikarmika-bodhisattva*). But when both conditions are absent, one should train in all [the precepts].
Even in that case, for one who is unable to train in a single precept, there is no offense due to the non-practice of the other precepts.
In the *Āryākṣayamatisūtra* it is also said thus:
"At the time of giving, there is the expectation of the integration of ethical discipline," and so forth.
One should not be lax in this regard, nor should one fail to fully realize the remaining perfections.
This is because it is stated in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*: "according to one's strength and according to one's capacity.
Furthermore, this restraint is also obtained by women who have weak afflictions and whose minds aspire to awakening;
for it is said in the *Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa*:
"Śāriputra, endowed with four qualities, bodhisattvas become speakers of truth. Beginning with this, he said:

"In this case, Śāriputra, a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having generated the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, dwells with aroused vigor for the sake of seeking wholesome dharmas"—this is the entirety of the instruction beginning from that point.
Furthermore, the undertaking of the vow should be performed in the presence of one who is observant of the vow and devoted to the practice of the bodhisattva training precepts.
For in this way, should he transgress a training rule, a powerful sense of shame and a fear of deceiving his teacher arise within him;
and therein, through effortless application, love and respect are perfected. This is the general dharma of the vow.
For this very reason, Bodhisattvas, desiring the accomplishment of one or another of the trainings in the presence of the Tathāgatas, undertake their formal acceptance.

In the absence of such a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), the vow (saṃvara) should be taken while cultivating the visualization of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas residing in the ten directions as being present before them, after having weighed the vow against one's own strength.
Otherwise, all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the world with its gods, would be deceived.

For in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, it is stated that one who fails to give even after having thought of giving just a little goes to the realm of hungry ghosts (*pretagati*), and for one who fails to give what was promised, the realm of hell (*narakagati*) is taught;
how much more so for one who, having promised the unsurpassed goal for the entire world, fails to fulfill it?
Therefore, it is said in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:
Noble son, a bodhisattva must be one for whom truth is the primary value.
Noble son, the recitation of truth is the recitation of the Dharma.

In this regard, noble son, what is truth? It is that which a bodhisattva, having generated the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, does not abandon that mind even for the sake of his life, nor toward sentient beings...
He acts contrary [to worldly standards];
this is the truth of the bodhisattva.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva, having generated the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, subsequently abandons that mind and acts wrongly toward sentient beings, this is called the bodhisattva’s base form of lying. This is also taught in the *Āryasāgaramatisūtra*.

Sāgaramati, it is as if, for example, a king or a royal minister were to invite all the citizens to a meal on the morrow, yet remain indifferent and fail to provide food and drink; thus he would truly deceive the entire body of people. Thereupon, not obtaining food and drink, they would depart while mocking him.

In the same way, Sāgaramati, if a bodhisattva reassures all sentient beings for the sake of crossing over those who have not crossed, for the sake of liberating those who are unliberated, and for the sake of encouraging those who are discouraged— yet does not apply himself to great learning, nor to the other factors conducive to awakening and roots of virtue,
this bodhisattva deceives the world together with its gods.
And thus, the deities who have seen previous Buddhas mock and deride him, saying:
"Rare are those masters of sacrifice who, having pledged a great sacrifice, fulfill it.
Therefore, Sāgaramati, a Bodhisattva should not utter such speech by which he would deceive the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Furthermore, Sāgaramati, a bodhisattva may be requested by someone regarding matters concerning the Dharma or practical duties.

In such a case, the bodhisattva has spoken a word such that even the sacrifice of one’s own self would have to be made by the bodhisattva; yet, in that situation, that sentient being must not be deceived.
Therefore, according to one's own strength, having undertaken even a single root of virtue, it must be protected.
As it is said in the *Āryakṣitigarbhasūtra*:
"Buddhahood is attained through these ten paths of wholesome action;
however, it is not for one who, even for as little as a single moment throughout their entire life, does not guard even a single path of wholesome action, yet nevertheless speaks in this way:"

"I am a follower of the Mahāyāna, and I seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment"—that person is an utter deceiver and a great liar; he is a fraud in the presence of all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and a proponent of nihilism to the world. That fool dies and goes to a state of ruin.
And for as long as one is able, for that long one should abide having undertaken what is wholesome.
And this is to be seen in the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha-sūtra*.

But that great being who, even having heard this, penetrates with wisdom the difficulty of the bodhisattva’s conduct and yet perseveres in bearing the yoke of protecting all suffering beings— by him [should be performed] the salutation, worship, confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, entreaty of the Buddhas, supplication, and the dedication toward awakening.

Having made a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and approached him, one should speak either by repeating what was said by that friend or by speaking for oneself. Having said, "Pay attention, O Teacher, I who am named so-and-so," one should generate the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) endowed with practice, just as it was generated by the Blessed One Mañjuśrī in his former birth narrative (*avadāna*) in the *Āryamañjuśrībuddhakṣetraguṇavyūhālaṅkārasūtra*.
For it was said by him thus:
For as long as the first limit of saṃsāra, which is devoid of end,
may last, for that long shall I practice an immeasurable course for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings.
In the presence of the Protector, we generate the mind set on perfect enlightenment;
I invite the entire world, for I shall liberate it from poverty.
From this day forward, until I attain enlightenment, I shall not harbor a mind of malice or stubbornness, nor shall I practice envy or stinginess;
I shall lead a life of celibacy and abandon all evil desires.
I shall train myself in accordance with the Buddhas in the restraint and discipline of ethical conduct;
I do not strive here to attain awakening in a hurried manner.
For the sake of even a single sentient being, I shall remain until the furthest limit of existence;
I shall purify a field that is immeasurable and inconceivable.
I shall establish a name renowned throughout the ten directions,
and I shall purify my actions of body and speech in every respect.
"I shall purify my mental action; I shall perform no unwholesome deed. Thus [he resolves].

Furthermore, one should not entertain any suspicion that taking this vow entails falling into a rebirth in another life due to its being for all time; for in this very sūtra, the vow of Akṣobhya is authorized, as it is said:
"Just as the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, formerly when he was a bodhisattva, spoke these words:
'May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, consider me to have been false if I do not go forth into homelessness in every birth.'"
For it has been said: "One birth must be thoroughly purified by one whose soul is awakened;
as for the other births until enlightenment, that very [first birth] will purify them."
In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva should train in emulation of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.

Training in this manner, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva goes forth into homelessness in every birth; whether Tathāgatas appear or do not appear, he necessarily departs from the life of a householder.
For what reason?
"Śāriputra, this indeed is the supreme gain, namely, the going forth from the household life;
even to the extent that he has no craving for wife, sons, or daughters."
How this fault does not occur in future births will be explained right here; let this matter rest for now.
Thus, the general characteristic of an offense for one who has undertaken the vows is stated;

by means of this characteristic of an offense, one should personally discern and avoid whatever object is endowed with it, and one should not be confused regarding those things that resemble offenses or those that resemble non-offenses.

A bodhisattva, for the sake of pacifying all present and future suffering and mental distress of all sentient beings, and for the sake of producing all present and future happiness and mental well-being, applies himself through body, speech, and mind with vigor and without deceit.
He exerts effort;

however, if he does not seek out the collection of conditions for that [effort], he does not strive to remedy those obstacles. He does not produce even a small amount of physical pain or mental distress that could serve as a remedy for great physical pain and mental distress, nor does he sacrifice a minor interest for the sake of accomplishing a great purpose; rather, he remains indifferent for even a moment.
One becomes guilty of an offense.
In brief, there is no offense regarding tasks that lie beyond one's own capacity, because since they would be fruitless in those cases, there is no prescription for training therein.
However, anything that is inherently reprehensible (*prakṛtisāvadya*) is indeed taken up [as an offense].
In a case where an offense might occur due to the capacity for renunciation even when it is beyond one's own power, that need not be considered;
for liberation from it occurs through the general confession of sins.
This is, in brief, the essence of the bodhisattva training;
however, in detail, its exposition extends for the duration of immeasurable eons.
Alternatively, in summary, there are two types of transgressions for a bodhisattva.
If one undertakes an action without considering whether it is appropriate or inappropriate according to one's capacity, but then desists and reflects upon it, one incurs an offense.
However, if after deliberation one transgresses what is fitting—even if urged by a *caṇḍāla* slave—one incurs an offense. Why is this so?
This is because of the statement in the *Adhyāśayasaṃcodana-sūtra*:
"Moreover, Maitreya, by four causes, eloquence is spoken by all the Buddhas... Here, Maitreya, eloquence is associated with truth."
It is associated with truth and associated with Dharma, not associated with untruth or non-Dharma;
it is a destroyer of afflictions, not an increaser of afflictions;
it demonstrates the qualities and benefits of Nirvana, not the qualities and benefits of Saṃsāra.
By these four [reasons]—the full passage being as follows:

"Maitreya, whoever has had, or will have, inspired eloquence through these four causes, there faith-inspiring sons of good family or daughters of good family should produce the perception of a Buddha; having formed the perception of a Teacher [toward them]," [they should act accordingly].
That Dharma should be heard.
Why is that?
Maitreya, whatever is well-spoken, all that is spoken by the Buddha.

In this regard, Maitreya, whoever should reject these inspired eloquences, saying, "These were not spoken by the Buddha," and should conceive a lack of respect for them out of hatred for the person [who spoke them], by that act they have rejected all inspired eloquence spoken by the Buddhas. Having rejected the Dharma, they go to the states of woe through karma conducive to the ruin of the Dharma.
Furthermore, for one who desires to master this for the sake of practice,
they should apply themselves to this *Śikṣāsamuccaya* at least for the purpose of training in the mere gateway of conduct, because the very commencement of training yields great fruit.
As it is said in the *Praśāntaviniścayaprātihāryasūtra*:

And suppose, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva were to give as a gift to each and every one of as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, having filled as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges with great wish-fulfilling king jewels, and were to continue giving such gifts for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.
Or, Mañjuśrī, suppose another bodhisattva, having heard such teachings as these, goes to a secluded place and reflects upon them with his mind, thinking, "I shall train in such teachings as these.
Even though he is not yet trained, Mañjuśrī, that bodhisattva who is intensely desirous of this training produces far more merit than the former;
indeed, that gift does not even equal this basis of meritorious action.
Therefore, seeing such benefits in this way, a bodhisattva should not turn back under any circumstances.
As it is said in this very context:

"In that regard, Mañjuśrī, suppose there were as many sentient beings as there are atoms in a great trichiliocosm, and each single sentient being among them were to become a king, a sovereign of Jambūdvīpa; and all of them were thus..."
They shall proclaim:
"Whoever shall take up, uphold, recite, master, or propagate the Mahāyāna, we shall shave his nails every month with a five-pala blade each day; and by this means, he shall be removed."
"We shall deprive you of life.
Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva, being addressed in this way, does not tremble, does not fall into terror—even for a single moment of thought—and is not afraid, does not despair, and does not doubt;
and if he further applies himself to the task of upholding the true Dharma, remaining devoted to its recitation and study; [then he is a bodhisattva].

Mañjuśrī, this bodhisattva should be called a hero of mind, a hero of generosity, a hero of ethical discipline, a hero of patience, a hero of vigor, a hero of meditative concentration, a hero of wisdom, and a hero of samādhi.
Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva does not become angry with those executioners, does not feel resentment, and does not give rise to a mind of stubborn malice,
then, Mañjuśrī, that bodhisattva is equal to Brahmā, equal to Indra, and is unshakable.
Furthermore, in this final age, respect for the training yields a great fruit of maturation;
for it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
"One may attend upon tens of millions of billions of Buddhas..."
With a serene mind, having given food and drink,
as well as parasols, banners, and rows of lamps,
for as many millions of eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
And whoever, while the true Dharma is perishing and the teaching of the Sugata is coming to an end,
should practice the training for even a single day and night;
This, therefore, becomes distinguished by merit.
Therefore, one should apply oneself with earnestness to this.
And the training precepts for bodhisattvas have been taught in the sūtras;
as it is said in the *Āryaratnamegha*:
"And how, noble son, do bodhisattvas become restrained by the vow of bodhisattva training?"
In this regard, a bodhisattva reflects as follows:
"It is not possible for me to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening through the mere restraint of the *prātimokṣa* alone.
Rather, it is by means of those modes of conduct for bodhisattvas which have been taught by the Tathāgata in various sūtras."
"The training precepts of a bodhisattva have been prescribed; I must train in each and every one of them"—such is the detailed account.
Therefore, the vow of a bodhisattva is difficult for one of dull intellect like myself to understand because it is taught so extensively.
Consequently, what is appropriate?
Therefore, one should know the vital points so that one does not incur an offense.
And what are those vital points which have indeed been taught in the sūtras for the benefit of those who delight in the Mahāyāna?
Namely:
[the relinquishment] of one's person, of enjoyments, of the merit occurring in the three times, and of the wholesome.
The relinquishing [of all things] for the sake of all sentient beings, their protection, and the increase of purity.
This is the summary of the bodhisattva vow,
wherein even transgressions committed during the intervals between a bodhisattva’s practices are formally established.
As it is said in the *Bodhisattvaprātimokṣa*:
"The path which has been undertaken by a bodhisattva for the sake of all sentient beings is one that leads into suffering.

Even if, while the bodhisattva remains established having undertaken that path, after the passing of ten million eons, a single thought of happiness should arise—even if it is merely the thought [of sitting] down."

In that regard, a bodhisattva should generate this thought: "Having taken upon myself the urgent needs of all sentient beings, I sit down even while avoiding this [action]. Mañjuśrī said: "He should indeed take it upon himself."

"O sons of the gods, there are these five acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) by which bodhisattvas, being endowed with these acts of immediate retribution, swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What are the five?

O sons of the gods, when a bodhisattva, having generated the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), does not in the interim generate the mind for the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha—this is [the first]."
O Devaputra, first is the immediate transgression:
having generated the thought of relinquishing all one's possessions, not to abandon that resolve midway due to a mind of stinginess—this, O Devaputra, is the second immediate transgression.
Having generated the thought, "I must rescue all sentient beings," not to falter midway—this, O Devaputra, is the third immediate transgression.

"Having generated the thought, 'I shall realize all phenomena as unarisen and unceasing,' one does not fall midway into the views of speculative dogmatism; O Son of the Gods, this is the fourth immediate transgression (*ānantarya*).
Having generated the thought, 'I shall realize all phenomena with wisdom conjoined in a single moment,' one does not stop midway nor falter before attaining omniscience;
O Son of the Gods, this is the fifth immediate transgression."
Therefore, in this way, the relinquishing, protecting, purifying, and increasing of one's person, enjoyments, and merit should be cultivated continuously and according to what is appropriate.

In that regard, first of all, for the sake of renunciation, one should generate dispassion by means of contemplating the faults of grasping, and one should contemplate the benefits of relinquishment. As it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
"Those fools who are thoroughly attached to this putrid body..."
In this life, which is flickering, uncontrollable, and comparable to an illusion or a dream.
"Having performed extremely fierce deeds while under the sway of delusion, those fools, having entered the vehicle of death, go to the terrible hells. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, it is said in the *Anantamukhanirhāradhāraṇī*:
Whatever sentient beings there may be who do not enter into conflict, the root cause therein is grasping; therefore, one should abandon that in which craving arises.
For one whose craving has been relinquished, indeed, there will be dhāraṇī.
It is said in the *Bodhisattvaprātimokṣa*:
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva produces the perception of 'belonging to another' toward all phenomena;
he does not grasp at any entity whatsoever."
For what reason?
Because clinging is indeed fear.
It is also said in the *Āryogradattaparipṛcchā*:
"That which has been given need not be guarded;
that which remains in the house must be guarded."
That which is given leads to the destruction of craving;
that which is kept in the house increases craving.
That which is given is without possession; that which is kept in the house is with possession.
That which is given is free from fear; that which is kept in the home is accompanied by fear.
That which is given serves as a support for the path to enlightenment;
that which is kept in the home serves as a support for Māra.
That which is given is inexhaustible;
that which remains in the house is perishable.
From what is given comes happiness; from what remains in the house, suffering begins.
That which is given leads to the abandonment of afflictions; that which remains in the house increases afflictions;
that which is given leads to great enjoyment.
That which remains in the house does not lead to great enjoyment;
that which is given is the deed of a true person,
while that which remains in the house is the deed of a base person.
That which is given is for the sake of capturing the mind of a true person;
that which remains in the house is for the sake of capturing the mind of a base person.
That which is given is praised by all the Buddhas.
That which is found in the house is praised by childish people.
Furthermore, if he should develop an even greater affection for his son than for other sentient beings, he must reproach his own mind with three reproaches.
With which three?
"Enlightenment belongs to the Bodhisattva who is correctly applied and possesses an even mind; it does not belong to one with an uneven mind, nor to one who is wrongly applied."
The awakening of a bodhisattva belongs to one who practices non-differentiation, not to one who practices differentiation.
Having reproached his own mind with these three reproaches, he should generate the perception of an enemy toward that [differentiation], thinking: "This is my enemy;
it is not a friend."
I, who have transgressed the training prescribed by the Buddha for this purpose, am producing an excessive degree of affection for this son,
not so toward other beings. Therefore, he should generate his mind in such a way that loving-kindness (*maitrī*), characterized by the love one has for a son, arises toward all beings.
Loving-kindness arises from concern for one's own welfare;
furthermore, he should investigate this with proper reasoning:
"This has come from elsewhere."
From another perspective,
all sentient beings have been my children,
and I have been the child of all sentient beings.
"Nothing whatsoever exists here for anyone, nor anything that belongs to another. Therefore, householder,
a householder bodhisattva should not exercise a sense of 'mine' or possessiveness toward any object whatsoever."
One should not harbor attachment,
nor fixed resolve, nor the latent tendency of craving.
Furthermore, householder, if a beggar should approach a lay bodhisattva and ask for some object or other:
If this object has not yet been relinquished by him,
he should not contemplate his mind in this way:
"Whether I relinquish this object or do not relinquish it, I will inevitably be separated from this object."
One must approach death without desire.
This object will abandon me, and I shall abandon it;
having relinquished this object, I shall pass away with my essence secured, and this relinquished thing will not remain obsessing my mind at the time of death.
"And this will produce for me at the time of death joy, gladness, and freedom from regret.
If, however, even while reflecting in this way, he is able to relinquish that object,
then he should satisfy that petitioner with four kinds of conciliatory speech.
By which four?
First, I am weak, my roots of virtue being unripened; I am a beginner in the Mahāyāna.
I am not a master of my own mind for the sake of renunciation; I possess views accompanied by grasping, and I abide in the notions of "I" and "mine."
Forgive me, O noble being!
Do not be distressed; I shall act accordingly, I shall practice accordingly, and I shall exert vigor accordingly.
"In such a way that I shall fulfill this intention of yours and that of all sentient beings as well.
Thus indeed, householder,
should the beggar be instructed by him.

And this "causing to understand" (saṃjñapana) was stated for the sake of avoiding future faults—lest there be a lack of faith on the part of the bodhisattva in that regard, or on the part of the petitioner toward the bodhisattva.
However, stinginess itself does not become blameless in this way; rather, it is something censured by the Blessed One for bodhisattvas.
As it is said in the *Bodhisattvaprātimokṣa*:
"Śāriputra, these four qualities are not found among bodhisattvas. What are the four?"
Deceit does not exist among bodhisattvas; stinginess does not exist among bodhisattvas;
envy and slander do not exist among bodhisattvas.
"I am not capable of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment"—
such a discouraged mind does not exist among bodhisattvas.
Śāriputra, one in whom these four qualities are found should be known as a wise person.
Truly, this man is a deceiver; truly, this man is a chatterer;
truly, this man has lost his moral integrity.
"Alas, this is a phenomenon of affliction! Alas, this one values worldly gain! Alas, this one is devoted solely to food and clothing!
Yet, Śāriputra, Bodhisattvas are indeed courageous in mind;
they even become those who give away their own hands and give away their feet.
One who renounces the nose;
one who renounces the head;
one who renounces the limbs and minor members.
One who abandons a son;
one who abandons a daughter;
one who abandons a wife.
One who renounces sensual pleasure,
one who renounces retinue,
and one who renounces the mind.
One who renounces happiness,
renounces the home,
and renounces material things.
One who abandons the country, one who abandons jewels,
and one who abandons all possessions.
Thus it is also said in the *Nārāyaṇaparipṛcchā*:
"One should not take up that object for which the thought of renunciation does not arise,
nor should the intention to give fail to proceed."

One should not take possession of that possession for which one does not conceive the thought of relinquishment; one should not accept that retinue for which the notion of possession arises when being asked by supplicants;
one should not accept that kingdom, nor those enjoyments, nor that jewel, nor indeed any object whatsoever that should not be accepted.
It is that object with regard to which a bodhisattva’s thought of non-renunciation arises.
Moreover, noble son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should generate this thought:
"This body of mine is surrendered and relinquished to all sentient beings;
how much more so external things—whatever thing will be needed by whichever sentient being, for whatever purpose."
To each and every one of them I shall give that which is truly available: I shall give my hand to those who seek a hand, my foot to those who seek a foot, my eye to those who seek an eye;

I shall give my flesh to those who seek flesh, my blood to those who seek blood, my marrow to those who seek marrow, my limbs and members to those who seek limbs and members, and my head to those who seek a head—I shall relinquish it all.

How much more so, then, regarding external objects—namely, wealth, grain, gold, silver, jewels, ornaments, horses, elephants, chariots, vehicles, villages, towns, market-towns, provinces, kingdoms, royal capitals, ports, male and female slaves, laborers, servants, sons, daughters, and retinues?
Indeed, whatever purpose any sentient being may have for whatever thing they require, I shall give that very thing to each such being from my own possession.
Without grieving, without regret, and without longing for the karmic result, I shall relinquish it.

"Without regard for [my own welfare], I shall give for the sake of favoring sentient beings, out of compassion for sentient beings, out of pity for sentient beings, and for the sake of gathering those very sentient beings together, so that these sentient beings, once gathered by me, may become knowers of the Dharma when I have attained awakening. [The rest is as before.]

It is just as if, noble son, when a medicinal tree is being taken from its root, or from its trunk, its branches, its bark, or its leaves; or when it is being taken from its flowers, its fruits, or its heartwood— it does not give rise to such a conceptual discrimination as, "I am being taken from my root," up to, "I am being taken from my heartwood."
Moreover, indeed, it is precisely through non-conceptualization that one removes the diseases of sentient beings—whether inferior, middling, or superior.
In the same way, noble son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should conceive of this body composed of the four great elements as medicine.
Whatever is needed by whichever sentient beings, let them take exactly that from me: those who need a hand, let them take a hand; those who need a foot, let them take a foot.
"Those seeking a foot" is as explained previously.
It is also taught in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*:
"This very body of mine must be exhausted in performing services for all sentient beings;
just as these external four great elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and [the wind element]—[are used for the benefit of others]."

And the wind element serves as various enjoyments for sentient beings through various pleasures, various methods, various objects, various requisites, and various consumptions. In the same way, I shall extensively [employ] this body— a collection of the four great elements— through various pleasures, various methods, various objects, various requisites, and various consumptions for the sake of all sentient beings.

Thinking, "I shall make it an object of enjoyment," he perceives this purposeful significance; he contemplates the suffering of the body, yet he does not become weary because of that bodily suffering due to his regard for sentient beings.
It is also said in the Noble Vajradhvaja Sūtra:

Thus, the bodhisattva, offering himself to all sentient beings as a benefactor through all roots of virtue, regarding all sentient beings with their own roots of virtue, bringing himself to all sentient beings like a lamp, and establishing himself as equal to happiness for all sentient beings— so it is.

Maintaining himself as equal to the womb of the Dharma throughout the entire world; following after all sentient beings as himself being like light; perceiving himself as equal to the foundation of the world;
following after the entire world as himself being the causal condition for roots of virtue;
and applying himself toward all sentient beings as himself being like a friend, [he regards] himself as equal to the path of unsurpassed happiness for all sentient beings.
Manifesting himself as equal to the support of unsurpassed bliss, purifying himself toward all sentient beings, making himself equal to the sun throughout the entire world,
and thus bestowing upon all sentient beings a self endowed with such qualities.

Perceiving ourselves as being at the disposal of others in all worlds, ready to be acted upon according to their wishes, we shall become the foremost shrines... perceiving ourselves as the sustenance for the entire world;
bringing about equanimity toward the entire world;
perceiving ourselves as a ford for all necessities.

Contemplating himself as the giver of happiness to all the world; resolving upon himself as the lord of generosity for the entire realm of beings; making himself equal to the wisdom of all the world; generating within himself the application to the conduct of a bodhisattva;
and disciplining himself through acting exactly as he speaks.
Contemplating himself as one clad in the armor for omniscience,
guarding the mind that was previously invited [to enlightenment],
establishing himself in right practice, attending to the bodhisattva’s mind of renunciation, and regarding himself as a pleasure garden for all sentient beings.

Manifesting himself as one whose very nature is delight in the Dharma throughout all worlds; establishing himself as a bestower of mental joy for all sentient beings; offering himself to the entire world as a producer of infinite gladness; maintaining himself in all worlds as a gateway to all pure dharmas;
and dedicating himself to all sentient beings as a giver of the enlightenment of the Buddhas.
Appointing himself as equal to a father toward all living beings,
he establishes himself within the realm of all sentient beings as the source for the non-deficiency of all necessary provisions.
For in this way, when a bodhisattva gives himself away to serve as an attendant, he maintains a humble mental attitude toward supplicants;

his mind is fixed on the ground as his bedding; he proceeds with the mental resolve to endure all suffering like the earth; he applies himself with a mind untiring in serving all sentient beings; he remains steadfast against the misdeeds of foolish people, being of a nature that endures and accepts them; he does not waver, being devoted to roots of virtue; and he is engaged in serving all world-systems without ceasing.
Karna, having abandoned his ears and nose to beggars who approached him— his mind born of the lineage of the Tathāgatas acquired through the practice of a Bodhisattva,

set forth in the dwelling of mindfulness of all Bodhisattvas, beholding all the three worlds as essence-less, his mental continuum unattached to his own body, dwelling in the mindfulness of all Buddha-dharmas which are without abode— he [gave] from his body, which was without essence...

For a bodhisattva who intends to extract the essence, when asked for his tongue, he— having seated that petitioner upon a noble lion-throne worthy of a king with a pleasing and expansive display of loving-kindness (*maitrī*)—
addresses him with a mind free from malice, a mind unharmed, a mind uninjured, a great-souled mind, and a mind born of the lineage of the Buddhas.
With a mind whose mental continuum was tranquil, possessing the empowerment of great strength, with a mind that was not attached to his body and a mind that did not cling to his speech,
he knelt upon his kneecaps; then, having made his entire body subject to the beggar,
he uttered words that were smooth, gentle, affectionate, and characterized by the practice of loving-kindness.
"Take my tongue and do with it as you wish;

act in such a way that you become pleased, with a joyful mind, delighted, thrilled, and filled with gladness and cheer. Thus, while relinquishing his head, he entered into the supreme knowledge—the pinnacle of all dharmas—and the awakening that is the head for the protection of all sentient beings.

...proceeding while desiring the incomparable wisdom that is the foremost head of all the world; aspiring to attain the King of Wisdom, the head of all directions; wishing to fulfill the state of being the crown of sovereignty over all unsurpassed dharmas; with a mind made radiant by joy for infinite supplicants—thus indeed does the Bodhisattva, when renouncing his hands and feet to supplicants, act with a conduct of grace through the hand of faith.

With the lion-like stride of a Bodhisattva, with hands outstretched in the practice of renunciation, delighting in relinquishment through the sacrifice of his own hands and feet, with the great placement of his feet as he strides forward, through his resolve in the conduct of a Bodhisattva, by remaining unassailed by painful sensations, and by the power of his serene faith in giving— he maintained the restraint of the arising of a stainless thought of enlightenment, possessing a body of Dharma characterized by non-obstructed knowledge, which was neither severed, nor divided, nor lost.
With a mind that is not base, his heart supported and strengthened by all the works of Māra and by non-virtuous friends, yet possessing a resolve for renunciation praised by all Bodhisattvas—
thus a Bodhisattva, having cast aside his own body and giving his blood to supplicants, possesses a mind thrilled with the thought of awakening,
a mind longing for the conduct of a Bodhisattva, a mind that does not seek personal gratification, and a mind that longs for the fulfillment of every supplicant.

With a mind free from aversion toward all recipients, having practiced the path of renunciation characteristic of all bodhisattvas, with a mind indifferent to his own body through irreversible joy and pliancy, he gave blood from his own body; his consciousness was directed toward the Mahāyāna, the sphere of gnosis, his mind undaunted by the Mahāyāna, his mind delighted, satisfied, joyful, glad, friendly, and blissful.
With a serene mind, filled with joy, gladness, and mental well-being, he renounced the marrow and flesh from his own body for the sake of beggars through a noble spirit of renunciation.
Addressing those beggars with words that fulfilled their desires, he said:
"May you, sirs, take the marrow and flesh from my body; let me increase your equal joy through a mind of renunciation that acts out of compassion according to your wishes."
By means of the great roots of virtue cultivated by the community of wise Bodhisattvas, which remove the stains of the world; by means of the most excellent resolute intention;

by means of the undertakings of great giving shared equally with all Bodhisattvas; by means of the objects of gift desired by the mind for all supplicants, with a heart free from regret; by means of the condition of the maturation of karma that is not scrutinized; and by means of the worship consisting of the array of ornaments adorning all Buddha-fields, without turning away from any world-system.
By means of compassion that protects and turns toward all the world;
by being oriented toward the awakening of all Buddhas;

by the practice of the ten powers; by the cultivation of a single root of goodness directed toward all bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present; and by roaring the bull-like lion’s roar facing toward all forms of fearlessness.

Facing the three times, with the knowledge of the equality of all times... facing the world, with the resolve for eons reaching to the furthest limit of the future, through the vow of a bodhisattva, facing without fear, and generating a mind free from weariness—
the bodhisattva, giving away his own heart to supplicants, has a mind trained in the power of generosity and a mind intent on the perfection of the perfections.
With a mind that is well-established and free from pride regarding all the giving of bodhisattvas;
with a mind that honors every supplicant through his empowerment;
he purifies his resolute intention.
Practicing the great vow which is the cause for maturing all the world, dwelling in the conduct of a bodhisattva,
and accumulating the equipment for omniscience without abandoning his aspiration, he there relinquished his liver,
spleen, and lungs to beggars, with a gaze full of faith toward those supplicants and eyes manifesting the form of clear joy.
With a love born of the Bodhisattva’s departure, with an unflagging mental attention, and with a mind that takes up the essence from this insubstantial body through renunciation;
contemplating the body as food for wolves, jackals, and dogs, he maintains mindfulness of the body until its end at the cemetery, regarding it with a mind focused on devotion to others.

With his body cast aside due to its impermanence and his consciousness focused entirely on the other, the bodhisattva, thus engaged in the mental application of the Dharma, gazes at those supplicants with unblinking eyes and thinks:
"If I were to give the intestines, liver, spleen, or lungs from this body to this supplicant,
or if I were not to give them," [he reflects upon the nature of the gift].
"At the end of the exhaustion of his lifespan, this body is not eternal; it culminates in the cemetery.

With a mental continuum thus satisfied by such reflection, with an intention characterized by knowledge of the Dharma, and established in the perception of the petitioner as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), he—desiring to take the essence from this essenceless body out of love for the Dharma—was about to give away even his own flesh and nails.
In this way, having made the renunciation of his own body, he dedicates that root of merit.
The relinquishing of enjoyments and merit is also taught in this very context:
"For thus a bodhisattva [acts] toward various recipients of offerings— toward diverse individuals coming from various directions, toward immeasurable wretched people and beggars,

toward those who have come upon hearing the report of a bodhisattva, toward those who have come having heard the word 'bodhisattva,' and toward those who have arrived seeking an opportunity for a connection with a bodhisattva."
Having heard the former vows of the Bodhisattvas regarding giving,
and being invited by the mind of the Bodhisattvas' vow,

he desires with his whole mind the relinquishment of everything; his intention is to honor the supplicants with satisfaction, and his intention is to apologize to the supplicants who have come to him.
"I myself would have gone there to receive you, so that you would not suffer the fatigue of the journey.

Thus, with a magnificent prostration, he asks for forgiveness from all the supplicants; having asked for their forgiveness, he bathes them and restores their bodies to rest, then bestows upon them whatever requisites they desire:
such as jeweled chariots filled with the most excellent jewel-like maidens of Jambudvīpa, and golden chariots filled with the pure jewel-like maidens of the various provinces.
Namely, these are chariots made of beryl, fully provided with the singing and instrumental music of the Vānaku clan;

likewise, there are crystal chariots filled with precious maidens who are beautiful to behold, pleasing, well-attired, well-adorned, and of excellent form. Furthermore, it is taught in this very same context that he gives jeweled chariots covered with nets of all kinds of gems and accompanied by noble thoroughbred elephants.
Giving away sandalwood chariots together with their mounts— chariots fitted with wheels of jewels, set upon jeweled lion-thrones, arrayed with canopies of various jewels,
covered by spread-out jeweled awnings, adorned on all four sides with banners and flags, and perfumed with various incenses...
They were anointed with ointments of the essence of sandalwood;

strewn with arrays of every kind of flower; drawn along by hundreds of thousands of maidens holding precious cords; moving without wavering and driven by steady, non-errant mechanisms; emitting fragrances that blew as pleasant and agreeable breezes; and attended with the respectful verbal service of devoted daughters and sons.
"Having performed services by means of various powders of fragrant substances."
Furthermore, it says in this very same place:

"Whether offering himself to all sentient beings, or undertaking service to all Buddhas, or renouncing his kingdom, or [offering] a city or capital adorned with every ornament, according to what is appropriate."

Relinquishing his entire retinue to those who ask, giving away his sons, daughters, and wife to supplicants, or surrendering his whole household; even so, giving away all objects of enjoyment and utility—
thus the Bodhisattva gives gifts of drink and gifts of flavors that are diverse, auspicious, sublime, and pure.

They were complete, bitter, salty, pungent, and astringent, endowed with various supreme flavors; they were very smooth, prepared through diverse methods of flavoring, capable of balancing the agitation of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and providing support for the strength of the mind and body. They generated affection, serenity, joy, and a sense of well-being, up to the point of warding off all external injuries and producing health free from all diseases.
In this way, the Bodhisattva bestows gifts of clothing, flowers, perfumes, ointments, and garlands;
gifts of beds, dwellings, couches, and lamps;
and he provides medicinal requisites for the sick, as well as various vessels and diverse provisions.

Giving to the Blessed Buddhas many bronze vessels, accumulated from immeasurable resources and filled with powders of gold, fine gold, and silver— his mind being resolved upon the inconceivable worthiness of such recipients— or giving to the jewels among Bodhisattvas, or giving to the Noble Saṅgha with the thought that a spiritual friend is extremely difficult to find;

Giving to a person for the sake of supporting the Buddha’s teaching; giving to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas with a mind of profound faith in their noble qualities; giving to one's mother and father with a mind intent on serving and attending to them; or giving to teachers, gurus, and those worthy of offerings, being engaged therein in the training and instruction regarding the equipment for the gurus.
Or, giving food and clothing to the wretched, beggars, and supplicants, he possesses an unobstructed eye toward all sentient beings because his mind is permeated with loving-kindness; [and so on].

Thus, indeed, the Bodhisattva, giving away noble elephant-kings— well-established on seven limbs, sixty years of age, endowed with six tusks, lotus-colored, pure of face, adorned with golden ornaments, their bodies covered by nets of gold,
their trunks arrayed with networks of various jewels and diverse ornaments, beautiful as gold, and lovely to behold.

Or giving noble steeds capable of traveling unwearyingly for thousands of yojanas— possessed of comfortable harnesses and comfortable bodies, endowed with speed and strength, capable of swift movement in the four directions, perfect in their stature, and adorned with all divine, auspicious, beautiful, and peerless ornaments—

he gives them away and relinquishes them with a mind of liberation, out of reverence to his elders, to spiritual friends, to his parents, to the wretched, to beggars, to supplicants, and to all beings who receive his gifts.
Giving, relinquishing with a mind that does not grasp, proceeding with a mental continuum suffused with great compassion toward the immeasurable qualities of a bodhisattva’s great renunciation,
and purifying the noble resolute intentions of a bodhisattva— thus indeed is a bodhisattva.

Giving the gift of seats, he renounced royal thrones with feet of lapis lazuli, supported by lions, canopied by nets of golden thread and jewels, spread with many cloths of exquisite touch, perfumed with the application of every kind of essential fragrance,
adorned with banners raised high by various supreme jewels, and arrayed with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of precious ornaments.

There were great thrones spread with canopies of golden nets, resounding with the charming sounds produced by the clashing of networks of golden bells; they were elevated, with eyes and teeth [inlaid] in gold, consecrated for sitting as the sole umbrella-rulers over the great earth.

He exercises unimpeded sovereign rule and dominion over all kingship, established upon a seat of certain sovereignty, wielding the teaching of the wheel of authority that governs the entire lordship of kings.

In this way, up to the point that the Bodhisattva, giving and relinquishing parasols, [gives those] adorned with arrays of great jewels, having jeweled handles, covered with networks of tinkling bells,

hung with necklaces and strings of gems and neck-ornaments made of precious threads, featuring the hanging of *vaiḍūrya* jewel garlands, provided with the pleasant sounds of joyful resonance, having pure canopies within golden nets, spread over hundreds of thousands of ornaments of jeweled spokes, and supported by jeweled cases.

He gave, relinquished, surrendered, and bestowed— without a mind of attachment— to those who were present, the finest essences of aloeswood and sandalwood, perfumed and incensed by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of supreme fragrances, pure and radiant as Jāmbūnada gold; such parasols adorned with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of ornaments, and even more, beyond count, adorned with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of ornaments.
Or for the purpose of adorning the reliquaries (caitya) of the Tathāgatas who have entered parinirvāṇa;

or for the sake of seeking the Dharma from the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) who are bodhisattvas, or from noble bodhisattva Dharma-preachers; or for one’s parents; or for the Jewel of the Saṅgha; or for the entire teaching of all the Buddhas; or even unto all recipients.
In this way, he dedicates that root of merit.
Just as it was taught in the very first dedication during the introduction to all roots of merit,
one generates this aspiration:

"How may these roots of merit become a source of sustenance and benefit for the entire world, culminating in the pure Dharma, so that by means of these roots of merit, there may be the cessation of the miserable states and hells for all sentient beings?"
They would turn them away from the mass of suffering belonging to the animal realm and the world of Yama.
While dedicating those roots of goodness, he dedicates that root of goodness in this manner:
By this root of merit, may I become the guide for all sentient beings in order to turn back the entire mass of suffering;
may I become the protection for all sentient beings by means of liberating them from all afflictions;
may I become the refuge for all sentient beings by means of guarding them against all fears.
May I become a refuge for all sentient beings by following along through all stages; may I become a final resort for all sentient beings by attaining ultimate security and peace;
may I become a light for all sentient beings by manifesting knowledge free from darkness.
May I become a torch for all sentient beings by dispelling the blinding darkness of ignorance; may I become a light for all sentient beings by establishing them in ultimate purity;
may I become a guide for all sentient beings by leading them into the inconceivable method of the Dharma.
May I become a guide for all sentient beings by leading them to the aggregate of unobstructed knowledge; [and so on].
And he dedicates that through his resolute intention, not by mere words;
and he dedicates it with an uplifted mind,
he dedicates it with a joyful mind.
With a serene mind, he dedicates;
with a joyful mind and an affectionate mind, he dedicates;
with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of endearment, a mind of assistance, a mind of benefit, and a mind of happiness, he dedicates.
And he dedicates it in this way:
"May this root of merit of mine lead to the purification of the destinies of all sentient beings;
may it lead to the purification of their rebirths."
It conduces to the purification of the greatness of merit;
it conduces to being unsurpassed;
it conduces to inexhaustibility.
It conduces to a mind that is difficult to assail;
it conduces to the non-forgetfulness of mindfulness;
it conduces to the definitive determination of one's course and intelligence.
It would lead to the non-measurability of the intellect;
it would lead to the fulfillment of all ornaments of virtue through the actions of body and the actions of mind.
By this root of merit of mine, may all those sentient beings please all the Buddhas; having pleased them, may they never displease them.
May they attain indestructible faith in those Blessed Buddhas, and may they hear the teaching of the Dharma in the presence of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
And having heard it, they shall dispel all doubts;
and as they have heard it, they shall retain it;
and while retaining it, they shall bring it to fulfillment through practice.
And they would please those Tathāgatas,
attain pliancy of mind,
and accomplish blameless deeds.
May they establish themselves in great roots of virtue, utterly eliminate poverty,
fulfill the seven attainments of wealth, train in accordance with all the Buddhas, acquire the attainment of excellent faculties,
and bring to perfection the equality of noble resolve.
May they obtain an opening into the wisdom of omniscience;
may they produce unimpeded vision throughout the entire world;
and may they obtain the perfection of the body adorned with the primary marks.
They should embrace the purity of speech, which is adorned with all virtues;
they should cultivate the restraint of the sense faculties, the application of the ten powers, and the fitness of mind; and they should fulfill the state of dwelling without fixed attachment.
And by whatever means of comfort all the Buddhas are endowed, may all sentient beings likewise obtain that same means of comfort.
Just as he dedicates by means of the method described in the sixth dedication:
"May all sentient beings have the sustenance of gnosis and possess minds engaged in non-attachment."

May all sentient beings be those who are diligent in food and wisdom, who do not become attached to food, who feed on joy, whose food is non-material, and who turn away from the thirst for sensual desires; may they rain down the cloud of the flavor of the Dharma upon all beings,
their mental continuums nourished by the delight in the unsurpassed Dharma.

May all sentient beings have tongues that perceive the finest of all flavors; may they be perceivers of the signs of flavor who are dedicated to the thought of the qualities of all Buddhas; may they possess unimpaired vehicles—the foremost vehicle, the supreme vehicle, the swift vehicle, the Great Vehicle.
May all sentient beings be insatiable in their vision, having attained the joy of the Buddhas.
May all sentient beings have their mental continuums unharmed by the sight of any spiritual friend.
May all sentient beings be shown the King of Medicines, the antidote. May all sentient beings turn back the poison of the afflictions.
May all sentient beings come to have a vision like that of the rising solar disc, because of their dispelling of the cataracts of darkness and ignorance for all sentient beings.
Thus, having compared oneself [to others], one should recite in accordance with one's own disposition:
"I dedicate [this merit] toward all sentient beings seeing what is pleasing;
I dedicate it toward their seeing what is joyful; I dedicate it toward their seeing what is auspicious."
I dedicate [this merit] toward the vision of what is desired, the vision that brings great joy, the vision free from dejection, and the endowment with the vision of the Buddha.
May all sentient beings be endowed with the fragrance of ethical discipline, possessing an uninterrupted morality and the morality of the perfections of a bodhisattva.
May all sentient beings be perfumed by generosity, relinquishing everything through total renunciation;
