may all sentient beings be perfumed by patience, having attained an unshakeable intention; may all sentient beings be perfumed by vigor, being armored for the vehicle of great vigor.
May all sentient beings be perfumed by meditative concentration, remaining in the presence of the Buddhas of the present and having attained samādhi.
May all sentient beings be perfumed by the dedication of the Bodhisattvas; may all sentient beings be perfumed by all pure dharmas and have abandoned all unwholesome dharmas.
May all sentient beings obtain celestial couches for the sake of attaining great gnosis.
May all sentient beings obtain the noble bed;
may all sentient beings obtain a peaceful bed because they are free from the habitual tendencies of the bodhicitta of ordinary worldlings;
may all sentient beings obtain a secure bed, being endowed with the touch of the desire for the Dharma, because they have completely abandoned all the sufferings belonging to the realm of saṃsāra.

May all sentient beings possess the illumination of completely pure Buddha-fields; may they be well-engaged in dwelling upon virtues and have departed from the abodes that are the dwellings of the noble ones;
may they never be separated from the supreme abodes of all Buddhas;
and may all sentient beings abide in the definitive realization of the Buddhas.
May all sentient beings possess infinite light regarding all the qualities of a Buddha; may all sentient beings have unimpeded radiance, pervading the entire realm of phenomena as one.
May all sentient beings have healthy bodies, having attained the body of a Tathāgata. May all sentient beings be like the King of Medicine, possessing the quality of ultimate non-conceptuality.
May all sentient beings become like unimpeded medicinal pillars, dedicated to the healing of the world.

May all sentient beings have the thorns of disease removed and attain the health of omniscience. May all sentient beings become skilled in the medicines for the entire world, applying medicinal treatments according to the inclinations of others.

I dedicate [this merit] for the sake of turning back all diseases among all sentient beings; I dedicate it for the sake of the state of having a body of infinite strength and power among all sentient beings; I dedicate it for the sake of the attainment of bodily strength in all sentient beings that is indestructible even by the Cakravāḍa mountains.
I dedicate [this merit] so as to be insatiable in supporting all the powers of all sentient beings.

May all sentient beings become immeasurable vessels, vast as the element of space, endowed with the faculty of mindfulness; through the comprehension of all worldly and transcendent speech, may they be undeluded in their grasping and recollection.
May all sentient beings cultivate auspicious purity, receiving with serene faith the unadulterated awakening of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
May all sentient beings be able to go wherever they wish, having attained the stage of a Buddha that leads everywhere.
May all sentient beings possess minds that are unimpeded toward all other sentient beings. May all sentient beings effortlessly travel to and pervade all buddha-fields.
May all sentient beings possess the power to traverse all phenomena in a single moment of thought; may they travel through all world-systems without weariness or fatigue,
having attained an unceasing mind-made body.
May all sentient beings be liberated through the path of happiness and enter into the conduct of all bodhisattvas.
By this root of merit, may all sentient beings never abandon the thought of not forsaking spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), being grateful and mindful of what has been done for them.
May all sentient beings share a single purpose with their spiritual friends by gathering together roots of merit that are common to one another.

May all sentient beings possess virtuous intentions, by virtue of dwelling in the excellence of living together with spiritual friends. May all sentient beings be purified through the ripening of the roots of merit of their spiritual friends, and may they share a single aspiration.
May all sentient beings be devoted to the Mahāyāna and set forth upon it, never obstructing their progress until they reach the culmination of omniscience.

May all sentient beings have their roots of virtue concealed, having attained the preservation of the state of all Buddhas. May all sentient beings be covered by the knowledge of qualities, having turned away from all worldly secondary afflictions. May all sentient beings possess pure dharmas that are uninterrupted and undistracted, with the stream of the Buddha-dharmas never failing.
May all sentient beings become like parasols, endowed with the canopy of the ten powers. May all sentient beings attain the seat of ultimate awakening.
May all sentient beings attain the lion throne of the Buddha’s stride, worthy of being beheld by the entire world.
It is also said in the *Āryagaganagañjasūtra*:
"May my roots of merit, or my skill in the knowledge of the Dharma, never fail to be a source of sustenance for all sentient beings."
The relinquishment of past and future virtues is taught in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*:
"The recollection of wholesome mental states and mental factors, and having recollected them, the dedication toward awakening—
this is skillfulness regarding the past."
That which is the mental application, the focused attention, and the bringing to presence of the resolve for enlightenment regarding future roots of virtue—
thinking, "Whatever wholesome productions of thought will arise in me, I shall dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment"— this is skillfulness regarding the future.

Thus, having fulfilled the resolve for total renunciation through such mental cultivation, one who has attained the momentum of a mind of relinquishment and abandoned all possessions through physical application is called "liberated," being freed from the suffering of existence which is rooted in all forms of grasping. Furthermore, for unsurpassed, immeasurable, and incalculable eons, one experiences rains of worldly and supramundane happiness and prosperity in various forms and infinite varieties.
And by means of that very personal existence and so forth—which, like bait on a hook, draws others even though it is not itself enjoyed with conscious intent—he causes others to cross over as well.
Therefore it is said in the *Ratnamegha*:
"For giving is the awakening of a bodhisattva."
The First Chapter: The Perfection of Generosity, from the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.
[II. Saddharmaparigrahaḥ] The second chapter of the Śīlapāramitā, titled "The Upholding of the True Dharma" (Saddharmaparigraha).
Thus, even though these things such as one's own person have been relinquished, they must still be protected. Why? Because:
One's own body and so forth are given for the enjoyment of sentient beings;
if they are not protected, how can there be enjoyment? What is given that is not enjoyed?
Therefore, for the sake of the enjoyment of sentient beings, one should protect one's own body and so forth.
For it is said in the *Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa*:
"Śāriputra, thinking 'I shall protect others,' one must protect oneself.
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva endowed with such a desire for the welfare of others does not commit an evil deed even for the sake of his life."
It is also said in the *Vīradattaparipṛcchā*:
"One should carry the burden solely with the thought of the Dharma, like a cart for the purpose of carrying a load.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Akṣayamatisūtra* as well.
And one does not become weary because of physical suffering, due to the consideration for sentient beings.
And how should one protect that physical existence and so forth?
By not abandoning the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra),
as stated by the noble Śrīsaṃbhava in the noble Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra.
Noble son, bodhisattvas who are sustained by spiritual friends do not fall into the miserable realms;
those who are attended to by spiritual friends do not transgress the training of a bodhisattva;
those who are shielded by spiritual friends rise above the world; and bodhisattvas who serve spiritual friends act without forgetfulness in all the practices of a bodhisattva.
Bodhisattvas who are embraced by spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) become invincible to karma and afflictions (kleśa).
Spiritual friends are awakeners; they prevent one from doing what should not be done and restrain one from states of negligence.
They are those who lead one out from the city of saṃsāra.

Therefore, noble son, with such a mental orientation and with a mind thus composed, you should approach spiritual friends with a mind like the earth, because it does not turn back under the weight of any burden; with a mind like a diamond, because its intention is indestructible;
and with a mind like the Cakravāḍa mountains, because it is not shaken by any suffering.
With a mind equal to that of a servant of the world, by not shrinking from undertaking any task;
with a mind equal to a dust-remover, by abandoning pride and arrogance;
with a mind equal to a vehicle, by carrying heavy burdens.
With a mind like the earth, by being free from anger;
with a mind like a boat, by not being terrified of coming and going;
and like a good son, by looking toward the face of the spiritual friend.
And you, son of good family, should conceive the notion of being ill regarding yourself, the notion of a physician regarding spiritual friends,
and the notion of medicine regarding their instructions.
One should conceive of spiritual practices as the eradication of disease,
and you, noble son, should conceive of yourself as a coward and of spiritual friends as heroes.
In the instructions, there is the perception of weapons;
in the practices, there is the perception of the destruction of enemies.
In this very *Vācanopāsikā-vimokṣa*, it is described:

"For a son of good family, a bodhisattva who practices according to the instructions of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), the Buddha Bhagavats become pleased in mind. For a bodhisattva who abides without contradicting the words of the spiritual friend, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) draws near."
For one who has no doubt regarding the words of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), spiritual friends draw near;
for one who is never separated from the mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward a spiritual friend, all goals become manifest.
For this very reason, the noble Sudhana, having bowed his head at the feet of the monk Sāradhvaja, [circumambulated him] many hundreds of thousands of times.
Having circumambulated the monk Sāradhvaja, looking at him, prostrating himself, and looking back again and again, he was certainly prostrating, paying homage, bowing down,
attending to him in his mind, reflecting, meditating, contemplating, uttering an inspired exclamation, and making cries of "Hā!"

Turning his attention toward his virtues, concluding [his discourse] there, remaining present, recollecting, strengthening [his resolve], not abandoning [the thought], bringing it to mind, fixing it in his heart,
directing his aspiration, entering into the vision, longing for [the sight of him], and grasping the signs of his voice, he departed from his presence.
Thus, perceiving omniscience as having come from the spiritual friend, with tears on his face and weeping, he departed from the presence of Megha the Dramida.
It is also said in the *Bodhisattvaprātimokṣa*:
"In this regard, Śāriputra, out of a love for the Dharma, there is no jewel in the world that a bodhisattva does not relinquish;
there is no service to the body that he does not perform."
There is no dispatching of messengers on foot that he does not undertake;
there is no verbal action that he does not undertake out of reverence for his teachers and preceptors.
...and so on, as before.
For what reason?
Because this Dharma leads to the severing of bonds;

this Dharma leads to the severing of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and dejection. Having thus generated the thought of it as a jewel and having generated the thought of it as medicine.
"This Dharma conduces to the pacification of the illness of all sentient beings;
therefore, we must seek such a Dharma as this for the very purpose of pacifying the illness of all sentient beings."

It is also said in the *Ugratattaparipṛcchā*: "Furthermore, householder, if a bodhisattva seeking the purpose of recitation and study should hear, explain, or memorize from someone else even a single four-line verse associated with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom..."
Or, for the sake of accumulating the equipment of a bodhisattva, he should show reverence for that teacher toward as many names, phrases, and syllables as have been taught in the verses;
even for that many eons, he should perform service and attendance upon that teacher with sincerity and with all forms of gain, honor, and worship.
Even now, householder, the teacher’s respect for the teacher has not been fulfilled;
how much less, then, can there be respect for the Dharma?
It is also said in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*:
"O son of good family, you should generate intense reverence toward spiritual friends and show them love."
Then, indeed, as the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita proceeded with such qualities and reflections of reverence, he gradually reached a certain city.
While he was in the middle of the marketplace there, this thought occurred to him:
"What if I were to sell this body of mine and, with the proceeds, perform an act of honor for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata?"

For a long time, indeed, throughout immeasurable saṃsāra, thousands of my own bodies have been broken, wasted, and sold; and for immeasurable reasons, on account of sensual desires and with sensual desires as their cause, I have experienced such things, yet never for the sake of these teachings, nor for the sake of honoring beings of such a kind.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, having come to the middle of a marketplace, raised his voice and proclaimed this cry:
"Who needs a man? Who needs a man? and so on, as before.
Then Māra, the Evil One, caused the brahmins and householders to be so situated that they did not hear that sound.
When he could not find a buyer for himself, he went to a secluded place, wept aloud, shed tears, and spoke thus:
"Alas! How difficult it is for us to obtain gain, since we cannot find even a buyer for our own body!
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, assuming the form of a young man, approached the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita and said this to him:
"Noble son, why do you stand here with a dejected mind and a yearning heart, shedding tears?"
Sadāprarudita spoke thus:
"Young man, out of a desire for the Dharma, I wish to sell this body of mine to perform a worship of the Dharma; however, I do not find a buyer for it. [The passage continues.]
Then that young man said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita:
"Noble son, I have no need for a man; rather, a sacrifice must be performed by my father.
For that, I require a man’s heart, his blood, and his marrow."
You shall give that to me for a price.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to Sadāprarudita:
"I have gained great gain; I know myself to be perfected in the perfections of wisdom and skillful means, since I have found a buyer for my own heart, blood, and marrow."
With a joyful heart, a serene mind, and a delighted spirit, he said this to the young man:
"Young man, I shall give you whatever from this body you require.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita took up a sharp blade and [prepared to cut] his right arm.
Having pierced it, he caused blood to flow; then, having pierced his right thigh and stripped it of its flesh, he approached the base of a wall in order to break the bone.
Then, a certain merchant’s daughter, who was on the upper terrace of her palace, saw the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita; having approached the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, she said this to him:
"Noble son, why indeed do you subject yourself to such treatment?"
When that girl heard the purpose of his worship, she spoke again:
"Noble son, what kind of excellence will arise for you from that?
He said this to her:
"Daughter, that son of good family will teach us the perfection of wisdom and skill in means;
there we shall train, and training therein, we shall become a refuge for all sentient beings. [And so on.]
Then the merchant’s daughter said this to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"It is marvelous, noble son, how sublime and excellent these dharmas have been proclaimed by you!"
"Noble son, for the sake of even a single such dharma as this, one should be willing to sacrifice selfhood in this manner for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.
Indeed, these dharmas you have proclaimed are so vast and sublime.
Nevertheless, noble son, I shall give you whatever you require—be it gold, a jewel, a pearl, or lapis lazuli—whatever it may be, by means of which you may [serve] that Bodhisattva Dharmodgata."
"You shall honor him.
[The Bodhisattva said: "In detail, you must go to visit that Dharmodgata together with that maiden and her retinue of five hundred."
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata rose from his seat and entered his own home;
for seven years he remained entirely absorbed in a single meditative concentration.
During those seven years, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita did not give rise to a single thought of sensual desire.
He did not give rise to thoughts of ill will or thoughts of harmfulness;
nor did he give rise to a craving for flavors, except with the thought:
"When indeed will the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata emerge from his meditative absorption?"

"We shall prepare a Dharma-throne for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, upon which this son of good family will sit and teach the Dharma; and we shall sprinkle and sweep that spot of earth and scatter various flowers over it," they thought.

The five hundred maidens, headed by the merchant’s daughter, following the example of the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, passed their time in two postures alone. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita heard a divine voice saying: "On the seventh day from now, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, having emerged from this samādhi, will be in the middle of the city."
"Having sat down, he will teach the Dharma.

Then, upon hearing that voice, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita was uplifted, overjoyed, and filled with gladness and happiness; together with the merchant's daughter and her companions, he cleared that area of ground.
Together with five hundred maidens, he prepared a Dharma-seat made of the seven precious gems.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, desiring to sprinkle that area of ground,
searched everywhere for water, yet he could not find any with which to moisten that spot of earth.

Just as if Māra, the Evil One, were to make all that water disappear, thinking, "Perhaps his mind, not obtaining this water, will become pained, or experience distress, or undergo a change of state, whereby his roots of merit might disappear or his roots of merit might not shine forth."
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita:
"What if I were to pierce my own body and sprinkle this place with my blood? For what reason?"
For this region of the earth is full of rising dust;
let not this element of dust fall upon the body of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata. What could I do with this physical form, which is necessarily subject to disintegration?
Indeed, it would be better for this body of mine to perish through such an act as this than through an act of inefficacy.

For the sake of sensual desires, with sensual desires as their cause, thousands of my own bodies have been shattered again and again as I wandered through the immeasurable cycle of existence. If they must be shattered once more, let them be shattered in such places of Dharma as these!
Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, having reflected thus, took a sharp weapon and, having pierced his own body all over, sprinkled that entire area of ground with his own blood;
likewise, it was done by those maidens as well.
And neither the mind of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita nor the minds of all those maidens underwent any change,
such that Māra, the Evil One, might find an opportunity to enter.
Therefore, it is also said in the *Caturdharmaka-sūtra*:
"O monks, a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) must not be abandoned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva for as long as life lasts, even for the sake of one's own life."
Thus, by not abandoning spiritual friends, one must perform such tasks as the protection of one's own person and so forth.
Furthermore, because of the constant examination of the sūtras, for the training precepts of a bodhisattva are generally found in the sūtras themselves;
this is because it is stated that "in those various sūtras, the conduct of a bodhisattva and the bodhisattva training precepts have been prescribed.
Therefore, lest one who has committed an offense fail to desist from it due to ignorance, one should always take care to examine the sūtras.
Thus, by this non-abandonment of spiritual friends and this seeing of the sūtras, the entire upholding of the true Dharma is explained.
As it is said in the *Āryasāgaramati-sūtra*:
"The retention and teaching of those syllables and expressions by which that ineffable Dharma is indicated—
this is called the upholding of the True Dharma (*saddharmaparigraha*)."

Furthermore, noble son, as for those Dharma-preachers who are the expounders of such sūtras as these and who take practice as their essence— one should attend upon them, associate with them, serve them, rise for them, wait upon them, show them respect, honor them, listen to them, protect them, and support them; and one should give them robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

Bestowing words of approval, protecting the master, protecting the side of wholesome qualities, speaking praise, and concealing dispraise—this too is the upholding of the true Dharma. [The rest is as before.]
Furthermore, noble son, that which is the supreme state of non-contention,
and the lawful subduing of those persons who speak of what is not Dharma as being Dharma—
this too is the upholding of the true Dharma.

Furthermore, noble son, for one whose mental continuum is unimpeded, whose intention is the liberation of all sentient beings, and whose mind is free from worldly motives, to give the gift of Dharma to others—this too is the upholding of the true Dharma.

Furthermore, noble son, whether caused by listening to the Dharma or caused by teaching the Dharma, even a single step taken, or even a single inhalation and exhalation—this too is the upholding of the true Dharma. [And so on.]
"O noble son, this mind is indeed cast down toward sense objects.

That which is its warding off, its protection, its one-pointedness, its self-mastery, its tranquility, its pacification, and its discipline—this is called the embracing of the true Dharma. [And so on.]
Furthermore, noble son, the non-appropriation and non-grasping of that very dharma by which any non-dharma arises—this too is the upholding of the true Dharma, and so forth.
In that context, by means of serving the Dharma-preacher and so forth, the non-abandonment of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) has been taught,
as well as the characteristics of a spiritual friend;
yet all of this [is impossible] without this upholding of the True Dharma (saddharma).
There is no protection, no purification, and no increase; therefore, he too would not be a bodhisattva. Thus, the upholding of the true Dharma must necessarily be performed.
For it is said in the *Śrīmālāsiṃhanāda-sūtra*:

"O Blessed One, even those bodhisattva vows which are as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā are all placed within, included in, and established upon a single great vow, namely, the upholding of the true Dharma."
"Thus, Blessed One, the upholding of the true Dharma has such a vast scope."
Furthermore, it says in this very same place: "O Goddess, it may be that even for a man of great strength, a small blow to a vital spot becomes piercing and causes affliction."
In the same way, O Goddess, even a small embrace of the true Dharma by Māra, the Evil One, becomes piercing, brings about sorrow,
and causes lamentation. O Goddess, I do not perceive any other single wholesome quality that is so piercing, sorrow-inducing, and lamentable for Māra, the Evil One,
as this small embrace of the true Dharma.

He spoke again: "Furthermore, O Goddess, it is just as Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, outshines all the surrounding mountain ranges and shines forth, shining brilliantly because of its height and vastness;

even so, O Goddess, the upholding of the True Dharma by one who has set out in the Mahāyāna—being indifferent to body and life and having no grasping mind—outshines all the wholesome qualities of those Mahāyānists who have newly set out in the vehicle and are still attached to body and life."
"It overcomes," and so forth.
Likewise, it is said in the *Ārya-sāgaramati-sūtra*:
"You are embraced by the Jinas, by the gods, the nāgas, and the kinnaras;
you are embraced by merit and wisdom because of upholding the True Dharma of the Tathāgatas."
...and so on in detail...
He is never born in empty realms; in every birth, he beholds the Jina.
Having seen him, he gains serene confidence in those Tathāgatas by upholding the True Dharma.

He becomes one who remembers his past lives, possesses the nature of a great being, and repeatedly attains the state of renunciation; he is pure in conduct, makes practice his essence, and upholds the true Dharma of the Tathāgatas.
...and so forth.

They become possessors of the dhāraṇīs of the wise; the merit they have acquired is not lost for hundreds of eons. They become possessed of eloquence and remain unattached, because they uphold the true Dharma of the Tathāgatas.
Then Śakra, as well as Brahmā, the World-Protectors, and the human king who is a universal monarch on earth—
by means of such happiness and bliss, he awakens to enlightenment through upholding the True Dharma of the Tathāgatas.
Thirty-two marks appear upon his body; the wise one possesses limbs beyond reproach.
Those who behold him never find satiety, for he upholds the true Dharma of the Tathāgatas.

His bodhicitta does not become deluded, nor is he lacking in vigor regarding the practices of the perfections; he remains unattached through hundreds of virtues because he upholds the true Dharma of the Tathāgatas.
The second chapter, titled "The Upholding of the True Dharma," in the Perfection of Ethical Discipline.
[III. Dharmabhāṇakādirakṣā] The Third Chapter: Protection of the Dharma-preacher and Others.

The general means for the protection and so forth of all three [the self, wealth, and dharma] have been stated. Now, however, the specific protections and so forth must be explained. Among these, what is the protection of one's person? It is the avoidance of that which is harmful.
In this context, while engaged in the upholding of the true Dharma, the protection of one's person is considered so that one does not cause harm to others;
and this avoidance of what is disadvantageous was spoken by Bodhisattvas intent on maintaining the true Dharma in the *Āryagaganagañjasūtra*.
"O Blessed One, after the Supreme among Men has entered parinirvāṇa, we are resolved to uphold the True Dharma, even at the cost of our bodies and our very lives."
Having renounced gain and honor, and having abandoned all intimacy,
yet not abandoning this Dharma which reveals the wisdom of a Buddha.
We shall endure with patience all insults, revilings, and harsh words, for the sake of upholding the true Dharma.
Mockery, threats, dispraise, and ill repute—all these we shall endure, upholding this principle... [etc.]
In such a time of great terror, when the king of monks is agitated and beings are undergoing destruction, we shall uphold the True Dharma.
Those who are not receptive to the profound sūtras associated with the fruit of liberation will instead take pleasure in various worldly tales. ... [pe] ...
We shall practice loving-kindness toward those who are unestablished in phenomena,
and we shall exercise compassion while upholding this method.
Seeing sentient beings of immoral conduct, established in desire and greed, we shall shed tears; for what destiny has been prepared for the blind?
And upon suddenly seeing that obstructer of the true Dharma,
we shall approach him from afar with friendliness, lest he indeed become enraged at us.
We shall protect [them] to the best of our ability, restrained in speech and action;
we will not speak with them while they remain established in this evil of their own.
Having thus ripened those men here through gifts and honors, we shall afterwards urge them on toward the reality that has its sphere in the states of woe.

Having completely abandoned the life of householders, dwelling in the remote forests as our proper sphere of activity, we shall become like deer—possessing few desires and having few undertakings. ...pe...
Having descended into this village, we— tamed, peaceful, and liberated—
shall teach the Dharma to those beings who seek the true nature of reality.
Even if we must travel very far, upon hearing those who desire the Dharma,
we shall act for the benefit of embodied beings, having attained delight in the garden of the Dharma.
Seeing there before us the many lapses of sentient beings,
we shall become observers of ourselves, established in the gentleness of the Dharma.
Whether treated with disrespect or with honor, becoming as steadfast as Mount Meru and remaining unsullied by the world, we shall become leaders of the world.
And having heard the censure of monks who have broken their conduct, [one should think]:
"We shall be masters of our own karma; let not the karma of these others ripen upon us."
For those who abide in these teachings, they will indeed employ obstacles;
yet these teachings do not exist for us in any way whatsoever.
For us ascetics, there are indeed no qualities of an ascetic;
yet, having heard a true reproach, they reject this sutra.
For those whose ears and noses have been cut off, how can this mirror be dear?
Having heard the exhortation according to reality, they reject that True Dharma.
Those monks who shall be receivers of the true Dharma will act accordingly; someone will hear this Dharma from them.
Kings will cause [this] to be accepted, and the great multitude will be inspired with awe;
through the empowerment of the Buddha, sentient beings will then hear this Dharma.
"At that time of hardship, having abandoned our bodies along with our lives, we shall uphold the True Dharma for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings. Thus [they vowed].
It is also said in the Noble Lotus Sutra of the True Dharma:
Guarding one's conduct and sphere of activity, one should remain unattached and pure;
one should always avoid intimacy with princes and kings.
Furthermore, those men who serve kings should not form intimate associations with outcasts,
boxers, drunkards, or any kind of heretics whatsoever.
One should not associate with those who are conceited, but should discipline those established in the Āgamas; one should avoid monks who are considered Arhats but are actually of immoral conduct.
One should always avoid a bhikṣuṇī who frequents frivolous conversation,
and one should also avoid laywomen who are openly unstable.
One should avoid intimacy with those beings who are women or eunuchs;
one should also avoid [intimacy with] young wives and maidens within families.
One should never greet them with joy, even when they inquire after one's welfare;
one should avoid intimacy with those who raise pigs or sheep.
One should avoid intimacy with those beings who support women,
as well as with actors, jhallakas, wrestlers, and any other people of that sort.
One should not serve courtesans or others who live by sensual enjoyment;
one should completely avoid socializing with them in every way.
And when a wise man should teach the Dharma to women,
he should not enter there alone, nor should he remain in a state of laughter.
And this other disadvantage would also arise, namely that which is described as the work of Māra in the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
"Māra, the Evil One, will exert a more powerful effort against that bodhisattva who has recently set out in the vehicle.
On this very point, it says:

Furthermore, Ānanda, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva applies himself to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom, at that time the wicked Māras bring about harassment toward the bodhisattva and produce fear;
they display and cast forth falling meteors and portents in every direction.
"May it be that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva might become discouraged or experience horripilation,
whereby even a single thought-moment of his toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment might perish.
Furthermore, others, perceiving them as having consciousness, will write [this] down and even master it.
Thinking, "We find no enjoyment here," they will rise from their seats and depart;
likewise, yawning and laughing loudly, they will continue until they have mastered [the teaching]—this is the work of Māra.
In this way, discursive thoughts concerning countries, villages, and so forth will arise.
In this way, there are mental attentions toward teachers, preceptors, parents, friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations;
likewise, there are mental attentions toward thieves;
and likewise, there are mental attentions toward robes and other such requisites.
Furthermore, the Dharma-preacher will be eager to have this profound *prajñāpāramitā* written down, up to being recited, while the listener of the Dharma will be weary; or it may be the reverse.
Moreover, the Dharma-preacher will desire to go to another country, whereas the listeners of the Dharma will not.
In this way, it should be understood that the Dharma-preacher will have great desires while the listener of the Dharma has few desires.
In brief, whatever discord there may be between the Dharma-preacher and the listener of the Dharma is all said to be the work of Māra.
It is also said in the *Āryagaganagañjasūtra*:
"In this way, everything from following unwholesome dharmas to the abandonment of wholesome dharmas is the work of Māra."
The *Āryasāgaramati-sūtra* also says:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva who is a forest-dweller delights in remote lodgings; he has few desires, is contented, is secluded, and does not associate with householders or renunciants.
Because his aims are few and his duties are few, he dwells in happiness, and he is not devoted to the pursuit of extensive learning."

He does not act for the sake of maturing sentient beings, nor does he consider it necessary to move toward listening to the Dharma, or to discourse on the Dharma, or to engage in discussions for the determination of its meaning when such occasions arise;
he is not of a nature to inquire.
He does not apply himself to any wholesome practice whatsoever.
Due to his dwelling in the forest and his delight in solitude, the afflictions do not manifest within him;
he finds satisfaction merely by the suppression of the outbursts of the defilements.
Nor does he cultivate the path for the sake of uprooting the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
In that regard, he has not set out for his own benefit, nor for the benefit of others.
Blessed One, this is the seventh hook of Māra associated with a bodhisattva’s dwelling in the forest. ... [as before] ...
Furthermore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva serves, associates with, and attends upon evil friends who merely resemble spiritual friends;
for these people dissuade him from the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), dissuade him from the accumulation of merit and the upholding of the true Dharma, and instead urge him toward solitude,
toward having few goals and few activities.
And they frequently teach him discourses associated with the disciples and the solitary buddhas.
And at the time when a bodhisattva might rise up toward the Mahāyāna by dwelling in solitude, at that time they enjoin that bodhisattva to the hindrance of service;
for service must necessarily be performed by a bodhisattva.
And at the time when a bodhisattva ought to be engaged in service, they instead engage him in solitude, saying to him:
"Awakening belongs to the bodhisattva who has initiated vigor, not to one who is indolent."
If you do not attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment within eight or nine eons,
it will no longer be possible for you to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
In that regard, Blessed One:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, it is indeed possible that a bodhisattva, through excessive exertion of vigor, might attain the fruit of nirvāṇa; this, Blessed One,
is the tenth hook of Māra for a bodhisattva, appearing in the guise of a spiritual friend."

Furthermore, those other persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who, pierced by the hook of Māra, practice among inferior qualities and find delight in their company— since they become followers of such [people], that practitioner of the base, having failed to attain distinction, goes to an inferior state; namely, the state of a barren person, or the state of one who is dull-witted and mute, up to the eleventh hook of Māra.

And because for one who has thus initiated vigor through a continuous stream, there arises from weariness a state that is in every way truly that of a bodhisattva, it is said for this very reason in the *Ratnamegha*:
"In this case, a bodhisattva initiates vigor in all modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*);
and he initiates it in such a way that he does not produce bodily exhaustion."
There is no weariness of mind;
this is called the bodhisattva’s continuous vigor.
What kind of vigor is that?
That by which weariness arises is this:

for one who is weak in strength, the undertaking of heavy tasks; or at an improper time; or for one whose resolve is not yet mature, the undertaking of difficult deeds, such as the giving of one's own flesh and so forth.
And he has already given away his very person.
However, he restrains them from using it at an improper time;

for otherwise, through the resulting weariness of those very beings toward the bodhisattva, the seed of the thought of awakening would perish, and there would be the destruction of a great mass of fruit.
And therefore, it is stated in the *Gaganagañjasūtra*:
"Expecting [the right time] at the wrong time is the work of Māra.
Nor is it that one should not produce the thought of relinquishing the self at the wrong time; for if one does not begin practice, one will never give anything at all.

Therefore, having established mindfulness in this way, one must protect one’s person from those who oppose the ripening of the thought of awakening— namely, from deluded ones, from those who destroy their own welfare, from flesh-eaters, and from those who perform [unwholesome] deeds. Just as the seed of the Sudarśana medicinal tree, which provides its roots and other parts for enjoyment, must be protected even after it has been given from being used at the wrong time, so too must the seed of the Perfectly Awakened One’s medicinal tree be protected.
This, in brief, is the harm caused by the deeds of Māra.
The relinquishing of this is explained in the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*:
"And how, noble son, does a bodhisattva here become skillful in the means for avoiding the deeds of Māra?
Here, a bodhisattva completely and utterly avoids an unvirtuous friend."
He completely avoids dwelling in unsuitable places, the cultivation of the study of Lokāyata mantras, and gain, honor, worship, service, and high esteem;
he completely avoids all other secondary afflictions that are obstacles to the path of the factors conducive to enlightenment,
and he cultivates their antidotes.
In this very context, the characteristics of an unwholesome friend (*akalyāṇamitra*) have been stated:
one should understand the avoidance of evil friends through the avoidance of persons who have failed in ethical discipline (*śīla*),
and likewise through the avoidance of persons who have failed in view (*dṛṣṭi*), conduct (*ācāra*), and livelihood (*ājīva*).
By avoiding persons who delight in socializing;
by avoiding persons who are indolent;
and by avoiding persons who take pleasure in cyclic existence.

By avoiding persons who are averse to awakening and by avoiding association with householders, one should understand that one is avoiding evil friends. Furthermore, noble son, while avoiding these situations, one should not give rise to a mind of malice toward those persons, nor a mind of resentment, nor a mind of contempt.
And in this way, he should establish his mind:
for it has been said by the Blessed One that beings, according to their elements, flow toward the realm of desire and other realms, are born therein, and through association with them, they perish.
Therefore, I shall avoid association.
The loss of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is also a disadvantage, and its cause is stated in the *Ratnakūṭa*:
"Kāśyapa, the thought of awakening of a bodhisattva who possesses four qualities becomes deluded. Which four?"

By deceiving teachers, gurus, and those worthy of offerings; by inducing remorse in others regarding matters that are not regrettable; and by uttering dispraise, infamy, and ill-repute against beings who have set out in the Mahāyāna—treating others with deceit and guile rather than with a resolute intention (adhyāśaya)—the avoidance of these is taught here.
Kāśyapa, for a bodhisattva endowed with four qualities, the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) manifests as soon as he is born in all his lifetimes.
And he does not become deluded in the interval until he sits at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
By which four?
Namely, even for the sake of his life, he does not knowingly utter a falsehood.
Even in jest,
he dwells with a resolute intention toward all sentient beings, free from deceit and guile, and conceives of all bodhisattvas as teachers;
furthermore, he proclaims their praises in the four directions.
And those beings whom he brings to maturity, he establishes them all in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
because he has no desire for a limited vehicle.
By these four, Kāśyapa...
It is also said in the *Siṃhaparipṛcchā*:
"He who never creates an obstacle to the gift of Dharma quickly attains union with the Lords of the World."
Likewise, O young man, know this from the gift of Dharma by which one remembers past births.
Likewise, in this very context:
"Therefore, he does not abandon the mind of awakening in any of his births;
even in the midst of a dream that mind remains, how much more so when he is awake?"
He said: "In whatever villages or cities there are places for abstaining [from unwholesome conduct], having undertaken [the vows] for the sake of awakening, one does not abandon that mind."
It is also said in the *Āryamañjuśrībuddhakṣetraguṇavyūhālaṃkārasūtra*:
"Endowed with four qualities, a bodhisattva does not waver from his vows... [and so forth].
"One becomes one whose pride is destroyed, one who abandons envy and stinginess, and one who is joyful upon seeing the prosperity of others.
This very reason for not forgetting the vessel-like mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is stated even more clearly in that same *Ratnakūṭa*:
"By means of the cultivation of the mind of awakening in all modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*)."
And by having the thought of awakening as its precursor.
For thus it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
"I announce to you, I make it known to you: in whatever way a person reflects extensively, in that very way his mind becomes inclined toward those reflections upon which it is dependent."
Despair is also a disadvantage, and its avoidance is seen in the *Ratnamegha*:
"In this regard, a bodhisattva does not give rise to such a thought:
'Awakening is difficult to attain for one who has become a human being.'"

Moreover, this vigor of mine is limited and I am indolent, yet awakening must be fully accomplished over many eons— many hundreds of eons, many thousands of eons— by one who is like [a person whose] head or clothing are on fire. Therefore, I do not have the strength to bear such a burden.
Rather, a bodhisattva should generate this thought:

"Those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who have already awakened, those who are currently awakening, and those who will awaken in the future— they all have awakened, are awakening, and will awaken by means of this very method, this very practice, and this very vigor."
"As long as they have not yet become Tathāgatas and attained full awakening,

I too shall strive and exert myself in such and such ways with vigor shared with all sentient beings and with vigor directed toward all sentient beings, so that I may attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening."
Furthermore, another disadvantage is seen in the *Ratnakūṭa*:
placing trust in beings who have not yet been matured is a lapse for a bodhisattva; revealing the sublime Buddha-dharma to beings who have not become fit vessels is a lapse for a bodhisattva.
It is a transgression for a bodhisattva to proclaim the Hīnayāna to sentient beings who are inclined toward the sublime;

it is a transgression for a bodhisattva to treat with contempt those who are established in right mindfulness, who possess ethical discipline, and who are of virtuous character, thereby gathering together those of immoral conduct and evil qualities.
Even conviction regarding the Dharma is not the ultimate goal.
As it is said in the *Rāṣṭrapāla-sūtra*:
"For one who lacks conviction, there is no conviction in the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha."
That evil-minded one, whose face is turned toward the lower realms, has no devotion for the trainings and vows.
Having passed away from here, that ignorant and deluded person, by the power of karma, indeed experiences suffering among humans,
or in the hells, the animal realms, and the realms of hungry ghosts.
Thus, its relinquishment is seen to have been declared in the *Ratnakūṭa*.
Furthermore, regarding those profound matters into which his intellect does not penetrate,
he does not reject them, considering that the Tathāgata alone is the witness therein.
Only the Tathāgata knows;
I do not know.
The awakening of the Buddhas is infinite, and the teaching of the Dharma by the Tathāgatas proceeds toward sentient beings according to their various inclinations.
One engaged in service (vaiyāvṛtya) must be skilled in avoiding what is unbeneficial.

For in the *Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa*, service is taught in relation to listening to the Dharma from a fellow practitioner of the Dharma and in the worship of the Tathāgata; the manner of conduct therein is derived from the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*.
In that regard, the monk serving as an attendant (vaiyāvṛtyakara) should please the minds of the entire community of monks.
Among them, for those monks who dwell in the wilderness (āraṇyaka) and those who frequent remote lodgings (prāntaśayyāsana),
the monk serving as an attendant must not, in any way whatsoever, assign them any manual labor.

Furthermore, if a forest-dwelling monk should receive a task pertaining to the Saṅgha that requires training, that task must be performed by this monk acting as an attendant himself, or another monk should be requested to do it; however, that forest-dwelling monk must not be burdened with it. In that regard, whoever...
If there is a monk who goes for alms, that attendant monk should share with him a portion of the choice foods.
In this regard, Kāśyapa, as for the monk who is a practitioner of yoga (yogācāra):
That monk serving as an attendant must provide him with suitable requisites and medicinal supplies for the alleviation of illness.
Furthermore, in whatever place that monk who practices yoga resides, no loud noise should be made;
the monk serving as an attendant must protect the monk who practices yoga.
He should provide him with a bed, a seat, and a support;
and he should offer him refined and pleasant foods for chewing and eating that are conducive to the stages of practice for a yoga practitioner. ... [as before] ...
Those monks who are devoted to great learning should be given encouragement;
indeed, they must be protected as well,
including those monks who will become preachers of the Dharma.
They must perform the duties of a gatekeeper;

they must urge the listeners of the Dharma [to attend], arrange the circle of the assembly, and clear the circle for discussion; furthermore, they must be full of frequent expressions of approval (*sādhukāra*). ... [as before] ...

One should not give rise to the notion of exercising authority over any object whatsoever. Even the most minor task must be carried out according to the consensus of the Saṃgha, and never according to one's own will; furthermore, property belonging to the Saṃgha must not be commingled with property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four quarters.
Thus, by way of contrast, there is likewise a prohibition against mutual commingling with what belongs to a stūpa.

Furthermore, if there should be a deficiency in the Saṅgha of the four directions and the property belonging to the Saṅgha should be in surplus, that monk serving as an attendant (vaiyāvṛtyakara), having made the Saṅgha of monks single-minded,
should perform the affairs of the Saṅgha of the four directions from the property belonging to the Saṅgha.
Likewise, even when a stūpa has fallen into ruin, this same procedure applies: having exhorted the donors or masters of generosity, it must be restored; such is the command.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, however great the property belonging to a stūpa may be, it must not be handed over by the *vaiyāvṛtyakara* to the Saṅgha or to the Saṅgha of the four quarters.
For what reason?
Because even a single thread belonging to a stūpa, once offered by the faithful who abound in serene confidence,
becomes a shrine for the world including its gods.
How much more so in the case of a jewel or what is considered a jewel, or whatever robe has been dedicated to a stūpa?
Let that very thing perish right there at the Tathāgata’s shrine through wind, heat, and rain;
one must not, however, exchange a robe belonging to a stūpa for its price in gold.

For there is no price whatsoever for what belongs to a stūpa, nor can there be any deficiency caused to a stūpa by anyone. Kāśyapa, if any monk who serves as an attendant, with a mind full of anger, issues commands out of a sense of authority over those who are virtuous and worthy of offerings,
he will, by that unwholesome karma, go to hell.

If he comes to the world of humans, he becomes a slave or a laborer for others, and he receives blows from sticks, slaps, and violent strikes... [and so on] ...he makes a monk fear the threat of punishment and physical force, dispatching him at improper times and giving him instructions at improper times.
By that unwholesome karma, he is reborn there in the individual hell named Bahuśaṅku (Many Spikes).
...until his body becomes pierced by a thousand [arrows], set ablaze, ignited, and fully consumed by flames. ...pe... [as before] ...pe...
His tongue becomes a hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth.
Upon that tongue-faculty, many hundreds of thousands of flaming iron spikes are driven in.
For any monk who acts as a steward, Kāśyapa, and who accumulates communal gains as they arrive rather than distributing them from time to time— [he shall suffer thus].
Having caused [others] to be terrified and having harassed them, he gives [a gift];
yet to some he does not give.
By that root of unwholesomeness, he is reborn in the preta-realm known as Jaṅghā, which is like a mass of excrement.
There, other hungry ghosts (preta) appear to him after taking food;
being terrified and gazing at that food with unblinking eyes, he— overcome by hunger and thirst—
experiences painful sensations, yet even in a thousand years he does not obtain that food.
Furthermore, whatever food is obtained at any time whatsoever becomes excrement, or pus and blood.
In the *Saṃgharakṣitāvadāna*, a harmful consequence is also mentioned:
"Saṃgharakṣita, those beings whom you saw in the form of walls were formerly monks.
They destroyed a wall belonging to the Saṅgha with phlegm."
Through the ripening of that karma, they have become like walls.
Those beings whom you saw, Saṃgharakṣita, appearing like pillars, were formerly monks.
They defiled a pillar belonging to the Saṅgha with their snot.
Because of that, they became pillar-shaped.
As for those beings whom you saw who had the form of trees, leaves, flowers, and fruits—they too were formerly monks.
They consumed the trees, leaves, flowers, and fruits belonging to the Saṅgha for their own private use; because of that, they became shaped like trees, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Those beings whom you saw in the form of ropes and brooms were monks;
because they used communal ropes and brooms for their own private enjoyment, they became transformed into the form of ropes and brooms.
The being whom you saw in the form of a water-jar was a novice monk.
He was scrubbing a wooden bowl when some visiting monks arrived.
They saw him and asked, "Novice, will this be a drink for the Saṃgha?"
With a mind overcome by stinginess, he said,
"Do you not see that the bowl has been wiped clean and the drink has been drunk?
Thinking that the time had passed, they fell into despair and departed with dejected and miserable faces.
As the ripening of that karma, he became shaped like a wooden mortar.
As for that being whom you saw in the shape of a mortar, he too was once a monk; a task involving his alms-bowl had presented itself to him,
and there a certain śrāmaṇeraka who was an arhat was appointed to guard the seal.
He said to him, "Novice, pound some oil-cake for me.
He replied, "Elder, wait a moment; I am busy, but later, after I have pounded it, I will give it to you."
Filled with indignation, he said:
"Novice, if it were permissible for me to touch a mortar, I would throw you right into that mortar and pound you;
how much more so for a mere handful of sesame!"
That novice reflected:
"This man is possessed by intense obsession; if I were to give him an answer, he would fall into even greater provocation. Thus, he remained silent.
When his outburst had subsided, [the other] approached him and said,
"Elder, do you know who I am?
He replied:
"I know you as a novice who has gone forth under the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa;
I too am an elder monk.
The novice said:
Even though this is so, nevertheless, that which was to be done by me as one who has gone forth has been done.
What has been done? The afflictions have been abandoned; I have severed all bonds and am completely liberated from every fetter.
Harsh words were uttered by you.
"Confess your transgression as a transgression;
perhaps by this, the exhaustion, attenuation, and total consumption of that karma might occur.
Yet, he did not confess his transgression as a transgression, and because of that karma, he became shaped like a mortar.
Those beings whom you saw in the shape of cooking pots were formerly *kalpikāraka* monks who served as attendants to other monks.
While they were boiling medicinal decoctions, they were addressed unpleasantly by the monks; becoming resentful, they broke the pots, and because of that, they have become shaped like cooking pots.
As for that being whom you saw cut in the middle and held together by a thread, he too was once a monk who was acquisitive and greedy; overcome by stinginess, he diverted his gains:
what was intended for the rainy season retreat he diverted to the winter, and what was intended for the winter he diverted to the rainy season.
As the ripening of that karma, he goes along being supported by a thread that has been snapped in the middle.
The third chapter of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, titled "Protection of the Dharma-preacher and Others."
[IV.
(The Fourth Chapter)] Other great misfortunes are also taught in the sūtras, such as those found,
for instance, in the *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra*.
Noble son, there are these five root downfalls for a consecrated Kṣatriya king.
By these root downfalls, the consecrated Kṣatriya king consumes all previously planted roots of merit;
he falls from his status, commits a defeat (pārājika), and becomes one who goes to the states of woe, deprived of the presence of all gods and humans.

What are the five? Noble son, whoever steals property belonging to a stūpa, or belonging to the Saṅgha, or belonging to the Saṅgha of the four directions, or that which has been dedicated [to them]—whether he steals it himself or causes it to be stolen; these are the five.
This is the first root downfall.

Furthermore, whoever rejects the Dharma— whether that which is spoken for the liberation of the Śrāvakas, or that which is spoken for the liberation of the Pratyekabuddhas, or that which is spoken for the liberation of the Mahāyāna— and rejects or denies it, this is the second root downfall.

Furthermore, whoever, on my account, robs— either personally or causes another to rob— the saffron robes of one who has shaved his head and beard and is clad in saffron garments, whether that person observes the precepts or not, whether he is immoral or virtuous;
or who makes him a householder, strikes his body with sticks, casts him into prison, or deprives him of life— this is the third root downfall.

Furthermore, if a kṣatriya intentionally deprives his mother of life, or deprives his father, an Arhat, or a disciple of the Blessed One of life; or if he causes a schism in the harmonious Saṅgha; or if, with a malicious mind, he intentionally sheds the blood of a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha—[these constitute the immediate transgressions].
If one commits any one of these five actions of immediate retribution, this is the fourth root downfall.
Furthermore, if a kṣatriya is a proponent of causelessness, indifferent to the next world,

and having undertaken the ten unwholesome paths of action, he practices them himself and also incites, disciplines, establishes, and settles many other beings in the ten unwholesome paths of action— this is the fifth root downfall. ...pe...
Furthermore, whoever causes division among villages, division among districts, division among cities, or division among kingdoms—this is a root downfall. ... [as before] ...
For sons of good family or daughters of good family who are beginners and have set out in the Mahāyāna, there are eight root downfalls.
By these root downfalls, when beginners who have set out in the Mahāyāna stumble, they burn away all previously planted roots of virtue.

Having fallen from their foundation and being defeated, they depart from the gateway of the Mahāyāna for gods and humans and go to the states of woe; deprived of spiritual friends, they languish in saṃsāra for a long time.

What are the eight? Those beings who, due to the cause of past misconduct, have been born into this afflicted world of five corruptions, and who, possessing only meager roots of virtue, hear this supreme and profound Mahāyāna by relying upon a spiritual friend.

And those sons of good family, though their intellects were limited, gave rise to the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Among them, those beginner bodhisattvas who hear, recite, and study this most profound sūtra associated with emptiness,
remember and elucidate it in detail before others— whose prior understanding is similar to their own— in its excellent meaning and excellent phrasing, exactly as they have heard and mastered it.
For those foolish ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet attained tranquility, upon hearing this, they become terrified, greatly alarmed, and fall into a state of dread.
Because of that dread, they turn their minds away from unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) and direct their minds toward the vehicle of the disciples (*śrāvakayāna*).
This is the first root downfall for a beginner bodhisattva.
By that root downfall, that son of good family consumes all previously planted roots of merit;
fallen from his foundation and defeated, he is deprived of the happiness of heaven and liberation,
and his bodhicitta becomes deceptive, leading him toward the miserable states.

Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having first understood the dispositions and latent tendencies of other individuals, should teach the Dharma to beings according to their dispositions in a gradual manner, just as one causes others to descend into the great ocean step by step. ... [as before] ...
Furthermore, a beginner bodhisattva might say this to someone:
"You are not capable of practicing the conduct of the six perfections;
you are not capable of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Quickly generate the aspiration for the vehicle of the śrāvaka or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha."
By means of that, you shall emerge from cyclic existence;
as previously stated, this is the root downfall regarding the knowledge of a beginner bodhisattva.

Furthermore, a beginner bodhisattva might say to someone: "O friend, what is the use of the Prātimokṣa discipline? What is the use of well-guarded ethical conduct? You should quickly generate the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
Recite the Mahāyāna!
Whatever unwholesome karma you have accumulated through body, speech, or mind due to the influence of afflictions, through this recitation there shall be purification and no ripening of results.
As previously stated, this is the third root downfall for a beginner bodhisattva.
Furthermore, noble son, some beginner bodhisattva will say this:
"Noble sons, avoid discourse on the vehicle of the śrāvakas;
do not listen to it, do not read it, and do not teach it to others."
Conceal the discourse on the Śrāvaka vehicle;
you will not obtain great fruit from it,
nor are you capable of bringing an end to the afflictions on that basis.
Have faith in the discourse of the Mahāyāna;
listen to the Mahāyāna, recite the Mahāyāna, and teach it to others.
Thereby, you shall pacify all paths leading to the miserable states and the lower realms.
And you shall swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If those who act according to his words should adopt such a view, there is a root downfall for both; this is the fourth root downfall of a beginner bodhisattva.
Furthermore, beginner bodhisattvas become double-tongued and display things otherwise;

for the sake of fame, reputation, and verses of praise, and for the purpose of gain and honor, they read, recite, memorize, chant, and teach this Mahāyāna, and they instruct others merely by what they have heard, saying thus:

"We are Mahāyānists, not others. Because they envy others for the sake of gain and honor— since they obtain enjoyments and articles of use from others due to those conditions— they become angry with them, utter dispraise of them, and revile, disparage, and loathe them.
They exalt themselves and do not [exalt] those [others]. Therefore, out of envy, they claim for themselves superhuman qualities (*uttarimanuṣyadharma*).

Consequently, by that act, they fall and are defeated from the bliss of the Mahāyāna; they incur this most grave offense (*mahāgurvī āpatti*), by which they become destined for the miserable realms (*apāya*).

Just as a certain man might set out for a jewel island and, having embarked upon the ocean by boat, should himself break that boat in the great sea and thus meet his death right there; even so, those beginner bodhisattvas who desire to embark upon the great ocean of qualities, yet speak out of envy, will— on account of that— break the boat of faith and suffer separation from the life of wisdom.
Thus, those foolish beginner bodhisattvas, for the sake of envy and based on falsehood, incur a very grave offense.
This is the fifth root downfall for a beginner bodhisattva.
Furthermore, noble son, in the future time there will be beginner bodhisattvas, both householders and renunciants,

who will uphold, recite, and study those Mahāyāna sūtras— which are profound and connected with emptiness, and which constitute the domain of great learned persons who have exerted themselves in the dhāraṇīs, patiences, samādhis, and stages that are the self-adornments of bodhisattvas.
Having recited and explained these teachings in detail to others, they say:

"I have realized these dharmas through my own intelligence, and thus, out of compassion for you, I teach them to you. Furthermore, you must cultivate them in such a way that you will become directly manifest in these profound dharmas."
"In this way, your knowledge and vision shall become just like mine.
However, at present, I do not grant it; for merely by reciting [this], I teach these most profound dharmas, but not through direct realization."
For the sake of gain and honor, one sells oneself; because of that,
one becomes guilty before all the Arhats, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, Bodhisattvas, and Noble Persons belonging to the three times,
and incurs a very heavy offense.
He deceives gods and humans regarding the Mahāyāna;
for him, even the Śrāvakayāna does not exist,
let alone the specific realization of entering the Mahāyāna.
How much more so, then, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening!

It is as if a certain man, setting out for a great forest and tormented by hunger and thirst, were to stand at a tree bearing large fruits. For the sake of food, having abandoned that noble fruit-tree which was endowed with fragrance and flavor, he would taste it not, but instead climb a poison-tree and eat its poisonous fruits; having eaten them, he would meet his end.
I declare those persons to be like unto him.
Those who, having obtained the rare attainment of human birth and relying upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), desire to enter the Mahāyāna,

yet for the sake of gain, honor, and fame, display themselves and disparage others— commit such a grave offense (*mahāgurvī āpatti*) that because of this heavy offense they become utterly despised by all wise people.
Furthermore, such individuals who are destined for the states of woe must not be associated with by any kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, or śūdras.
Whoever associates with them commits an offense against all wise ones.
Noble son, this is the sixth root downfall of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, noble son, in the future time there will appear among the kṣatriyas outcaste priests, outcaste ministers, and outcaste soldiers who are fools yet imagine themselves to be wise;

though possessing great wealth, they will be seen engaging in various meritorious deeds consisting of giving. Intoxicated by the pride of renunciation and by the arrogance of conceit and haughtiness, they will cause dissension between the kṣatriyas and the śramaṇas.
Relying upon those kṣatriyas, they cause the śramaṇas to be punished;
they plunder their wealth by means of punishment.

Because of that affliction, those monks—whether it be property belonging to an individual, to the Saṅgha, to the Saṅgha of the four directions, or to a stūpa—are made to pay back what has been seized by the śramaṇas as a gift for them.
Furthermore, those Caṇḍālas will present [themselves] to the Kṣatriya;
both of them incur a root downfall— namely,
those Kṣatriya-Caṇḍālas who become hostile toward the Śramaṇas and will promulgate such a doctrine.
Or, having abandoned non-dharma for the sake of dharma, disregarding the training of the Sūtras and the Vinaya, abandoning the timely instructions and the great principles,

and setting aside the training in great compassion, the guidance of the eye of wisdom, the perfection of wisdom, skillful means, and whatever other trainings are taught in other sūtras; [he acts] by abandoning these.
They establish such a formal rule of Dharma with the prior intention of harassing the monks—
those rules by which the harassment of monks occurs,
which obstructs the mental application devoted to the practice of tranquility and insight.
They become full of malice and abound in ill will.
For that reason, even the already pacified afflictions of the monks do not subside and do not diminish.
Furthermore, at that time, those monks become corrupted in their intention and corrupted in their ethical discipline.
They become fallen in conduct, they become fallen in view; for that reason, they become lax, they become luxurious, and though not being true śramaṇas, they claim to be śramaṇas.
Those who do not lead the holy life, yet claim to do so, whose conduct is like that of a conch-blower, and who teach the Dharma only when questioned—
they become increasingly honored, revered, and worshipped by the kṣatriya along with his retinue;
and they utter dispraise regarding householders in the presence of monks who are devoted to spiritual exertion.
And that kṣatriya, together with his retinue, becomes resentful and speaks ill of the monks who are devoted to spiritual exertion;
yet they hand over whatever resources and enjoyments belong to those monks engaged in exertion to the monks who delight in recitation.
Both of them incur a root offense.
For what reason?
A meditating monk is a fertile field;
they do not depend on recitation or service, nor are they intent upon study.
Having become vessels through the stages of the junctions, the dhāraṇīs, and the patiences, they are worthy of offerings and worthy recipients;
they are makers of light for the light and instructors in the path. They deliver sentient beings from the field of karma and the field of afflictions.
And they establish [beings] on the path leading to nirvāṇa.
These, noble son, are the eight root transgressions.
The escape from these [faults] is stated in this very sūtra:
if those bodhisattvas, having heard the name of the bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, should desire to see him,
out of fear of falling into the miserable states (apāya) and desiring to reveal their root transgressions.

If they should pay homage to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha and proclaim his name, that son of good family will, according to their fortune, stand before them in his own form, or he will stand before them in the form of a brahmin, or even in the form of a young girl.
He confesses those offenses as they have arisen for that beginner Bodhisattva.
And his skill in means is profound; he demonstrates the practice in the Mahāyāna and establishes them on the stage of non-retrogression. ... [pe] ...
If he does not grant them a face-to-face audience,
that beginner bodhisattva who has committed an offense and requested an interview should rise from his seat in the final watch of the night, stand facing the east, and burn incense.
The divine son Aruṇa should be entreated, and it should be said:
"Aruṇa, Aruṇa! O Greatly Compassionate One, O Fortunate One, O Greatly Exalted One! Out of compassion, cover me with your light in Jambudvīpa."
"Quickly awaken Ākāśagarbha, the Great Compassionate One, with my words! Reveal that means to me within my dream, by which means I may confess my transgression;
thus, O Noble One, I shall obtain skillful means and wisdom in the Mahāyāna."
At that time, he should be made to sleep upon his bed; as soon as the dawn has risen here in Jambudvīpa, there occurs a meeting here with the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha in his own physical form.

Standing before that beginner Bodhisattva in the midst of a dream, he causes him to confess that root downfall by means of the Mahāyāna method, and he likewise demonstrates to him such skillful knowledge of means.
By means of which skillful method that beginner bodhisattva attains therein the samādhi called "non-forgetfulness of the thought of awakening" and becomes firmly established in the Mahāyāna,
and so forth.
Alternatively, this ritual procedure should be performed with that mantra of entreaty which was previously mentioned in this sūtra;
it should be done in this manner.
In a forest, a grove, or an open space, one should burn *agara*, *tagara*, or *kālānusāri* incense.
Then, with palms joined and having prostrated in the five-pointed manner (*pañcamaṇḍalaka*) toward all the cardinal and intermediate directions, these mantra-words should be recited:
namely as follows:
Reflect,
O compassionate one;
let it proceed.
O you who wander,
who move about,
O compassionate one!
Murara! Murara! O bearer of speed, O compassionate one, fulfill my every hope; O compassionate Cintāmaṇi, establish [it] for me! O bearer of the command, be swift! sphugu!
O Guṇa, who delights in solitude! O Guṇa, who delights in the vision [of truth]! Fulfill me, O Compassionate One; fulfill my aspiration!
And in every way, O Aśokagati, svāhā!
The ritual procedure is as before;
it should be performed for the warding off of all diseases, sufferings, fears, and the destruction of all necessary resources, and for the accomplishment of all desired goals.
If even kṣatriyas and others are bodhisattvas, how can there be a fixed rule regarding their downfalls while others have more? Or, if they are [bodhisattvas] by virtue of that vow,
how is the classification of their downfalls established?
Or how is it that even those who possess vows (sāmvarika) are included because of that fault?

This is not a fault; for those in whom [the faults] most frequently occur are mentioned there by their specific names—as seen in the case of the "unwholesome courses of action"—in order to instill fear.
However, one must avoid all transgressions by means of all [the methods], each in turn.

Alternatively, because certain actions are by their very nature great offenses (*prakṛti-mahāsāvadya*), one becomes incapable [of liberation] and has one's roots of virtue severed even without having formally undertaken the vow; therefore, they are all the more subject to restraint (*sāmvarika*). Enough with this deliberation.
In the *Upāyakauśalyasūtra*, a root downfall is also described:
"Furthermore, noble son, a bodhisattva training in the *prātimokṣa* precepts might subsist on roots and fruits for even a hundred thousand eons,
and might endure the well-spoken and ill-spoken words of all sentient beings."

If a bodhisattva dwells with mental orientations associated with the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, this is a grave root downfall for a bodhisattva. Just as, noble son, a follower of the Śrāvaka vehicle who has committed a root downfall is incapable of attaining parinirvāṇa with those very aggregates,

even so, noble son, one who has not confessed and relinquished this downfall, and who has not abandoned those mental orientations of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, is incapable of attaining parinirvāṇa on the level of a Buddha.
And for the sake of easily grasping and retaining these root downfalls, as well as for the purpose of summarizing the various opinions of different schools, the summary verses are now stated.
The first offense involving defeat is considered to arise from stealing the property of the Three Jewels;
the second was taught by the Sage as resulting from the rejection of the True Dharma.
Even for a monk who is immoral, [the offense is incurred] by stealing his saffron robes, by beating him,
by casting him into prison, or by causing him to leave the religious life.

The root downfall taught by the Victor occurs through committing one of the five acts of immediate retribution, through the adoption of wrong views, or through the destruction of villages and the like.
And because of the teaching on emptiness to those beings who have developed wisdom,
or because of turning back from perfect enlightenment those who have set out for Buddhahood.
Because of abandoning the Prātimokṣa and enjoining [others] to the Mahāyāna,
or because of the misconception that the Disciple Vehicle does not lead to the abandonment of passion and the other afflictions.
Either by seizing the property of others, or again by proclaiming one's own virtues,
or by disparaging others for the sake of gain, honor, and fame.
Furthermore, by falsely claiming, "I possess profound patience," one might cause the śramaṇas to be punished or cause them to be expelled from the Three Refuges.
One may accept what is being offered, or again, by relinquishing [distractions] for the sake of tranquility;
and one may enjoy seclusion by announcing it to those engaged in recitation.
For these root offenses are the causes for rebirth in the great hells;
they must be confessed in a dream while standing before the noble Ākāśagarbha.
Through the abandonment of the thought of awakening, by not giving to a petitioner,
through intense stinginess and greed, or through striking a sentient being out of anger;

Even when being conciliated with effort, one does not exercise patience toward sentient beings—either because of a desire for fame, out of compliance with others, or due to the description of a counterfeit of the true Dharma. Thus it is said.

It is also said in the *Āryakṣitigarbhasūtra*: "O Mahābrahman, if a monk who has gone forth on my account is immoral and of evil conduct, one who is like rotten wood, a non-śramaṇa claiming to be a śramaṇa, a non-celibate claiming to be celibate, ruined, fallen, and defeated by various afflictions; [even so, he is not to be abandoned]."

Moreover, even though that monk of immoral conduct and evil behavior remains until today a revealer of the treasures of merit for all gods down to all humans, and a spiritual friend— despite having become an unworthy vessel— nevertheless, by the mere sight of his shaven head and face, his wearing of the saffron robes, and his dignified deportment, he provides support for the various roots of virtue in many beings and becomes a guide to the path of happy rebirths.

Therefore, whether he be virtuous or immoral, I do not permit even a universal monarch’s command regarding one who has gone forth on my account; nor do I permit, even in accordance with the Dharma, that a physical blow be dealt to the body of one who has gone forth on my account, or that he be cast into prison.
To maim limb by limb, or to deprive one of life—
how much more so, then, by means of unrighteousness?
Furthermore, although one is said to be "dead" in this Dharma and Vinaya,
nevertheless, that person is like *gorocanā* and musk;
regarding this very point, it is said:
"Those who cause harm to those who have gone forth on my account—whether they be worthy vessels or unworthy vessels—all of them commit a grave offense against all the Buddhas of the three times;
their roots of merit are severed, their mental continuums are scorched, and they are destined for the Avīci hell.
Regarding this very point, it is said:
"This red saffron robe is the banner of liberation, empowered by all the Buddhas.
And in this very [text] it is said:

"Furthermore, at that time, many hundreds of thousands of millions of śrāvakas and many hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas [disclosed] such previously committed karmic obstructions in the presence of the Blessed One."
They confessed:

"Venerable Blessed One, we too, in the teachings of many former Tathāgatas, have reviled and disparaged those persons belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle who were worthy vessels and those who were not worthy vessels among the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones."
We became enraged and uttered words of dispraise and infamy;
because of that karmic obstruction, we have experienced various kinds of intense, fierce, and painful sensations within the three lower realms.
...and so forth.
