"We shall now, in the presence of the Blessed One, confess the remainder of that karmic obstruction.
Some said,
"We have threatened and reviled the disciples of the Blessed One with our words."
Some said,
"We have struck the Blessed One’s disciples who were unworthy vessels as well as those who were worthy vessels.
Others said:
"We have stolen their robes.
Some said,
"We have seized the articles of enjoyment and use belonging to the Blessed One's disciples."
Some say:
"We have caused householders to go forth under the Blessed One; therefore, we have incurred an improper situation.
Others say: [the same].
“Blessed One, we have heard that the disciples of the Blessed Buddhas—both those who were worthy vessels and those who were not, as well as those who had committed offenses—were cast into prison.
Because of that karmic obscuration, for many eons we have experienced various intense, fierce, and painful sensations within the three lower realms. [pe]
Therefore, we now confess before the Blessed One the remainder of our karmic obstructions;
may we undertake restraint for the future.
May the Blessed One accept this from us out of compassion.
"May the Blessed One deliver us from endless evils," and so forth in detail.
The disadvantage is also stated in the *Pravrajyāntarāya-sūtra*:
"Mahānāman, a householder endowed with four qualities falls into an unfavorable state:
he is born blind, or dull-witted, or tongueless, or a caṇḍāla; he is never happy, he is frequently slandered, he is a eunuch, he is a paṇḍaka, and he is a perpetual slave."
And she becomes a female dog, a pig, a donkey, a camel, and a venomous serpent in various births.
What are the four?

Here, Mahānāman, a householder creates an obstacle for beings who have performed services under previous Victors, regarding their thought of renunciation, their thought of going forth, and their thought of the Noble Path.
This is the first.

Furthermore, a householder, out of greed for wealth or greed for his children, lacking faith in the ripening of karma, creates an obstacle to the going forth of a son, a daughter, a wife, or a circle of kinsmen while they are established in a position of power;
this is the second [obstacle].
The other two are:
rejecting the true Dharma and hostility toward ascetics and brahmins.

The ten unwholesome paths of action are harmful; they should be regarded as having bitter maturation because they obstruct the application of mindfulness to the true Dharma. Therefore, a brief excerpt from a sutra is indicated here.
First, regarding the minor portion of the maturation of taking life:

as it has been said, for example, there are birds called "Fire-Flame-Walkers" who, though situated in the midst of fire-flames, are not burned; and being exceedingly joyful, they pierce the skulls of the hell-beings and drink their blood.
There are birds called *kapālāntaracara* who, having pierced the skull, drink the glowing brain matter;
there are birds called *jihvāmiṣabhuja* who, having torn open the tongue, devour it on all sides.
Even that tongue, once consumed, grows back again, more tender than a lotus petal.
Thus, there are those with perceptions corresponding to their objects: those called "tooth-pullers," those called "throat-duct-extractors," the "lung-eaters," and the "stomach-seizers."
The spleen-transformers,
the intestinal-cavity-eaters,
and those called the spine-walkers.

There are birds called *marmaguhyaka* who, having pierced all the vital points (*marman*) and openings, cut through the vital organs and enter the cavities to drink the marrow-essence of those who are crying out.
There are birds called *sūcīchidra* who, with beaks like needles, drink the blood.
Likewise, there are those that eat from the openings of the bones and those that consume the six layers of skin.
The *nakhanikṛntakas* are fat-eaters who specialize in tendons;
the birds named *keśoṇḍukas* pluck out the roots of the hair.
That region of the Avīci hell, extending for three hundred thousand yojanas, is named Pakṣibhairavapakṣa (Terrifying Winged Birds).
There, together with those other denizens of hell, he is devoured and reborn for many hundreds of thousands of years.
Somehow or other, having been released from that place, he remains encompassed by a net of all kinds of suffering.
He goes toward the second region, named Śvabhraprapāta (The Precipice of the Abyss).
Seeking protection, seeking refuge, and seeking deliverance, he is surrounded on all sides by eleven masses of flames;
friendless, bound by the fetters of the noose of karma, and hemmed in on every side by enemies, he has entered a wilderness, [fleeing] from everything.
Having encountered a calamity even greater than that of the mass of hells, he runs toward that region called the Abyssal Precipice (*śvabhraprapāta*).
When he falls, his foot dissolves completely;
yet when it is lifted, it is formed once again.
Extremely delicate and tender, he is overwhelmed by harsh and intense pains.
As his face becomes distraught with fear and his hands, feet, and all his major and minor limbs begin to dissolve, that region called the Abyssal Precipice (Śvabhraprapāta) appears before him.
He falls into that place, and having fallen, he plunges three thousand yojanas down into the abyss.
Again, he is tossed upward by wind produced by karma;
as he falls, he is devoured by herons, crows, vultures, and owls.
In this manner, as he is being tossed up and falling down, many hundreds of thousands of years pass for him.
Having somehow escaped from that, he runs toward a region called the "Wheel-marked Cavity.
In that region, thousands of wheels appear—having adamantine hubs, sharp flames, and rapid rotation—which, as soon as he enters them, reach his body and spin there. ...pe... [as before] ...pe...
Crushing every limb one by one, they burn him, and his soles are pierced with spikes;
thus it is on Mount Makkoṭaka,
where he is devoured inside and out, down to the level of atoms, by creatures of the species known as makkoṭakas.
Each time he eats, it grows back even more delicate;
because of that delicacy, he experiences even greater pain.
With each successive meal, his skin and flesh emerge in even greater abundance.
That is the fruit which arises from the accumulation of that act of taking life.
He describes the ripening of the taking of what is not given:

This very person, who practices the course of evil deeds, sees a vast collection of objects—consisting of heaps of jewels, garments, wealth, and grain—which is like a whirling firebrand, a magical creation, a city of the Gandharvas, or a mirage.
To him, thus overcome by greed and deluded by his own karma, it occurs as follows:
Thinking "this is mine," that evildoer, thus deluded, leaps over pits of blazing coals and runs after that wealth.

He is seized by the henchmen of Yama created by his own karma; falling into a net of weapons, he is split apart limb by limb and member by member, slaughtered, and burned until nothing but his bones remains.
And even that greed of his, which has been active since beginningless time, does not diminish even when he has reached such a state.
Concerning sexual misconduct, it is said:
Having somehow escaped from that perilous place of weapons, this evildoer, led astray by his own karma, crosses over the Pit of Embers and reaches another region.
There, he sees a woman created by karma named "False Vision," whom he had previously seen when his mindfulness was lost.
Upon seeing them, the fire of passion, practiced since beginningless time, arises within him; driven by it, he runs toward those women,
who are actually iron women created by karma.
He is seized by them;
having seized him, they consume him starting from the lips in such a way that not even a portion the size of a mustard seed remains in his body.
Again it comes into being; again it is enjoyed.
Experiencing that bitter and harsh sensation, he does not turn away from the fire of passion.
He runs again toward those women;

yet the pain of them does not afflict him as much as the fire of passion. Then those women, whose limbs are made of adamant and iron and are ablaze, seize that man with their entire bodies wreathed in garlands of flames and crush that denizen of hell like a handful of wet flour.
It arises once again, as before... [etc. ...as previously described.
Women are the root of the lower realms and of the total destruction of wealth; for those men who are subject to women, how could there be happiness? ...pe...
To such an extent that woman is the destruction of all things, both in this world and in the next;
therefore, women should be avoided by one who desires his own happiness.
Concerning false speech, he said:
He is seized by those men of Yama; having seized him, they tear open his mouth and pull out his tongue from it.
And by the power of karma, that tongue becomes five hundred *yojanas* in length.
By the power of that false speech, at the time she emerges together with him, those men of Yama cause him to be dragged across the ground made of blazing iron.
A thousand ploughs produced by his own karma appear, joined with flaming tips and drawn by powerful oxen; they drag him through the interior of his tongue.
There, rivers flow, discharging pus, blood, and worms. ... [pe] ...
And that tongue was so delicate as the eyes of the gods.
As he stretches out, cries out, and wails from the sensation [of pain], and no one removes that suffering of his— so it is said in detail—
while he thus experiences such fierce sensations for many hundreds of thousands of years, that tongue is dragged [out]; somehow or other, it enters the mouth of that hell-being.
With his face overwhelmed by fear, he flees hither and thither, sinking as he is burned in pits of glowing coals.
While he is thus afflicted by suffering, without refuge or resort, the men of Yama appear once more, hammers and swords in hand;
they crush that man from his head down to his feet, and so forth.
The ripening of malicious speech is just like that of false speech; [the tongue] extends for three hundred *yojanas*, though there is this distinction:
the henchmen of Yama, taking up swords with blazing edges, cut off the tongue, and in another place, it is devoured by jackals.
He experiences extremely bitter sensations; he cries out and wails with indistinct syllables, being deprived of his tongue, and so forth.
He describes the ripening of harsh speech:
they tear open the mouth and seize that tongue;
having seized it, they cut it with sharp-edged weapons and cast it back into his mouth as food to be chewed.
Afflicted by the desire to kill and with a face emaciated by hunger, he devours that very tongue of his from which his own blood and saliva flow;
and by the power of karma, that tongue, though severed, grows back again.
Then, tormented by pain, he rolls about on the ground, writhes, and cries out.

For him who is thus afflicted by sensation, whose pupils are rolling, who is tormented by suffering, wretched, helpless, and alone, experiencing the fruits of his own deeds, the messengers of Yama utter this verse of instruction from their tongues:
"This is the fruit that has come to you for that harsh speech which was seen by you as 'harshness,' like a sharp arrow of words released from the bow of the tongue."
Thus is the detailed exposition.
He speaks of the maturation of frivolous speech.
That blazing [fire], red as molten copper, burns his tongue;
having burned the tongue, it burns the throat;
having burned the throat, it burns the heart; having burned the heart, it burns the intestines.
Having burned those as well, it burns the receptacle of digested food;
having burned the receptacle of digested food as well, it exits through the lower part of the body.
The messengers of Yama spoke this verse:
"This fruit has now arrived for that which was spoken by you— words bound together neither before nor after, meaningless, incoherent, and unconnected."
"That tongue which is not always truthful and not devoted to the study [of the Vedas],
is seen by the wise as nothing more than a mere piece of flesh.
Thus is the detailed explanation.

He speaks of the maturation of covetousness: then he sees much wealth, produced by karma, which is empty, hollow, and devoid of essence, yet possessed by another; to him, who is thus deluded by the impulse of his own karma, the thought occurs:
"May this be mine!"
Then that hell-being runs toward that very object.

This is the fruit of that unwholesome mental state called covetousness (*abhidhyā*), which he has practiced, cultivated, and frequently indulged in; namely, that he perceives things perversely in hell.
As he perceives them thus, being full of covetousness, a weapon appears in his hand, and with it he runs.

For those other hell-beings as well, weapons appear in their hands; he fights with them using those weapons until his flesh is cut away from his body so that not even a portion the size of a mustard seed remains, leaving him as nothing but a skeleton. ... [pe] ...
"I thought, 'May the prosperity of others be mine';
the fruit of that poison arising from covetousness has now arrived."
He speaks of the fruit of ill-will (*vyāpāda*):
lions, tigers, and serpents made of karma, overcome by anger, stand before one;
terrified by them, one flees hither and thither.
How can he possibly escape from his unwholesome karma?
He is seized by them;
having been seized, he is first devoured from the head down to the sides, being bitten again and again by snakes with venomous fangs until he is consumed.
"He is devoured from behind even by tigers;
his feet are burned by fire; he is pierced from afar with arrows by the messengers of Yama," and so forth in detail.
Furthermore, the fruit of wrong view is immeasurable;
however, the recitation is abbreviated here.
One is slain by rains of weapons, showers of javelins, rains of thunderbolts, lightning strikes, and showers of stones.
It is continuously burned by eleven masses of flames and by the fire of hunger and thirst, which issues forth easily.
Since all misfortunes have their root in sensual desire, one should feel revulsion toward them alone;
as it is said in this very context:
"There is a hell named Agnikuṇḍa."
In that regard, by what karma are beings reborn there?

It is by the karma of one who, though not a true ascetic, claims to be an ascetic, and having heard the sound of women dancing, singing, or wearing ornaments—with a mind distracted by improper mental attention—upon hearing those sounds of laughter, dalliance, and play, emits impurity. [Pe.]
There, those hell-beings are pulverized in every limb and member by a rain of iron, and they are cooked and burned by a rain of glowing coals, and so forth.
Thus, due to the recollection of the relish of past sensual pleasures and the recollection of things that occurred in dreams, the hell named Paduma is described;
there, those hell-beings are cooked in cauldrons.
"They are struck with iron pestles upon mortars," and so forth in detail.
Thus, due to the dedication of one's celibacy through the longing for celestial nymphs (apsarases), the hell named Mahāpaduma is described.
There flows a river called Kṣāranadītaraṅginī;
in that river, the bones [of the damned] serve as its stones.
That which was moss is your hair;
that which was mud is your flesh;
and that which was water is the boiled copper.
"Those who are fish are hell-beings," and so forth.
Thus, immeasurable and groundless particularities are taught regarding a man’s sexual misconduct with another man.
Likewise, regarding his misconduct with children, he sees infants being carried away in the River of Caustic Ashes;
they cry out to him.
He plunges into that river due to the force of grief and suffering arising from an intense bond of affection for those children;
likewise, sexual misconduct with cows, mares, goats, sheep, and so forth, which is inherently blameworthy, is taught to have an extremely harsh ripening.
Through the birth canal of those very cows, mares, and so forth—which are made of heated iron and produced by unwholesome karma—that one who indulges in animal lust enters.
He is steamed and cooked within their bellies, which are filled with heaps of blazing coals, for many hundreds of thousands of years; this should be understood in detail.
In this way, it is taught that those who commit misconduct even with other nuns who have been destroyed fall into the great hells;
likewise for those who go with their own wives by a non-vaginal route,
as well as with the wives of others who have been carried off by force, or with maidens who have been obtained.

Thus, it is taught that from sexual misconduct with women who are observing a fast, or with the wives of teachers, or with those honored as kinswomen, there arise intense and immeasurable falls into the great hells.

It is also said in the *Saptamaithunasaṃyuktasūtra*: "In this case, O Brahmin, a certain person claims for himself the status of a celibate practitioner (*brahmacārin*). He does not engage in sexual union with a woman here in this very life; rather, he gazes upon and looks at a woman by means of his eye."
At that time, he relishes it, becomes intent upon it, and having become intent, remains therein.
O Brahmin, this one is called a "brahmacārī" who is joined with the practice of sexual intercourse and not separated from it;
he leads an impure holy life.
Thus, for one who sports with a woman, who makes amorous sounds, and who relishes [the experience], impure celibacy is said to have been practiced.
Likewise for one who relishes the attendance upon a woman.
Likewise, for one who relishes the sound of a woman’s dancing, singing, and so forth, even when she is behind a wall or behind a curtain, it is said that there is sexual union.
Thus, he observed another who was enjoying himself, fully provided with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Thus, by dedicating his celibacy toward the states of the gods and so forth, he is joined with the dharma of sexual union and not separated from it.
And since these sensual desires are thus harmful even when they have merely become objects of memory and longing, for that very reason it was stated in the *Kāmāpavādaka-sūtra*:
"O monk, restrain the mind from sensual desires!
For this path is full of fear, fraught with peril, thorny, overgrown, a wrong path, a bad path, and a track of suffering."
This path is frequented by wicked persons; it is not frequented by virtuous persons. You do not think in this way.
Why did the Blessed One say that sensual pleasures have little gratification,
but much suffering, many calamities, and much despair;
and that the disadvantage therein is great?

"Monks, sensual pleasures are a disease, an abscess, a thorn, intoxication, the root of intoxication, and a baited hook of flesh. Sensual pleasures are impermanent, hollow, characterized by falsehood and deception, and like a dream;
they are merely toys for children. ... [and so forth] ...
Just as a snare is for the binding of deer, a net for the binding of birds,
a fish trap for the binding of fish,
sticky resin for the binding of monkeys, and a mass of fire for the binding of moths;
In this way, sensual pleasures are [like a dream]. ... [as before] ...

For one who has long pursued the search for sensual pleasures, there is no known end to being tossed about in the mouths of lions; likewise, there is no known end to being tossed about in the mouths of cattle-slaughterers and cowherds;
and likewise, there is no known end to being tossed about in the mouths of snakes while still being frogs.

For a long time, those who have indulged in sensual pleasures have been seized as thieves and, having had their heads cut off, their end has not been known. Those who have been seized as adulterers, highwaymen, village-destroyers, country-destroyers, and even as pickpockets, and having had their heads cut off, their end has not been known. The intense, sharp, harsh, and bitter suffering they have experienced, and the blood that has flowed and streamed forth, is more abundant than the water in the four great oceans... [pe] ... [The Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any limit to the blood that has been shed by sentient beings over a long period of time, who, having committed various evil deeds, were seized as thieves, adulterers, highwaymen, village-destroyers, country-destroyers, and even pickpockets, and had their heads cut off? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One. The Buddha said: "Subhūti, it is because of this that one should know: all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all conditioned phenomena are suffering; all conditioned phenomena are empty and selfless. Subhūti, for this reason, a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having heard this Dharma teaching, should train themselves in this way: 'We shall practice the holy life under the Tathāgata so that, upon the exhaustion of this present body, we shall not again experience such suffering.'"
For this body has many dangers:
it is a collection of bones bound together by sinews, smeared with flesh, enveloped in skin, covered by a hide, riddled with holes, inhabited by swarms of worms, useless to sentient beings,
and the locus for afflictions and karma.
In this body various afflictions arise, such as eye disease, ear disease, and so forth, up to hemorrhoids, boils, and fistulas... [etc. ...pe... [as before] ...pe... [as before].
Bodily afflictions are bodily suffering;
they consist of the body's decrepitude, brokenness, and humpbackedness; baldness, graying hair, and an abundance of wrinkles.

The maturation of the sense faculties, the breaking down of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), their becoming ancient and their falling into decay; as long as you ought not to indulge in this body which is thus oozing and trickling, loathsome... [pe] ...as long as you ought not to indulge in it.
"O monk, what desire do you lack that is not yet appeased?
And who is seducing you? How have you become so incited, infatuated, obsessed, and fallen into such attachment?"
When I have passed into parinirvāṇa and the True Dharma has disappeared,
you will have indulged in sensual pleasures and fallen into a state of ruin.
When will you completely liberate yourself from old age and death?
"Enough, monk! Restrain your mind from sensual desires. This is not the time for the pursuit of sensual pleasures;
this is the time for the pursuit of the Dharma."
It is also said in the *Ugratattaparipṛcchā*:

"One who has desisted from sexual misconduct must be content with one's own wife, have no longing for the wives of others, not look with lustful eyes, and possess a mind of revulsion [toward them], thinking:
'Sensual desires are exclusively suffering.'"
Thus, by being constantly engaged in mental attention,
even when a thought of sensual desire should arise toward his own wife,
he then regards his own wife as impure with a mind full of trepidation.
Sensual pleasures should be indulged in only under the influence of the afflictions (*kleśa*),
and not out of attachment or obsession, while maintaining the constant perception of them as impermanent, selfless, and impure.
Furthermore, he should establish mindfulness in this way:
"I shall act in such a way that I will not enjoy sensual pleasures even through mere mental intentions,
let alone through the union of the two sexual organs or through the communication of the limbs."
Furthermore, it says in this very same place:
"A bodhisattva should produce three perceptions toward his own wife.
Which three?"
She is a companion for amorous play, not a companion for the next world;
she is a companion for food and drink, not a companion for experiencing the ripening of karma;
she is a companion for pleasure, not a companion for suffering.
Likewise, there are another three:
the perception of an obstacle to ethical discipline, the perception of an obstacle to meditative concentration, and the perception of an obstacle to wisdom.
There are three others:
the perception of them as thieves, the perception of them as executioners, and the perception of them as hell-wardens.
It is also said in the *Candrottarādārikāparipṛcchā*: "Then,

having seen that great multitude of people running toward her, the girl Candrottarā at that moment rose into the sky through the air to the height of a palm tree, and having remained there, she addressed that great multitude of people."
He addressed him with verses.
Behold this body of mine, so pleasing to the mind, golden-hued, and radiant as a blazing fire;
for the beautiful form of a human being whose heart is stained with passion is not perceived.
Those who, being ungreedy for sense objects, abandon desires that are as fiercely blazing as pits of fire;
and those who, restrained by the control of the six sense faculties, practice the auspicious holy life (brahmacarya).
Indeed, those who, upon seeing the wives of others, conceive the perception of them as mothers or sisters,
become graceful, beautiful to behold, and eternally most charming.
"You know this city clearly on all sides, as do my pores; yet this exquisite fragrance was not acquired by me through a mind of passion, but is rather the fruit of generosity and self-restraint."
No thought of lust arises in me; do not conceive passion for those who are free from passion.
Before me stands this Lord of Munis as witness that I know the truth and never speak falsely.
In the past, you were my fathers,
and I was your mother;
there were brothers, sisters, and fathers as well— who could conceive a mind of passion for their own mother?
Previously, all of you were slain by me,
and formerly I was slaughtered by you;
all enemies are the executioners of another.
But how indeed does a mind of passion arise?
For through passion they do not become beautiful;
those with passionate minds do not go to a happy rebirth, nor do those with passionate minds attain nirvana. Therefore, passion must be completely abandoned.
For the sake of desire they fall into hell;
through passion they become hungry ghosts or animals.
Those whose minds are overwhelmed by passion become kumbhāṇḍas, yakṣas, asuras, and piśācas.
Those who practice the base conduct of sensual desire become one-eyed, lame, tongue-tied, and indeed deformed; they become partakers of various kinds of defects.
That they attain the state of a universal monarch (cakravartin), become Śakras, lords of the thirty-three gods,
Brahmās, Īśas, or Vaśavartins— that is the result of having practiced that vast celibate life (brahmacarya).

Those who are always lustful for sensual pleasures indeed become blind from birth, deaf, and senseless; they become dogs, pigs, camels, donkeys, and monkeys; or they become elephants, horses, cows, tigers, moths, and ants.
They become exalted lords of the earth, excellent merchants, householders, and ministers;
those who practice extensive celibacy increase in happiness and mental well-being.
For those enslaved by desire indeed seek out heated iron beds, smoke-chambers, as well as bonds, beatings, and threats;
they even undergo the cutting off of their heads, ears, hands, eyes, noses, and feet. Thus it is said.
And in the *Udayanavatsarājaparipṛcchā*, sensual pleasures are described as being loathsome.
Just as a fly runs toward a wound upon seeing it,
just as a donkey runs toward filth upon seeing it, and just as dogs run toward a slaughterhouse for the sake of meat; so too do they run toward sense objects.
In the very same way, the ignorant run after women with delight.
Fools are covered by ignorance and enveloped in a mass of darkness;
thus deluded, they are attached to women like crows to filth.
For this is the domain of Māra, by which one sets out for an evil rebirth;
those who perceive it as a relish and are greedy for it are like worms in a place of filth.
Just as a variegated jar of insects, wherever it may be seen,
is filled with urine and excrement, or like a leather bag inflated with wind.
With their heads drenched in phlegm, mucus,
and saliva, foul odors flow from the bodies of fools as if they were honey.
The gateway of the mouth is filled with bones and covered with flesh, skin, and the like;
for this body is like a goiter, loathsome and smelling of raw flesh.
Just as a cheek might be filled with various small creatures,
even so is this body a vessel for impurities such as excrement.
For the belly is filled with the final intestines, crowded with liver and lungs,
the two kidneys, blood, bile, brain matter, bones, and marrow.
There are eighty thousand families of worms that dwell within;
the fools do not see them, being shrouded by the net of delusion.
From the nine openings of the wounds, impurities flow out with a putrid stench;
yet fools seize upon signs both in speech and in sight.

It has been said that those fools who speak after they have eaten do not understand that place which is utterly contemptible; these children frequent the realm of excrement and consume phlegm and snot.
They are attracted to what is loathsome, like flies to a wound;
sweat exudes from the armpits, and a foul odor wafts forth.
They perform evil deeds by which they go to an evil destiny,
indulging in base sensual pleasures and practicing base qualities.
Having gone to Avīci, those of poor wisdom experience painful sensations;
women have been proclaimed by the Buddhas to be as foul-smelling as excrement.
Therefore, for one who is base, association with base women occurs,
just as when one takes up a bag of excrement and enters the dwelling of a fool.
Whatever kind of action one performs, such is the fruit one obtains.
Thus it is said in this very same [text]:

"In this way, they are unable to give gifts to ascetics and brahmins, to the wretched, the needy, and beggars— being those who have sought wealth through such forms of suffering for the sake of their own livelihood, yet are controlled by women and conquered by women."
Those who are subdued by women are slaves to women;
because of that very love for her, they are unable to give gifts or undertake ethical discipline (*śīla*) for the sake of supporting her alone.
Being thus attached to her, he endures the insults of women, and he even endures their threats, glares, and rebukes.
When that man is threatened by a woman, he becomes despondent and dejected, yet he gazes upon her with pleasure.
For the sake of sensual desire, and with sensual desire as its cause, he falls under her power.

Great King, this is the fault of a man who is greedy for sensual pleasures, who regards the pleasure of excrement as supreme, who delights in impurity, and who acts without clear comprehension. ... [pe] ...
Having heard such a stirring discourse, they do not attain tranquility;
instead, filled with delight, they again form associations with women.
They pursue what leads to suffering and speak what is loathsome.
Having heard the Dharma, those who are deluded regarding its meaning speak well-spoken words,
yet their minds remain fixed on women, like a cat’s toward a mouse.
Having heard what was spoken by the Jina, he experiences a momentary sense of spiritual urgency;
yet his passion flares up again, like the deadly Hālāhala poison.
Like a pig, his momentary terror subsides;
having seen the excrement, he indeed conceives a greedy desire for it.
Thus, fools seeking pleasure abandon the teaching of the Victor and indulge in base sensual desires, by which they go to an evil rebirth.
Those who are stained by passion and intoxicated by sensual desires, having committed very evil deeds and betrayed those possessed of virtuous conduct, go afterwards to an evil destiny.
For that man who, having understood such a principle of Dharma,
feels no attraction toward women,
the path to heaven is eternally purified for him.
For him, the supreme and foremost enlightenment is not difficult to attain.
"Having obtained this opportune moment and having heard such a Dharma as this, the wise person, having abandoned all sensual desires here, should go forth into the homeless life. Thus it is said.
In the *Praśāntaviniścayaprātihāryasūtra* as well, another disadvantage is stated:
Mañjuśrī, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to deprive all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa of their lives and take away all their possessions;

yet, Mañjuśrī, suppose another son of good family or daughter of good family were to create an obstacle for a single wholesome thought of a bodhisattva—even if it were merely a root of merit associated with giving a single morsel of food to one born as an animal. [The latter would incur far greater demerit than the former.]
This person produces a sin even more incalculable than that.
Why is this?
Because they stand as an obstacle to the roots of merit that give rise to the appearance of a Buddha.
Mañjuśrī, whoever among those in other families should harbor envy or stinginess toward a bodhisattva, at that time and on that account, three fears are to be expected for them.
What are the three? They are:
the fear of rebirth in hell, the fear of being born blind, and the fear of rebirth in a border region.
He spoke again:
Whatever person might do him harm, or speak dispraise of him whether true or false;
whoever, with an angry mind, should speak harshly to him, or even further cause him agitation—[to all such he would respond with patience].
With a ruined self, that evil-minded one is reborn in the hells with a massive physical form; he experiences agonizing sensations.
His height becomes five hundred yojanas; surrounded by ten million [beings], he is constantly and violently devoured by dogs.
There shall be five thousand heads for this slanderer,
and on each single head there shall be five hundred tongues.
And upon each and every tongue, five hundred plows with flaming tips are driven; they plow his tongues for having spoken evil speech.
And those who, being unattached [to virtue], inflict oppression upon Bodhisattvas, are cooked in the Pratāpana hell, which is filled with the fire of intense suffering.
For them, rebirth in the animal realm along with the hells will not be difficult to encounter for hundreds,
thousands, and millions of billions of eons.
Falling from there, they become fierce and extremely dreadful serpents with terrible venom;
overcome by hunger and thirst, they perform cruel deeds.
Even having obtained food and drink, he does not attain satisfaction;
when he passes away from there, if he is reborn among human beings...
A man who has spoken ill-spoken words— harsh speech that offends the noble ones— becomes blind from birth, dull-witted, evil-minded, and unrestrained.
Having passed away from among humans, he goes once again to a miserable rebirth;
for thousands of millions of eons, he does not see a Buddha born.
Furthermore, it says in this very same place:
"Mañjuśrī, for as many moments as a bodhisattva gives rise to thoughts of resentment or thoughts of contempt toward another bodhisattva,
for that many eons must he don his armor and dwell in the great hells."
“Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva cannot be caused to fall by any other action except for the very act of slandering a bodhisattva.
Mañjuśrī, it is just as a diamond-jewel (*vajramaṇiratna*) cannot be broken by any other wood or clod of earth except by another diamond;
in the same way, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva cannot be caused to fall by any other action except for the very act of slandering a bodhisattva.”
It is also said in the *Ārya-śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*:
Mañjuśrī, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to angrily cast all sentient beings in all the world-systems throughout the ten directions into darkness and bondage;
and suppose another son of good family or daughter of good family, being angry with a bodhisattva, were to turn their back on them and say,
"I will not look upon this evil-natured one"— the latter incurs a far more incalculable amount of sin than the former.
It is said in this very [text]:

"Mañjuśrī, if someone were to take away all the possessions of every being in all of Jambudvīpa, and another were to revile a bodhisattva in whatever manner possible, the latter would incur incalculably more demerit than the former.
It is said in this very [text].
Mañjuśrī, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to destroy or burn as many stūpas as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā;

yet another son of good family or daughter of good family, having conceived a mind of malice, stubbornness, and anger toward a bodhisattva who is devoted to the Mahāyāna, were to revile or abuse them— this latter person produces incalculably more demerit than the former.
For what reason?
Because the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are produced from Bodhisattvas, and from the Buddhas are produced the stupas, all articles of comfort, and all the assemblies of gods.
By showing disrespect to a Bodhisattva, one shows disrespect to all the Buddhas.
By honoring a bodhisattva, all buddhas are honored.
One who wishes to worship all buddhas with unsurpassed worship must worship bodhisattvas.
And this ripening of the merit from such worship is declared in the *Praśāntaviniścayaprātihāryasūtra*.
But he who provides righteous protection for these speakers of Dharma,
having abandoned all miserable rebirths, becomes Śakra, the king of the gods.
Having been Brahmā, as well as a Yāma, Tuṣita, and Vaśavartin deity again and again,
he is born among humans and becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin).
He becomes a merchant or a householder, wealthy and possessing great riches;
endowed with wisdom and mindfulness, he is happy and free from affliction. Thus it is said.
Now, with reference to what kind of bodhisattva is this reflection on benefit and harm intended?
It is intended for the ordinary person (pṛthagjana) alone.
As it is said in the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*:

"Mañjuśrī, if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to give divine food of a hundred flavors and divine garments day after day to as many sentient beings as there are atoms in all world-systems, and were to continue giving in this manner for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges..."
One might give gifts for oceans of eons;

yet another son of good family or daughter of good family, having formed the conviction that "this person is trained in the training of the Blessed Buddha," might give a single meal for one day to a single lay follower who does not follow another teacher and is endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action. [The latter would generate far greater merit.]
This person generates merit that is even more incalculable than that.

Mañjuśrī, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to give every day divine food of a hundred flavors and divine garments to as many lay followers as there are atoms in all world-systems— lay followers who are endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action— and were to give them such gifts for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges; [if another were to do otherwise...]
And if another son of good family or daughter of good family were to give food for a single day to a single monk,
this person would produce incalculably more merit than that.
The *Niyatāniyatāvatāramudrāsūtra* also says:

"Mañjuśrī, suppose that, by way of conceptualization, all sentient beings in all world-systems in the ten directions were to have their eyes plucked out. Then, if some son of good family or daughter of good family, with a mind of loving-kindness toward all those sentient beings, were to restore their eyes by way of conceptualization..."
Or, Mañjuśrī, if another son of good family or daughter of good family, with a mind full of faith, should behold a bodhisattva who is devoted to the Mahāyāna,
this person generates incalculably more merit than that.

Mañjuśrī, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to release all sentient beings throughout the ten directions who have entered prisons and establish them in the happiness of a universal monarch or the happiness of the state of Brahmā;

yet, Mañjuśrī, another son of good family or daughter of good family might, with a mind of faith and longing for a vision, speak the praises of one who is devoted to the Mahāyāna. [The latter would generate far more merit than the former.]
This person generates merit that is even more incalculable than that.
Likewise, it is said in the *Kṣitigarbhasūtra*:

"Furthermore, O Venerable Blessed One, whether it be a virtuous kṣatriya, a virtuous minister, a virtuous soldier, a virtuous ascetic, or a virtuous brahmin, whoever protects others protects himself and protects the next world."

Within the teaching of the Blessed One, whether one is a worthy vessel or not, as long as one protects even a shaven-headed person clad in a fragment of saffron robe, one will hear and honor the discourse on the Śrāvakas; likewise, one will hear and honor the discourse on the Pratyekabuddhas,
and the discourse on the Mahāyāna, as well as those persons who have set out in the Mahāyāna— those who are virtuous, rich in qualities, and possessed of appropriate and liberated eloquence.
He delights, plays, inquires, and questions with them; he considers that what they have to say should be heard and what they propose should be carried out. ... [as above] ...
"Blessed One, how much evil will it destroy?"
The Blessed One said:
It is as if, noble son, some man were to appear who,

having filled the entire Jambudvīpa with the seven precious jewels, were to give it as a gift to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, remaining present; and in the same way he would give a gift at the time of midday, and likewise at the time of evening— in this manner, by such a method.
If one were to give such a gift for a hundred thousand years,
what do you think, noble son— would that person produce much merit?
He said.
"Venerable Blessed One, that person would produce a vast heap of merit—immeasurable and incalculable.
No one at all would be able to grasp the measure of that heap of merit, except for the Tathāgata."
The Blessed One said:
But whichever noble son, whether a virtuous kṣatriya or as previously described, [acts in this way], he produces a much greater merit; indeed,
he produces a mass of merit that is more vast, more immeasurable, and more incalculable.
Whoever protects the guidance of the True Dharma during my final five-hundred-year period protects himself;

he protects others, he protects the next world, and he protects my teaching— protecting both those who are worthy vessels and those who are not, even including those with shaven heads and clad in saffron robes, whom he protects and does not harm.
It causes one's own kingdom and the kingdoms of others to flourish;
it exhausts the lower realms;
it leads one to the abode of the gods; and it protects one's lifespan for a long time.
He burns away his own afflictions and the afflictions of others;
he supports the path to perfect enlightenment and the six perfections;
and he abandons all miserable rebirths.
He does not wander long in saṃsāra;
he is constantly in the company of spiritual friends, and of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas.
Constantly never separated from spiritual friends, before long he will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment in the Buddha-fields according to his aspirations.
Then, at that very moment, all the lords of the gods with their retinues,

up to the lords of the *piśācas* with their retinues, rose from their seats, bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, and spoke thus: "Venerable Blessed One, those who in the future time, even unto the final five-hundred-year period, shall be noble kṣatriyas, up to noble householders— [pe]..."
Thus they are protectors of the true Dharma and thus kindlers of the lineage of the Three Jewels...
We too, all together with our retinues, shall protect, preserve, and increase that noble kṣatriya, up to and including the noble householder, in ten ways.
By what ten?
We shall increase his lifespan and, through the Dharma, ward off obstacles to his life;
we shall increase his health, his retinue, his mass of wealth, his enjoyments and resources, his sovereignty, his fame, his spiritual friends, and his perfection of wisdom.
"By these ten," and so forth in detail.
Thus, this detailed exposition of the maturation of results should be understood as applying specifically to those who have not yet entered the stages.
Also in the Avalokanā-sūtra:
"Having generated the mind set on perfect enlightenment for the sake of the welfare of all living beings,
whoever here performs a circumambulation of the stūpa of the Lord of the World..."
Having thus spoken at length on these benefits, he said:
"But the man who would do what is displeasing to these sons of the Buddha—
excluding gods and humans, hell shall be his domain."
Thus the detailed explanation is as before.
And since no specific reason can be shown for this [distinction], enough with such conceptual proliferation.

In the *Karmāvaraṇaviśuddhi-sūtra* as well, the word "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*) is used to denote misfortune: "Mañjuśrī, obscuration is said to be passion; obscuration is hatred; obscuration is delusion; obscuration is giving; obscuration is ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom... and so forth. Why is that? Mañjuśrī, when foolish ordinary people give gifts, they produce a lack of faith in those who are stingy.
Due to that lack of faith, they give rise to a mind of resentment;
through the fault of such stubborn resentment, they are reborn in the great hells.
While guarding their own precepts, they revile and abuse those who are immoral.
They speak dispraise of them;
having heard their faults, they cause a lack of faith among many people;
through that lack of faith, they become destined for the miserable realms.
Cultivating patience, they exalt themselves with the intoxication of patience and become heedless, thinking,
"We are proponents of patience, whereas these others have malicious minds."
For those who are intoxicated with the pride of their own patience, sufferings rooted in negligence arise.
Exerting themselves in vigor, they exalt themselves and disparage others, saying:
"These monks dwell in idleness, lacking application, yet consuming what has been given out of faith."
They do not even deserve a water bowl;
by that exertion of vigor, they exalt themselves and disparage others.
I call them fools.
As they enter into meditative absorption, they conceive a longing for that attainment of dhyāna;
it occurs to them:
"We are dwellers in samādhi."
"These other monks dwell with distracted minds;
how could they ever become Buddhas? and so forth.
In the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa* it is also said:
"If a bodhisattva accuses another of an offense,
he becomes distant from awakening."
He also embraces karmic obstructions,
is rebuked by his own conduct,
and becomes distant from enlightenment.
One who reproaches another by way of their deportment distances themselves from awakening.
If a bodhisattva conceives a notion of inferiority toward another bodhisattva while conceiving a notion of superiority toward themselves, they destroy themselves and incur a karmic obstruction.
In this regard, a bodhisattva who advises or instructs another bodhisattva should do so having established the notion that the other is the Teacher.
A bodhisattva should not give rise to a mind of contempt toward another bodhisattva,
provided that his own awakening has not been abandoned.
O Devaputra, a bodhisattva never utterly cuts off his roots of virtue.
Regarding the phrase "by relying on a non-dual bodhisattva":

even in the case of a sentient being who is merely capable of awakening but has not yet generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), disparagement is forbidden; how much more so, then, in the case of one who has already generated that thought?
As it is said in the Śūraṅgamasamādhi-sūtra:
"In that regard, Dṛḍhamati, what is the prophecy for one who has not yet generated the mind of awakening?"
In this regard, Dṛḍhamati, that person is born within the saṃsāra of the five destinies—
whether in the hells, or in the animal realm, or in the world of Yama, or among the gods, or among humans—
and that person possesses sharp faculties.
He possesses noble resolve;

the Tathāgata knows him thus: "This person will, after this many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. ... [as above] ...
And after this many hundreds of thousands of incalculable eons, he will fully awaken to enlightenment... [pe] ...
This, O Dṛḍhamati, is called the prophecy for a bodhisattva who has not yet generated the thought of awakening. Then, the venerable Mahākāśyapa said this to the Blessed One:
"From this day forward, Blessed One, we should conceive the notion of the Teacher toward all sentient beings.
For what reason?
Because this knowledge does not function within us."
"Of which bodhisattva do the faculties that ripen enlightenment exist,
and of which do they not exist?
Therefore, O Blessed One, being ignorant of this, we might conceive a notion of inferiority toward such individuals."
By that we would be harmed.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa! These words of yours are well-spoken.
And it is, Kāśyapa, seeing this very purpose that I have taught the Dharma to you in this way."
"Monks, one person should not judge another person;
for a person who judges another person quickly comes to ruin, monks—
unless it be I who should measure a person, or one who might be like me."
By this teaching, Kāśyapa, whether a bodhisattva or a śrāvaka, should conceive the notion of the Teacher toward all sentient beings.
One should not think, "If there should be some person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, I must protect myself from him.
However, one must especially guard against contempt toward those who possess the certain signs of attaining awakening.
As it is said in the noble *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"With joy, they build stūpas for the Jina out of bricks or heaps of clay;
or, even with heaps of dust, they construct them in forests and difficult terrains."
Furthermore, those children who, in various places, built toy stūpas made of clay or sand, dedicating them to the Jinas,
have all become attainers of enlightenment.
...up to...
Those who fashion images upon variegated walls,
with limbs complete and endowed with the marks of a hundred merits;
Whether one writes it oneself or causes it to be written,
all such persons have become attainers of awakening.
And those who at that time were training,
even while diverting themselves with playful delights;
You have fashioned figures with your fingernail or with wood— men or boys upon the walls.
And they all became attainers of enlightenment... [etc. ...
Even those who had cymbals struck,
or water-drops, or even cakes,
offered for the sake of worship directed toward the Sugatas, sang songs that were sweet and pleasing to the mind.
And they all became Buddhas in the world.
Having performed various kinds of worship to the relics,
what is the use of one who trembles only slightly before the relics of the Sugatas,
even if they play but a single musical instrument?
Indeed, by worshipping with even a single flower,
they shall successively behold tens of millions of Buddhas;
and likewise for those who have joined their palms in reverence there at the stupa.
Or, with the strength of a single palm-strike fully exerted,
one should lower the head for a moment,
and likewise lower the body once.
Homage be to the Buddha even once;
those who, at that time, within those repositories of relics,
[utter it] even once, even with distracted minds— [for them there is great merit].
They all attained this supreme enlightenment at that time, under those Sugatas,
whether they had already entered parinirvāṇa or were still remaining in the world.
"Those beings who hear even the names of these dharmas shall all become attainers of enlightenment. Thus it is said.
It is also said in the Mahākaruṇā-sūtra:

It is just as when a fisherman, for the sake of catching fish in a large lake, casts a baited hook; and immediately after it is cast, it is swallowed by a fish. Even though that fish still swims about in the lake, it must nevertheless be said to be already caught, because it is firmly bound by a strong line attached to a pole standing on dry land. When the fisherman arrives, he knows [the fish's situation] through the tension of that line.
Thinking, "A fish has been caught," one takes it from the line and brings it onto dry land for use and enjoyment according to one's desire.
In the very same way, those beings who, having developed a mind of serene faith toward the Blessed Buddhas, plant roots of merit;
Even if it is but a single thought of serene faith;
moreover, even though those beings may have been born in the unfavorable states due to their evil deeds and karmic obstructions, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
having taken hold of those beings with their Buddha-knowledge and the thread of the articles of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), draw them out from the lake of the waters of *saṃsāra*.
They establish [beings] in the state of nirvāṇa.
Therefore, one should regard them as the Teacher;
and when they pay homage, they should be mentally honored.
For even a novice is worthy of veneration by virtue of the power of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
For example, even though Megha was a great bodhisattva, he prostrated with his entire body and paid homage to the novice Sudhana.
And this is of definitive meaning;
for instance, in the *Adhyāśayasaṃcodana* and other such texts, it is permitted to pay homage to all individuals belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle.
Since the word "all" includes oneself as well,
how is it that the state of being both the object of worship and the worshiper is not contradictory in one and the same person?
It is because one takes another as the very object of worship.
For this very reason, by not tasting the food, there is an absence of demerit.
Furthermore, this is also accepted for the Buddhas,
so that there may be no infinite regress.
And there is no deficiency in one [of the two].
In the *Āryasarvadharmavaipulyasaṃgrahasūtra* as well, this disadvantage is stated:
"For subtle, Mañjuśrī, is the karmic obstruction of rejecting the true Dharma.
For whoever, Mañjuśrī, forms the notion that some part of the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata is superior [to another]," [that person incurs such an obstruction].
In some cases, perceiving [the teaching] as unwholesome, he rejects the true Dharma;
by rejecting the true Dharma, he slanders the Tathāgata and the Dharma is rejected.
The Saṅgha is thereby slandered.
Whoever speaks thus, "This is reasonable; this is unreasonable," rejects the True Dharma.
I have not taught any separate dharma associated with the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Mahāyāna.
Then those deluded persons will differentiate this Dharma of mine,
saying, "This was taught for the śrāvakas, this for the pratyekabuddhas, and this for the bodhisattvas. By means of such perceptions of diversity, they reject the true Dharma.
"This is the training of a bodhisattva;
this is not the training of a bodhisattva"—thus one rejects the true Dharma.
"The Dharma-preacher possesses eloquence; he lacks eloquence"—thus one rejects the true Dharma.
To explain the Dharma according to its true nature [and thereby deny its efficacy] is to reject the True Dharma.
To say that when a Buddha has not appeared in the world there is no attainment of *dhāraṇī* is to reject the Dharma. To say that a Dharma-preacher does not attain *dhāraṇī* is to reject the Dharma.
One defiles the conduct of a Dharma-preacher and rejects the Dharma;
one rejects the Dharma by saying that the Dharma-preacher is not endowed with correct practice;
one rejects the True Dharma by reproaching him on account of his negligence.
One rejects the true Dharma by censuring it on account of [another's] deportment;
one rejects the Dharma by censuring it on account of verbal conduct or a failure in morality;
and one rejects the Dharma by claiming that [the speaker] merely succeeds through rhetorical eloquence.
One rejects the Dharma by thinking, "The light of these phenomena has not been well understood.

One rejects the Dharma by responding while failing to understand one mantra through another mantra. One rejects the Dharma by thinking, "I do not penetrate the teaching of the Tathāgata because of my preoccupation with the notion of syllables."
To contradict one sutra with another is to reject the Dharma;
to contradict one verse with another is to reject the Dharma;
to apply a particular interpretation to some syllables while not applying it to others is to reject the Dharma.
To divert the discourse for the sake of a Dharma-preacher is to reject the Dharma. To act so as to deprive him of his vision is to reject the Dharma.
To speak while engaging in idle chatter is to reject the Dharma.
To say, "He has such conduct here" or "He does not have such conduct here," is to reject the Dharma.
To say, "This is well-spoken" or "This is ill-spoken," is to reject the Dharma.
To say, "There is no practice by means of this," is to reject the Dharma.

"To say, 'By this [person] the Buddha's word was spoken, but by this [other person] the Buddha's word was not spoken,' is to reject the Dharma. For indeed, Mañjuśrī, to the extent that one causes any [teaching] to be destroyed, to that extent one rejects the Dharma.
Whether it be a monk, a nun, a layman, or a laywoman, they think and speak thus: "This is the characteristic of a Dharma-preacher."
"He rejects the entire True Dharma," and so forth.
And it is said in this very place:
"O son of good family, if any Tathāgata who has entered final nirvāṇa should have the inspiration to teach the Dharma to sentient beings according to their inclinations,
and if in that assembly even a single being should experience the bristling of a single hair or the shedding of a single tear, all of that is through the power of the Tathāgata."

In that regard, deluded persons who are not bodhisattvas, yet claim to be bodhisattvas, who revile bodhisattvas and are thieves of the Dharma and hypocrites, will say this to those who teach the Dharma:
"What are these people? Do they not understand? ... [and so forth] ...
I do not declare that there is an end to the hell for those who treat Bodhisattvas with contempt.
Why is that?
The bodhisattva who reviles a Dharma-preacher reviles the Buddha, rejects the Dharma, and despises the Saṅgha.
He who has no respect for the Dharma-preacher has no respect for the Buddha;
he who does not wish to see the Dharma-preacher does not wish to see the Buddha.
He who speaks dispraise of a Dharma-preacher speaks dispraise of the Buddha;
he by whom the Buddha is abandoned is he who harbors a mind of resentment even toward a bodhisattva who has first generated the thought of awakening. ... [as before] ...
Furthermore, Maitreya, regarding this complete realization of the six perfections for the sake of the enlightenment of bodhisattvas, those deluded persons will say:
"A bodhisattva should train only in the perfection of wisdom;
what is the use of the remaining perfections?"
They consider other perfections to be something that should be disparaged.
What do you think, Ajita? Was that King of Kāśi not of poor wisdom, who gave his own flesh to the hawk for the sake of the dove?
Maitreya said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Maitreya, as for those roots of merit associated with the six perfections that were accumulated by me while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva—was any harm done by those roots of merit?"
Maitreya said,
"Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "Ajita, you yourself have practiced for sixty eons in the perfection of generosity, sixty eons in the perfection of ethical discipline,
sixty eons in the perfection of patience, sixty eons in the perfection of vigor, and sixty eons in the perfection of meditative concentration."
For sixty eons he has fully realized the perfection of wisdom.
Yet those deluded persons will speak thus:
"Awakening is by means of a single method alone, namely, the method of emptiness."
"They will become completely purified in their practices," and so forth.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.
[V. Avoidance of What is Unbeneficial] The fifth chapter: The Avoidance of What is Unbeneficial in the Perfection of Ethical Discipline.
The disadvantage has been stated in brief.
Its avoidance is as described in the *Adhyāśayasaṃcodana-sūtra*.
Beginner bodhisattvas, who are terrified by the fear of hearing about such disadvantages, should act in accordance with how the commitments were undertaken.
For thus they said:
"O Blessed One, from this day forward, in the presence of the Tathāgata,
we make this formal undertaking."

“Blessed One, if from this day forward we should reproach a person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle— whether a householder or one who has gone forth— with an offense, whether true or false, we would have deceived the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Blessed One, if from this day forward we should despise a person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle or speak ill of them, we would have deceived the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
“Blessed One, if from this day forward, upon seeing a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle— whether a householder or one who has gone forth—

sporting with and indulging in the five strands of sensual pleasure, we should feel a lack of serene confidence, or give rise to mental distress, or produce a lack of respect, and fail to conceive the perception of them as the Teacher; [may we not attain enlightenment].”
The Tathāgata would be deceived by us,

O Blessed One, if from this day forward we were to cause physical or mental suffering to persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle on account of families of friends or families from whom alms are sought. The Tathāgata would be deceived by us.
“Blessed One, if from this day forward, upon seeing a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, we should address them with even a single unpleasant word, we would have deceived the Tathāgata.

Blessed One, if from this day forward, three times during the night and three times during the day, we should not pay homage to a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, we would have deceived the Tathāgata.”
"Blessed One, if from this day forward, for the sake of undertaking this vow, we were not to relinquish our acquisition of a kingdom, or our acquisition of wealth, or even our bodies and lives,
we would have deceived the Tathāgata. Blessed One, if from this day forward we were to hold in contempt any person belonging to the vehicle of the disciples or the vehicle of the solitary buddhas,"
If we were to think, "We are more distinguished and they are not," the Tathāgata would be deceived by us.
Blessed One, if we were to dwell with lowly minds, with minds like those of outcasts, the Tathāgata would be deceived by us.
Blessed One, if from this day forward we were to exalt ourselves or disparage others, the Tathāgata would be deceived by us.

"Lord, if from this day forward, when moved by fear of malice or strife, we do not flee for even a league or a hundred leagues, we would be deceiving the Tathāgata. Lord, if from this day forward we claim ourselves to be virtuous, or learned, or possessed of the ascetic qualities (dhuta-guṇa), or if we exalt ourselves by any other quality whatsoever, we would be deceiving the Tathāgata."
“Blessed One, if from this day forward we were to dwell concealing our virtues and revealing our evils, we would have deceived the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.”
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:
"Maitreya, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to exhaust their karmic obstructions should make this formal commitment, just as it was made by these sons of good family."
It is also said in the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa*:
Three times during the night and likewise during the day,
he should bow his head in salutation to those Bodhisattvas;
he should not look for any fault or lapse in them whatsoever.
For he always practices his conduct according to his own will.
When one sees him enjoying the qualities of sensual pleasure,
one should not seek out any fault in him;
for his practice of supreme awakening is infinite in its virtues.
In time, he too shall touch what is beneficial.
Through the sequence of reasoning and the sequence of practice,
one may indeed become a Jina; it is certainly not by a single word,
for this takes many millions and billions of eons.
The armor and the setting forth are not non-existent.
In this very regard, it says: "O son of good family, those who do not desire such an obscuration of karma should not act improperly toward any of the practices of a second bodhisattva;
all his actions should be accepted."
One should generate the thought:
"I do not know the minds of others; the conduct of sentient beings is difficult to discern.
Indeed, O son of good family, it is seeing this significant purpose that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma in this way.
One person should not be judged by another person.
Either I myself would judge a person, or someone who might be like me.
O sons of good family, he who wishes to protect himself must not scrutinize the conduct of anyone,
nor should he engage in disparaging others by saying,
"This one is like this," or "That one is like that."
One should be devoted to the Buddha's teachings day and night, with a mind entirely absorbed in the Dharma.
Likewise, it is also said in the *Kṣitigarbha-sūtra*:
"Then, at that very moment, many hundreds of thousands of wise beings rose from their seats, bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, and spoke thus:
'Venerable Blessed One, we make this vow before you: for as long as we must wander in saṃsāra, Venerable Blessed One, may we not desire [anything other than] the attainment of patience.'"
May we obtain the position of a king; may we obtain the position of a minister;
may we not obtain the position of a city elder.
May there be no position as the elder of a village; may there be no position as the elder of a town;
may there be no position as the chief priest; may there be no position as a royal minister.
May there not be for me the preeminent position of a caravan leader; may there not be the preeminent position of a preceptor; may there not be the preeminent position of a śramaṇa.

"May we not obtain the position of a senior householder, nor the position of a senior family head, nor indeed any position of sovereignty over sentient beings until we have attained patient acceptance (*kṣānti*).
For on account of such a cause, we would be casting aspersions upon the teaching of the Buddhas by performing such extremely grave karma."
Thus is the detailed exposition.
In the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra* as well, the avoidance of what is unwholesome is stated:
"O youth, there shall be no evil that you will not commit; therefore, in the future age, you must not cultivate intimacy with them."
When conversing or engaging in dialogue, you should show no respect toward them;
remaining unattached, you should treat them with indifference for the sake of supreme enlightenment.
Having inquired about the seniority of the rainy-season retreat (*varṣāgra*), you should show reverence to whoever is more senior than you by bowing your head at their feet.
One who gazes upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) should not observe their lapses;
one should not give rise to resentment, but should always maintain a mind of loving-kindness (maitracitta).
If one should see a lapse in these [beings], one should not proclaim their faults;
for whatever kind of action one performs, such will be the fruit one receives.
With a moon-like face brightened by a smile, one should always be the first to speak toward both the elders and the novices, and should be entirely free from pride.
"You should provide them with assistance through robes and alms-food;
you should direct your mind thus: 'All shall become leaders.'"
Furthermore, for one in whom neither reverence nor serene faith arises toward those who have generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*),

it is necessary— out of a desire to protect oneself from the fear of falling into miserable rebirths, for the sake of experiencing joy in both the seen and the unseen worlds, for the purpose of purifying the turbidity of one's own mind, and for the attainment of mental health and mental flexibility—
to cultivate the qualities of those who have generated the thought of awakening, as described in the *Āryagaṇḍavyūha*.
These [qualities] were elucidated by the Blessed Noble Maitreya with reference to the teacher Sudhana; they should be cultivated in that same manner.
Having seen living beings afflicted by old age and disease, oppressed by hundreds of sufferings,
and tormented by the fear and grief of birth and death, he whose mind is set on compassion acts for their sake.
Having seen the world oppressed by the machinery of suffering within the wheel of the five realms of existence,
this firm vajra of yours, consisting of primordial wisdom, shatters the machinery of suffering and the wheel of rebirth.

Seeking to purify the field of sentient beings, which is filled with the weeds and stumps of passion and hatred and overgrown with the thickets of many attachments to views, he seeks the firm plow of wisdom.
The world has a mind dense with delusion and ignorance, its guide lost through the destruction of the eye of wisdom;
for it, there will arise a Lord, a caravan leader, who acts as a guide toward the direction of security.
Carrying the vehicle of patience, the Dharma, and the three liberations, he will subdue the enemy of the afflictions with the sword of wisdom;
a hero among teachers, he will indeed become a guide for the world, bestowing fearlessness.
This one, well-trained on the path to the ocean of wisdom, gathers the ship of Dharma;
he is the helmsman in the ocean of the three realms, leading to the island of the supreme jewel of peace.

This sun of a Buddha is proclaimed as having arisen in the sky of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), possessing a mandala of vows and rays of wisdom that illuminates the abodes of all sentient beings.
Cool with the concentration of the sandalwood of loving-kindness, possessing the beautiful radiance of a mind equal toward all sentient beings,
this Buddha-moon is seen rising, its orb completely filled with pure dharmas.
Established upon the firm foundation of the resolute intention, the conduct of awakening has gradually arisen;
for this is indeed a mine of the jewels of all dharmas, and it shall become the supreme essence of wisdom.
Born from the king of serpents that is the thought of awakening, it has arisen in the sky of the realm of phenomena;
it simultaneously rains down clouds of Dharma, increasing the harvest of all white fruits.

I, though obscured by the darkness of the three impurities, shall kindle the lamp of Dharma— pure in its wick, a firm vessel for the oil of loving-kindness and mindfulness, and brilliantly radiant with the stainless fire of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta).
With the *kalala* of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), the *arbuda* of compassion, the *peśī* of loving-kindness, and the *ghana* of unwavering intention,
this embryo of the Buddha (*buddhagarbha*)— the gradual arising of the factors of enlightenment— grows.
He will cause the womb of merit to increase and purify the womb of wisdom;
such is this one who shall manifest the womb of knowledge, born from the womb of his own vows.
Those whose nature is endowed with such compassion and loving-kindness, whose intent is the liberation of beings, and whose disposition is beneficial—
such as this one of pure mind, are rare in the world of gods and humans.
Established with such excellent roots of intention, increased by such firm application,
and possessing such power to cover the three realms of existence, this tree of knowledge that yields fruit is extremely difficult to find.
Seeking the arising of all virtues, seeking to inquire about all dharmas,
and seeking to tear asunder all doubts, he tirelessly attends upon all spiritual friends.
This one is the destroyer of Māra, the age of strife, and the afflictions; this one is the purifier of the stains of views and the afflictions;
this one is intent upon liberating the entire world; this one is always your distinguished wise man.
He will purify the miserable realms, show the path to heaven,
and lead the world to the path of liberation, established as he is upon the path of such virtues.
He is the liberator from all that suffering;
he is the bestower of happiness in all realms of existence;
he is the cutter of the snares of all fears.
"You shall become the destroyer of the Blessed One," [he said].
Thus, by means of this cultivation, the avoidance of what is disadvantageous becomes easy to accomplish.
Likewise, the avoidance of what is disadvantageous is also taught in the *Adhyāśayasañcodana-sūtra*:

"Maitreya, a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who is endowed with four qualities will, when the final five-hundred-year period of the disappearance of the True Dharma is occurring, remain unhurt, unassailed, and in safety."
He will be completely liberated.
By which four? By examining one's own transgressions;
and by not accusing other persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle of their offenses.
By not looking toward families that are not those of one's friends when seeking alms; and by abstaining from speech that is not well-considered— by these four, Maitreya, it is as before.
By another four: by which ones?
By avoiding sentient beings who have heard little of the Dharma.
By not clinging to the assembly, by resorting to remote lodgings and seats,
and by being devoted to the practice of self-taming and tranquility.
"By these four," and so forth in detail.
Furthermore, it says in this very same place:
"Maitreya, a beginner bodhisattva who has attained the empowerment of the power of wisdom should be one who avoids gain and honor, and perceives the faults of gain and honor. [etc.]
One should avoid delighting in social company and instead perceive the faults in delighting in social company;
one should avoid delighting in talk and instead perceive the faults in delighting in talk;
one should avoid delighting in sleep and instead perceive the faults in delighting in sleep.
One should be free from delighting in action and should see the fault in delighting in action;
one should be free from delighting in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and should see the fault in delighting in conceptual proliferation... [and so forth]...
In this regard, Maitreya, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should reflect that gain and honor give rise to passion;
he should reflect that gain and honor cause the destruction of mindfulness;
he should reflect that gain and honor cause one to fluctuate between elation and dejection depending on whether gain is obtained or not.
One should reflect that gain and honor give rise to delusion;
one should reflect that gain and honor involve attachment born of envy for [other] families;
one should reflect that gain and honor give rise to deceit through the pursuit of accomplishing one's own interests.
One should reflect upon gain and honor as producing a lack of shame and a lack of dread of blame by way of abandoning the four noble lineages;
one should reflect upon gain and honor as being disapproved of by all the Buddhas;
one should reflect upon gain and honor as giving rise to pride and intoxication.
The disparagement of gurus is gain and honor;
gain and honor belong to the side of Māra;
gain and honor are the sole root of negligence and the plunderer of the roots of virtue.

Gain and honor are like a wheel of lightning or a thunderbolt; they are heavily entangled with and defiled by worldly attachments. They involve looking toward the families of friends and those who provide alms, which gives rise to mental distress.
Gain and honor cause the delusion of the intellect; because they lead to the transformation of beloved things, gain and honor are vessels of sorrow.
Gain and honor cause the loss of the four foundations of mindfulness, weaken wholesome qualities, bring about the decline of the four right efforts,
cause the loss of supernormal powers and higher knowledges,
and result in being honored at first and then being dishonored later.
Gain and honor consist of honoring enemies and abandoning friends;
because they involve deceiving others, they are like a courtesan;
and they result in the abandonment of meditative concentration and the immeasurables.
Gain and honor cause one to fall into the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama;
gain and honor should be scrutinized as being the same conduct as that of Devadatta and Udaka.
Maitreya, these are the kinds of disadvantages in gain and honor that a bodhisattva should reflect upon;
having reflected upon them, he should delight in having few desires and not be distressed.
Why is that?
For one who has few desires, Maitreya, such faults as these do not exist, nor do obstacles arise to the qualities of a Buddha.
He does not become despondent toward householders or those who have gone forth into homelessness. And, abiding in a state of pure intention, he becomes worthy of being protected by gods and humans.
He becomes fearless regarding all falls into miserable destinies; he becomes unconquerable, being free from intimidation;
and he becomes unassailable, being liberated from the realm of Māra.
He becomes invincible against all calamities;
he becomes desirable to gods and humans, established in the practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);

he becomes transparent, having abandoned deceit and guile; he becomes vigilant, seeing the faults of the five strands of sensual pleasure; and, established in the lineage of the noble ones (*āryavaṃśa*), he acts exactly as he speaks.
And one becomes desired by wise fellow-practitioners.

Having understood these benefits of such a kind, Maitreya, a wise bodhisattva should, with resolute intention, delight in having few desires and cultivate fewness of desires for the sake of abandoning all gain and honor.
Concerning socializing, it is said:
Having abandoned passion and having abandoned hatred, the yogi does not remain amidst social gatherings;
he becomes inclined toward them and flows toward them.
One should not take delight in this fault;
for in social gatherings, all these things— restlessness, laughter, and discursive thoughts— arise.
For he who cultivates worthless social company acts in a confused manner and remains unrestrained.
Fools take delight in worldly mantras;
fools fall away from the foremost discourses here.
Their discursive thoughts being excessive, they increase their malice.
Because of this fault, it does not shine there.
A monk does not increase in learning by taking delight in improper incantations;
therefore, one should abandon such improper incantations.
Find delight in the Dharma at all times.
Thousands of times my own limbs have been sacrificed by me; therefore, aspire for enlightenment. And I am not yet satiated while hearing the Dharma.
They will fall into weariness while listening to the Dharma.
All improper mantras and unrefined mantras should be avoided in every way; instead,
you should generate delight in that supreme Dharma.
He who is difficult to encounter even in many hundreds of eons.
By one dwelling in the forest who seeks virtue,
