the faults of others must certainly not be observed; [one should not think],
"I am distinguished," or "I alone am the best."
The mind itself should not be grasped.
This intoxication is the root of all negligence;
one must not despise monks who are inferior,
for this is the gradual path here in the teaching.
One does not attain awakening in a single lifetime.
Regarding this very point, concerning one who delights in the commentary (bhāṣya), it is said:
"He becomes disrespectful, intoxicated by his learning,
and becomes intent upon the spells of dispute."
Furthermore, one whose learning has been stolen away and who lacks clear comprehension— these indeed are the faults of one who delights in mere talk.
One becomes very far removed from internal reflection;
neither the mind nor the body becomes serene,
and one undergoes many fluctuations of pride and dejection.
For these are the faults of one who delights in talk.
But fools, having fallen away from the mind of the true Dharma, become extremely harsh and unaffectionate in heart;
they remain far removed from both insight and tranquility.
For these are indeed the faults of one who delights in talk.
He is always disrespectful toward his teachers; having conceived a delight in worldly entanglements, he dwells in what is essence-less and is deprived of wisdom.
For these are the faults of one who delights in talk.
He is not honored by the qualities of the gods,
nor do they conceive any longing for him;
he becomes one who is bereft of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
For these are the faults of one who delights in talk.
And he is also censured by the wise:
"For whoever exists as a mere witness to a separate body,
his life is meaningless."
For these are indeed the faults of one who delights in talk.
That fool grieves as he passes away, thinking, "I am deficient in practice; what shall I do now?
He becomes deeply distressed, having failed to find a firm footing.
For these are the faults of one who delights in speech.
He becomes as unsteady as a blade of grass shaken by the wind;
he wavers in this way, of this there is no doubt.
His intellect never becomes firm.
For these are indeed the faults of one who delights in talk.
Just as an actor standing in the midst of the theater proclaims the virtues of other heroes,
yet he himself remains devoid of any actual practice.
For these are indeed the faults of one who delights in talk.
He becomes deceitful and quickly loses hope; again and again he initiates disputes. He remains far from the noble Dharma.
For these are indeed the faults of one who delights in talk.
When honored, one of little strength becomes overjoyed; when treated with hostility, the ignorant person trembles. Like a monkey, his mind becomes restless.
For these are the faults of one who delights in talk. ... [pe] ...
Even after delighting in and discoursing upon it for a long time,
one finds neither joy nor personal happiness here; indeed,
the contemplation of even a single verse is better.
Wherein one may obtain endless joy in every step.
There is no pith at all here in the skin of the sugarcane;
its pith is found within, which is most delightful.
Having consumed the skin, it is not possible here to obtain it again.
To obtain the excellent sugarcane juice by a man.
Know that the commentary is like the bark,
and the investigation of the meaning here is like the sap;
therefore, abandon attachment to the commentary.
Always reflect upon the goal with constant heedfulness.
Regarding one who delights in sleep, it is said: "He increases the great net of delusion;
he becomes a skeptic, though having attained [a certain] view."
Many views arise for him because he finds delight in sloth.
Their wisdom becomes exceedingly weak;
their intelligence declines and does not flourish,
and they are constantly deprived of knowledge.
Because one finds delight in drowsiness.
The indolent, the ignorant, the lazy, and the unwise—non-human beings find an opportunity to enter him; they harass him as he dwells in the forest, because he finds delight in sloth.
One who always lacks interest in wholesome states of mind has no desire for the Dharma; moreover,
such a person comes to possess a body of unrighteousness because they take pleasure in sloth.
The fool who is devoid of desire for the true Dharma and is deluded is deprived of all virtues;
he destroys his own purity and falls into darkness,
because he takes delight in sloth.
He becomes unconfident and his mind is dejected;
joy does not abide in him constantly;
seized by sleep, he becomes slack-limbed.
Because one finds delight in drowsiness.
But the self, having become aware [of this] and fallen into indolence, envies those endowed with the power of vigor;
it speaks dispraise of those possessed of vigor, because it takes delight in torpor... [etc.]...
That which destroys all suffering and darkness,
which is the root by virtue of avoiding the lower realms,
and which is always praised by all the Buddhas.
Constantly cultivate that noble vigor.
With reference to one who delights in karma, it is said:
When exhorted by his teachers, he becomes difficult to speak to; he does not accept their instruction with respect,
and his moral conduct quickly falls into ruin.
These faults arise in one who delights in action.
He is constantly filled with longing, always brooding over the affairs of a householder; for him,
there is no need for meditation or spiritual exertion.
These faults arise for one who delights in karma.
Intense passion arises within him;
seized by the flavors of flavors, he becomes infatuated.
He finds no satisfaction in one thing after another.
These faults arise in one who delights in action.
He is delighted by a large assembly,
but he becomes distressed when deprived of it;
he becomes confused, just like a donkey here in this world.
Day and night, with no other thought,
he is constantly intent on food and clothing;
yet, he is always seeking after virtuous qualities.
These faults arise in one who delights in karma.
He asks about worldly affairs and finds pleasure in improper counsel;
yet he finds no pleasure in proper counsel.
These faults arise for one who delights in action... [etc. ...pe... [as before] ...pe... [end].
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, those bodhisattvas will be of very limited wisdom and deficient in wisdom who, having abandoned the supreme dharmas, will undertake inferior activities."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:
"It is so, Maitreya;
it is just as you say. Those bodhisattvas will be of very limited wisdom who, having abandoned the supreme dharmas, will undertake inferior actions."
Moreover, Maitreya, I announce to you, I declare to you:
those are not bodhisattvas who have gone forth in the teaching of the Tathāgata for whom there is no application, no meditation, no abandonment, no study, and no pursuit of great learning.
Rather, Maitreya, the teaching of the Tathāgata is characterized by meditation and abandonment; it is fashioned by knowledge, concentrated in knowledge, and characterized by diligent application.
It is not characterized by the busyness of household affairs;
for those who are improperly engaged and delight in cyclic existence, this activity— namely, busywork and entanglement in worldly tasks—
is not something in which a bodhisattva should conceive a desire.
If, Maitreya, a bodhisattva devoted to service were to fill this trichiliocosm with stupas made of the seven precious gems,
I would not be pleased by that, nor honored, nor even venerated.
...pe... In that regard, suppose Jambudvīpa were filled with Bodhisattvas acting as attendants;
all of them together should perform service and attendance for a single Bodhisattva who is devoted to teaching and recitation.

Furthermore, Bodhisattvas equal in number to those filling Jambudvīpa and devoted to teaching and recitation should perform service and attendance for a single Bodhisattva who is devoted to solitary meditation. ...pe...
For what reason?

Because this task is difficult—namely, the task of wisdom—which is supreme, unsurpassed, distinguished above all the three worlds, and exalted. Therefore, Maitreya, a bodhisattva who seeks yoga and desires to exert vigor should apply himself to wisdom.
Thus it is said.
With reference to one who delights in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is said:
"The eight inopportune states (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*) are not far from him;
for him, the excellence of the opportune moment (*kṣaṇasaṃpad*) does not exist."
These misfortunes constantly befall him; these are the faults of one who wanders in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). ... [etc. ...

Having correctly understood these faults, the wise person should completely abandon all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*). For those who move within conceptual proliferation find misfortunes easily;
therefore, one should not dwell with conceptual proliferation.

One should travel even a hundred yojanas to reach a superior place where there is neither conceptual proliferation nor dispute; one should not make a dwelling or a home there, nor stay for even a moment where affliction exists.
Those who have gone forth do not seek wealth, but seek virtue; do not engage in dispute with evil minds. For you there is no field, nor agriculture, nor trade.
For whose sake these conceptual proliferations exist.
You have no son, no daughter, nor do you have a wife; you have no friend, nor any circle of kinsmen;
you have no female slaves, no male slaves, and no lordship.
Do not engage in dispute after having gone forth into homelessness.
Having taken up the saffron robes with faith— garments indeed frequented by those who are peaceful and thoroughly calmed—
be you peaceful, thoroughly calmed, and serene.
Having abandoned conceptual proliferation, you should generate patience.
Guard against venomous snakes of fierce mind;
for hell, the animal realm,
and the domain of Yama are not far from one who dwells in conceptual proliferation.
Therefore, one should indeed generate vigor regarding patience... [and so forth] ... // pe //
By this yoga one may obtain purity, having exhausted the obstructions of karma without remainder;
that wise person who subdues Māra along with his army and his mounts generates patience for that very [teaching]. Thus it is said.
In brief, the avoidance of what is harmful has been explained therein.

Therefore, Maitreya, a son of good family or a daughter of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, who wishes to be liberated safely, unhurt, and unharmed during the final five hundred years when the true Dharma is in the process of perishing—

One who wishes to exhaust all karmic obstructions should delight in non-association; one should dwell in forest retreats and remote wildernesses, avoid those beings who are not diligent, seek out one’s own faults rather than seeking out the faults of others, delight in silence, and delight in dwelling in the perfection of wisdom.
In the *Āryaratnamegha* as well, the avoidance of what is disadvantageous is stated:
"He wanders for alms only so long as his purpose is accomplished,
except in those places where there are fierce dogs, cows with young calves, or animals of the animal realm who are by nature ill-behaved."
Or, with the intention of causing harm, [one avoids] women, men, boys, and girls, or loathsome places;
one avoids all of these in every respect.
By this it is shown that even when such a subverting factor is perceived,
an offense occurs for one who does not avoid it.

Now, as for this avoidance of what is useless that has been described above, by what means is it attained? It is attained by avoiding all flow that is fruitless; for "fruit" here refers to the welfare of others, and one avoids any flow that does not conduce to that end.
Because it is fruitless, it should be avoided.
As it is recited in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra* within the section on bodily restraint:
"One does not fidget with the hands, nor does one fidget with the feet; one is restrained in hand and foot."

Likewise, it is also taught in the *Daśadharmaka-sūtra*: "The flinging of the hands, the flinging of the feet, running, running about, leaping, and jumping—this is called bodily corruption (*kāyadauṣṭhulya*)."

In the *Āryadharmasaṃgītisūtra*, however, it is clearly elucidated that no activity whatsoever is appropriate for bodhisattvas other than the welfare of others: "O Blessed One, whatever bodily action, whatever vocal action, and whatever mental action of bodhisattvas there may be, all of them proceed with regard for sentient beings and are governed by great compassion."
It has as its cause the empowerment for the welfare of beings, and it proceeds from the resolute intention for the welfare and happiness of all beings.
With such an intention for their welfare and with such a perception, he thinks:
"I must practice a conduct that brings about the welfare and happiness of all beings. ... [pe] ...
Practice consists in contemplating the sense-bases as being like an empty village,
yet one does not long for the abandonment of those sense-bases.
It is also said in the *Āryagaganagañjasūtra*: "Just as wind enters through a hole,
even so, from whatever opening there is in the mind, from that very place Māra gains an entrance."
Therefore, a bodhisattva should always possess an unbroken mind;
therein, this "unbroken-mindedness" consists in the complete fulfillment of emptiness and the knowledge of all aspects.
What, then, is this emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects?
It is that which is being practiced, or has been practiced, without abandoning the conduct of a bodhisattva.
The emptiness of all phenomena;
this has been explained in detail in the *Ratnacūḍa-sūtra*.
Likewise, it is shown in the *Akṣayamati-sūtra*:

"In this context of generating the desire for the abandonment of evil, unwholesome dharmas, whatever other things there may be that cause distraction of the mind and which act as adversaries to the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*)," [so it is said].
This is called the adversary of concentration;
these are what are called evil, unwholesome states.
In the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, within the chapter on the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), this is the fifth chapter: "The Avoidance of What is Harmful."
[VI. Protection of the Person] The sixth chapter: Protection of the Person.
The avoidance of fruitless outflows has been explained.
How is this established? He says:
"This would be established by constant mindfulness."
These twelve kinds of mindfulness lead to the avoidance of fruitless outflows;
namely:
mindfulness that honors the maturation of not transgressing the commands of the Tathāgata.
It is the recollection of the entire body’s state of being established in an immovable nature.

When there is a purpose for sentient beings, whatever limb is not required [for that task] is rendered motionless through a superior resolve based on a very firm mindfulness; this is the mindfulness of all steadfast movements.
Furthermore, even in the confusion of circumstances involving fear, festivals, and the like, he does not lose mindfulness of his limbs.

There is mindfulness that projects and examines the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*). From time to time, there is mindfulness that observes the perfection of conduct for the sake of guarding against its disturbance. And at the time of speaking, there is mindfulness that restrains excessive and unseemly distortions of the hands, feet, head, and face resulting from the influence of extreme serenity, agitation, impetuosity, partiality, and so forth.
The listener should speak with only as much sound as is necessary for the hearer to understand the meaning;
beyond that, one should not speak with excessive intonation, lest there arise the fault of others suspecting one's motives.
In the difficulty of encountering untrained people, one should maintain mindfulness focused on clarifying one’s own mind and the minds of those others.
One whose mindfulness is constantly bound to the pillar of *śamatha*— the elephant of the mind alone—
and who possesses the mindfulness that repeatedly examines the state of the mind;
who, even by abandoning most other activities in the midst of a great crowd, maintains a commitment to guarding the aforementioned mindfulness.
In this way, by means of these forms of mindfulness, the avoidance of fruitless wandering is accomplished.
And that mindfulness should arise from intense respect (*ādara*). In this context, respect is the orientation toward the tasks with one's whole being.
It is the antidote to contempt.
Furthermore, this respect arises through application once one has understood the greatness of *śamatha*.
What, then, is this so-called "calm" (*śama*)?
That which is called "calm abiding" (śamatha) in the Noble Akṣayamati Sūtra.
In this regard, what is the inexhaustibility of calm abiding?
It is the tranquility and complete pacification of the mind, the absence of distraction, the restraint of the sense faculties, and the state of being free from agitation.

Absence of arrogance, lack of fickleness, lack of instability, gentleness, guardedness, adaptability, thoroughbred-like nature, one-pointedness, delighting in solitude, avoidance of socializing, delight in seclusion, physical seclusion, non-confusion of mind, mental attention directed toward the forest, fewness of desires, and so forth, up to the guarding of deportment,
knowledge of the proper time, knowledge of the right occasion, knowledge of moderation, and knowledge of liberation.
"Ease of maintenance," "ease of nourishment," and so forth.

What, then, is the greatness of this tranquility? It is the power to generate knowledge of things as they truly are; for the Sage has said that one who is concentrated understands things as they truly are.
As it is said in the *Dharmasaṃgīti*:
"For one whose mind is concentrated, there is vision of things as they truly are;
for the bodhisattva who sees things as they truly are, great compassion toward sentient beings arises."
And he thinks thus:
"I must bring about for all sentient beings this entrance into meditative concentration and the vision of all phenomena as they truly are.
Urged on by that great compassion, he fulfills the trainings in higher ethics, higher mind, and higher wisdom, and awakens to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, one should think: "I must be well-established in ethical discipline, unshakable and not lax.

Having understood this greatness of tranquility—which consists in the transcendence of the infinite sufferings of the miserable realms for oneself and others, and the attainment of the ultimate excellence of infinite mundane and supramundane happiness—one should cultivate it with ardor through a longing for that [attainment].
Just like one who has entered the midst of a burning house and longs for cool water,
he develops intense reverence for the trainings;
through that, mindfulness becomes established.
One whose mindfulness is established avoids what is fruitless;
and for one who avoids what is fruitless, misfortunes do not arise.
Therefore, by one who desires to protect their own person, having sought the root of mindfulness, one must always possess established mindfulness.
Therefore, in the *Ugraparipṛcchā*, with reference to a householder bodhisattva, it is said:

"One should abstain from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence; one should be sober, not intoxicated, not fickle, not wavering, not confused, not talkative, not arrogant, not haughty, and possessed of established mindfulness and clear comprehension.
And in that very same text, with reference to a renunciant bodhisattva, it is said: "The non-distraction of mindfulness and clear comprehension."
In this regard, mindfulness is taught in the *Āryaratnacūḍasūtra*:
it is that mindfulness by which the manifestation of all afflictions does not occur,
and that mindfulness by which one does not allow any entry for the activities of Māra.
That mindfulness by which one does not fall onto a wrong path or a bad road,
and that mindfulness acting as a gatekeeper which allows no opportunity for any unwholesome mental states or mental factors— this is called right mindfulness.
Clear comprehension, however, is explained in the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
"When walking, one clearly knows, 'I am walking';
when standing, one clearly knows, 'I am standing.'"
He discerns, "I am lying down when lying down.
He discerns, "I am sitting when sitting. And in whatever way his body is positioned, he discerns it exactly as it is. ... [as before] ...
Whether going forward or returning, he acts with clear comprehension; in looking ahead or looking aside, in bending or stretching, in carrying his outer robe,

inner robe, and bowl, in eating, drinking, chewing, and dispelling drowsiness and fatigue, in coming and going, in standing and sitting, in sleeping and waking, in speaking and remaining silent, and in seclusion, he acts with clear comprehension.
For ethical discipline leads to concentration.
As it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
"One quickly attains the stainless samādhi;
such is the benefit in this pure ethical discipline."
From this it is understood that whatever applications are causes for meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are included within ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Therefore, one who seeks concentration must possess the ethical discipline of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*);
likewise, even one who seeks ethical discipline must exert effort toward concentration, because of the statement in that very same sutra.
For it is recited among the benefits of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*):
"He does not become one of improper conduct; his conduct is well-established.
The practitioner moves within his proper range and avoids what is not his range."
Dwelling free from feverish distress, guarded and with sense-faculties restrained. Thus it is said.

And through these two—ethical discipline and meditative concentration—which mutually foster one another, there is the perfection of mental action. This training of a bodhisattva consists precisely of this: the cultivation of the mind, because it is the root of all benefits for sentient beings.
For it is said in the *Āryaratnamegha*:
"All phenomena are preceded by the mind;
when the mind is thoroughly understood, all phenomena become thoroughly understood."
Moreover, the world is led by the mind; the mind does not see the mind.
By the mind is karma accumulated, whether it be wholesome or unwholesome.
The mind wanders like a whirling firebrand;
the mind wanders like a horse;
the mind burns like a divine conflagration.
It carries away the mind like a great flood.
Examining in this way, he dwells with mindfulness well-established in the mind; he does not fall under the power of the mind, but rather the mind itself comes under his power.
When the mind has been brought under his control, all phenomena come under his control.

Likewise, it is also said in the *Āryadharmasaṅgītisūtra*: the Bodhisattva Mativikrama said, "This phenomenon which is called 'phenomenon' does not abide in a location, nor does it abide in a specific place; rather, it is dependent solely upon one's own mind."
Therefore, by me, the Dharma must be practiced such that my own mind is well-pleased, well-sustained, well-initiated, and well-restrained.
Why is that? Because wherever there is mind, there are virtues and faults.
In the state of mindlessness, there is neither virtue nor fault;
therein, the bodhisattva restrains the mind from faults and directs it toward virtues.
Thus it is said: "Dharma is dependent on the mind; awakening is dependent on Dharma."
"O Blessed One, this undertaking of the Dharma leads to the easy realization of perfect enlightenment."
It is also described in the Noble Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra:
"The basis of one's own mind is the entire conduct of all bodhisattvas; the basis of one's own mind is the ripening and disciplining of all sentient beings. ... [as above] ...
Regarding this, noble son, it occurred to me:
"One's own mind alone must be supported by all roots of virtue;
one's own mind alone must be moistened by the clouds of Dharma."
"One's own mind alone must be purified of obstructive phenomena;
one's own mind alone must be made firm through vigor," and so forth.
Likewise, in this very context, when the noble Sudhana became distressed by not seeing Queen Māyā, the city goddess Ratnanetrā gave him this instruction for the sake of seeing her:
"Noble son, you must become skilled in protecting the city of the mind by not dwelling in delight with any of the objects of saṃsāra.
Noble son, you must apply yourself to adorning the city of the mind by taking as your objective support the ten powers of the Tathāgatas."
Noble son, you must be devoted to purifying the city of the mind by removing envy, stinginess, and deceit.
Noble son, you must be intent on expanding the city of the mind by increasing the great force of vigor that constitutes the equipment for omniscience.

Noble son, you must be devoted to accomplishing the invincibility and impenetrability of the city of the mind by not being crushed by any afflictions, the hosts of Māra, evil friends, or the wheel of Māra.
Noble son, you should be intent upon expanding the city of the mind by pervading the entire world with great loving-kindness;
noble son, you should be intent upon covering the city of the mind by bringing forth the vast parasol of the Dharma as an antidote to all unwholesome phenomena;
noble son, you should be intent upon opening the city of the mind by bestowing all internal and external things upon the entire world.
Noble son, you must apply yourself to establishing firm stability within the city of the mind by means of the complete disappearance of the continuity of all unwholesome dharmas.
To this extent, noble son, a bodhisattva who is devoted to the purification of the city of the mind is able to attain the gathering of all roots of virtue.
Why is that?
For indeed, when that bodhisattva’s city of the mind is thus purified, no obscurations whatsoever stand before him—
neither the obscuration to seeing the Buddha nor the obscuration to hearing the Dharma, and so forth. Therefore, it is established as follows.
The training of a bodhisattva is precisely the cultivation of the mind,
and that belongs to one whose mind is not fickle.
And the mind should not waver from tranquility due to the cessation of external activity.
The mind of one who is dependent on a lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) and whose mindfulness is lost wavers, because it is led away from the intended object to another.
However, when external activities have been turned back by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension, then, being under their control, it remains bound to a single object for as long as desired.
And from that, there follows the detailed expansion of benefits as previously described.
And even in the present day, he remains indeed capable of benefiting sentient beings because he inspires faith; how so?
By speaking everywhere with speech that is steady, gentle, measured, and affectionate,
one wins over worthy people and becomes someone whose words are accepted.
And this indeed is the duty of a bodhisattva, namely, the winning over of sentient beings,
as elucidated by the noble Bodhisattva Priyadarśana in the *Āryadharmasaṃgītisūtra*.
In such and such a way, Blessed One, should a bodhisattva practice so that sentient beings may become inspired with faith at the very first sight of him.
For what reason?
Blessed One, there is no other duty for a bodhisattva than the winning over of sentient beings.
"O Blessed One, this very maturation of sentient beings is the Bodhisattva’s communal recitation of the Dharma."
Furthermore, he states what the fault would be if this were not done:
"But the world, having despised that sprout of the Conqueror as unworthy of offerings,
shall be cooked in the hells and other realms, like fire covered by ashes."
Just as was previously demonstrated.
And because such contempt causes him harm, as stated by the Victor in the *Ratnamegha*, he should therefore maintain the vow in brief:
"One should diligently avoid that which causes the loss of faith among sentient beings."
As it is said: "And what are those practices of a bodhisattva? In this regard, a bodhisattva does not dwell in an improper place, nor at an improper time;
he does not speak at an improper time, he does not know the improper [occasion], and he does not know the improper location."
For the reason that sentient beings might experience a lack of faith toward him, he—
out of a desire to protect all sentient beings and for the sake of fulfilling his own equipment for enlightenment— possesses perfected deportment, speaking softly and speaking sparingly.
He is one who abounds in non-association,
is intent upon seclusion,
and has a very serene countenance.
For this very reason, it is taught in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:
"He who protects sentient beings protects his ethical discipline (*śīla*).
By [acting thus] with this young woman, protection of the world would also have been accomplished through staying in private and so forth.
Likewise, one should not discharge urine, feces, phlegm, pus, or other loathsome things in water or on land, whether in secret or in public, for the sake of protecting the minds of gods and humans.

Furthermore, in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna*, it is taught that one who, having set aside leftovers in a secluded place, does not give those leftover foods [to others], will go to the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Likewise, in the *Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa*, the avoidance of lack of faith is also stated:
"One should not chew a tooth-stick in front [of others], nor should one spit in front.
And this rule of respect and modesty is to be observed toward all, not only toward those living the holy life (*brahmacārin*).
In this sutra, however, the section concerning the celibate student (brahmacārin) is intended to demonstrate the fear of the most grave transgressions among them.
As it says in this very same [text]: "One should not be a loud speaker."
Furthermore, this injunction is not limited in scope;
likewise, it is stated in the *Brahmaparipṛcchā*: "A bodhisattva must not be one who resembles a killer.
Similarly, even from the *Prātimokṣa*, whatever is found to cause lack of faith among the world should be avoided.
That is not so, at least for now.
One should not eat with the mouth full, nor with noise, nor with the face stretched out; one should not sit with legs dangling, nor rub the arms together.
Thus, having reflected for oneself and having seen or heard [of such things], one should protect against the loss of public confidence.
Since it is not easy to avoid speech that causes a lack of confidence, this is demonstrated for the purpose of awakening mindfulness.
It is taught in the *Āryasāgaramati-sūtra*:
He does not speak with hesitation; he does not speak in a confused manner; he does not speak with a faltering voice.
He does not speak with inflammatory words; he does not speak with words led by passion;
he does not speak vulgar words.
He does not speak words that are unprotected; he does not speak words that incite malice;
he does not speak fickle words.
He does not speak with frivolity; he does not speak like a performer on a stage; he does not speak words that cast false blame based on mere hearsay.
It is also said in the *Āryatathāgataguhya-sūtra*:

"Furthermore, noble son, the speech of a bodhisattva is not passionate, nor hateful, nor deluded, nor afflicted; it is not a confused exposition, nor does it consist of words that exalt one's own side."
Either speech that refutes the positions of others,
or speech that is attached to praising oneself, or speech that is resentful toward the praise of others.
Or it is a statement for fulfilling a vow;
or it is a statement of prophecy for those possessed of overweening pride.
It is also said in the *Āryadaśabhūmikasūtra*:
"Having abandoned that speech which is unpleasant and destructive to one's own continuum and the continua of others,
one should employ that speech which is smooth, soft, pleasant, sweet, endearing, agreeable, and beneficial."

Pleasant to the ear, heart-pleasing, affectionate, clear in its syllables, intelligible, worthy of being heard, independent, beloved by many people, dear to many people, agreeable to many people, praised by the wise, bringing welfare and happiness to all sentient beings, uplifting the mind, gladdening the mind,
causing joy to one’s own and others’ mental continuums, and pacifying all afflictions such as passion, hatred, and delusion.
He utters such speech that he avoids even those words preceded by traditional history (itihāsa) that ought to be avoided.
In the *Āryagaganagañjasūtra*, it is said:
"By not disregarding the words of one's guru and by not cutting off the speech of others, one becomes a person whose words are worthy of being accepted and taken to heart."
It is also said in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:
the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja said,
"A bodhisattva should not utter such speech by which another might be provoked to malice."
One should not speak that speech by which another is tormented;
a bodhisattva should not speak that speech which another might understand;
one should not speak that speech which is meaningless or devoid of purpose.
A bodhisattva should not utter that speech by which one does not produce knowledge;
he should not utter that speech which does not reach the hearts of sentient beings, which is not refined, or which is not pleasant to the ear. Such speech should not be uttered.
In brief, however, the protection of others' faith is taught in the *Āryasāgaramati-sūtra*:
"There is one further quality that leads to the integration of the Mahāyāna: by means of reflecting upon one's own transgressions, one protects all sentient beings."
This is the protection of one's own person,
so that it may not be destroyed by others,
and so that one does not destroy others.
However, this summary of the extensive treatise must be constantly held in mind by the bodhisattva.
It is perfectly steady, very serene, firm, respectful and reverent, modest, fearful [of wrongdoing], peaceful, and intent upon pleasing others.
"Always under my own control regarding blameless things, I maintain this mind like a magical creation, free from pride. Thus.
Is the protection of the person (ātmabhāva) merely this much?
No, indeed not; rather, it is together with medicine, clothing, and so forth.
In that regard, medicine is of two kinds:
constant medicine and medicine for the occasion of illness.
Concerning constant medicine, it is stated in the *Āryaratnamegha*:
From that alms-bowl, he sets aside one portion for his fellow practitioners of the holy life;
a second for those who are suffering; a third for those who have fallen into misfortune; and the fourth he consumes himself.
Consuming it, he does so without attachment, unclinging, free from greed, and without being obsessed by it.
Except for as much as is necessary for the maintenance and preservation of the body,
he consumes food in such a way that he does not become overly emaciated.
Nor should the body be excessively emaciated.
For what reason?
Because one who is too emaciated becomes averse to the side of wholesome qualities.
One whose body is excessively heavy becomes overcome by drowsiness;
therefore, having consumed that alms-food, one should remain intent upon the side of wholesome qualities, and so forth.
It is also said in the *Āryaratnarāśi*:
"When he wanders for alms in a village, city, or town, he should wander for alms having donned the armor of the Dharma.
In that regard, what is the armor of the Dharma?"
Having seen unpleasant forms, one should not react with aversion;
having seen pleasant ones, one should not react with attraction.
Likewise, when pleasant or unpleasant sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles are perceived, one should neither be attracted nor repelled.

With the sense faculties well-restrained, with eyes not cast about but looking only a yoke’s length ahead, with a mind like that of a well-trained noble steed, and without abandoning the prior mental attention to the Dharma, one should wander for alms with a mental continuum not distracted by worldly things; one should also proceed in a continuous sequence. Wherever alms-food is obtained, one should not feel attachment; wherever it is not obtained, one should not give rise to resentment.
If, upon entering ten households, alms are not obtained even from the eleventh household, one should nevertheless not be distressed; rather, one should generate this thought:
"These ascetics, brahmins, and householders have many duties; it is not necessary that they must give to me."
"This is already a marvel that they even take notice of me;
how much more so that they will give alms!
Therefore, one should wander for alms without being distressed in this way."

And whatever beings come into the range of his vision—whether men, women, boys, or girls, or even those belonging to the animal realm—he should generate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward them.
He should resolve: "I shall act in such a way that those beings who come into my sight, or who give me alms-food, I shall establish in a happy rebirth."
I shall attain such a yoga;
by means of it, having gathered alms-food, whether coarse or refined, he should look all around in the four directions:
"Who here in this village, town, or market-town is a poor being?"
From whichever alms-food I shall make a distribution,
if he sees a poor being, he must make a distribution from that alms-food;
however, if he does not see any poor being at all, [he should give it away].
Therefore, he should generate this thought:
"There are sentient beings who have not come into the range of my vision and do not appear before my eyes;
for them, I set aside the foremost portion from this alms-food."
Let them enjoy what has been given as alms.

Having taken that alms-food, he ascended to that forest retreat; with washed hands, possessing excellent conduct, having attained the state of the ritual rules for the life of a śramaṇa, and being sustained by his spiritual resolve, he sat cross-legged and partook of that alms-food.
It should be used. ... [as before] ...
And while consuming it, one should generate this mental attention:
"In this body there are eighty thousand families of worms;
may they dwell in happiness and comfort through this very nourishment."
"Now I shall gather them together with material gifts;
and once I have attained awakening, I shall gather them together with the Dharma.
Furthermore, if his alms-food is coarse, he should generate this thought:
"By means of coarse food, my body will become light, capable of exertion, and my discharge of excrement and urine will be minimal;
my consumption of what is given in faith will be minimal,
and I shall possess lightness of body and lightness of mind."
I shall have little weariness and drowsiness.
Furthermore, when he has received an abundant amount of alms-food, he must eat with moderation and practice the quality of relinquishment.
Then, having stepped down onto a certain stone slab after that alms-food, he should generate this thought:
"Whatever flocks of beasts and birds there are who desire food consisting of meat, let them enjoy it after having been given this gift."
It says further: "By all that, the perception of taste should not be produced... [etc. ...".
I must become like a candala youth;
pure in mind and body,
but not pure in food.
For what reason?
No matter how exquisite the food may be when eaten,
it all results ultimately in putrid secretions, results in foul odors, and results in that which is repulsive.
Therefore, I should not be one who longs for exquisite food;
he should not give rise to such a thought as:
"A man gives me alms-food, not a woman."
A woman gives me alms-food, not a man;
a boy gives me alms-food, not a girl;
a girl gives me alms-food, not a boy.
"I obtain what is excellent, not what is coarse; I obtain it with honor, not without honor;
I obtain it without difficulty, not with hardship; and as soon as I have entered, they pay me attention."
May I have no distraction whatsoever;
may I obtain well-prepared, exquisite foods of various flavors;
may I not receive inferior or poor food; and may men, women, boys, and girls come out to meet me.

For generally, beings who are greedy for flavors, having committed evil deeds for the sake of food, are reborn in the hells. However, those who are contented, free from greed, uncorrupted, who have stilled their craving for flavors, and who are satisfied with the faculty of the tongue— contenting themselves even with very coarse food—
when they pass away and die, their rebirth is in the heavenly realms.
There is a journey to a happy destination among gods and humans;
those born as gods enjoy ambrosia.

In the same way, Kāśyapa, a monk who goes for alms, having turned away from craving for flavors, should not feel distressed while eating even well-cooked boiled beans with a mind of resolute contentment.
For what reason?
"I should consume food for the sake of sustaining the body and for the sake of sustaining the path. ... [as before] ...
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, if a monk who wanders for alms should find himself unable to go out for food during a time of cloudy skies and heavy rain, he should—

equipped with the sustenance of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and established in mental attention to the contemplation of the Dharma— remain without food for two or three nights and generate this perception:
"There are hungry ghosts (*preta*) of the Yama realm who, having performed difficult deeds, do not obtain even a morsel of phlegm as food for a hundred years."
Therefore, established in this fundamental reflection on the Dharma, I must not give rise to physical weakness or mental weakness.
I shall endure hunger and thirst, and I shall not slacken my vigor in the cultivation of the Noble Path... [etc.]...

In whichever family one has a pure alms-offering prepared, one should sit upon a seat in that family and deliver a discourse on the Dharma. As long as that alms-offering has not been purified, the mendicant monk, Kāśyapa, having taken the alms-food, should rise from his seat and depart; he should not be a seeker of fame, nor should he engage in flattery or hypocrisy.
In that regard, what is "illumination"?
It is when one speaks these words to others:
"My alms-food was coarse, my alms-food was rough, and I did not eat as much as I required."
"My alms-food was made common to many people;
I have eaten little and am hungry"—
whatever sign of such an appearance as this there may be.
This is called mental hypocrisy;
all of this should not be done by a monk who goes for alms,
remaining in a state of equanimity.

Whatever has fallen into the alms-bowl—whether coarse or refined, auspicious or inauspicious—that should be consumed without regret, with a pure intention, and with frequent reflection upon the Dharma.
That alms-food should be consumed for the sake of maintaining the body and for the sake of supporting the Noble Path.
Likewise, it is also said in the *Āryograparipṛcchā*:
"If, having consumed alms-food from someone, one is unable to fulfill the welfare of oneself and others, I permit that bodhisattva who wanders for alms to accept an invitation."
In this way, one should first protect the physical body with constant medicine;
even in that regard, one must not use fish or meat, as they are prohibited in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
For it has been said:
"I declare that all meat is unfit to be eaten by a Bodhisattva whose nature is compassion. ... [etc. ...
Due to its kinship, due to its potential for transgression, and because it arises from semen and blood,
a yogi should avoid meat, which causes revulsion among living beings.
A yogi should always avoid meats, onions, various kinds of intoxicants, leeks, and garlic.

One should avoid applying oil as an ointment and should not sleep where one has been pierced by a thorn; nor should one stay in the dwellings of beings—whether they have faults or no faults—which are places of great danger. //pe//
A living being is killed for the sake of profit, and wealth is spent for the sake of meat;
both of those who perform such evil deeds are cooked in the Raurava and other hells.
...up to...
That evil-minded person who, though initiated into the teaching of the Śākyas, would transgress the word of the Sage and eat meat, acts for the sake of destroying both worlds.
Those evildoers go to the most terrible hell;
the eaters of flesh are cooked in the fierce hells, such as Raurava and others.
Meat that is pure according to the three criteria—unimagined, unasked for, and unsolicited—does not exist at all; therefore, one should not eat meat.
A yogi should not eat meat, for it is censured by me and by the Buddhas;
beings who devour one another are born into the families of carnivorous creatures.
...up to...
One is born foul-smelling, contemptible, and even insane,
again and again among the families of Caṇḍālas, Pukkasas, and Ḍombas.
That lowest of men is born into the womb of a *ḍākinī* and into a family of meat-eaters; he is also born into the wombs of bears and cats.
In the *Hastikakṣya*, the *Mahāmegha*, the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Aṅgulimālīka*,
and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, meat has been condemned by me.
If one who is shameless eats what is censured by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas, he will always become insane.
By abstaining from meat and other such things, one is born among brahmins or in the family of yogis, endowed with wisdom and wealth.
One should avoid all meat due to doubts regarding what has been seen or heard;
logicians, born into the lineage of carnivores, do not understand this.
Just as this passion becomes an obstacle to liberation,
so too do meat, alcohol, and the like become obstacles.
In a future time, meat-eaters who speak out of delusion will say:
"Meat that is permissible, blameless, and praised by the Buddhas [is allowed]."
A yogi should partake of alms-food with moderation, regarding it as medicine or even like the flesh of his own son, and perceiving it as something disagreeable.
For one who dwells constantly in loving-kindness, cohabiting in one place with lions, tigers, deer, and other such creatures is in every way censured by me.
Therefore, one should not eat meat, which causes agitation among men;
for it is the banner of the Noble Ones, being consistent with the dharma of liberation.
As for the fact that meat-eating is mentioned in the *Jñānavatī-parivarta*, it is faultless because it accomplishes a great purpose.
For it has been said thus:
"If this monk had passed away,
even the sound of 'samādhi' would have ceased in Jambudvīpa."
If it had always existed for sentient beings once it was ceased,
this samādhi would have been obtained by me through medical treatment.
And because he is devoted to great compassion, there is not even a suspicion of ill-will toward him; thus, there is no fault.
Even though it is stated in the *Āryaratnamegha* that "one who dwells in cemeteries (*śmāśānika*) must be free from worldly desire (*nirāmiṣa*)," [the following applies].
This is for the purpose of demonstrating that there are other beings of a similar kind;
furthermore, that which is permitted even in the Vinaya refers to eating that is pure in three respects, and it does not constitute an obstacle to abandonment.
This is intended to dispel the conceit of those who hold a view of purity by means of such renunciation.
And that was for the sake of ensuring that the teaching would not fail to enter among those capable of liberation due to their advanced age.
For it is said in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:
"In various places in the scriptural teachings, the sequence of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) is bound together by means of the arrangement of steps on a ladder;
having bound them according to the three limits (*trikoṭi*)."
In that regard, those things specifically prescribed were prohibited; consequently, even those that were naturally mortal were prohibited.
The constant medicine has been explained;
that medicine for the occasion of illness is indeed to be used.

Even in the *Śrāvaka-vinaya*, it is taught that for the sake of one's own welfare and for the sake of living the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one may even sell one’s bowl and robes to sustain the body; how much more so, then, for the sake of protecting immeasurable beings, regarding the body of a Bodhisattva— how rare is such a festival-perfection of obtaining this opportune moment!
And for the purpose of demonstrating this, the Blessed One himself exhibited the use of medicine there.

And it is said in the *Āryaratnameghasūtra*: "When they have set out [on their journey], whether at the proper time or not, they do not obtain such means for sustaining the body as food and drink— namely, ghee, oil, the juice of roots, the juice of stalks, or the juice of fruits— to consume."
Nor does he give rise to a mind of aversion upon seeing others consuming food. Furthermore, if a bodhisattva who observes the practice of eating after the meal becomes ill—

such that his illness would cause an obstacle to life or an obstacle to the side of wholesome qualities— he should, being free from remorse and free from doubt, cultivate the thought of medicine and partake [of it].
The purpose for wearing and using [robes] is stated in the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra*:

"Those who possess a sense of shame and dread of blame, for the sake of concealing the private parts and for the sake of manifesting the mark of a śramaṇa, should properly wear these saffron robes as a shrine (*caitya*) for the world of gods, humans, and asuras, and for the sake of the shrine itself."
These are colored by the passion for cessation and dispassion, not colored by sensual passion;
these are conducive to tranquility.
They are not conducive to inflaming the afflictions.
By means of these saffron robes, we shall have our evils laid bare;
we shall be performers of well-done deeds, not devoted to the practice of adorning our robes.

Considering that these saffron robes are conducive to the equipment for the Noble Path, we shall act in such a way that we do not wear the saffron robes upon our bodies while possessing defilements (kaṣāya), even for a single moment.

And the reason for this is stated in the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*: "Furthermore, Kāśyapa, those who are like vaidūrya stones— unrestrained, cast out from these qualities and dharmas of a śramaṇa, yet wearing saffron robes on their bodies,
and who do not give rise to reverence toward them."

In that regard, Kāśyapa, there is a particular hell called "Resembling the Appearance of a Śramaṇa. There, Kāśyapa, in that particular hell, those punishments are inflicted upon them in the form of figures resembling śramaṇas; their garments are ablaze, their heads are ablaze, their alms-bowls are ablaze, their seats are ablaze, and their beds are ablaze. Whatever objects of enjoyment or use they have there, all of them are ablaze, fiercely burning, and become a single mass of flame.
There, they experience painful sensations while appearing in the form and appearance of ascetics.
It is also said in the *Āryaratnamegha*:
"If a bodhisattva who dwells in the open air should become ill or physically weak, he must generate this thought while remaining in his monastery:
'The ascetic qualities were prescribed by the Tathāgata for the purpose of counteracting the afflictions.'"
"I shall act in such a way that I will strive for the abandonment of the afflictions within this very monastery;
and in that monastery, I shall produce neither attachment nor fixation.
And thus it occurs to him:
"We must show favor to the donors; we should not be merely those who look after themselves."
Furthermore, it says in this very same [text]:
"When they prepare their beds, they prepare the bed on their right side;
placing one foot upon the other, with their bodies covered by their robes, they remain mindful."
Being fully aware, they lie down with the perception of rising and the perception of light; they do not relish the pleasure of sleep nor the pleasure of reclining,
except for the sake of maintaining and nourishing these great elements.
In this manner, all enjoyments should be consecrated for the sake of sentient beings;
however, from enjoying them out of self-attachment, a defiled transgression arises.
As it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
"Having obtained food that is delicious, flavorful, and excellent, they eat it while lacking application in yoga."
For them, that food becomes a cause for bondage,
just as unwashed poison is for young elephant calves.
Thus.
In the *Āryaratnarāśisūtra* as well, when the Blessed One had proclaimed [the gravity of] consuming what has been given out of faith (*śraddhādeya*),
then in that very assembly, two hundred monks who were practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*) wept upon hearing this Dharma-discourse and spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, we shall pass away;
we will not consume even a single morsel of alms-food given out of faith until we have attained the fruit."
The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, sons of good family! It is through such forms of modesty, endowed with remorse, and by seeing the fear of blame in the world beyond, that this teaching is adorned."
But rather:
“Kāśyapa, I permit the gift of faith for two kinds of persons. Which two? For one who is disciplined and for one who is liberated.”
Monks, if a monk who is disciplined, a practitioner of yoga, established in my training, seeing impermanence in all conditioned phenomena,

understanding the suffering in all conditioned phenomena, resolved upon the selflessness of all dharmas, and longing for the peace of nirvāṇa, were to consume offerings given out of faith in morsels as large as Mount Sumeru,
that gift of his would be utterly purified.

And for those donors and masters of generosity from whom he has consumed what was given in faith, there arises for those donors and masters of generosity a very great ripening of merit and great splendor. Why is that?
This attainment of a mind of loving-kindness (*maitracitta-samāpatti*) is the foremost among the bases of meritorious action consisting of material things (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*).

In this regard, Kāśyapa, if a monk, having partaken of robes and alms-food from a donor or patron, enters the immeasurable concentration of the mind, then an immeasurable ripening of the merit of that donor or patron is to be expected.
Kāśyapa, it may be that the great oceans in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system could come to an end, but there would be no end whatsoever to the outflow of that merit.
Thus, at these three points— at the start of going for alms, or at the start of eating— one should establish mindfulness: toward the favor shown by the donors,
toward the nourishment of the worms within the body,
and toward the upholding of the True Dharma which accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings.
However, in order to fulfill the command of the Tathāgata, mindfulness must be maintained in all activities;
by the word "and so forth," it is implied that protection should also be performed with mantras.
Therein, first of all, one should recite this vidyā spoken in the *Trisamayarāja* for the purpose of the maṇḍala commitment:
*Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānām. Oṃ viraji mahācakraviraji. Sata sārata trapi vidhamani.*
Sabhajani / Saṃbhajani / Taramati /
O Siddha, you are foremost; svāhā!
By this, one becomes entered into all maṇḍalas.
Alternatively, one should recite the Tathāgata-hṛdaya eight thousand times; one then becomes one who has entered both mundane and supramundane maṇḍalas.
And what is that?

Homage to the Tathāgatas of the three times, who possess the power of the nature of phenomena through the attainment of unimpededness everywhere. Āṃ! O you whose teaching is the attainment of the infinite in every direction, peerless among the peerless!
Hara! Smara! O you whose mind is free from passion through mindfulness, the nature of the Buddhas! Sara! Samabalā! Hasa!
Traya / O protector of the great mountain of the sky / Blaze, blaze in the ocean, svāhā!
This is the very embodiment of all the Tathāgatas;
herein, one should cultivate unsurpassed reverence.
By means of this, even beginners perform infinite Buddha-activities for the sake of sentient beings.
This very [mantra] provides supreme protection against Māra and all malevolent beings;
by means of a hand-clap, ashes, mustard seeds, water, or even by sight or thought, one establishes a boundary.
In cases of diseases, one should employ medicine and water after consecrating them with mantras.
Or, with a concentrated mind, one should offer forest flowers at a shrine, before an image, or to a book of the True Dharma.
Through the application of these practices, one is liberated from great diseases.
It should be recited with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as one's object of focus, with a mind desiring the welfare of all sentient beings, and preceded by the ritual of the *Bhadracaryā*.
This procedure is to be observed at the conclusion of this ritual manual (*kalpa*).
For one who recites the mantra according to the three samayas, there is no fault according to the tradition.
Even for one who has consumed leftovers or is impure, there is no fault.
One should neither eat nor step over the forms of the mudrās.
One must not mount a bed,
nor drink intoxicants.
The practice of resolute conviction succeeds even for one who was previously immoral, provided they are unwavering and free from doubt regarding the precepts of training.
Whether for the wise or the unwise, it is certain to succeed.
And thus it is said in this very same place:
"For one whose bodhicitta is firm and whose mind is free from attachment, no doubt should ever be entertained; for such a person, this will certainly succeed."

And here, the firmness of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is mentioned for the purpose of stabilizing the wavering mind of ordinary beings, but it is not with reference to those who have entered the [Bodhisattva] stages.
For it has been said here:
"By one who desires to obtain the state of withdrawal and the state of illumination,
and by one who desires to enter from great darkness into light."

"Since that which is to be accomplished is mostly achieved by one who has fallen [into lower realms], how could there be success for me, a person of little merit?"— this is the refutation of a lowly mind. Furthermore,

this aforementioned fault does not apply to one who has transcended the miserable destinies, who possesses many waves of enthusiasm, who has accumulated an immeasurable mass of merit, and who has entered the spiritual stages (*bhūmi*).
And in this case, due to the ignorance of the mantras, there is no fault in reciting with additional syllables,
nor is there the fault of deficiency,
nor the fault of deviating from the prescribed rule.

However, taking as one's standard the force of faith, the force of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), and the force of total renunciation, one should proceed without deliberation; thus, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will certainly appear right here, and one's every desire will be accomplished.
Alternatively, one should perform protection with this mantra of all Vajradharas:
*Namaḥ traiyabdhikānāṃ tathāgatānāṃ sarvavajradharāṇāṃ caṇḍāla cala!*
Vajra,
Śāntana, Phalana.
Move! Kill!
Vajra-daṃṣṭra phaṭ!
O Lalitaśikhara, you who possess the vajra everywhere!
Blaze!
Homage be to you, the foremost among the most fierce commands! Raṇa haṃ phula sphāṭa, O supreme vajra, svāhā!
By the mere recitation of this, all obstacles and obstructing spirits (vināyakas) do not approach;
gods, nāgas, and others cannot prevail against it.
Furthermore, one may protect food, drink, bedding, seats, clothing, and ritual implements by means of consecrated water, or through sight, or through the mind.
Or one may perform all this with a steady mind.
And this is that.
Homage to all Vajras! Trāṭ!
O Amogha Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, shatter it, hūṃ! Cause it to revolve, hūṃ!
Trāṭa hūṃ / māṃ / Oṃ, I bestow strength upon you, O Tejomālinī; svāhā!
With this, one should first eat the first morsel, having consecrated it eight times while recollecting the state of being the King of Medicine of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
But as for the counteracting of poison:
It is as follows: ilimitte,
tilimitte, ililitimitte.
O dull-witted one!
O difficult-to-tame one!
O you who are difficult to subdue!
In dumbālīye, in takke, in tarkkaraṇe.
In Marmme, in Marmaraṇa,
and in Kaśmīra.
O you who have liberated Kaśmīra!
O you who are free from clouds!
O you who are thick with clouds!
O Ilmilīye! O Akhāpye! O Apāpye Śvete!
O white-beaked one!
O you who do not protect! Svāhā!
Whoever hears this vidyā even once will not be bitten by a snake for seven years,
nor shall poison enter his body.
And if a snake should bite him, its head would split into seven pieces like the cluster of blossoms on an arjaka tree.
Whoever maintains this knowledge shall not be bitten by a snake for as long as they live,
nor shall poison enter their body. Furthermore, these mantra-words must not be recited in the presence of a snake, because the snake would die.
They are as follows: Illā,
Cillā, and Cakko.
Bakko!
Koḍā koḍeti!
Nikuruḍā nikuruḍeti!
Poḍā causes affliction; moḍā and moḍeti [likewise].
Puruḍā puruḍeti / phaṭa rahe / phuṭṭaṇḍa rahe /
Nāgarahē / Nāgaṭṭaṇḍarahē / Sapparahē /
O you who are like the tip of a serpent's hood!
O pure one!
O you who destroy deceit and poison!
Śītavattāle / Halale / Halale /
taṇḍi, taḍa, tāḍi.
mala / sphuṭa / phuṭu / svāhā //
Thus, monks, when this Jāṅgulī spell has been recited in the presence of all beings, it is entirely such as it is, not false, not otherwise, true, unerring, and not inverted:
"Let this poison become non-poison;
let it go to the giver!"
May it go to the fangs;
may it go to fire;
may it go to water.
Let him go to dry land; let him go to a pillar; let him go to a wall.
May he pass to the ground;
may he go to peace, svāhā!
For protection against thieves and other such threats, one should recite the Mārīcī mantra.
That is to say: you are valor;
you are rising; you are enmity; you are light.
You are the deer;
you are the forest; you are the concealment.
Protect me on the path; protect me from the wrong path; protect me from the crowd.
Protect me from the thief;
protect me from the king;
protect me from the lion.
Protect me from the tiger; protect me from the serpent; protect me from the snake.
Protect me from all sides!
Protect me and all sentient beings from all fears, from all calamities, and from all misfortunes, svāhā!
Uṃ vaḍili, I bow to the knot of all the wicked; svāhā!
Homage to the Triple Gem!
Homage to the deity Mārīcī!
I shall now recite the heart-mantra of the deity Mārīcī.
It is as follows: battāli,
badāli, badāli.
Barāli! Varāhamukhi!
Ward off all the wicked ones!
Bind the mouth, svāhā!

One should employ this vidyā as well—which possesses great power, consists of fifty-seven syllables, is contained within the Vidyādhara Piṭaka, and is the cause for remembering infinite births—for the purpose of protection from all fears.
It is as follows: aṭṭe, baṭṭe, naṭṭe.
Kunaṭṭe / ṭake / ṭhake /
Ṭharake / Urumati / Rurumati.
Turu / hili mili / Sarvajñodupadagga.
Homage to all the perfectly enlightened ones! May my mantra-words be successful, svāhā!
This protection of one's own person by means of medicine, clothing, and so forth,
must be undertaken only preceded by the mindfulness of the welfare of sentient beings.
But from the enjoyment of craving for a self, a defiled transgression arises.
For a bodhisattva has relinquished everything to all sentient beings.

In that regard, if one consumes another's property by forgetting it out of a thirst for self-sustenance, one incurs an afflicted offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*). However, if one consumes it without such thirst, or while being attached to something else, having kept in mind the task of sentient beings, one does not incur an afflicted offense.
If one consumes it with the perception that it is another's property, but for one’s own sake, one incurs an offense of theft (*steyāpatti*).
According to the full valuation [of the object], one becomes defeated (*pārājika*) in the *Prātimokṣa*.
However, there is no fault in the case where one protects one's own person with possessions that have sentient beings as their owners, for the person itself has sentient beings as its owners.
For a slave who is constantly occupied with the master’s work has no property of his own by which he might subsist.
And it is said in the *Dharmasaṅgīti-sūtra*:
"A bodhisattva should be like a servant, by way of accomplishing whatever needs to be done for all sentient beings."

Furthermore, there is no fault whatsoever in a slave who, being entirely devoted to his master’s interests and whose mind is overwhelmed by illness or other afflictions, consumes [food] even without the master’s permission;
nor is it appropriate for anyone who knows the circumstances to feel displeasure toward a Bodhisattva acting in this way, because they fail to recognize his intention to abandon stinginess.
Nor is any doubt appropriate regarding this principle;
for the universal relinquishment was already established previously by the direct words of the Blessed One,
and likewise, the protection of one's own person was taught solely for the sake of sentient beings.
This logical principle has been applied for the sake of making that [point] clearly understood, and not out of regard for its own intrinsic purpose.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, "Protection of the Person," in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.

[VII. Protection of Wealth and Merit] The seventh chapter is the protection of wealth and merit. Thus far, the protection of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) has been understood; now, however, the protection of wealth must be explained.
In this regard, because of the training rule that "one should undertake well-performed actions and be moderate in all things," the protection of his enjoyments is not difficult.
For in the *Ugraparipṛcchā*, a training rule is stated:
"One should act with well-considered actions and act with well-performed actions;
thereby, there will be no misplacement of wealth and one will exercise foresight regarding the afterlife."
The prohibition of contempt is thereby established;
and by way of introducing *śamatha*, moderation and knowledge of the proper method have been explained.
Thus, this is established:
when a task can be accomplished even with a small and inferior amount of resources, one should not— either personally or through others— neglect the destruction of many superior resources.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Ugraparipṛcchā*:
"By means of the proper utilization [of wealth] for one's sons, wives, female and male slaves, laborers, and servants.

Likewise, one should not practice either giving or non-giving if they cause obstacles to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) or to the learning and other virtues of oneself and others.

It is thus established that for a bodhisattva who possesses either superior or equal capacity for the welfare of sentient beings, neither giving nor not giving should be performed if they would cause an obstacle to superior or equal merit.
And with this in mind, it is stated in the *Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa*:
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, how should a bodhisattva who has gone forth from the household life and is devoted to the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) give gifts?
What kind of gift should he give?"
To what extent should a gift be given? ... [etc. ...
One should be a giver of the Dharma, a master of the gift of Dharma.

Śāriputra, suppose a householder bodhisattva were to fill as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā with the seven precious jewels and offer them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
And, Śāriputra, whichever bodhisattva who has entered the religious life should proclaim even a single four-line verse, he produces far more merit than that.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata has not authorized the giving of material gifts by one who has gone forth. ... [pe] ...
Furthermore, Śāriputra, whatever gain there may be that has come into one’s bowl or is contained within one’s bowl— righteous and obtained in accordance with the Dharma—
one should eat it in common together with one’s fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Moreover, if someone should come and ask for either a bowl or a robe:
If he should have anything in excess of the three robes authorized by the Buddha,
it should be given away as a relinquishment.
However, if his robe should be deficient— that is, if he lacks the robes upon which the practice of the holy life depends— [he should not give them away].
Therefore, it must not be abandoned.
For what reason? Because the Tathāgata has declared that the three robes are not to be relinquished.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva, having renounced the three robes, should become preoccupied with beggars, he has not cultivated fewness of desires.
On the other hand, Śāriputra, that bodhisattva who has gone forth from the household life must cultivate the Dharma; he should not be devoted to that [preoccupation with beggars].

Otherwise, for the sake of gathering a single being, there would be a loss of great benefit—the obstruction of the cultivation of the bodhisattva’s intention for that great mass of beings and for that individual being as well.
For this very reason, it is called a "defilement" because it involves the abandonment of the vast side of wholesome qualities.
Such, then, is the prohibition against giving.
There is also a prohibition against excessive giving.
Just as in the *Āryasāgaramati-sūtra* it is taught that having many gains is an obstacle to the Mahāyāna,
how is it known that this method prescribed for oneself is also to be applied to another bodhisattva?
It is because it has been taught in the *Āryograparipṛcchā*.
The abandonment of one's own task because of being made to perform another's task.
Likewise, it is also said in the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa*:
"By one who is terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, what should be relied upon?
He replied:
"Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva who is terrified by the fear of saṃsāra should rely upon the majesty of the Buddha. He asked:
"One who wishes to abide in the majesty of the Buddha, where should they abide?"
He said:
"One who wishes to abide in the greatness of the Buddha should abide in equanimity toward all sentient beings.
He said:
"Where should one who wishes to abide in equanimity toward all sentient beings abide?
He replied,
"One who wishes to abide in equanimity toward all sentient beings should abide for the sake of the liberation of all sentient beings."
And so, in the *Dharmasaṅgīti*, the Bodhisattva Sārthavāha said:
"O Blessed One, that bodhisattva who desires awakening for all sentient beings before himself—
this, O Blessed One, is the true *dharmasaṅgīti*."
By its very renunciation, the absence of self-interest in this [bodhicitta] is established.
However, out of fear of abandoning the welfare of sentient beings, one does not impose the easy-to-bear upon an unsuitable being.

But where one perceives no loss of the welfare of sentient beings, what difference is there between that which is performed by oneself and that which is practiced for the benefit of the world by another?
That he does not relinquish his own merit for the sake of accomplishing the virtue of another bodhisattva,
while fearing the suffering of his own miserable rebirths— yet that very same suffering applies to the second as well.
If, however, one remains indifferent [thinking], "I have no affliction from that suffering," one becomes guilty of an offense according to the aforementioned sūtras.

And as it is said in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, beginning with: "Kāśyapa, these four are counterfeit bodhisattvas," it is stated: "One seeks one's own happiness, but does not seek the removal of the suffering of all sentient beings."

Therefore, according to the procedure in the *Ugraparipṛcchā*, one should reproach oneself as before; however, this training of a bodhisattva is as it was taught in the *Ārya-nirārambha-dharmasaṅgīti-sūtra*:
"How, noble sons, should one who stands in practice be known?
He replied:
When they do not act wrongly toward sentient beings.
He asked:
"How do they not act wrongly toward sentient beings?"
He said: "Because they do not abandon loving-kindness and great compassion.
Subhūti said:
What is the great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) of the bodhisattvas? He replied:
It is when they surrender their own body, life, and all roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*) to all sentient beings, and yet do not expect any recompense.
He asked: "What is the great compassion of the bodhisattvas?
It is that they desire awakening for sentient beings even earlier than for themselves."
And regarding this very point, it is said:
"All the trainings of a bodhisattva have great compassion as their root.
Furthermore, the Blessed One would certainly not have prohibited this.
It is certain that he teaches out of necessity, even without being requested, for the sake of any one bodhisattva;
for by this, the donor’s vast expansion of an ocean of great merit is seen through the gift of great benefit to one who is a supreme field of merit.
Otherwise, however, there would be nothing but the death of those who cause such obstruction.
As for that which was taught in the *Praśāntaviniścayaprātihāryasūtra*:

"O Great King, whatever expenditure of yours has been incurred here over a hundred thousand years, if all of that were combined, it would suffice as the sustenance for a single monk; and in this same way, it would suffice for each and every monk.
Furthermore, a Bodhisattva who is devoted to the recitation and study [of the Dharma], who is respectful and intent on the Dharma, should take food given out of faith and generate this thought:"
"By this [gift], I shall apply myself to the quest for the Dharma"—
this renunciation of the gift of merit does not approach even a hundredth part of that virtue.
That was said with reference to the purification of the pleasures of the household life;
however, there is no fault whatsoever according to the method previously described.
The protection of enjoyments has been explained in brief;
now the protection of merit must be discussed.
In that regard, through freedom from craving for the ripening of one's own self-interest, the wholesome becomes well-protected.
As it is said in the *Nārāyaṇaparipṛcchā*:
"He does not guard his ethical discipline for the sake of himself,
nor for the sake of heaven."
Not for the sake of the state of Śakra;
not for the sake of enjoyments;
not for the sake of sovereignty.
Not for the sake of physical form, not for the sake of complexion, nor for the sake of fame... [and so forth].
One does not guard ethical discipline out of fear of hell, and so forth.
Thus, one does not guard morality out of fear of the animal realm; rather,
one guards morality for the sake of establishing the guidance of the Buddhas,
and so on, guarding morality while seeking the welfare, happiness, yoga, and security of all sentient beings.
Endowed with such a mass of ethical discipline, that bodhisattva does not fall away from ten things.
From which ten?
That is to say: he does not fall away from the sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
And therein he becomes heedful, longing for awakening and desiring the vision of the Buddhas.
Thus, from the state of Brahmahood, through the attainment of the indestructible vision of the Buddhas and the hearing of the Dharma, he does not fall away;
and so on, until, for the sake of accomplishing practice according to what has been heard, he does not fall away from the undertaking of the bodhisattva vows.
Due to his unhindered eloquence, he does not fall away from the meditative concentrations that seek all wholesome qualities.
Thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the aggregate of ethical discipline is always honored by the gods, always praised by the nāgas,
and always honored by the yakṣas.
He is always honored by the gandharvas and always revered by the lords of the nāgas and the lords of the asuras; he is always highly esteemed by brahmins, kṣatriyas, guild-leaders, and householders;
and he is always sought out for audience by the wise.
He is always attended by the Buddhas; he is esteemed as a teacher by the world including its gods; and he is compassionate toward all sentient beings. ... [pe] ...
He does not go to the four destinies.
Which four?
Namely, he does not go to the destiny of the unfavorable conditions, except for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
He does not go to a Buddha-field devoid of a Buddha;
he does not go to rebirth in a family of wrong views;
he does not go to any state of miserable rebirth.
In this way, one must protect even previously relinquished merit that is being taken up again under the influence of the afflictions.
Furthermore, regarding the merit derived from the gift of merit itself, one should not pray for its ripening except for the sake of others.
Moreover, why would one wish to protect merit?
One should not feel regret later.
As it is said in the *Ugraparipṛcchā*:
"And having given, one should not give rise to a mind of regret."
Weakness arises from weakness of back;
the intention is that through remorse, there may be a depletion of merit just as there is of evil. And one should not, having performed [an act], proclaim it.
For in many ways the Blessed One has praised the concealment of one's virtues and the disclosure of one's faults;
therein, the destruction of what is disclosed is understood.

There is no transgression for one who, for the sake of sentient beings, reveals [the teaching] with a mind free from worldly desire, even if sin occurs through mental distress or merit occurs through mental joy.
As stated in the *Ratnamegha* by way of the analogy of the physician, self-exaltation is said to be faultless.
Furthermore: "One who desires to protect merit should fear gain and honor; he should always avoid arrogance. A Bodhisattva should be serene and should cast away doubt regarding the Dharma."
And this is stated in the *Ratnakūṭa*:
"Kāśyapa, when a bodhisattva is possessed of four qualities, the wholesome dharmas that have arisen repeatedly decline;
and being deprived of those four, he does not increase in wholesome dharmas."
What are the four?
Namely: by the pursuit of Lokāyata mantras for one who is conceited;
and by looking toward [famous] families for one who is intent upon gain and honor.
By harboring malice toward and slandering Bodhisattvas,
and by rejecting sūtras that have not been heard and have not been taught.
And it is recited among the Noble Sarvāstivādins:
"Behold, monks, this monk who, having prostrated with his entire body at the stūpa of hair and nails, is inspiring his mind with serene faith.
"So be it, Venerable Sir."
"Monks, for as many grains of sand as there are within this earth— extending eighty thousand yojanas downward from where it is stepped upon by this monk, down as far as the golden wheel—
so many thousands of reigns as a universal monarch (cakravartin) must be enjoyed by this monk.
Then, the venerable Upāli, having bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One in this way:"
Regarding what was said by the Blessed One: "This monk has such great roots of merit;
