where, Blessed One, do these roots of merit go to attenuation, exhaustion, and total depletion?
"Upāli, I do not perceive any such injury or destruction [of the Dharma]."

Just as when a fellow practitioner gives rise to a malicious thought toward another fellow practitioner—Upāli, in this case these great roots of merit undergo diminution, exhaustion, and total destruction.
Therefore, Upāli, you should train yourself thus: "We shall not allow our minds to become corrupted even toward a burnt pillar."
How much more so, then, in the case of the body endowed with consciousness?
The *Āryamañjuśrīvikrīḍitasūtra* also says:
"Anger, anger—it destroys the roots of virtue accumulated over a hundred eons; therefore it is called 'anger'."
And in the *Āryagaṇḍavyūhasūtra*, while the night goddess Samantasattvaparitrāṇyojas narrates her former life story, she said:
"By that root of unwholesomeness arising from mutual contempt, they were deprived even of the measure of their lifespan;
they were also deprived of their complexion and their strength."
And here, the word "always" (sadā) is used for the purpose of demonstrating that pride should never be displayed at any time.
However, gain and honor may sometimes even be accepted,
as it is said in the *Āryaratnamegha*:
"In this regard, noble son, a bodhisattva, upon receiving a heap of jewels even as large as Mount Sumeru, accepts it."
Even when obtaining a very inferior object,
for what reason does this occur? It is because he thinks as follows:
These beings are stingy, greedy, and overcome by greed;
because of that, with that as the condition, and with that as the cause, they rise and sink in the ocean of saṃsāra like those overwhelmed by a great mass of water.
This will be for their long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness.
Having accepted everything, he does not take possession of it;
he does not give rise to a mind of greed,
but rather performs services toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha for the common benefit of all sentient beings.
Just as he makes himself a source of livelihood for all suffering sentient beings,
he also inspires and gladdens that donor.
Likewise, it is said in this very same place:
"And by that gift, he does not become arrogant."
Furthermore, it says in this very same place:

"If, moreover, on account of that cause, with that as its condition, and with that as its source, he gains fame, renown, and verses of praise, he does not become conceited, does not become arrogant, and does not become intoxicated.
And he thinks thus:"
Before long, this sound of the verse of his fame—those by whom it was raised, that which was raised, and the sound of the verse of fame itself—all three of these will cease to exist in every respect.

In this regard, what person of wise nature would produce a mind of attachment, become haughty, or be arrogant and conceited toward phenomena that are impermanent, unstable, non-abiding, and unreliable?
Thus, a bodhisattva dwells with mindfulness well-established regarding gain, honor, fame, and the sound of verses of praise.
Furthermore, it says: "They dwell in the world like outcaste children with a most debased mind;
they have fallen into pride, intoxication, and arrogance because the perception of malicious speech is constantly and perpetually present."
It is further said:

"In this case, noble son, a bodhisattva who has gone forth from the household life and entered homelessness becomes one whose pride is humbled, thinking: 'I am like a corpse to my friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relatives.
He becomes one whose pride is humbled, thinking: 'My disfigurement has appeared; I am clothed in discolored garments, and my appearance has become altogether different.'"

"Shaven-headed and with bowl in hand, I wander from family to family for the sake of alms, on account of alms"—thus his pride is humbled. "With a very lowly mind, like that of a Caṇḍāla boy, I go about for alms"—thus his pride is humbled. "I am a mendicant, one who is restrained."

Thinking, "My livelihood is dependent on others," his pride is humbled. Thinking, "I accept what is rejected and despised," his pride is humbled. Thinking, "The teachers, gurus, and those worthy of offerings must be propitiated by me," his pride is humbled.
"My fellow practitioners of the holy life should be satisfied with this and that conduct, sphere of activity, and behavior"— thus he becomes one whose pride is humbled.
"I shall practice those dharmas which I have not yet attained and which I have not yet mastered"— thus he becomes one whose pride is humbled.
Thinking, "I shall dwell amidst beings who are angry and of malevolent mind, abounding in patience," one becomes one whose pride is destroyed.
It is also said in the *Āryasāgaramati-sūtra*:
"He becomes pure of the view of a self-existent body (*satkāya*);

his limbs are adorned with the primary marks, his hands and feet are soft and tender, his body is the natural outflow of well-distributed merit, his faculties are unimpaired, and all his major and minor limbs are complete."
Nor does he become intoxicated by pride in his physical form,
nor is he devoted to the practice of adorning his body.
Out of a desire to receive the Dharma, he bows down and pays homage even to those beings who are inferior or deficient in physical form.
Furthermore, it is said in this very same place: "It is just as if, Blessed One, when the great ocean settles, it settles in a low-lying region of the earth;
because of that lowliness, all rivers and all springs flow into it with little difficulty."

In the same way, Blessed One, for a bodhisattva who is free from pride and possesses reverence for those worthy of honor and gifts, those profound joys of the Dharma come into the range of the sense of hearing with little difficulty and remain fixed in mindfulness.

Therefore, Blessed One, it should be understood that whichever bodhisattva is puffed up with pride, stiffened by conceit, and does not bow down or pay homage to those worthy of honor and gifts, has been pierced by the hook of Māra.
"Ah, this is truly a Bodhisattva!"
And it is said in the *Āryalokottaraparivarta*:
"O Son of the Victor, these ten are the deeds of Māra for bodhisattvas. What are the ten?"

This is the work of Māra: namely, a lack of respect toward those who are worthy of honor and offerings—teachers, parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, those who have gone rightly, and those who practice rightly;

and not bowing down before the Dharma-preachers who have attained distinguished realization of the Dharma, who teach the sublime Dharma, who have mounted the Mahāyāna, who know the methods of the path to nirvāṇa, and who have obtained the *dhāraṇīs* and the kings of sūtras.
He becomes arrogant and stubborn;
he does not conceive reverence for the Dharma-preacher,
nor does he show a desire to hear him or treat him with esteem.

When one is seated for hearing the Dharma or for discussion, and a powerful surge of the sublime Dharma has arisen, yet one does not offer praise to the Dharma-preacher, thinking, "Let no one else praise him," this is the work of Māra.
Having generated conceit, one grasps at a self and does not grasp others;
furthermore, one does not enter into the knowledge of the self.
One does not produce mental composure; this is the work of Māra.
Giving rise to overweening pride, not knowing and not understanding, one conceals the praise of those persons worthy of praise and speaks dispraise;
nor does one become glad at the praise of another's virtues. This is the work of Māra.
He knows: "This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the authentic word of the Buddha";
yet, out of hatred for the person, he harbors hatred for the Dharma and rejects the true Dharma.
And one causes others to dispute; this is the work of Māra.
With an uplifted mind, he prays for the quality of being exempted from duties; he does not seek [to avoid them],
but approaches the service of others and rejoices in it.
Not rising for or going out to meet the elders and seniors who have long practiced the holy life is the work of Māra.
Furthermore, he has a frowning face;
he does not have a smiling face,
nor does he speak with gentle and sweet words.
Always having a harsh mind, he seeks out faults.
Seeking an opportunity for entry; this is the work of Māra.
And having fallen into conceit, he does not approach the wise;
he does not serve them; he does not honor them.
He does not attend upon them; he does not inquire further;
he does not ask questions.
"What is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is to be done? What, when performed, leads for a long time to welfare, benefit, and happiness?
Or what, when not performed, leads for a long time to misfortune, harm, and suffering?"—thus he becomes dull-witted, even more dull-witted.
An array of delusion, grasping at pride,
seeing no way out— this is the work of Māra.
Overcome by pride, he becomes indifferent toward the appearance of a Buddha;
he exhausts his former roots of merit and does not produce new ones.
He explains that which is inexpressible;
he initiates disputes and becomes full of contention. For one who dwells in such a manner regarding the Dharma, it is possible that he may fall falsely into a great abyss.
Moreover, although one attains sovereignty by depending on the power of the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*),
if for hundreds of thousands of eons one does not encounter the appearance of a Buddha,
how much less could one hear the Dharma?
This is the tenth work of Māra.
O Son of the Conqueror, these are the ten deeds of Māra;
by avoiding them, Bodhisattvas attain the ten deeds of gnosis,
and it is precisely within these deeds of gnosis that they ripen.
Humility toward all sentient beings.
It is also said in the *Āryarāṣṭrapālasūtra*: "The ground of the miserable states, rebirth in the [eight] unfavorable conditions,"
Poverty,
birth into a low family,
blindness from birth, weakness, and likewise a lack of physical vigor.
Those deluded ones grasp [at things] through the power of pride.
Thus [it is said].
It is also said in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:

"The field of sentient beings is the Buddha-field of a bodhisattva, for it is from that Buddha-field that the acquisition and attainment of the Buddha-dharmas occurs; I ought not to act wrongly toward it."
And it occurs to him:
"All good conduct and misconduct proceed depending upon sentient beings;
and from the exhaustion of misconduct, the miserable states of existence arise."
Because they rely on good conduct, they are called gods and humans.
For this very reason, it is also said in the *Ratnolkā-dhāraṇī*:

"In this regard, O sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening generates ten kinds of mind toward all sentient beings from the very beginning. What are these ten kinds?"

That is to say: he generates this tenfold mind— namely, a mind of benevolence, a mind of happiness, a mind of generosity, a mind of affection, a mind of love, a mind of assistance, a mind of protection, a mind of equanimity, a mind toward [them] as teachers, and a mind toward [them] as instructors.
It is also said in the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*:
"I stand firm in accepting all sentient beings as my disciples,
and I shall establish others in accepting all sentient beings as their disciples"— thus one gains consolation.
...and so forth.
"I am established in bowing down and prostrating before all sentient beings," as before.
In that regard, humility and prostration consist of being free from pride toward all sentient beings.

Likewise, in the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa*, it is taught that for the sake of being reborn in a completely pure buddha-field, one should maintain love for all sentient beings as if they were the Teacher.

However, for the sake of protecting the faith of the world, even while performing acts such as washing the feet of his seat, a bodhisattva must practice love and respect toward women, those who have reached an unfavorable state, or those who have fallen into ruin, even with his mind [focused on the aforementioned goal].
It should be performed.

For it is said in the *Gaṇḍavyūha*: "As soon as he had sat down upon that great lion throne, the entire assembly of people stood facing him with palms joined in reverence, paying homage to that very king. ... [pe] ...

Indeed, upon merely seeing those supplicants, King Sarvadharmanirnādacchatramaṇḍalanirghoṣa became even more delighted than by his acquisition of the sovereignty of a universal monarch over the triple-thousandfold world system lasting until the end of limitless eons,
or even by the dwelling in the gateways of liberation and peace of the Śuddhāvāsa deities lasting until the end of boundless eons.

It is like this, noble son: suppose there were a man of exclusively lustful temperament who, having been separated for a long time from his mother, father, brothers, sisters, friends, ministers, kinsmen, blood relations, sons, daughters, and wife, had become lost in a vast wilderness forest;
longing to see them, upon their reunion, a great joy and intense attachment would arise in him because he could not be satiated by the sight of them.

In the same way, noble son, as soon as King Sarvadharmanirnādacchatramaṇḍalanirghoṣa saw those supplicants, a great surge of joy arose within him; a blissful satisfaction entered his mind, and a powerful impulse of mental exaltation appeared, such that he perceived all those supplicants as his only son, as his parents, as those worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*), as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), as beautiful, and as rare to encounter.

The perception of them as performers of what is difficult, the perception of them as those of great benefit, the perception of them as supreme benefactors, the perception of them as supports for the path to awakening, and the perception of them as teachers and instructors should arise.
Thus, when there is the possibility of beings coming before one to pay homage and so forth while one is in another state, one should remember the renunciation of everything:
"This body belongs to these very beings;
let them do with it as they wish."

It is for the sake of one's own happiness, as in the case of cleaning and smearing the ground; or else, like one who fears the displeasure of a master and desires his favor, one should keep in mind the fulfillment of his commands,
since even when performing service for the Blessed One, there is no other recourse.
The sick monk accepted it.
As it is said in the *Bhikṣuprakīrṇaka*:
the Blessed One said, "Do not fear, monk; do not fear, monk."
"I shall attend upon you, O Bhikṣu; bring me the robes so that I may wash them for you.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda spoke thus to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One not wash the robes of this sick man, which are smeared with impurities;
I, Blessed One, shall wash them.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Ānanda, you must wash this monk's robes;
the Tathāgata will pour the water.
Then the Venerable Ānanda washed the robes of that sick monk.
The Blessed One poured water. ... [as before] ...
Then indeed, the venerable Ānanda, having properly and thoroughly supported that sick monk, carried him outside and bathed him,
saying, "The Blessed One is pouring water. And he said:
Since by pleasing these one attains greatness, while by displeasing them one meets with grievous calamity, is it not indeed right to satisfy them even at the cost of sacrificing one's life?
These indeed are those beings, having inspired faith in whom many have attained accomplishment;
there exists no other field of accomplishment in the world than sentient beings.
These are wish-fulfilling gems, auspicious jars, and cows that yield all desires;
therefore, they should be propitiated like a teacher and like a deity.
Furthermore, for those who are sincere friends and immeasurable benefactors,
what other recompense could there be than the act of pleasing sentient beings?
In the past, the Protector, becoming motionless through great effort, bore upon his head with his matted locks those beings who resided there, according to their desire.
They shatter their own bodies and enter the Avīci hell for the sake of those [beings]; whatever is done for them, that is truly done.
Therefore, even toward those who have done great harm, one should practice only what is entirely beneficial toward them.
Since my masters themselves are indifferent even toward their own selves for the sake of this [Dharma],
how can I not adopt the state of a servant toward those various masters, instead of maintaining pride?

Those in whose happiness the Lords of Sages find joy, and in whose suffering they enter into grief—by pleasing them, all the Lords of Sages are pleased; by harming them, an injury is done to the Sages.
Just as one whose body is ablaze on all sides finds no joy even through all sensual desires,
likewise for those of great compassion, there is no means of finding pleasure even when sentient beings are suffering.
Therefore,
whatever suffering I have caused to all those of great compassion by means of the suffering of living beings, I now confess that sin; may those sages, who were troubled by it, forgive me.
Today, for the sake of propitiating the Tathāgatas, I enter into servitude in this world with my whole being;
let the multitudes of people place their feet upon my head or even strike me down—may the Lords of the World be satisfied.
This entire world has indeed been made their own by those whose very nature is compassion; there is no doubt about this.
Are these beings who are seen before us not themselves the Protectors? Why, then, is there such disregard for them?
This alone is the propitiation of the Tathāgatas; this alone is the accomplishment of one’s own welfare;
this alone is the remover of the world’s suffering; therefore, let this alone be my vow.
Just as a single king’s man crushes a great multitude,
the far-sighted multitude is unable to retaliate.
Since he is not truly alone— his strength being the king's army— he would not, even if weak, cause humiliation to anyone who has committed an offense.
Since the guardians of hell and those endowed with compassion possess that power,
one should therefore please sentient beings, just as a servant pleases a fierce king.
What could an angry king do that would cause the suffering of hell,
which is experienced precisely through the mental distress caused by harming sentient beings?
What could a gratified king give that would be equal to Buddhahood—
that which is indeed experienced through bringing joy to sentient beings?
Let alone the future Buddhahood that arises from pleasing sentient beings;
do you not see even in this very life the good fortune, fame, and well-being [that result]?
One who is patient, as they wander through cyclic existence, attains a pleasing appearance, health, joy, long life, and the abundant happiness of a universal monarch.
That a person of loving disposition is worthy of worship is itself the greatness of sentient beings;
that merit which arises from faith in the Buddha is itself the greatness of the Buddha.
For this very reason, the fruit of cultivating loving-kindness is proclaimed in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
"Whatever various and immeasurable offerings one might make throughout hundreds of millions of buddha-fields."
Having performed that worship of the incomparable Leaders,
it does not equal even a fraction of the merit in a mind of loving-kindness.
Therefore, one should always avoid arrogance toward such great objects of veneration;
for this arrogance arises from improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
One should make an effort to prevent its non-arising,
as it is said in the *Ratnamegha*:
"And how, noble son, does a bodhisattva become free from improper mental attention?"
In this case, a bodhisattva, being alone, having gone into seclusion, and established in solitude, does not give rise to such a thought as:
"I am dwelling without confusion;
I am established in solitude."
I have entered the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata;
but as for those other ascetics or brahmins, they all dwell in confusion, are full of worldly attachments, and have strayed from the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata.
In this way, indeed, the bodhisattva becomes free from improper mental attention.
Furthermore, it is said in this very same place:
"In this regard, a bodhisattva, while exerting vigor, does not relish that great vigor,
nor does he exalt himself on account of that vigor."
He does not disparage others;
rather, he thinks to himself:
"For what person of a wise nature, being himself devoted to his own duty, would ever reproach others?"
In this way, a bodhisattva possesses unswerving vigor.
This, however, is the summary of the protection of merit: namely, its dedication toward awakening.
For it is said in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*:
"Indeed, there is no exhaustion whatsoever in the interim of a root of merit dedicated toward awakening until one sits at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Reverend Śāradvatīputra, it is just as, for example, with a drop of water fallen into the great ocean: there is no exhaustion in the interim until the end of the eon."
Thus ends the seventh chapter, "The Protection of Wealth and Merit," in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.
[VIII. Purification of Evil] The eighth chapter is the purification of evil.
The protection of all three—beginning with one’s own person—has been explained.
Purification must now be explained.
For what purpose?
So that the enjoyment of the purified personal existence will become wholesome.
It is like perfectly prepared, husk-free rice for embodied beings.
As it is said in the *Āryatathāgataguhya-sūtra*:
"And in those great charnel grounds that exist within great cities, which are crowded with many hundreds of thousands of living beings,
there too that bodhisattva mahāsattva displays his own great body as dead and deceased."

There, those beings born in the animal realm, having consumed as much meat as they required, at the end of their lives, having died and passed away, are reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world among the gods.
And that very act becomes for them the cause, leading even unto final nirvana. That is to say:
This was due to the purification of the former vow of that very Bodhisattva,
by whom such a vow had been made for a long time:
"May those who consume my flesh after I have died and passed away [be benefited]."
That very [virtue] shall be the cause for that person of virtuous conduct to attain rebirth in heaven, up until their final nirvana;
their intention succeeds, and their aspiration succeeds.
The aspiration succeeds.
Furthermore, it is said in this very same place:
"Manifested by the Dharma-body, he benefits sentient beings even through being seen;
he benefits sentient beings even through being heard and even through being touched."

Śāntamati, it is just as if the physician-king Jīvaka, having gathered all medicinal herbs, had fashioned from that collection of medicinal trees the form of a maiden— graceful, beautiful to behold, well-crafted, perfectly finished,
and highly refined— who would come, go, stand, sit, and lie down.

There, those who come—afflicted persons, great-souled ones, kings, or royal ministers, guild-leaders, householders, counselors, or vassal princes—Jīvaka, the king of physicians, unites them with that maiden Bhaiṣajya.
As soon as they have entered into union with her, all their diseases are stilled; they become free from passion, happy, and free from disorder.
Behold, Śāntamati, the knowledge of Jīvaka, the king of physicians, regarding the treatment of worldly diseases— if it were possessed by other physicians!

In the very same way, Śāntamati, as many beings— whether men, women, boys, or girls— as are tormented by passion, hatred, and delusion, and touch the body of that bodhisattva who is manifested through the Dharma-body, their every affliction is stilled the moment they are touched, and they perceive their bodies as free from torment.
This is because that very bodhisattva’s previous vow is thoroughly purified;
for this purpose, the personal existence (ātmabhāva) must be cleansed.
Furthermore, he states the fault in not purifying [the mind]:
"Just as grain covered by weeds withers through diseases and does not flourish,
so the sprout of a Buddha does not attain growth when shrouded by the afflictions (kleśa)."
The intention is that [this is done] both for the sake of dispelling opposing views and for the sake of increase.
What is the purification of the personal existence?
It is the cleansing of evil and afflictions by means of the essential meaning of the words of the Perfectly Awakened One.
But in the absence of effort, one goes to the states of woe.
In that regard, the purification of evil is taught in the *Caturdharmaka-sūtra*:
"Maitreya, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with four qualities overcomes evil that has been committed and accumulated. What are these four?"
Namely:
by means of the practice of revulsion, by means of the practice of the antidote,
and by the power of restoration.
And by the power of the basis.
In that regard, the practice of revulsion consists in frequently feeling remorse for whatever unwholesome action one has committed.
In that regard, the practice of the counteragent consists in applying oneself with extreme diligence to wholesome action even after having committed unwholesome action.
The power of restoration is the attainment of the restraint of non-action through the undertaking of vows.

In this regard, the power of the basis consists in taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and not relinquishing the thought of awakening. By relying on such a powerful support, one cannot be overcome by evil.
Maitreya, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these four qualities overcomes evil that has been committed and accumulated.
In that regard, how should the practice of revulsion be cultivated?
As it is stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*:
May the Buddhas, whose minds are filled with love and compassion, attend to me—
those supreme among bipeds who dwell throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Whatever evil karma I have previously committed, however terrible it may be,
I shall confess it all while standing before the One Endowed with the Ten Powers.
Whatever evil has been committed by me through ignorance of my parents, through ignorance of the Buddhas, and through ignorance of what is wholesome.
Whatever sin has been committed by me while intoxicated by the pride of power, by the pride of noble lineage and enjoyments, and by the intoxication of youth;
Whatever evil has been committed by me through ill-considered thought, ill-spoken word, or even through a misdeed, because I failed to perceive its danger;
By acting with the intellect of a child, with a mind shrouded by ignorance,
under the influence of evil friends, and with a mind agitated by the afflictions.
Whatever sin has been committed by me through the power of attachment to play and pleasure, or under the influence of grief and disease, or due to the fault of insatiable greed for wealth;
Whatever sin has been committed by me through association with ignoble people, on account of envy and avarice, and due to the fault of deceit and poverty;
In this time of the onset of calamity, out of fear regarding sensual desires,
whatever sin has been committed by me even while possessing food and sovereignty;
Whatever sin has been committed by me, whether under the influence of a restless mind or of desire and anger, or even while afflicted by hunger and thirst;
Whatever sin has been committed by me for the sake of drink, for the sake of food, for the sake of clothing, or on account of women, through the various torments of the afflictions;
Whatever evil of body, speech, and mind, the threefold misconduct, and whatever [evil] was done by such thoughts and forms— all that I confess.
Whatever disrespect I may have shown toward the Buddhas, the Dharmas, and likewise toward the Śrāvakas, all of that I now confess.
Whatever disrespect I may have shown toward Pratyekabuddhas or Bodhisattvas, all of that I now confess.
Whatever disrespect I have shown toward preachers of the true Dharma or toward others who possess virtuous qualities, all of that I now confess.
The true Dharma would have been rejected; by that, ignorance has always been mine.
My lack of respect for my mother and father—all that I confess.
Through my foolishness, my childishness, and being shrouded by pride and arrogance,
as well as by passion, hatred, and delusion— I confess all of that.
May the Buddhas, with their attentive minds, look upon me;
may they, whose hearts are surrendered to compassion, accept my transgression.
Whatever evil was previously committed by me during hundreds of eons—
for the sake of that, my mind is filled with grief, and I am wretched, afflicted by fear.
I am constantly dejected in mind among those of evil deeds;
wherever I may go, I possess no strength at all.
May all the compassionate Buddhas, who remove all fear from the world,
accept my transgression and deliver me from fear.
May the Tathāgatas cause the flow of my afflictions, karma, and its fruit to cease;
may the Buddhas bathe me with the waters of the river of compassion.
I confess all evil that was previously committed by me, and whatever evil I have now; all that I confess.
I undertake restraint for the future regarding all misdeeds;
I do not conceal that evil which may have been my wrongdoing.
Whatever threefold bodily action, fourfold verbal action,
and threefold mental action I have committed, all of that I confess.
Whatever tenfold karma has been committed through body, speech, and thought, all of that I confess.
And whatever evil karma of mine yields undesirable fruit,
all that I shall confess, standing before the Buddhas.
Whatever extremely terrible evil I have committed with my childish intellect amidst the perils of existence and the realms of rebirth—
standing now before the One Possessed of Ten Powers, I confess all that evil.

And I confess that evil which I have accumulated during the perils of birth, through the various perils of bodily conduct, in the peril of cyclic existence, in the peril of the world, in the peril of a fickle and restless mind, and in the peril of afflictions produced by foolish children.
In the peril of encountering evil friends,

in the perils of fear and passion, and even in the perils of the darkness of hatred and delusion; in the peril of the [fleeting] moment, in the peril of time, and even in the perils of failing to acquire merit—
he stands facing the peril of the Victorious One.
I confess all that evil.
Specifically, the confession of the grave and light transgressions of Bodhisattvas is taught in the *Āryopāliparipṛcchā*.
What, then, is the grave root transgression?
But it has been stated there in general terms:

"Upāli, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna should incur offenses associated with passion as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, yet should incur even a single offense associated with hatred—provided he has made the Bodhisattvayāna his standard... [etc.]"
This offense, which is associated with hatred, is more serious than those [other offenses].
Why is that? Because this hatred, Upāli, leads to the abandonment of sentient beings.
Passion conduces to the gathering of sentient beings.
In that regard, Upāli, as for that affliction which conduces to the gathering of sentient beings, therein the bodhisattva has neither deception nor fear... [and so forth].
Therefore, Upāli, whatever offenses are connected with passion, I declare them all to be non-offenses.
What is the intention here?
It is because the gathering of sentient beings has already been specifically emphasized.
For this instruction is intended for one who possesses resolute intention and compassion.
For immediately thereafter it says:
"In that regard, Upāli, those bodhisattvas who are unskilled in means fear transgressions associated with passion;
whereas those bodhisattvas who are skilled in means fear transgressions associated with hatred, but not those associated with passion."
Who, then, are those skilled in means?
They are those who, by means of wisdom and compassion, are prevented from abandoning sentient beings;
for in both ways, the abandonment of sentient beings occurs.
Because one realizes the emptiness of suffering through wisdom alone,
and because compassion alone— due to the power of the afflictions— is lost without delay.
As it is said in the *Upāyakauśalya-sūtra*:
"For example, noble son, suppose a man who is a master of mantra-vidyā were bound by a king with a fivefold bond.
When he desired to depart, he would cut all his bonds by the power of a single mantra-vidyā and go forth."
In the same way, noble son, a bodhisattva skilled in means finds delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure and dwells surrounded by them.
Yet, whenever he so desires, through the power of wisdom and by means of the single mind of omniscience, he enjoys all sensual pleasures and, upon passing away, is reborn in the Brahma-world.
Why is it not accepted that the same applies to hatred? Because hatred is by nature a great transgression,
and because when compassion is absent, skillful means itself is impossible.

One who is convinced that the accomplishment of the welfare of others is more important than one's own welfare will, even when under the sway of anger while instructing another, give rise to a vow for the future preceded by remorse. What fault is there in anger that wards off what is harmful?
There is the fault of the loss of compassion, due to the defect of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of that [anger] arising from giving it an opportunity.
We shall demonstrate later that by cutting it off, there would be the fault of cutting off the root;

for even if that were beneficial for that particular being, nevertheless, through the loss of the Bodhisattva’s compassion, there would be a loss of the great continuity of the welfare of sentient beings.

In the *Āryasatyaka-parivarta* as well, the analogy of the son should be understood as being established solely upon compassion. Furthermore, the prohibition of pity found there is for the purpose of winning over the world through skill in means regarding the welfare of the world.
If one who is being restrained were to harbor resentment toward a Bodhisattva who desires their benefit, that Bodhisattva would bring about harm to both.
Furthermore, a fault regarding passion is also recited:
"A person who indulges in sensual desires becomes blind;
he is a slayer of mother and father."
One may indulge in sensual pleasures or even kill those who possess virtue;
therefore, one should always avoid them.
And it is observed that through attachment to one's own happiness, there is indifference toward the suffering of others.
It is true that it has been seen;
for one by whom the suffering of others has not been practiced as one's own suffering,
but rather by one by whom it has been so practiced.
For him, both faults are impossible.

As it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*: "For example, Ānanda, suppose a certain man were to be ablaze from the sole of his foot up to his head, burning intensely and becoming a single mass of flame; then another man, approaching him, were to say:"
"Come, my good man! With this extinguished body, provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, play, enjoy yourself, and amuse yourself!
What do you think, Ānanda?
Would that man, with an unextinguished body, play, enjoy himself, and amuse himself with the five strands of sensual pleasure?
Ānanda said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

"Ānanda, that man might play, rejoice, and enjoy himself, provided for and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, by means of a physical existence that has not yet attained final nirvāṇa, on account of his conceptual construction."

But it was not so for the Tathāgata; while formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, upon seeing sentient beings suffering in the three lower realms or being impoverished, he experienced neither mental joy nor clarity of mind, and so forth.
Even in the world, when a son is being impaled on a stake,
it is observed that his parents, while watching him, have no attachment to their own happiness due to the power of compassion corresponding to their [relationship].
In that case, would there not be sexual misconduct even in secret with women who have a husband, those who have no husband, or those protected by the banner of the Dharma?
When there is a purpose for the benefit of sentient beings and no harm to sentient beings, it is faultless after having examined the subsequent consequence.
Because her purpose has been fulfilled by those who practice the holy life correctly, she is to be avoided from afar;
furthermore, she is to be honored like a mother or a sister.
If that is so, then this same [conclusion] would apply to a monk as well.
Because he accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings through no other mode of holy life than that.
For it is said in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*:
"Furthermore, he should practice equanimity regarding both the proper and improper times."
If, however, one should perceive a benefit for sentient beings even greater than that,
one may set aside the training.
In the *Upāyakauśalya-sūtra*, concerning the young brahmin Jyotis who had practiced celibacy for forty-two thousand years, it is said: "While standing at the seventh step, compassion arose in him:
'Even if I should break this vow and be destined for hell, I am nevertheless willing to experience the suffering of hell so that this woman may be happy.'"
"Do not die!
Thus, noble son, the young brahmin Jyotis turned back, took that woman by her right hand, and said to her:
"Arise, sister; I shall do for you whatever you desire. ... [as before] ...

Thus, noble son, through the arousal of a mind of great compassion, yet for a brief moment associated with sensual desire, I turned my back on [the path] for ten thousand eons. Behold, noble son, that which is karma leading to rebirth in hell for others becomes,
for a bodhisattva skilled in means, karma leading to rebirth in the Brahma-world.

Furthermore, it says in this very same place: "If a bodhisattva were to produce a root of virtue for a single sentient being, yet were to incur such an offense that by incurring that offense he would be cooked in hell for a hundred thousand eons—
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva must indeed endure incurring that offense and that suffering of hell."
But one should never abandon the welfare of even a single sentient being.
Furthermore, it says in this very same place: "In this regard,
noble son, when a bodhisattva skilled in means should at any time or on any occasion incur an offense through the influence of a spiritual friend of evil character, he reflects upon it as follows:"

"I am not to attain final nirvana by means of these aggregates; rather, I must don this armor once again: 'I shall wander through the furthest limits of the future for the sake of maturing sentient beings.'"
I shall not allow my mind to burn with distress;
rather, as I wander through cyclic existence, I shall bring sentient beings to maturity.
Furthermore, I shall remedy this transgression according to the Dharma.
"I shall undertake restraint for the future.
Noble son, if a bodhisattva who has gone forth, having formed an intention, should transgress all four root downfalls, yet dispel them through this skill in means,
I declare that there is no downfall for that bodhisattva.
And this is clear from the *Āryaratnamegha*, because it authorizes the killing of a person who intends to commit an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
Even in the Śrāvaka Vinaya, it is stated that there is no offense when one releases deer and other animals out of compassion, even in a situation that constitutes a root downfall.
And this is the merit in passion: by generating passion toward a bodhisattva, one attains a happy rebirth, but not through anger.
As it is said in the *Upāyakauśalya-sūtra*,
concerning the girl Dhavvyottarā who was infatuated with the bodhisattva Priyaṃkara:
"Furthermore, whatever woman, with a mind full of passion, should repeatedly gaze upon Priyaṃkara’s vow..."
Having completely abandoned the state of womanhood, she would become a man such as that noble being.
Behold, Ānanda, such are his qualities!
By that very [conduct] through which other beings go to hell, by generating passion for heroes, they go to heaven and even to human status. ...pe...
Who would give rise to hatred toward those Bodhisattvas of great renown, the kings of medicine,
for whom even their afflictions are givers of happiness?
How much more so, then, for one who would honor them? Thus it was said.
Thus, when there exists another means for the welfare of sentient beings, an offense born of passion is declared to be no offense.
And in the *Upāyakauśalya-sūtra*, it is explained in detail that a bodhisattva who has accomplished his purpose, like a courtesan, abandons that sentient being without further regard.
This reflection belongs to one who has not yet attained the [bodhisattva] stages but has practiced the six perfections;
it does not belong to anyone else. Let this incidental discussion suffice.
Therefore, no opportunity for hatred should be given.
For it is said in the *Upāliparipṛcchā*:
"Śāriputra, there are two offenses for bodhisattvas that are greatly blameworthy."
Which two? Those accompanied by hatred and those accompanied by delusion.
In this regard, Śāriputra, the first offense is to be confessed straightforwardly before a group of ten.
The offense of taking the hand within a group of five is grave and must be confessed.
Śāriputra, the grasping of a woman’s hand or looking at her with lustful intent constitutes an offense; one should confess that grave offense to a single person or to two.
A bodhisattva who has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution, or the offense of a woman, the offense of a girl, the offense of a hand,
the offense against a stūpa, the offense against the Saṅgha, or other such offenses, must alone, day and night, confess those grave transgressions before thirty-five Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
In this regard, the instruction is as follows: "I, [name], go for refuge to the Buddha;
I go for refuge to the Dharma."
I go for refuge to the Saṅgha.
Homage to Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Homage to Vajrapramardin. Homage to Ratnārcis.
Homage to Nāgeśvararāja! Homage to Vīrasena!
Homage to Vīranandin!
Homage to Ratnaśrī!
Homage to Ratnacandraprabha!
Homage to Amoghadarśin!
Homage to Ratnacandra!
Homage to Nirmala!
Homage to Vimala!
Homage to Śūradatta!
Homage to Brahmā!
Homage to Brahmadatta!
Homage to Varuṇa!
Homage to the god Varuṇa!
Homage to Bhadraśrī!
Homage to Chandanaśrī!
Homage to Anantaujas! Homage to Prabhāsaśrī!
Homage to Aśokaśrī!
Homage to Nārāyaṇa! Homage to Kusumaśrī!
Homage to the Tathāgata Brahmajyotirvikrīḍitābhijña.
Homage to Dhanaśrī. Homage to Smṛtiśrī.
Homage to the one whose glorious name is well-proclaimed! Homage to Indraketudhvajarāja!
Homage to Suvikrāntaśrī!
Homage to Vicitrasaṃkrama!
Homage to Vikrāntagāmin! Homage to Samantāvabhāsavyūhaśrī!
Homage to Ratnapadmavikrāmin!
Homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnapadmasupratiṣṭhitaśailendrarāja!

May all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, headed by these, who currently reside, remain, and maintain themselves throughout all world-systems—may those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, attend to me: whatever evil karma I may have committed, caused to be committed, or rejoiced in while wandering through this present birth or other births in the beginningless cycle of existence; may they bear witness to it.
Whether property belonging to a stūpa or the Saṅgha has been stolen, or was caused to be stolen, or is being stolen, and one has rejoiced in it;
or whether the five acts of immediate retribution have been committed, or caused to be committed, or are being committed, and one has rejoiced in them;
or whether one has undertaken and practiced the ten unwholesome paths of action, or incited others to undertake them, or they are currently being practiced [by others].

or have rejoiced in [the commission of such acts], by which karmic obstruction I might be hindered so as to go to hell, or to the animal realm, or to the domain of Yama; or be reborn among the borderlands or among the barbarians; or be born among the long-lived gods; or fall into the impairment of the sense faculties; or embrace false views; or cause the non-appearance of a Buddha.

I confess all those karmic obscurations in the presence of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— who have become wisdom, who have become eyes, who have become witnesses, who have become authorities, and who know and see— and I reveal them; I do not conceal them, and I undertake restraint for the future.

May those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, attend to me: whatever gift I may have given in this life, or in other lives, or while wandering through the beginningless cycle of births and deaths— even as much as a single morsel of food given to one born in the animal realm— or whatever morality I may have observed, and whatever root of merit from my dwelling in the holy life, and whatever root of merit from my ripening of sentient beings.

Whatever root of merit of mine consists of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and whatever root of merit of mine consists of unsurpassed knowledge— having gathered all that together, weighed it, and condensed it— I dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening through a progressively superior dedication, just as it was dedicated by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, and just as the Buddhas of the future will dedicate it.
Just as the Blessed Ones— the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones currently existing in the ten directions— now dedicate [their merit], so do I also dedicate;
I rejoice in all merit.
I entreat all the Buddhas:
may I attain unsurpassed wisdom!
Those Tathāgatas who have passed away, those who have not yet come, and those supreme among men, the Victors, who currently abide—[I entreat them all].
With palms joined in reverence, I go for refuge to all those of infinite color, who are like oceans of virtue;
those heroic Bodhisattvas endowed with the power of compassion who wander the world for the benefit of sentient beings—may they protect me, a constant evildoer.
To those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, I go for refuge.

Thus, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva should effect the purification of evil by taking these thirty-five Buddhas as the foremost and attending upon all the Tathāgatas with mental orientations that follow them.

When his every evil is thus purified, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest their faces to him solely for the sake of liberating sentient beings; they manifest various forms and appearances for the purpose of maturing confused, foolish, and ordinary people. ... [pe] ...

It is not possible for the assemblies of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas to purify the state of remorse for an offense as a Bodhisattva does— by holding and proclaiming the names of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, day and night, and by setting in motion the Dharma discourse of the Three Aggregates— thereby emerging from the remorse for offenses and attaining meditative concentration.

The practice of revulsion has been explained; now the practice of the counteragent is being described. In that regard, through familiarity with profound sūtras, there comes about the destruction of evil.
As it is said in the Vajracchedikā:
"Subhūti, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who shall take up such sūtras as these, and even master them, they will be despised, indeed thoroughly despised."
For what reason?

Because those actions performed by those beings in previous lives which were conducive to rebirth in the miserable states will be exhausted in this very life through that contempt, and they shall attain the awakening of a Buddha.
Even through conviction in emptiness, purification of evil occurs, according to the statement in the *Tathāgatagarbhasūtra*:

"Kāśyapa, if one were to deprive of life one who is both a father and a pratyekabuddha, this is the foremost of acts of killing. This is the foremost of acts of taking what is not given, namely, the seizing of the property of the Triple Gem."

This is the foremost of sexual misconducts, namely: that one’s mother should be an Arhat. This is the foremost of false speech, namely: the slandering of a Tathāgata. This is the foremost of divisive speech, namely: the disparagement of the Noble Saṅgha.
This is the foremost of harsh words: namely, the reviling of the noble ones.
This is the foremost of frivolous chatter: namely, the distraction of those who desire the Dharma.
This is the foremost of ill-will: namely, the drawing near of the immediate transgressions.
This is the foremost of covetous thoughts: namely, the intention to steal the gains of those who have attained the right path.
This is the foremost of wrong views: namely, the view of impenetrable density. These, Kāśyapa, are the ten unwholesome paths of action that are most blameworthy.
Kāśyapa, if a single sentient being were endowed with these ten unwholesome paths of action, which are so greatly blameworthy,
yet were to enter into the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma associated with causes and conditions—
realizing that herein there is no self, no sentient being, no life-principle, and no person who acts or experiences [the result]— [he would be liberated].

For he enters into the uncreated, non-conditioned illusory nature of phenomena, the nature of non-defilement, and the natural luminosity of all phenomena; he places his faith in and resolves upon all phenomena as being primordially pure.
Of such a being, I do not say that he will go to the states of woe.
It is also said in the *Karmāvaraṇaviśuddhi-sūtra*:
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, that bodhisattva who perceives an offense as no offense, and perceives what is not discipline as discipline..."
He perceives affliction and purification;
he perceives the realm of saṃsāra and the realm of nirvāṇa;
he attains the purification of the obstruction of karma.
In the *Trisamayarāja* as well, the practice of the counteragent to evil is taught.
Closing one's eyes, with the mind focused upon the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra eight thousand times.
While the eyes remain closed, one sees the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and becomes free from evil.

Alternatively, while circumambulating a stūpa, one should recite it eight thousand times; having placed either a stūpa, an image, or a book of the True Dharma before oneself, this is the same procedure.
Alternatively, one should recite the Cundā-dhāraṇī until one perceives signs of the destruction of evil in a dream;
namely, by vomiting, or by eating curds, milk, and so forth, one becomes free from evil;
or by spitting up [the food], or by seeing the moon and sun, or by traveling through the sky, or by defeating a blazing fire, a buffalo, or a black man.

From seeing the community of monks and nuns, from climbing down from a milk-tree, an elephant, a bull, a mountain, a lion-throne, or a palace, and from hearing the Dharma, the destruction of evil deeds is to be recognized.
In the *Tathāgataguhya-sūtra* (The Chapter on the Image of the Tathāgata), the practice of the antidote is also taught as follows:

"Just as a man smeared with excrement, having bathed thoroughly and washed himself clean, is then anointed with perfumes—his foul odor is thus vomited up and eliminated; even so, the evil of one who has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution is eliminated."

Even one who is endowed with the ten unwholesome paths of action, if they obtain faith in the Tathāgata and have an image of the Tathāgata made, even their sin is not perceived; especially so for one endowed with the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), especially for one who has gone forth from the household life, and especially for one possessed of ethical discipline.
It is also said in the *Puṣpakūṭadhāraṇī*:
"Furthermore, if someone were to attend upon the Tathāgata Siṃhavikrīḍita in person for a year, or a thousand years, or a hundred thousand years, providing all the requisites for happiness;

and if another were to place even a single flower at the stūpa of a Tathāgata who has entered parinirvāṇa, while being embraced by the thought of awakening (bodhicitta)—[the latter would generate far greater merit]."

For the sake of worshipping the Tathāgata, one might raise joined palms toward the people, or sprinkle water, or offer a blade of grass, or remove the faded flowers, or perform the offering of anointing, or the offering of flowers, or the offering of lamps, with a joyful mind; or, having stepped forward even a single stride, one utters these words:

"Oṃ, homage to that Buddha, the Blessed One!"— if, upon merely saying this, there should be any hesitation, doubt, or uncertainty regarding the Lion’s Play [Samādhi], such that one might fall into the miserable states of existence for an eon, or a hundred eons, or a thousand eons— that is impossible.
It is also stated in the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha-rāja-sūtra*: "Those who uphold the five precepts,
and those who uphold the ten precepts..."
And those who uphold the fourth hundred training rules of the bodhisattva vow;
furthermore, those monks who have gone forth from the household life and uphold two hundred and fifty training rules;
and those nuns who uphold five hundred training rules.
And those who have fallen away from any of the precepts of the training vows as they were undertaken—

if, being terrified by the fear of miserable rebirths, they should hold the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaiḍūryaprabharāja, and perform worship according to their means— then no further descent into the states of woe is to be expected for them.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Do you have faith, Ānanda? Do you believe?"
As I describe the virtues of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaiḍūryaprabharāja,
may you have no doubt, uncertainty, or hesitation regarding this profound sphere of the Buddha.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Blessed One, I have no doubt, nor perplexity, nor uncertainty regarding the discourses spoken by the Tathāgata. Why is that?"
There is no lack of purity in the conduct of body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgatas.
Blessed One, these very sun and moon, so possessed of great supernatural power and such great majesty, might fall to the earth;
Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, might move from its place.
But the word of the Buddhas can never be otherwise.
However, Venerable Blessed One, there are sentient beings deficient in the faculty of faith who, upon hearing of the Buddha’s domain, do not believe it; they think to themselves:
"How can such qualities and benefits arise from that Tathāgata by the mere recollection of his name?"
They do not believe it, they do not trust it,
and they reject it.
For a long time, this will lead to their misfortune, harm, suffering, and downfall.

The Blessed One said: "It is impossible, Ānanda, it is out of the question that those into whose ears his name should fall would go to a state of woe or an evil rebirth. And, Ānanda, the range of the Buddhas is difficult to believe."
And that which you, Ānanda, believe and trust in— this should be seen as the power of the Tathāgata;
for this is not the domain of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, with the exception of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas who are bound to only one more birth.
And it is said in this very same place:
"Furthermore, other faithful sons of good family or daughters of good family who observe the fast endowed with the eight limbs,
or who maintain the precepts for one year or for three years."
Those who have such an intention and such a vow:
"By this root of merit, may we be reborn in the western direction, in the world-system Sukhāvatī, where the Tathāgata Amitābha resides"—
and by whom the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaiḍūryaprabharāja, has been heard.
At the time of their death, eight bodhisattvas will come by means of their supernatural power and show them the way;
they will appear there through spontaneous birth upon lotuses of various colors,
while some will be reborn in the world of the gods.
For those who have been reborn there, that previous root of merit is not exhausted,
and they will have no fear of falling into the miserable states of existence.
Having passed away from there, they become kings in this human world.
As universal monarchs, lords of the four continents,
they establish many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings in the ten paths of wholesome action;
others, moreover, are reborn in great kṣatriya families.
They are reborn in families of great brahmins,
or they are reborn in families of great householders who possess abundant wealth, grain, treasuries, and storehouses;
they become endowed with physical beauty.
They become endowed with a retinue.
It is said in that very same place: "Furthermore, by whichever woman the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaiḍūryaprabharāja, shall have been heard or taken up..."
This should be expected to be his final existence as a woman.
It is also said in the *Mañjuśrībuddhakṣetraguṇavyūhālaṃkārasūtra*: "With devotion, I bow down to Jñānottaraprabhāketu, Praṇidhānamati, Śāntendriya, and Mañjughoṣa."
Whoever should hold in mind the names of these bodhisattvas,
for that woman, the state of being female will no longer exist.
The practice of the antidotes has thus been explained in brief.
The power of restoration is now being explained.

As it is said in the *Āryakṣitigarbhasūtra*: "The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, abstaining from taking life, grants fearlessness to all sentient beings; he is without terror, without distress, and without horripilation by virtue of that root of merit and the ripening of that karma."

Whatever karmic obscuration, afflictive obscuration, or dharma obscuration may have been committed, caused to be committed, or approved by him— through the causes of taking life, whether by body, speech, or mind, mounted upon the wheel of the five destinies throughout the limit of the past and flowing in the river of saṃsāra—
all that he crushes into total ruin by means of this wheel of abstaining from taking life.
Until it has been fully ripened without remainder,
one becomes dear to gods and humans within that same class of beings, free from affliction, and long-lived.

Furthermore, noble son, whichever bodhisattva refrains from taking what is not given for as long as life lasts gives fearlessness to all sentient beings; he dwells satisfied with his own gains, without effort or agitation. Having no desire for unrighteous enjoyments, by that root of merit he crushes and utterly destroys the karmic obstructions caused by taking what is not given, until they are rendered entirely without fruition.
... [and so forth] ...
Thus, all ten wholesome paths of action are taught therein as destroyers of their respective opposites, the unwholesome.
Likewise, in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*, it is heard that through the abandonment of malice, all evil is exhausted,
as it says:
"I shall endure here the false reviling of fools."
The Leader will endure both verbal abuse and threats.
"I shall exhaust the evil karma that was committed by me in the past,
[thinking] 'I have generated malice toward other bodhisattvas.'"
The power of restoration has been explained.
However, the power of the basis must now be explained.
In this regard, the *Sūkarikā-avadāna* should be cited:
"Those who go for refuge to the Buddha do not go to an evil rebirth;
having abandoned their human bodies, they obtain divine bodies."
Thus, by taking refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha in this manner, there is the destruction of evil.
In the *Āryamaitreyavimokṣa*, however, the purification of evil through the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is taught:
it is like the fire at the end of an eon because it incinerates all misdeeds;
it is like the underworld (*pātāla*) because it brings all unwholesome phenomena to exhaustion. ... [and so forth] ...
It is like this, noble son: there is a type of elixir called *hāṭakaprabhāsa*.
A single *pala* of it turns a thousand *palas* of iron into gold;
yet that single *pala* cannot be exhausted by those thousand *palas* of iron.
It cannot be turned into copper.

In the very same way, this single essence-element of the resolve for omniscience, when embraced by the knowledge of the dedication of roots of merit, exhausts all the metals of the obscurations of karma and afflictions, and renders all phenomena the color of omniscience.
Furthermore, the flavor-element of the resolve for omniscience cannot be defiled or exhausted by the metals of all karma and afflictions.
For example, noble son, just as a single lamp, when brought into any house or dwelling, dispels even the darkness accumulated over a thousand years the moment it enters and provides illumination.
In the same way, when this single lamp of the resolve for omniscience is introduced into the dense thicket of a sentient being’s disposition— which is permeated by the blinding darkness of ignorance—
it dispels, upon its entry, even the blinding darkness of the obscurations of karma and afflictions accumulated over hundreds of thousands of inexpressible eons,
and it brings forth the light of wisdom.
Just as, noble son, for the great nāga kings who wear crowns of the king of wish-fulfilling jewels there is no fear of harm from others,

even so, for bodhisattvas who have bound on the crown of the king of wish-fulfilling jewels of the thought of awakening and great compassion, there is no fear of harm from others regarding the miserable states or the lower realms.
It is also said in the *Āryopāliparipṛcchā*: "In this regard, Upāli, if a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna should incur an offense during the morning time,
but should dwell at the time of midday unseparated from the mind of omniscience, the aggregate of ethical discipline of that bodhisattva remains indeed limitless."

If one should incur an offense at the time of midday, but at the time of evening remains undissociated from the mind of omniscience, the aggregate of ethical discipline of that bodhisattva is indeed limitless. This rule has been stated for every watch of the day.
For in this way, Upāli, is the training with its exemptions for those bodhisattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna.
In that regard, a bodhisattva should not give rise to an excessive obsession with remorse, nor should he be one who feels excessive regret.

However, if a person belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle repeatedly commits an offense, it should be understood that the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha) of that Śrāvaka person has been destroyed. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, "Purification of Evil," in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.
[IX. The Perfection of Patience] The Ninth Chapter: The Perfection of Patience (Kṣāntipāramitā)

Thus, protecting against the arising of wickedness—which proceeds incessantly and brings much suffering—and likewise removing the obstruction of karmic hindrances, one should strive for the purification of the afflictions.
In that regard, one should first of all practice patience.
For the vigor of one who lacks patience is obstructed in study and the like, because of an inability to endure weariness;
and one who has not studied does not know the means for meditative concentration.
Nor is it the means for purifying the afflictions;
therefore, one should seek learning without weariness.
For even from the perspective of knowledge, it is difficult to achieve meditative concentration for one who wanders amidst distractions.
Then one should resort to the forest;
even there, the mind of one who is not devoted to the pacification of distraction does not become concentrated,
and thus one should apply oneself to concentration.
And for one who is concentrated, there is no fruit other than the purification of the afflictions;
therefore, one should cultivate the meditation on the foul and so forth.
Thus, these are the summary headings for the purification of the afflictions.
Now the exposition is stated.
In that regard, three kinds of patience (*kṣānti*) are taught in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:
the patience of enduring suffering (*duḥkhādhivāsanakṣānti*).
These are: the patience of reflecting on the Dharma and the patience of enduring harm from others.
Among these, the opposite of the patience of enduring suffering is the fear of suffering resulting from the arrival of what is undesirable.
Furthermore, there is the occurrence of the frustration of what is desired and attachment to pleasure; from those two arises mental distress, and from that, hatred and dejection.
Therefore, it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
"Non-attachment to pleasure;
non-aversion toward suffering."
It is also said in the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*:
"Whatever these internal sorrows, lamentations, sufferings, dejections, and despairs may be, he endures them and tolerates them."
It is also said in the *Āryogradattaparipṛcchā*:
"Furthermore, householder, a lay bodhisattva should be free from attachment and aversion, and unsmeared by the eight worldly dharmas.
He should neither be uplifted nor exultant because of the acquisition of enjoyments, or the acquisition of a wife and children, or the acquisition of wealth, grain, and property."
In all misfortunes, he should not be dejected, nor should he become despondent; rather, he should reflect in this way:
"All conditioned phenomena are like illusions, characterized by the appearance of mental fabrications."
For these— namely mother, father, son, wife, female and male slaves, laborers, servants, friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations— are produced by the ripening of karma;
they are not my own.
"I am not one of these."
Moreover: if there is indeed a remedy for it, what is the use of despondency? Even when there is a remedy, one who is dejected and overwhelmed by anger may become deluded.
Or, due to despondency, one whose enthusiasm is destroyed is seized by supreme calamity;
through constant reflection on that, one's short life passes away in vain again and again.
Therefore, through practice, one should abandon this [mind], which is useless and fraught with harm.
And how is the relinquishing of mental distress practiced? By means of the gradual and gentle relinquishing of the mind.
As it is said in the *Ugratattaparipṛcchā*:
"Because the mind is like something from which cotton-wool has been removed."
It is also said in the *Āryagaṇḍavyūha*:
"O girl, you should generate an invincible mind for the destruction of all afflictions;
an unconquerable mind for the shattering of all attachments."
The unshakable mind [is maintained] even when one has entered the whirlpools of the ocean of uneven dispositions.
Moreover, there is nothing whatsoever that is difficult for practice.

For instance, even among those who are most dull-witted— such as porters, fishermen, and farmers— their minds, marked by calluses formed through the habituation to hardship, are not overcome by despondency even when the object [of their labor] yields only a meager result.

How much more so, then, regarding an action that has as its fruit the attainment of all the happiness of cyclic existence, the happiness of all bodhisattvas, and the state of unsurpassed enlightenment?
Even ordinary people, when struck by their own misdeeds against those who have done them some slight harm—those who are themselves dying—still engage in combat despite the pain of severe blows.

How much more so, then, toward those who cause harm over the longest duration of time, who steal even a fraction of the wealth of virtue acquired through suffering, and who are the slayers of those who should not be killed, namely, those in the hells?

Even toward those who are the wardens of the prison of existence, who destroy the direction of the door of escape, who cause intense affliction even when appearing favorable, and who are enemies that have harbored enmity for countless eons— enemies who, like food, have bound one with firm hatred— there would be no enthusiasm to strike them back, nor any endurance of suffering.
This is especially true for one who has girded his loins for the conquest of the three worlds, fighting to liberate the world-captives held by the savage Māra.
In that regard, through the prior practice of [contemplating] one's own suffering, the practice of what is difficult and even more difficult becomes accomplished;
just as, by the power of habituation, sentient beings perceive suffering as pleasure.
Likewise, through the practice of establishing the perception of happiness in the arising of all sufferings, only the perception of happiness becomes established.
This is its outflow fruit, and he attains the samādhi called "Pervaded by the Happiness of All Dharmas."
For it is said in the *Pitāputrasamāgama*:
"Lord, there is a samādhi called 'Transcending All Phenomena into Bliss. By the attainment of this samādhi, a bodhisattva experiences only pleasant feeling toward all objective referents."
Nor does he experience anything that is neither painful nor pleasant;

even when undergoing the tortures of hell, the perception of pleasure alone arises within him. Even when undergoing human tortures—whether his hands, feet, ears, or nose are being cut off—the perception of pleasure alone arises within him.
Even when being struck with canes, or even with half-caned whips, or even with leather straps, the perception of pleasure alone arises; even when cast into prisons... [etc. ...pe... [as before].
Whether being cooked in oil,
or being crushed like sugarcane,
or being pressed like reeds, or being set ablaze by an oil lamp, or being set ablaze by a lamp of ghee or a lamp of curd— only the perception of pleasure is present.
It occurs as if one were being carried off by a firebrand-mouthed [demon], or being carried off by a lion-mouthed [demon], or as if a dry wick were being burned. ... [etc. ...

Whether being cut with a kārṣāpaṇa coin, or being ground in a mill, or being trampled by elephants, only the perception of pleasure arises. Even when having one’s eyes plucked out, or being subjected to the "living stake" torture, or being executed in every way, or having one’s head struck down, only the perception of pleasure arises;
the perception of suffering does not.
Nor is there the perception of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
For what reason?
Because for a long time, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, this was his vow:
"May those who feed me..."
May they all become attainers of the bliss of tranquility and peace—

those who would protect me, honor me, revere me, respect me, and worship me. And may even those who would revile me, insult me, strike me, cut me with weapons, or even deprive me entirely of life, all become attainers of the bliss of perfect enlightenment.
May they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Endowed with these mental orientations, by means of this action, and possessed of these aspirations, he cultivates, practices, develops, and frequently exercises the perception of happiness that extends toward all sentient beings.
As the maturation of that action, he attains the samādhi called "Pervaded by the Happiness of All Dharmas."
At the time when the Bodhisattva has attained the samādhi called "Pervaded by the Bliss of All Dharmas," at that time he becomes unshakeable and cannot be led away by any of the deeds of Māra;
such is the detailed account.
For this practice fulfills all renunciations;
it accomplishes all conduct and the difficult practices; it strengthens all forbearances; it establishes all vigor;
and it is the accumulation of the factors of all meditative concentrations and wisdom.
Therefore, one should be constantly joyful.
As it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
"One should always be respectful and joyful in mind;
one should always abide in a gentle gaze."
And it is said in the Akṣayamati-sūtra:

"In that regard, what is sympathetic joy (*muditā*)? It is the joy, clarity, and gladness arising from the recollection of the Dharma; it is the mind's lack of dejection, its lack of depression, and its lack of thirsting."
It is the removal of delight in all sensual pleasures and the foundation for delight in all dharmas;
it is joy of mind, exultation of body, gladdening of the intellect, and elation of the spirit;
it is the delight in rejoicing at the body of a Tathāgata and skill in seeking the adornment of the primary marks and secondary characteristics.
It is tirelessness in hearing wholesome dharmas;
joy, serene confidence, and gladness in the practice that takes the true dharma as its refuge; the surging forth of the dharma for one who rejoices;
and constant, unimpeded intelligence regarding sentient beings.
Intense aspiration;
not relinquishing that desire for the Dharma in the pursuit of the Buddha-dharmas;
and resolute conviction in the sublime Buddha-dharmas.
Liberation is the production of a thought that is not drawn back by limited vehicles; it is the production of a thought uncontracted by stinginess;
and it is the desire to give when requested.
Rejoicing in generosity that is purified by the three spheres, both while giving and having given; always maintaining serene confidence toward those who possess ethical discipline;
and feeling affectionate compassion for those who lack ethical discipline.
Through the purification of one's own ethical discipline, there is the consolation of transcending all foul odors;
this consists in dedicating it toward the ethical discipline of a Tathāgata and being firm and indivisible.
An unobstructed state of mind toward the paths of speech consisting of the ill-spoken and the ill-conceived; patience and gentleness; and freedom from pride.
It is showing respect and bowing down before teachers;

always having a smiling face and being free from frowning; being the first to speak, being without hypocrisy, and being without guile; having a pure intention, and being without harshness of mind or crookedness.
Seeing the benefits in all things, reflecting upon one's own transgressions, not reproaching others for their offenses, conforming to the qualities that inspire affection,
and regarding Bodhisattvas with the same love as for the Teacher.
Love for the teachings as love for oneself; love for the Tathāgatas as love for one's life;
love for teachers as love for one's parents.
Love for all beings like that for one's own son; love for teachers and preceptors like that for a Buddha;
and love for spiritual practices like that for one's own head.
The love for one's hands and feet is directed toward the perfections;
the love for all jewels is directed toward the Dharma-preachers;
and the love for all delights and play is directed toward the instructions.
Love for health is found in contentment;
love for medicine is found in the search for the Dharma;
and love for a physician is found in those who exhort and remind.
Thus, that state in which the faculties are not depressed among all the sense-faculties is called "joy," and so forth.
And in this regard, this statement adorns those bodhisattvas who have been trained, as it is said in the *Āryamahāmegha*:
"They possess the discipline of constant mental concentration upon the state of rebirth in hell; they are fond of the state of rebirth in hell; they are like merchants traveling to the city of hell;
they are eager for hell; they are greedy and stingy regarding hell; and their minds are well-accustomed to the fires of hell."
The patience of enduring suffering has been explained.

In the *Āryasāgaramati-sūtra*, however, all three types of patience (*kṣānti*) are taught: "In this regard, Sāgaramati, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is being harassed, provoked, agitated, or threatened by ignoble beings of immoral conduct, or by Māras, or by deities belonging to the retinue of Māra, or by those possessed by Māra, or by messengers of Māra— [all] with respect to the jewel that is the production of the mind set on omniscience— "
Though being struck, it is not broken;
therefore, the arousal of the mind of resolute intention is not broken because of the undertaking of great compassion and vigor for the liberation of all sentient beings.
It is not broken because of the prowess in ensuring that the lineage of the Three Jewels is never interrupted.
It is not divided from the skillful application of gathering all dharmas;
it is not divided from the accumulation of the equipment of merit directed toward the perfection of the primary marks and secondary characteristics;
it is not divided from the zeal brought forth by the accomplishment of the purification of the buddha-field.
He does not waver from his dedication to relinquishing body and life for the sake of non-appropriation of all phenomena;
he does not waver from his dedication to maturing all sentient beings through his lack of attachment to his own happiness.
Being thus endowed with such high resolve, he endures insults from all sentient beings.
He endures the disrespect and contempt of all sentient beings; he endures their abuse, reviling, and the paths of speech consisting of harsh words and insults.
He endures the affliction of all sentient beings and bears the burdens of all sentient beings, rescuing them without ever becoming weary.
And he does not shrink back,
he does not cower,
and he does not despair.
He displays strength,
generates power,
and exerts vigor.
He exerts valor;
he generates enthusiasm;
he restrains the deluded mind.
When reviled, he does not revile in return;
when struck, he does not strike back;
when provoked to anger, he does not respond with anger.
He does not respond with anger to one who is angry;
in this way, he girds himself with the armor of mental reckoning.
... Furthermore, even if all those beings as many as are manifest throughout the ten directions were to follow closely behind me, each equipped with swords, spears, javelins, and maces...

In whatever place on this earth he may stand, sit, walk, or lie down, and wherever he shall generate the thought of awakening, or the thought of generosity, up to the thought of wisdom, or the thought of roots of merit derived from learning— in that very spot on the earth, we shall cut his body into a hundred pieces the size of jujube leaves, dismember it, and destroy it.

If all those sentient beings were to revile me, abuse me, despise me, disparage me, address me with untruthful words or harsh words, or— if possessed by harmful intent— cut, break, mangle, and destroy my body into a hundred pieces the size of jujube leaves; [even so, I would remain unmoved].
Thus, I must not give rise to a disturbed mind toward any sentient being.
Why is that?
Because the prior limit of saṃsāra has been rendered immeasurable, wherein this body of mine existed even when I was in the realms of hell and even when I was in the animal realm.
Whether in the realm of Yama or in the human realm, being obsessed with the nutriment of sensual desires, having not heard the Dharma, dwelling in the sphere of a wrong livelihood,

living a life devoid of purpose, and having my limbs and members cut, split, and hacked into a hundred pieces, and being made to undergo various forms of torture— I have not, on that account, accomplished the welfare of myself nor the welfare of others.
