Furthermore, even if all these sentient beings were to repeatedly cut, break, scatter, and destroy me until the very end of the future limit, nevertheless, omniscience would not be abandoned by me;
all sentient beings would not be abandoned;
and the wholesome desire for the Dharma would not be abandoned.
For what reason?
Because all this bodily affliction and bodily transformation does not approach even a hundredth part of the suffering of a denizen of hell; indeed, it does not even bear comparison.
I would even endure dwelling in the hells;
yet I must never abandon the Buddha-dharmas, nor the great compassion that takes all sentient beings as its object... [etc.]...
Whatever cause might give rise to ill-will again, that phenomenon we shall abandon.
And what is that phenomenon?
Namely: affection for the body, dwelling in the body, and attachment to the body;

yet, having relinquished the body, he has relinquished ill-will. Thus, Sāgaramati, a bodhisattva who is engaged in the reckoning of phenomena endures all harm from sentient beings... [pe] ... The final "pe" indicates an ellipsis, suggesting that the passage continues with further details regarding the bodhisattva's practice of patience and endurance.
That which is the relinquishing of the body, the renunciation of the body, and the lack of regard for the body—
this is his perfection of generosity.
When his body is being cut, he pervades all sentient beings with loving-kindness and is not distracted by the sensations;
this is his perfection of ethical discipline.
When his body is being cut, he endures it for the sake of the very liberation of those who cut his body;
yet his mind is not harmed, and he demonstrates the power of patience—this is his perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
By means of that vigor, he does not abandon his aspiration for omniscience; he embraces it as dependent upon the power of the mind, continues to follow the cycle of existence itself,
and undertakes the very initiation of the roots of virtue.
This is his perfection of vigor.
When the body is being dismembered, that jewel of the resolve for omniscience does not become confused; it looks only toward awakening and contemplates only peace and utter tranquility.
This is his perfection of meditative concentration.
When the body is being cut, he contemplates the body as being like grass, wood, or a wall, and like a mere reflection; he enters into the illusory nature of the body.
He thoroughly reflects upon the body’s true impermanence, its true suffering, its true selflessness, and its true peace.
This is his perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and so forth. ... [pe] ...
Furthermore, it occurs to him:
"This being is indolent and devoid of wholesome qualities;
he reviles and abuses me."
"Come now, we shall become those who have initiated vigor;
unsatiated and devoted to the pursuit of roots of goodness,
I myself must first establish this very being upon the seat of awakening."
"Afterwards, I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. ... [as before] ...
For the sake of such beings who are untamed, unguarded, and unpacified, we must don our armor. ... [as before] ...
"Come now, we shall rely upon the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Who here reviles, or who is reviled?
Searching for it, he does not perceive that phenomenon."
He who either reviles or is reviled is one who, being free from the view of apprehension that perceives neither self nor others, practices patience.
It is also said in the *Bhagavatī*:
"One generates the thought in this way:
'By me, the disputes of all sentient beings must be dispelled.'"
Thus, I myself engage in dispute.
It is a misfortune for me that I prattle back in response to what is said.
For I ought to be a bridge for all sentient beings, yet I even speak the words, "You! to another.
"I shall not give harsh retorts;
this must certainly not be spoken by me, who am like one who is dull-witted.
In quarrels and disputes, I must remain like one who is mute as a sheep."
When hearing from others words that are ill-spoken, ill-received, or ill-articulated, one should not harbor malice in the mind.
Toward others, one should think: "It is neither good nor fitting for me that I should give rise to a sense of fault in another;
it is not fitting for me even to consider listening to the faults of others."
For what reason?

Because I must not disturb my intention, by which I must bring happiness to all sentient beings through every provision of happiness and lead them to final nirvana after I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
yet here I am becoming ill-tempered.
I must not harbor malice even toward others who have wronged me;
it is for me to fall into delusion and agitation—that is what I am doing.
But this is what I ought to do: [to remain undisturbed].
One should exert oneself with firm valor;
even if my life were being cut short, I must not allow myself to be disturbed,
nor should I knit my brows in a frown.
It is also said in the *Bodhisattvaprātimokṣa*: "Those beings who are angry, he comforts them, asks their forgiveness, conciliates them, and satisfies them with the Dharma."
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Perfection of Patience, in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.
[X. The Perfection of Vigor] The Tenth Chapter: The Perfection of Vigor (vīryapāramitā).
Thus established in patience, one should exert effort in learning;
otherwise, that very learning leads to one's own ruin.
As it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
"However many Dharma-discourses one may master, if one does not guard moral discipline while bowing to learning,
that person cannot be saved by great erudition when proceeding toward an evil rebirth due to immoral conduct."
The benefits of learning, however, are stated in the *Nārāyaṇaparipṛcchā*:
"For indeed, noble sons, for one who has learned there is the attainment of wisdom;
for one who possesses wisdom there is the pacification of the afflictions."
Māra finds no opportunity against one who is free from afflictions.
And here, having related the Jātaka of the Great Seer Uttara in detail, it says: "For those who desire the Dharma, O Vimalatejas..."

Vimalatejas, for those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who possess reverence and respect, even the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones residing in other world-systems, manifest their faces and cause the Dharma to be heard by those who desire the Dharma.

For the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, Dharma-treasuries have been deposited within mountains, caves, and among trees. Infinite gateways of the Dharma, committed to books, come to be held in the palms of their hands.
For those Bodhisattvas of stainless splendor who desire the Dharma and have beheld previous Buddhas, deities bring forth the inspired eloquence of the Buddha. ... [pe] ...
For those whose lifespan is exhausted, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the deities bestow longevity and strength.
Through the empowerment of the Buddhas and the empowerment of the deities, they remain for a thousand years, as long as they so desire. ... [pe] ...

For as long as an eon, or for the remainder of an eon, or for as long as they desire, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, remove even old age and remove diseases from those bodhisattvas who have conceived reverence for the Dharma; they bestow mindfulness upon them.
They bestow movement, intelligence, and eloquence... [etc. ...
They dispel their dogmatic views and establish right view out of reverence for the Dharma.
Vimalatejas,
for bodhisattva mahāsattvas there are no fears arising from any external attacks.
Therefore, Vimalatejas, a bodhisattva should be one who is devoted to skill in the equipment of learning.
In what form is learning praised in the Bodhisattva-vinaya?
As it is stated in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*:
"Learning consists of an entry into eighty aspects."

That is to say: the aspect of aspiration, the aspect of intention, the aspect of resolute intention, the aspect of application, the aspect of emanation, the aspect of the immeasurable, the aspect of the spiritual friend,
the aspect of reverence, the aspect of circumambulation, the aspect of pleasant speech, the aspect of attendance, the aspect of lending an attentive ear, and the aspect of mental engagement.

It has the aspect of non-distraction, the aspect of stability, the aspect of perceiving [the Dharma] as a jewel, the aspect of perceiving it as medicine, the aspect of pacifying all diseases, the aspect of cultivating mindfulness, the aspect of awakening to the goal, the aspect of illuminating the intellect, the aspect of entering into wisdom, the aspect of insatiable hearing of the Buddha-dharma,
the aspect of increasing renunciation, the aspect of being a well-trained and noble steed, the aspect of attending upon the learned, and the aspect of experiencing joy in performing what is true.
The aspect of physical exhilaration; the aspect of mental refreshment; the aspect of listening without weariness; the aspect of listening to the Dharma; the aspect of listening to the practice;

the aspect of listening to the instructions of others; the aspect of listening to what has not been heard before; the aspect of listening to the superknowledges (*abhijñā*); the aspect of listening without longing for other vehicles;
the aspect of listening to the *prajñāpāramitā*; the aspect of listening to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; and the aspect of listening to the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

The aspect of hearing skill in means; the aspect of hearing the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*); the aspect of hearing mindfulness and clear comprehension (*smṛti-saṃprajanya*); the aspect of reverence; the aspect of hearing skill in arising; the aspect of hearing skill in non-arising; the aspect of the foul (*aśubha*); the aspect of hearing loving-kindness (*maitrī*); the aspect of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); the aspect of impermanence (*anitya*); the aspect of suffering (*duḥkha*); the aspect of selflessness (*anātman*); the aspect of peace (*śānta*); and the aspects of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness (*śūnyatā-nimitta-apraṇihita*).
It has the aspect of non-accumulation of food; the aspect of wholesome formative activity; the aspect of empowerment over sentient beings; the aspect of non-wastage; the aspect of self-mastery;

the aspect of guarding one’s own mind; the aspect of non-laxity in vigor; the aspect of profound reflection on the Dharma; the aspect of being the antidote to the afflictions; the aspect of drawing in one’s own side; the aspect of subduing the afflictions of the opposing side; the aspect of converging upon the seven riches; and the aspect of severing all poverty.

It has the aspect of being praised by all the wise; the aspect of being celebrated by the learned; the aspect of being esteemed by the noble ones; the aspect of inspiring faith in those who are not noble;

the aspect of the vision of truth; the aspect of avoiding the faults of the aggregates; the aspect of weighing the defects of the conditioned; the aspect of relying on the meaning; the aspect of relying on the Dharma; the aspect of refraining from all evil; the aspect of benefiting oneself and others; and the aspect of not regretting well-performed deeds.
It has the aspect of proceeding toward distinction and the aspect of attaining all the qualities of a Buddha.
Furthermore, it says in this very same place: "That which is the application of the equipment of Dharma (*dharmasaṃbhāra*) is itself his equipment of knowledge (*jñānasaṃbhāra*).

In that regard, what is the application of the equipment of Dharma? It is this: having few aims, few activities, speaking little, and having few requisites; and for one who is devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, it is the thorough reflection upon the meaning of what has been heard."
Repeated and continuous investigation;
clarity of mind;
and the suppression of the hindrances.
Knowledge of the escape from transgressions,
freedom from remorse,
and the absence of obsessive mental afflictions.
The essence of practice;
being inclined toward the Dharma, leaning toward the Dharma, and tending toward the Dharma;
being endowed with heroic exertion, like one whose head or clothing are on fire, in the pursuit of knowledge.
Dwelling in that [state], having a relaxed discipline, not casting off the burden, progressing toward excellence, avoiding social crowds, delighting in solitude,

directing the mind toward the forest, contentment with the noble lineages, immovability in the ascetic virtues (*dhutaguṇa*), taking pleasure and delight in the garden of the Dharma, and not recollecting worldly mantras.
The pursuit of supramundane dharmas, the non-forgetfulness of mindfulness,
the following of the course of meaning,
and the conformity to the path through intelligence.
Through steadfastness and the conditions of restraint, there is the following of knowledge;
through shame and dread of blame, there is the adornment;
and through the following of knowledge, there is the essence.
The dispelling of ignorance;
the purification of the eye of wisdom for one who is enveloped by the cataract of the darkness and gloom of the delusion of nescience;
and the state of perfectly pure intelligence.
The vastness of the Buddha’s wisdom, the non-contracted nature of his wisdom, the unimpeded nature of his wisdom, and the direct perceptual nature of his wisdom.
The state of having qualities that are not dependent on others;
the absence of pride regarding one's own qualities;
and the proclamation of the qualities of others.
Performing well-done deeds,
being unshakable regarding the ripening of karma,
and the knowledge of the purification of karma.
What is to be heard?
It was said by the Blessed One in the *Jñānavaipulyasūtra*:
"One should study treatises that are meaningful."
Those that are meaningless should be avoided. Namely:

the treatises on materialism (lokāyata), the treatises on statecraft (daṇḍanīti), the treatises on sorcery (kārkheda), the treatises on the art of debate (vādavidyā), the treatises on children’s games, and the treatises on the science of sorcerers (jambhakavidyā). ... [as before] ...
Furthermore, whatever other treatises there may be that are contrary to liberation and lead to delusion—all these must be avoided by one who has set out upon the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Thus, having heard this, one who wishes to purify the mind should resort to the forest.
But how is it that even for one endowed with the right intention, living at home is permitted in the *Ugradattaparipṛcchā*?
Because of incapacity despite one's effort.
In that case, would there not be no offense even regarding the wives of others and so forth?
No; for although one may lack the capacity, those acts are inherently corrupt (*prakṛti-duṣṭa*), whereas living as a householder is a fault by convention (*prajñapti-sāvadya*).
Thus ends the tenth chapter, on the Perfection of Vigor, in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.
[XI. araṇyasaṃvarṇanaḥ] The eleventh chapter, titled "The Praise of the Forest."

Thus, having contemplated the faults of the household life according to the method of the *Ugradattaparipṛcchā*, it is established that one who possesses learning must resort to the forest in order to purify the mind.

And so it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*: "One who indulges in sensual desires, having generated craving for sons and wives, and who dwells in a loathsome home, shall never attain the unsurpassed, supreme enlightenment."
Those who avoid sensual desires as they would a pit of fire, having abandoned craving for children and wives,
and who go forth from their homes in fear— for them, this supreme enlightenment is not difficult to attain.
No Buddha existed in the past, nor will there be one in the future who remains [in this world];
yet by those very ones who remained in the midst of the household life, this supreme, foremost enlightenment was attained.
Having abandoned kingship like a lump of spittle, one who desires solitude should dwell in the forests;
having abandoned the afflictions and struck down pride, they awaken to the stainless, unconditioned enlightenment. ...pe...
The Jinas, the supreme among men, are not served by means of food, drink, robes, flowers, perfumes, and ointments in the same way as they are when one has gone forth and practices the Dharma.
And whoever, longing for awakening and out of weariness with conditioned things for the sake of sentient beings,
should walk seven steps toward the forest, this person's merit becomes superior to that [former one].
If, however, one should delay in entering seclusion due to attachment to dissimilar beings, or out of a desire for company, or a desire for gain and the like—for that reason it is said right here:
"The wise do not engage in disputes with fools; they avoid fools with respect."
And with malice toward me, they do not associate with those who possess the qualities of the foolish.
The wise do not cultivate intimacy with fools, having understood the continuous nature of fools' character;
however long they may be well-served, fools once again become like enemies.
The wise do not place their trust in fools here, having understood the nature and continuity of fools;
since fools are by nature alienated, how indeed can there be a friend among ordinary persons?

When addressed with words consistent with the Dharma, they manifest anger, malice, and lack of confidence; these are the characteristics of fools, for having understood this matter, they do not place their trust.
For fools indeed associate with fools, just as filth mingles with filth;
but the wise associate with wise people, just as clarified butter blends with the cream of ghee.
And furthermore, it says in this very same place:
"Those people in the world of men who always possess nothing pleasant or unpleasant are truly well-happened;
and those who do not take delight in mountain caves experience the sublime happiness of the ascetic life."
But those in whom there is nothing whatsoever of mine,
and in whom there is no grasping at all—
like rhinoceroses they wander through the world, moving like the wind in the sky.
Happy indeed are those in the world of men whose minds do not cling to the world;
their hearts here are always like the wind, and they have no attachment to the pleasant or the unpleasant.
Dwelling with those who are unpleasant and suffering, and separation from those who are pleasant and suffering—
having abandoned both of these at the end, they are happy, delighting in the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is said in this very same place:

"The practitioner who is constantly engaged in few activities, having abandoned all faults along with their manifold qualities, never engages in dispute; such are the qualities that belong to one disciplined in yoga who dwells in the forest."
He is always disenchanted with the conditioned; he has no longing for anything whatsoever in the world.
There is no increase of the outflows for him, and these benefits accrue to him who dwells in the forest.

For one who always delights in tranquility and dwells in seclusion, no legal dispute ever arises; for one who is restrained in speech, mind, and body, many virtues come to pass through dwelling in the forest.

Liberation becomes favorable for him; he swiftly penetrates peaceful resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). For one who dwells in the forest and cultivates resolute conviction, all these qualities of a forest-dweller arise.
Furthermore, it says: "Always resort to secluded forest groves, abandoning delight in villages and towns;
always remain like a peerless rhinoceros, and before long you shall attain the supreme samādhi. Thus it is said.

The *Ārya-rāṣṭrapāla-sūtra* also says: "Having abandoned the home, which is a thicket of infinite faults, those virtuous ones— free from anxiety, with peaceful senses and gentle natures— always find delight in the forest."
Neither the company of women nor that of men is ever found among them;
solitary like rhinoceroses, they dwell with pure intentions and stainless minds.
They feel no joy because of gains, nor does their own mind sink under losses;
having few desires, they delight in one another, being free from deceit and hypocrisy.
It is also said in the *Ugratattaparipṛcchā*:
"I must not form an attachment to sentient beings; for I should not cultivate roots of virtue for only a single sentient being," and so forth.
Furthermore, if one who has heard [the Dharma], having attained this perfection of the opportune moment, remains attached to gain and the like and does not purify his mind,
he alone would be deceived in the world including the gods.
For it is said in the *Āryaratnakūṭa*:
"Kāśyapa, it is just as if some man, being carried away by a great ocean of water, were to die of thirst for water.
In the same way, Kāśyapa, here some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, having taken up and mastered many teachings, do not dispel the thirst of passion."
They do not dispel the thirst of hatred nor the thirst of delusion;
being carried away by the great ocean of Dharma, they nevertheless pass away through the thirst of the afflictions.
They become those who go to the miserable destinies and the states of ruin.
Therefore, one must certainly take refuge in the forest.
And he should resort to such places as those where the alms-round for food is neither too far nor too near;
and where there are waters that are clear, pure, stainless, easy to obtain with little effort, and pleasant to use for drinking.

And he should resort to such places as are well-provided with trees, well-provided with flowers, well-provided with fruits, well-provided with leaves, free from wicked beasts of prey, well-provided with caves, well-provided with mountain slopes, pleasant for walking about, peaceful, and solitary.

Resorting to those places, he recites three times during the night and three times during the day what has been previously studied by him; neither with too loud a voice nor with too low a voice, with his sense-faculties not agitated and his mind not wandering outward, subsisting on clarity, retaining the text, grasping the signs, and warding off drowsiness.
If a king, a royal official, or others— whether Brahmins, Kshatriyas, merchants, or country folk— should approach a forest-dwelling monk,
he should perform a hospitable greeting for them with respect,
and he should speak to them as follows:
"Sit down, Great King, on the seat as it has been prepared. If he sits down, both of you should sit down; if he does not sit down, neither of you should sit down."

If one's faculties are restless, they should be uplifted: "It is a great gain for you, O Great King, well-attained by you, that in your territory there dwell virtuous, meritorious, and learned śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas,
and that they are free from harassment by thieves, soldiers, and the like."
If he is steadfast, disciplined, with senses calmed, and capable of receiving the teaching of the Dharma, then a varied exposition of the Dharma should be presented to him.
If he does not take pleasure in the varied exposition, then an exposition of the Dharma conducive to spiritual urgency (saṃvega) should be presented.
If he does not take pleasure in that which is conducive to spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), then the most sublime and magnificent qualities of the Tathāgata’s greatness should be taught.
Furthermore, when brahmins, kṣatriyas, merchants, or country folk approach him, he should perform appropriate actions for each according to their station.
Being thus one of great learning, he is capable of satisfying the minds of those who come to hear the Dharma.
And those beings, in his presence, obtain joy, serene confidence, and gladness.
It is also said in the *Ugratattaparipṛcchā*:
"Furthermore, householder, a bodhisattva who has gone forth and is dwelling in the forest should investigate in this way:
'For what purpose do I dwell in the forest?'"
One does not become a śramaṇa merely by dwelling in the forest;
many who are undisciplined, untrained, unapplied, and lacking in application also reside there.
For example:
Herds of deer, flocks of birds, thieves, and outcastes dwell there, yet they do not possess the qualities of a śramaṇa.
Nevertheless, I must fulfill that purpose for which I dwell in the forest—namely, the purpose of the śramaṇa state. ... [pe] ...
Furthermore, householder, a bodhisattva who has gone forth and dwells in the forest should investigate in this way: "For what purpose have I come to the forest?
He should examine it thus:
I have come to the forest terrified by fear.
Terrified by what fear?
Terrified by the fear of social entanglement.

He was terrified of social entanglement; he was terrified of the fear of passion, hatred, and delusion; he was terrified of the fear of pride, intoxication, hypocrisy, and burning anguish; he was terrified of the fear of greed, envy, and stinginess; he was terrified of the fear of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles;
he was terrified of the fear of the notions of "I" and "mine";
and he was terrified of the fear of restlessness and doubt.
Terrified by the fear of the Māra of the aggregates, terrified by the fear of the Māra of the afflictions, and terrified by the fear of the Māra of death.
He is terrified by the fear of the Māra who is a son of the gods;

he is terrified by the fear of the perversion that perceives the impermanent as permanent; he is terrified by the fear of the perversion that perceives the non-self as self; he is terrified by the fear of the perversion that perceives the impure as pure;
and he is terrified by the fear of the perversion that perceives suffering as happiness.
Terrified by mind, intellect, and consciousness;
terrified by the hindrances, obstructions, and obsessions;
terrified by the view of a self-identity; and terrified by evil friends.

He is afraid of gain and honor; he is afraid of the fear of untimely mantras; he is afraid of the fear of claiming to have seen what was not seen, afraid of the fear of claiming to have heard what was not heard, afraid of the fear of claiming to have thought what was not thought, and afraid of the fear of claiming to have cognized what was not cognized; he is afraid of the pride of being a *śramaṇa* when he is not a *śramaṇa*, afraid of the fear of mutual hatred, and afraid of the fear of the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.

Terrified by the fear of birth in all states of existence and destinies, terrified by the fear of the hells, the animal realm, and the world of hungry ghosts—in short, terrified of all unwholesome mental engagements—it is out of fear of such terrors and horrors as these that I have come to dwell in the forest. ... [as before] ...

Furthermore, householder, a bodhisattva who has gone forth and dwells in the forest, if he is afraid or terrified, should train himself thus: "Whatever fears arise, they all arise from grasping at a self. ... [as above] ...

Furthermore, if, while dwelling in the forest, I were not to abandon the grasping at a self, the adherence to a self, the appropriation of a self, the source of a self, the craving for a self, the perception of a self, the clinging to the doctrine of a self, the view of a self, the basis of a self, the conceptualization of a self, and the protection of a self; [then I would not be fulfilling my purpose].
"My dwelling in the forest would be purposeless; moreover, householder, for one who perceives a self, there is no dwelling in the forest, nor for one who perceives another. ... [as above] ...
"Householder, what is called 'dwelling in the forest' is dwelling in the non-arising of all phenomena; it is dwelling in non-attachment to all phenomena... [etc. ... "

"Just as, householder, the grasses, shrubs, herbs, and forest trees dwelling in the wilderness do not fear, are not startled, are not terrified, and do not fall into a state of panic; even so, householder, a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in the wilderness should conceive of his body as being like grass, shrubs, herbs, forest trees, wood, or a wall, and should conceive of it as a mere reflection, and should generate a mind that is equal to an illusion."
Who is afraid here?
Who is terrified in this?
One who is thus frightened or terrified should examine the body in this way with proper attention:
In this body there is no self, nor a sentient being, nor a living soul, nor a nourisher, nor a person, nor a human, nor a man.
This which is called "fear" is merely an unreal conceptualization;
that unreal conceptualization must not be conceptualized by me.

Therefore, just as grasses, shrubs, herbs, and forest trees dwell in the wilderness— without "mine-ness" and without possessiveness— in the very same way, one should dwell having attained and realized that all phenomena are indeed like the wilderness, being without "mine-ness" and without possessiveness. For what reason?
Cutting off strife, dwelling in the forest, being without "mine-ness," and without possession. ... [etc. ...
Furthermore, householder, a renunciant bodhisattva, knowing that dwelling in the forest is authorized by the Buddha, should dwell in the forest;
for herein the fulfillment of pure qualities occurs.
Having established the roots of virtue, I shall afterwards enter villages, towns, market towns, provinces, and royal capitals to teach the Dharma... [as before]...

Furthermore, householder, if a renunciant bodhisattva enters a group for the purpose of instruction and recitation, he should be respectful and reverent toward his teachers and preceptors, and he should behave with courtesy toward the elder, middle-ranking, and junior monks. He should be untiring, self-reliant, and not cause distress to others; nor should he be one who makes a heavy burden of receiving service.
And he should investigate in this way:

"Even the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—who is honored by the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and by this generation of recluses and brahmins—is worthy of offerings from all beings; yet even he does not accept service from anyone."
How much more so for us, who are untrained yet desire to train!
Rather, we ourselves shall become attendants to all sentient beings;
we ourselves shall perform service and attendance for others, and we shall never accept service and attendance from anyone else.
For what reason?
Because, householder, for a monk who values personal attendance, the cultivation of virtuous qualities perishes; and those whom he favors will think thus: [“He is partial to us”].
For the sake of providing service, he gathers us together.
Furthermore, it says in this very same place:

"Householder, if a forest-dwelling bodhisattva, desiring to hear the Dharma, or desiring to see his preceptors and teachers, or wishing to inquire after the sick, should come to a lodging within a village, he should set out to return there by evening."
And he should generate this thought:
"If, moreover, his recitation or study is dependent upon others, then while dwelling in a monastery, he should have a mind inclined toward the forest.
This indeed is his dwelling in the forest: perceiving all things as the forest and being insatiable in the search for the Dharma."
It is also said in the *Āryaratnarāśisūtra*:
"Furthermore, if fierce beasts should approach that ordinary person who has not yet attained the fruit while dwelling in that forest hermitage,
he should not give rise to fear or terror therein."
And one should generate this thought:
"Previously, I already approached forest dwelling having renounced body and life;
I should not be afraid here."
One should not be terrified;
rather, having generated loving-kindness, I shall abandon malice and dispel fear.
Even if, despite doing so, those wild beasts were to deprive me of life and devour me, [I would remain undaunted].
Therefore, I should generate this thought:
"It is a great gain for me, a true acquisition for me, that I shall extract the essence from this essenceless body.
Furthermore, these predatory beasts cannot be satisfied by me with mere bait; rather, having devoured my flesh, they will dwell in comfort. ... [as above] ...
Furthermore, if non-human beings— whether of beautiful appearance or ugly appearance— should approach him while he is dwelling in that forest hermitage,
he should neither be attracted by them nor repelled by them.
If deities who have seen previous Buddhas should approach a forest-dwelling monk and put questions to him, [he should remain composed].
In that regard, that forest-dwelling monk should teach the Dharma to those deities according to his ability, according to his strength, and for the sake of their realization of the Dharma.
However, if they should ask questions so profound that the forest-dwelling monk is unable to answer them, he should speak these words with humility: "I am untrained; you must not despise me."
"I shall apply myself and strive in the teaching of the Buddha.
There will come a time, there will come an occasion, when, having heard the realized Dharmas, I shall set aside all talk.
Nevertheless, let your inspired eloquence flow forth."
"We are listeners of the Dharma," [and so on].
While dwelling there in that forest hermitage, he should grasp the sign of the grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, and forest trees.
How do these come to be?
Just as for these things—which are without an owner, without "mine-ness," and without possession—there occurs arising and destruction despite being devoid of volition and devoid of activity.
And there is no one who produces these, nor anyone who causes them to cease.

In this very way, this body is like grass, wood, a wall, or a reflection; it is without an owner, without "mine-ness," without possession, motionless, and devoid of activity, arising through the conjunction of causes and conditions.
It ceases due to the deficiency of causes and conditions;
however, herein no phenomenon whatsoever arises or ceases from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Furthermore, it is said:
while dwelling there in that forest hermitage, he should generate this thought:
"Even though I have come to the forest alone, without a second."
I have no companion whatsoever who might reproach me for my good or evil deeds.
Nevertheless, there are these gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and the Blessed Buddhas who know the disposition of my mind;
they are my witnesses.

Thus, while dwelling here in this forest retreat, I fall under the power of unwholesome thoughts. If, having come this far alone, without a second, unpropped up, without "mine," and without possessions, I were to think thoughts of sensual desire, or think thoughts of ill-will, or think thoughts of cruelty, or think any other unwholesome thought; [then I would have failed].
"I would become no different from these beings who delight in social contact and worldly company;
thus, those gods, nāgas, and yakṣas would have been deceived by me, and the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, would be displeased."
Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, titled "The Praise of the Forest."
[XII. Purification of the Mind] The twelfth chapter: The Purification of the Mind.
Thus, dwelling in the forest in this manner, one should apply oneself to meditative concentration.
For it is said in the Bhagavatī:
"For the sake of those very sentient beings, while practicing the perfection of meditative concentration, he becomes undistracted in mind. Why is that?"
For it occurs to him thus:
"Even the attainment of mundane meditative absorption is difficult for one whose mind is distracted;
how much more so, then, is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Therefore, I must remain with an undistracted mind until I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, it is said in this [sūtra]:

"Moreover, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of meditative concentration, enters into meditative absorption with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects."
Having seen forms with the eye, he does not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics.
For, if he were to dwell unrestrained with respect to the faculty of the eye, covetousness, dejection, or other evil, unwholesome states might take possession of his mind;
therefore, he practices for the sake of restraint over them.
He guards the faculty of the eye;
likewise, having heard sounds with the ear,
and having smelled odors with the nose.
Having tasted flavors with the tongue,
having touched tangible objects with the body,
and having cognized mental phenomena with the mind, one does not grasp at their signs.
He does not grasp at secondary characteristics.
Since, on account of this, evil states might follow upon his mind when it is unrestrained by the faculty of the mind,
he practices for the sake of their restraint.
He guards the faculty of the mind;
whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or speaking, he does not abandon the state of composure even when in a state of non-composure.
He becomes one who is not fickle with his hands.
He does not fidget with his feet, he does not fidget with his face, and he does not speak incoherently.

His sense faculties are undistracted; he is neither arrogant nor haughty, neither restless nor lazy. His body is unagitated, his mind is unagitated; his body is tranquil, his speech is tranquil, and his mind is tranquil.
Whether in seclusion or in public, he maintains the deportment of one who is content. ... [as before] ...
Easy to support, easy to nourish,
with simple needs, his conduct and sphere of activity are excellent;
even amidst social company, his sphere of activity is solitude.
He is equanimous and unchanging in gain and loss;
neither elated nor dejected,
even so in pleasure and pain.
He is equal— unchanging, neither elated nor dejected— in praise and blame, in fame and infamy, and in life and death.
Thus it is toward enemy and friend, toward those who act agreeably... toward the noble and the ignoble.
He is equanimous and unchanging toward sounds, whether they are confused or distinct, and toward forms, whether they are pleasant or unpleasant;
he is neither elated nor dejected.
He is free from attraction and aversion.
Why is that?
Because he perceives all phenomena as empty of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), unarisen, unestablished, and unproduced; such is the detailed explanation.
In that regard, when the mind is sluggish, one should apply stimulation through the cultivation of sympathetic joy;
but when it is agitated, there should be pacification through mental attention to impermanence.
And for the sake of counteracting both [extremes], one should recollect the verse spoken by the noble Rāṣṭrapāla:
"A Buddha, the Great Sage who benefits the world, appears only once in many millions of eons.
That most excellent moment has now been obtained; if you desire liberation, abandon negligence today."
Likewise: "Having observed that this conditioned world is like an illusion and false, and like a dream, before long there will be separation from all that is dear;
nothing here is eternal.
Therefore, exert yourselves and strive constantly in the perfections, the stages, and the powers."
Never let your vigor slacken until you awaken to supreme enlightenment. Thus it is said.
It is also said in the *Ārya-lalitavistara*:
"The three worlds are ablaze with the sufferings of old age and disease, set on fire by the flame of death;
this world, without a protector, is always deluded regarding the escape from existence and wanders like a bee trapped inside a jar."
The three worlds are unstable, resembling autumn clouds; birth and death in this world are like a theatrical stage.
Life in the world passes with a swift and fleeting speed, like a mountain stream or lightning in the sky.
On earth, in the city of the gods, and on the path of the three miserable realms, the multitude of beings, driven by the thirst for existence and ignorance,
wander through the five destinies, unawakened like the revolving wheel of a potter.
O noose of the Kali age, this world is constantly drenched with forms that are dear, with pleasant sounds, with auspicious scents and tastes, and with the blissful touch of excellence—
just like a monkey caught in the snare of a deer-hunter.
The qualities of sensual desire are fraught with fear, full of refuge-seeking, and always productive of enmity; they bring forth much sorrow and calamity.
They are like the edge of a sword and resemble poisonous leaves; they are abandoned by noble persons, just as one discards a jar of excrement.

The qualities of sensual desire always cause the loss of mindfulness, create darkness, and are the cause of fear; they are the constant root of suffering and the means for the growth of the creeper of craving for existence. They are fraught with danger and are ever subject to affliction.
Just as blazing pits of fire are full of terror, so too have these sensual pleasures been understood by the noble ones;
they are like a great mire, like a sword-blade, and like the edge of a razor smeared with honey.

Just as a serpent’s head, just as a jar of excrement, so are these sensual pleasures known by the wise; like a stake for impalement, like the flesh of a bird, like a dog’s leg-bone, and like the moon reflected in water— these qualities of desire are like a reflection, like an echo from a mountain, like a mirage, like a theatrical stage, and like a dream, so they are understood by noble persons.

These qualities of sensual pleasure are momentary and deceptive; they are like an illusion or a mirage, like a false bubble on water or foam. They are unreal, arisen from conceptual construction, as the Buddhas, the wise, have understood.
In the first stage of life, possessing excellent form, beloved and desired, and acting with youthful playfulness,
people abandon one whose vitality and body have been struck down by the sufferings of old age and disease, just as deer desert a dried-up river.
Though he was once excellent in wealth and grain, powerful with many possessions, dear, and beloved— engaging in the ways of a youth—
men abandon him when his wealth has perished and he has fallen into distress, just as they would a desolate wilderness.
Just as a flowering tree or a fruit-bearing tree is a source of joy to people who delight in giving, so too is one who possesses wealth;
but when that seeker is destitute of riches and afflicted by old age, he then becomes as unpleasant as a vulture.
One who is powerful through lordship and wealth, possessing excellent form, bringing delight through union with loved ones and gratifying the senses—
when afflicted by the suffering of old age and disease and his wealth exhausted, he then becomes as unpleasant as death itself.
Wasted by old age and past the prime of life, one becomes like a tree struck by lightning;
like a house decayed by age and full of peril, O Sage, quickly tell us the refuge from old age.
Old age withers the multitude of men and women, just as the māluva creeper dries up a dense grove of śāla trees;
old age robs one of vigor, prowess, and speed, like a man sunk in the mud.

Old age makes the beautiful form ugly; old age robs one of radiance, strength, and stamina; old age constantly takes away happiness and brings about humiliation; old age brings death and robs one of vitality.
The world is afflicted by hundreds of various diseases and the intense suffering of manifold ailments, like deer caught in a fire;
seeing the world overcome by old age and sickness, O Hero, quickly teach the way out of suffering!
Just as in the cold season the great mass of snow robs the vigor of grasses, shrubs, forests, and medicinal herbs,
so too this disease robs the vigor of the world, causing the faculties, physical form, and strength to decline.
In this world, disease brings about the destruction and end of great wealth and grain; it causes humiliation and is ever-present.
It creates obstacles and hatred for what is dear, and it produces a burning fever like the sun in the sky.

Death, passing away, dissolution, and the end of time; constant separation from beloved things and people; and the state of never returning or reuniting—these are like the leaves and fruits of a tree or the current of a river.
Death brings those who possess mastery under its power; death carries them away like a river sweeps away wood.
A man goes forth without a companion, alone and helpless, following the fruit of his own karma.

Death devours many hundreds of living beings, as a sea-monster does the hosts of creatures in the ocean; it swallows them as Garuḍa swallows the serpent, as the king of beasts swallows the elephant, or as fire consumes the grass, herbs, and the multitude of living things. Thus it is said.

It is also said in the *Rājāvavādaka-sūtra*: "For example, O Great King, suppose four mountains were to come from the four directions— solid, substantial, unbroken, without holes, without cavities, well-knit, compact, and touching both the sky and the earth."

Scratching away all grass, wood, branches, leaves, and foliage, and crushing all beings, creatures, and living things— it is not easy to escape from them by speed, nor to turn them back by means of strength, substances, mantras, or medicinal herbs. In the same way, O Great King, these four great terrors approach, from which it is not easy to escape by speed, nor to effect their turning back by means of strength, substances, mantras, or medicinal herbs.
Which four?
Old age, sickness, death, and misfortune.
Old age, Great King, approaches, crushing youth;
disease, Great King, approaches, crushing health;
death approaches, crushing life.
Misfortune, O Great King, approaches, crushing all prosperities.
For what reason?

It is just as when, O Great King, a lion, the king of beasts—endowed with beauty, endowed with speed, and formidable with well-formed claws and fangs—enters among a herd of deer, seizes a deer, and does with it as he pleases.
He does so; and that deer, having encountered the mouth of an exceedingly powerful beast of prey, becomes helpless.
Even so, O Great King, for one who has been pierced by the arrow of death, whose intoxication has departed, who is without refuge, and whose vital organs are being cut asunder—

As the joints are being loosened and the flesh and blood are drying up; as his face becomes overwhelmed by burning heat and thirst; as he is occupied with the flailing of hands and feet, rendered inactive and powerless;

as he is smeared with saliva, snot, pus, urine, and excrement; as only a slight remnant of life remains; as he clings to a new existence from the state of karma; as he is terrified by the fear of the messengers of Yama; as he has fallen under the power of the Night of Time (*kālarātri*); and as his final inhalations and exhalations are being obstructed.
And for this solitary one— without a second, without a companion— who leaves this world and enters the next, who travels upon the great path,

enters the vast wilderness, plunges into the great thicket, encounters the great darkness, is tossed by the great ocean, is carried away by the winds of karma, and proceeds toward a direction where no sign exists, there is nothing else [to rely upon].
There is no other protection, no other refuge, and no other final resort than the Dharma.
For at that time, O Great King, the Dharma becomes the protection, the shelter, the refuge, and the final resort—
just as the heat of fire is for one afflicted by cold.
The non-extinguishing of the fire for one who has lost it;
coolness for one afflicted by heat;
and a cool grove of shade for one who has set out upon a journey.
Cool water for one who is thirsty,
or exquisite food for one who is hungry,
and physicians, medicines, and attendants for one who is ill.
For one who is terrified by fear, the powerful become companions and the virtuous become a refuge.

In the same way, Great King, for one pierced by the arrow of death— devoid of intoxication, without protection, without shelter, and without a resort— there is no other protection and no other resort except for the Dharma.
Therefore, O Great Kings, you must be those who perceive impermanence, who perceive decay and exhaustion, and who are terrified by the fear of death.
O Great King, you must rule the kingdom solely according to the Dharma, not according to what is contrary to the Dharma.
For what reason?
O Great King, even though this body of yours has been thus well-protected for so long, and has been so long satiated and served with pure, exquisite foods— both solid, soft, and relishable—

it will come to its end overcome by hunger and thirst. Likewise, though it was once clothed in various fine garments such as those from Kāśī, Kauśeya silk, fine linen, wool, and flax, at the time of death, while lying upon the final bed, it will be covered in clothes soiled and drenched by the various fluids of perspiration.

It will come to pass, O Great King, that even though your body is thus bathed, anointed, perfumed with incense, adorned with flowers, and made fragrant with sweet scents, it will before long become foul-smelling. Likewise,
even while you are in the midst of your harem, surrounded by a throng of women, and entertained with various songs, instrumental music, and the sounding of drums.
While you are sporting, enjoying yourself, and being entertained with a cheerful mind, yet terrified by the fear of death, your passing will occur amidst extreme suffering and mental distress—
even though, O Great King, your houses are plastered with ointments, well-secured with bolts, and their windows well-shut.

Having reclined upon couches that were illuminated by many incenses, perfumes, flowers, and oil lamps; draped with clusters of silk ribbons and garlands; strewn with loose blossoms; perfumed by incense burners; and provided with footstools, woolen rugs, *goṇika* blankets, *kācalindika* coverlets, inner curtains, and pillows made of both types of fine cloth.

Furthermore, O Great King, though you are currently mounted upon the shoulders of elephants, the backs of horses, or chariots, with conchs and kettledrums being beaten, a parasol being held aloft, and yak-tail fans being waved; though you are followed by many elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, and are being saluted with hundreds of thousands of joined palms—nevertheless, when your vital activity has ceased, your body will lie helpless upon the earth in a cemetery most loathsome and filled with jackals, crows, vultures, and corpses, along with flesh, bones, hair, blood, and fat. Even so, O Great King, your body will remain.

Having experienced the departure [of life], before long he became motionless and was laid upon a bier for the dead; lifted up by four men and carried out through the southern city gate, his mother, father, brothers, sisters, wife, sons, daughters, friends, female and male slaves, laborers, and servants— whose hearts were overcome with grief, whose hair was disheveled, and whose arms were raised— beat their breasts and wailed most piteously.

While the citizens and country-folk were wailing, "Alas, son! Alas, lord! Alas, father! Alas, master!", he was led to the cremation ground while being looked upon with contemptuous glances; there he was devoured by crows, vultures, dogs, jackals, and other scavengers. Furthermore, those bones—whether burnt by fire, buried in the earth, moistened by water, or pulverized by wind, heat, and rain—[are all gone].
"Cast away in every direction and intermediate direction, they will return to that very place as purified beings;
thus all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, thus they are unstable," and so forth in detail.
In that regard, the primary afflictions are attachment, aversion, and delusion; one should first cultivate the antidote for whichever one of these is predominant and avoid its cause.
In that regard, the *Āryaratnamegha* states:
"He cultivates the antidote to passion and avoids the conditions for the arising of passion."
And what is that antidote to passion? And what are those conditions for the arising of passion?
The cultivation of the foul (*aśubhā*) is the antidote to passion.
The most beautiful woman of the land is the condition for the arising of passion. And what is that cultivation of the foul?
It is this: in this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, dirt, filth, skin, flesh, bones, sinews, veins, kidneys, heart, spleen, and lungs.
The intestines, the mesentery, the stomach, the receptacle for digested food, the spleen, the liver, feces, tears,

sweat, saliva, mucus, fat, synovial fluid, marrow, adipose tissue, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, the brain, the brain-matter, and urine— in these things, the Bodhisattva is by nature one who investigates.
As he examines it in this way, it occurs to him:
"Even one who might be a fool, deluded, incapable, and unskilled—even such a person, having understood these things, would not give rise to a mind of passion;
how much more so one of a wise nature?"
For in this way, a bodhisattva becomes one who is abundant in the cultivation of the foul.
It is also said in the *Bhagavatī*:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom understands this very body as it truly is.
For example, Subhūti, just as a butcher or a butcher’s apprentice, having slaughtered a cow and divided it into four quarters with a sharp blade, examines them while standing or sitting."
In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom understands this very body, as it really is, according to its elements:
"In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and also the air element," and so forth.
Furthermore, he said:
"Subhūti, it is just as if there were a farmer’s sack full of various grains: rice, paddy, sesame, husked rice, mung beans, black gram, barley, wheat, lentils, and mustard seeds."
A man with sight, examining these, would recognize:

"This is rice of such a kind; this is *vrīhi*; these are sesame seeds; these are grains; these are mung beans; these are black gram; these are barley; these are wheat; these are lentils; these are mustard seeds."

In the same way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom contemplates this very body, from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by the nails, hair, skin, and body hairs, as full of various kinds of impurity, according to reality: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, and so on, up to the brain, eye-secretion, and ear-secretion," and so forth.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, having gone to a cemetery, sees various forms of dead bodies cast away in the cemetery, abandoned on the bed of the corpse—
those dead for one day, or dead for two days, or dead for three days, or dead for four days, or dead for five days; bloated, discolored, festering, and torn asunder.
He applies this very body to that [state], thinking:
"This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character;
it cannot transcend this natural law."
For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells contemplating the body in the external body... [and so on]...
Furthermore, when he sees dead bodies discarded in a cemetery—
those deceased for six nights being devoured by crows, or by ospreys, or by vultures, or by dogs, or by jackals, or by various other kinds of living creatures—
he applies this very same body to that situation.
This body, too, is of such a nature and such a character;
it cannot transcend this natural law.
Furthermore, when he sees dead bodies discarded in a cemetery—devoured, impure, and foul-smelling—he applies this very same body to that [situation], as described before. ... [pe] ...
Furthermore, when he sees dead bodies on a charnel ground— a skeleton smeared with flesh and blood, bound together by sinews—
he applies this very same body of his as before.
Furthermore, when he sees dead bodies on the charnel ground that have become mere skeletons, with the flesh, blood, and binding of tendons all gone—
he compares this very body as before.
Furthermore, when he sees bones scattered in the various directions and intermediate directions on the charnel ground—
namely, foot-bones in one place and shank-bones in another;
With one [hand] the thigh bones,
with another the pelvic bowl,
with another the backbone, and with another the ribs.
With one [part of his mind] he [contemplates] the bones of the neck; with another, the bones of the arms.
He applies this very same body [as an analogy], as before... [etc. ...up to... [end].
Furthermore, when he sees bones on a cemetery path that have been many years old, dried out by the wind, and resembling conch shells, he applies this very body to that [situation] as before:
"This body, too, has such a nature, such an intrinsic character; it does not transcend this natural law."

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom sees bones on a charnel ground that have been there for many years— disappeared, blue-black, pigeon-colored, putrid, reduced to powder,
and leveled with the dust of the earth— he applies this very body to that situation: "This body, too, is of such a nature and such a character."
One does not transcend this true nature of phenomena.
This, then, in brief, is the antidote to the manifestation of attachment.
For hatred, the antidote is loving-kindness (maitrī) and not seeing sentient beings as unpleasant.

Alternatively, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the production of affection through a shared purpose such as eating together; in that regard, it is the aspiration, the prayer, the longing, and the rejoicing for the happiness of others.
The meaning is that it is an unafflicted affection (*sneha*), being free from both sensual desire and the motive of seeking a return favor.
That [loving-kindness] is described as threefold in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*:

loving-kindness directed toward sentient beings belongs to bodhisattvas who have first resolved upon awakening; loving-kindness directed toward phenomena belongs to bodhisattvas who have entered into the practice.
The love that has no objective support belongs to those bodhisattvas who have attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena.
Furthermore, it has as its objects (ālambana) the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and sentient beings.

Among these, regarding that which has sentient beings as its object: having previously practiced meditative absorption (dhyāna) by bringing about welfare and happiness for a beloved sentient being, one should then extend loving-kindness (maitrī) toward one who is neutral.
Then toward acquaintances; then toward neutral persons;
then toward neighbors.
Then [he dwells] among those living in his own village;
likewise in another village;
and in this way, having resolved upon and suffused one direction, he dwells having attained it.
Thus it is in the ten directions;
however, for one who takes the Buddhas and others as their object of focus, this effort does not exist.
And that was explained in the *Vajradhvaja-pariṇāmanā*:

"While practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, whatever forms are seen— whether they be pleasing or repulsive— and likewise sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects— whether they be pleasing or repulsive— "
Whether they are blameless, pure, auspicious, noble, and radiant, by means of which gladness arises,
happiness enters,
and clarity is born.
Joy arises; gladness becomes established; rapture manifests.
Mental distress ceases;
mental pliancy appears;
the mind becomes serviceable.
The intention becomes gentle; the faculties attain refreshment;
experiencing constant happiness, one dedicates [the merit] in this way.

By means of this dedication, may those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to a still greater degree be endowed with the inconceivable bliss of the Buddha-abodes, be well-sustained by the incomparable bliss of the Buddha-concentrations, and be supported to a still greater degree by infinite bliss.
May they be endowed with the immeasurable bliss of the Buddha-liberations;
may they be well-sustained by the boundless bliss of the Buddha’s miraculous powers;
may they be well-protected by the inconceivable bliss of the Buddha’s unattached dwelling.
May they be covered by the invincible bliss of the bull-like majesty of the Buddhas; may they be supremely happy through the immeasurable bliss of the powers of the Buddhas;
and may they possess the bliss of their spiritual commitment through the bliss of non-arising, wherein all sensations are stilled.
May they possess unshakeable happiness through the Tathāgata’s bliss—which is characterized by non-dual conduct and is perpetually concentrated in an unattached dwelling.
In this way, having dedicated that root of merit to the Tathāgatas, the bodhisattva dedicates it to the bodhisattvas;
that is to say, he dedicates it for the fulfillment of unfulfilled intentions,
and for the complete purification of unpurified resolute intentions toward omniscience.
For the sake of bringing to completion all the perfections that have not yet been completed;
for the empowerment of the production of the adamantine-like thought of awakening;
and for the non-relaxation of the irreversible armor of omniscience.
For the sake of seeking the roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas;
for the fulfillment of the great vow that abides in the equality of all worlds;
and for the attainment of all the dwellings of the bodhisattvas.
For the sake of the sharpness of the superknowledges of all bodhisattvas' faculties;
for the sake of the attainment of omniscience by means of all bodhisattvas' roots of virtue.

Having thus dedicated that root of merit for the sake of the bodhisattvas, he dedicates that very same root of merit among all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who practice within the Buddha’s teaching: "Whatever beings hear even the sound of the word 'Buddha' for as long as it takes to snap one's fingers, or hear the sound of the Dharma, or perform service to the noble Saṅgha—to them he dedicates that root of merit for unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening; he dedicates it for the fulfillment of the recollection of the Buddha."
He dedicates it for the sake of the application of the recollection of the Dharma;
he dedicates it for the sake of reverence for the noble Saṅgha;
he dedicates it for the sake of not being long deprived of the sight of the Buddha.
He dedicates it for the purification of the mind; he dedicates it for the penetration of the Buddha-dharmas;
he dedicates it for the realization of immeasurable qualities.
He dedicates [the roots of merit] for the sake of purifying all supernormal knowledges and wholesome qualities; he dedicates them for the sake of turning back doubt regarding the Dharma;
and he dedicates them in accordance with those who practice within the Buddha’s teaching.
And likewise, the bodhisattva dedicates that root of merit to all sentient beings, including the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
That is to say, he dedicates it for the purpose of turning back from the path to the hells; he dedicates it for the purpose of cutting off rebirth in the animal realm;
he dedicates it for the sake of the happiness of severing the world of Yama.
He dedicates it for the purpose of severing rebirth in all states of woe and all destinies without exception.
And he dedicates it so that the aspiration for unexcelled enlightenment may increase in all those sentient beings;
he dedicates it so that they may attain the mind of omniscience through resolute intention;
he dedicates it so that they may not reject any of the qualities of a Buddha.
He dedicates [the merit] for the sake of attaining the stage of ultimate bliss and omniscience; he dedicates it for the sake of the ultimate purification of all sentient beings;
he dedicates it for the sake of the attainment of infinite knowledge by all sentient beings... [and so forth].

Whatever activity there is of his—whether it be the procurement of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; coming and going; attending to the body; sitting and so forth; the engagement with the bases of practice; the maintenance of the postures; the non-disturbance of the postures; bodily action, vocal action, and mental action; the conduct accompanied by these; the restraint of the six sense-faculties; and the acts of covering, massaging, and bathing his own body—all this constitutes his [practice].

Whether eating, drinking, chewing, contracting or extending [the limbs], looking forward or looking around, sleeping or waking, or attending to his own body— all these activities of the Bodhisattva who is engaged with the objective of omniscience are not at all untransformed toward omniscience,
for he possesses a mind intent on the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings. ...pe...
He whose mind is intent on protecting the entire world, whose roots of merit are constantly applied, and who has transcended intoxication and negligence... [pe] ...

He is one who has turned his back on all afflictions, whose mind emulates all bodhisattvas, who is unimpeded on the path to omniscience, who cultivates the stages of knowledge, and who delights in dwelling with the wise... [and so forth].
Like a bee [gathering nectar], he was one who accumulated roots of merit, whose mental continuum had transcended the entire world, and who was non-attached to all conditioned phenomena... [etc.]
Even if it be as little as a single grain of rice or a single morsel of food given to others,
even to those born in the animal realm, he dedicates all of that for their very benefit and for their complete liberation—
from that animal birth, from that ocean of suffering, from that grasping at suffering, and from that mass of suffering, and from that painful sensation.

Therefore, for the sake of turning those beings away from that accumulation of suffering, from that formation of suffering, from that cause of suffering, from that root of suffering, and from that basis of suffering, he dedicates [his merit]; and by means of that objective support, he takes all sentient beings as his objective support and brings them to mind.
He makes that root of virtue the precursor therein.
That which he dedicates toward omniscience,
receives through the arousal of the thought of awakening,
and therein brings to maturity that root of virtue.
It turns one back from the wilderness of saṃsāra;
it brings one face-to-face with the unhindered bliss of a Buddha;
and it causes one to emerge from the ocean of saṃsāra.
"He pervades with a loving-kindness dedicated to the Buddha-dharma," and so forth.

And all these verses spoken in the *Suvarṇabhāsa*, which have loving-kindness and compassion as their essence, should be contemplated with reverence and cultivated, at least by means of reciting them aloud.
By means of the *Suvarṇabhāsottama* drum, may sufferings be pacified in the triple-thousandfold world system:
the sufferings of the miserable realms, the sufferings of the world of Yama, and the sufferings of poverty here in this triple world.
By this resounding sound of the drum, may all calamities in the world be pacified;
and may sentient beings become free from fear, just as the Lords of Sages are fearless and their fears have been stilled.

Just as all the noble ones are endowed with virtues and are great oceans of omniscience within saṃsāra, so may all beings become oceans of virtue, endowed with the qualities of meditative concentration and the factors of enlightenment.
By this resounding sound of the drum, may all sentient beings possess the voice of Brahmā;
may they realize the supreme and most excellent awakening of Buddhahood and turn the auspicious wheel of Dharma.
May they remain for inconceivable eons and teach the Dharma for the benefit of the world;
may they destroy the afflictions, dispel sufferings, and pacify passion, as well as hatred and delusion.
May those beings who dwell in the realms of misery, their limbs and bones burning and aflame, hear the proclamation from the drum and utter these words: "Homage to the Buddha!"
May all sentient beings be rememberers of their past lives throughout hundreds of births, thousands of births, and tens of millions of births;
may they constantly recollect the Lords of Sages and hear their sublime speech.
By this resounding sound of the drum, may they always obtain union with the Buddhas;
may they indeed avoid evil deeds and practice wholesome and auspicious actions.
May all the sufferings of all living beings in all fields throughout the world be pacified;
and may those beings who have impaired faculties or missing limbs now possess all their faculties complete.
May all those who are diseased, with weak and emaciated limbs, lying in every direction without protection,
be swiftly liberated from their illness and regain health, strength, and their faculties.

May all those beings who are threatened by kings, thieves, and soldiers; who have been condemned to death; who are beset by hundreds of various fears; and who are fallen into calamity—may they all, who are suffering from such misfortune, be liberated from those hundreds of most terrible fears.
Those who have been beaten, bound in fetters, and tormented, who remain amidst various calamities;
those agitated by many thousands of miseries, and who have encountered diverse, terrifying, and dreadful sorrows.

May they all be released here from their bonds; may those who are being beaten be freed from the beatings; may those condemned to death be reunited with life; and may all who have fallen into calamity become free from fear.
May those beings who are tormented by hunger, thirst, and parching heat obtain various kinds of food and drink;
may the blind see diverse forms, and may the deaf hear delightful sounds.
May those who are naked obtain garments; may destitute beings find a treasure;
and may all sentient beings be happy with abundant wealth, grain, and various jewels.
May no one experience painful sensations; may all sentient beings be endowed with happiness.
May they possess beautiful, pleasing, and gentle forms, and may they always be filled with manifold joys.
May food and drink be abundantly provided for them through their mere thought, as they possess such well-accumulated merit;
may there be lutes, drums, cymbals, and sweet-sounding instruments, as well as springs, lakes, lotus ponds, and reservoirs.
May golden lotuses, blue lotuses, and lotus ponds appear for them by mere thought;
and may there be perfumes, garlands, ointments, garments, powders, and various flowers.
May they rain down from trees at the three times of day; may those beings receive it and become joyful, and may they perform inconceivable worship to all the Tathāgatas in the ten directions.
May they entrust the Dharma and awakening to the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas;
may sentient beings avoid low rebirths and transcend the eight inopportune states.
May they approach the supreme King of Jinas and always obtain union with the Buddhas;
may all women constantly become men, and may they be brave, heroic, wise, and learned.
May they all always practice for the sake of awakening; may they practice the six perfections.

May they behold the Buddhas in the ten directions, seated in bliss upon the lords of jewel-trees, sitting upon thrones of lapis lazuli gems, and may they hear the Dharma as it is being proclaimed. Thus.
This is loving-kindness in brief.
It is the antidote to the manifestation of hatred.
The vision of dependent origination is the antidote for the underlying tendency toward delusion.
In this regard, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is explained in the *Śālistamba-sūtra*.

Therein, what is the causal connection (*hetūpanibandha*) of internal dependent origination? It is as follows: conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*) are the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and so on, up to: conditioned by birth (*jāti*) are aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
If ignorance did not exist, volitional formations would not be perceived;
likewise, up to: if birth did not exist, aging and death would not be perceived.
Thus, when ignorance exists, there is the manifestation of volitional formations.
Thus, as long as birth exists, the production of aging and death occurs.
In that regard, ignorance does not think:
"I am producing the formative forces."
The formative forces (*saṃskāra*) also do not think in this way:
"We have been produced by ignorance. And so on, up to birth (*jāti*), which does not think in this way.
"I bring about old age and death," nor does it occur to old age and death, "I am produced by birth."
And yet, when ignorance exists, there is the production and manifestation of volitional formations;
and so on, until: when birth exists, there is the production and manifestation of old age and death.
In this way, the causal connection of internal dependent origination is to be understood.
How is the conditional dependence of internal dependent origination to be viewed? It is through the coming together of the six elements. Through the coming together of which six elements?
This should be seen as the conditional dependence of internal dependent origination resulting from the combination of the elements of earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness.
In that regard, what is the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*) of internal dependent origination?

That which produces the state of solidity through the cohesion of the body is called the earth element. That which performs the function of supporting the body is called the water element (*abdhātu*).
That which digests what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted by the body is called the fire element (*tejodhātu*).
That which performs the function of inhalation and exhalation for the body is called the wind element (*vāyudhātu*).
That which brings about the state of internal cavities within the body is called the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).

That which brings about name-and-form by means of the union of a bundle of reeds—namely, the five bodies of consciousness together with the tainted mental consciousness—is called the element of consciousness.
When conditions are absent, the arising of the body does not occur.
When the internal earth element is unimpaired, and likewise the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are unimpaired,
then from the conjunction of all these, the arising of the body occurs.
In that regard, it does not occur to the earth element, "I bring about the solid state of the body.
It does not occur to the water element [in this way].
The fire element does not think,
"I perform the function of digesting what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted by the body."
It does not occur to the wind element, "I perform the function of inhalation and exhalation for the body. It does not occur to the space element [in this way].
"I create the porosity within the body"—
the consciousness element does not think in this way; "I am produced by these conditions"— it does not think in this way either.
Nevertheless, when these conditions are present, the arising of the body occurs. In that regard,
the earth element is not a self, not a sentient being, not a living soul, not a creature, not a human, not a person, not a woman, not a man, not a neuter, and it is not "I."
It is not mine, nor does it belong to anyone else whatsoever.
Thus, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element are neither a sentient being nor a living soul.
It is neither a creature, nor a human, nor a man, nor a woman, nor a male, nor a neuter; it is not "I," nor "mine," nor indeed anything belonging to anyone else.
In this context, what is ignorance?

It is the notion of unity, the notion of a whole, the notion of permanence, the notion of stability, the notion of eternity, the notion of pleasure, and the notion of a self with regard to these very six elements; it is the notion of a sentient being, a living soul, a human, or a person; and it is the notion of "I" and "mine."
Such various forms of non-knowing as these are called ignorance (*avidyā*).
When ignorance exists in this way, attachment, aversion, and delusion arise toward objects.
Among those, the attachment, aversion, and delusion directed toward objects are called formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Consciousness is the distinct cognition of objects.
The four formless aggregates that arise simultaneously with consciousness are "name";
together with form—referring to the form derived from the four great elements and the form derived from them, which are condensed together as one—that is "name-and-form."
The sense faculties based upon name-and-form constitute the six sense bases;
the coming together of the three factors is contact;
the experiencing of contact is feeling.
Attachment to sensation is craving;
the expansion of craving is grasping;
and the action born from grasping is that which produces renewed existence.
Existence (*bhava*).
The manifestation of the aggregates (*skandha*) caused by that [existence] is birth (*jāti*).
The maturation of the aggregates is aging (*jarā*), and their destruction is death (*maraṇa*).
Sorrow (*śoka*) is the internal burning of a fool who, at the point of death, is possessed by self-attachment.
Lamentation (*parideva*) is the act of wailing.
Suffering (*duḥkha*) is the experience of the unpleasant associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness.
Mental suffering and dejection associated with mental attention (*manasikāra*), as well as other such secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), are called despair (*upāyāsa*). ... [etc. ...
Furthermore, non-comprehension of reality, false comprehension, and ignorance are what constitute *avidyā*.

When *avidyā* exists in this way, three kinds of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are produced: those leading to merit, those leading to demerit, and those leading to the imperturbable. These are called "formative forces conditioned by ignorance."
For volitional formations leading to merit, consciousness leads to merit; for volitional formations leading to demerit, consciousness leads to demerit;
for volitional formations leading to the imperturbable, consciousness leads to the imperturbable.
This is called "consciousness conditioned by formative forces. Likewise for name-and-form.
Through the growth of name-and-form, functional activities proceed by way of the six sense bases.
That is called "the six sense bases conditioned by name-and-form.
From the six sense bases, the six groups of contact arise; this is called "contact conditioned by the six sense bases.
Whatever the nature of the contact is, a feeling of that same nature arises.
This is called "feeling conditioned by contact. That which experiences it, specifically relishes it, rejoices in it, adheres to it, and becomes fully established in it.
That is called "craving conditioned by feeling":
it is the relishing, the delighting in, and the attachment [to it],
with the thought, "May I not be separated from what is pleasant and agreeable."
Non-relinquishment and repeated longing—
this is called "clinging" (upādāna) conditioned by craving (tṛṣṇā).
Thus longing, one instigates karma that produces renewed existence through body, speech, and mind.
This is called "existence conditioned by grasping.
That which is the manifestation of the aggregates produced from karma is called "birth conditioned by existence.
That which is the destruction of the aggregates manifested through birth, resulting from their accumulation and maturation, [is called aging-and-death].
