Thus, this aging and death are said to have birth as their condition... [etc. ...
Thus, this twelve-linked dependent origination has mutual causes and mutual conditions;
it is neither impermanent nor permanent,
neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
It is not a feeler;
it is neither subject to exhaustion, nor subject to cessation,
nor subject to dispassion.
Having proceeded from beginningless time, it continues uninterrupted like the flow of a river.
Furthermore, four members of this twelvefold dependent origination function as causes for the act of conjunction.
Which four? Namely:
Ignorance, craving, karma, and consciousness.
Among these, consciousness is the cause by virtue of having the nature of a seed;
karma is the cause by virtue of having the nature of a field.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), by virtue of having the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*), are the cause.
Karmic actions and afflictions together produce the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Among these, karma performs the function of the field for the seed of consciousness.
Craving moistens the seed of consciousness;
ignorance sows the seed of consciousness.
In the absence of these conditions, the production of the seed does not occur.
In this regard, it does not occur to karma: "I am performing the function of a field for the seed of consciousness. Nor does it occur to craving: [“I am performing the function of moisture”].
"I moisten the seed of consciousness"—
thus it does not occur to ignorance either:
"I cast down the seed of consciousness."
The seed of consciousness also does not think, "I am produced by these conditions.

Rather, when the seed of consciousness is established in the field of karma, moistened by the moisture of craving, and covered by ignorance, it grows in the womb of a mother at the junction of the various places of birth;
thus, the sprout of name-and-form comes into being.

And that sprout of name-and-form is not self-made, nor made by another, nor made by both; it is not created by a Lord (Īśvara) or the like, nor transformed by time, nor dependent on a single cause, nor is it arisen without a cause.

Nevertheless, through the union of mother and father, the convergence of the season, and the assembly of other conditions, the seed of consciousness—impregnated by craving—produces the seed of the sprout of name-and-form within the mother’s womb.

In phenomena that are without an owner, without "mine-ness," without possession, without adversaries, equal to space, and having the nature of the characteristic of illusion, [all things arise] due to the non-deficiency of causes and conditions.
For example, visual consciousness arises through five causes.
What are these five?
Dependent upon the eye, and dependent upon visible forms, light, space, and the mental attention arising therefrom, visual consciousness arises.
In that regard, the eye performs the function of being the basis for visual consciousness;
visible form performs the function of being the object;
and light performs the function of illumination.
Space performs the function of non-obstruction;
the attention born thereof performs the function of mental engagement.
In the absence of these conditions, visual consciousness does not arise.

When the internal sense-base of the eye is unimpaired, and likewise when visible form, light, space, and the attention arising from them are unimpaired, then, through the complete assembly of all these factors, the arising of visual consciousness occurs.
In that regard, it does not occur to the eye,
"I perform the function of being the basis for visual consciousness," nor does it occur to visible form.
It does not occur to the eye-consciousness, "I perform the function of being an object";
nor does it occur to the light,
"I perform the function of illumination."
It does not occur to space either:
"I perform the function of non-obstruction for the visual consciousness.
Nor does it occur to the attention produced thereby: [the same].
"I perform the function of attending for visual consciousness," nor does the visual consciousness think,
"I am produced by these conditions."
And yet, when these conditions are present, the arising and manifestation of visual consciousness occurs;
the same should be applied accordingly to the remaining sense faculties.
In this regard, no dharma whatsoever transmigrates from this world to the next world;
yet there is the discernment of the fruit of karma,
due to the non-deficiency of causes and conditions.
Just as fire does not burn due to a deficiency of fuel,
even so the seed of consciousness, produced by karma and afflictions, brings forth the sprout of name-and-form in the mother’s womb at the moment of linking to various places of birth,

because there is no deficiency of causes and conditions among phenomena that are without an owner, without "mine-ness," without possession, without an adversary, equal to space, and having the nature of the characteristic of illusion.
Therefore, internal dependent origination should be viewed through five reasons.
By which five?
Not from the perspective of permanence, not from the perspective of annihilation, not from the perspective of transmigration;
because a vast fruit is produced from a small cause, and because there is a continuous succession of similar [states].
How is it not eternal?
Because the aggregates at the time of death are one thing and the aggregates belonging to the state of rebirth are another;
it is not the case that the very same aggregates which are at the time of death are the very same aggregates which belong to the state of rebirth.
Moreover, as the aggregates at the time of death cease, the aggregates pertaining to rebirth manifest;
therefore, it is not eternal.
How is it not from annihilation?
It is not that the aggregates belonging to the state of rebirth appear once the [present] aggregates have ceased, nor do they appear while they have not yet ceased;
rather, the aggregates at the moment of death cease and the aggregates belonging to the state of rebirth appear.
It is like the rising and falling of the arms of a balance scale;
therefore, it is not through annihilation.
How is it not by way of transmigration?
For, from a dissimilar class of beings, aggregates of a similar kind are produced in another birth;
therefore, it is not by way of transmigration.
How is it that from a small cause there arises a vast fruit? A small action is performed, yet a vast ripening of the fruit is experienced;
therefore, there is the production of a vast fruit from a small cause.
How is it [established] by way of a continuous succession of similarity?
Just as the karma to be experienced is performed,
so too is the ripening to be experienced experienced.
Therefore, it is also [defined] by its similarity and its continuity.

"Venerable Śāriputra, whoever [sees] this dependent origination, rightly formulated by the Blessed One, thus as it really is with right wisdom— constantly and continuously as being without a living soul, devoid of a living soul, as it truly is, unerring, unborn,
unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, non-obstructive, unobscured, auspicious, fearless, unassailable, imperishable, and non-ceasing..."
He perceives it as being without intrinsic nature;
he regards it as unreal, empty, void, insubstantial, harmful, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
He does not turn back toward the past limit.
Did I exist in the past, or did I not exist in the past?
Who indeed was I in the past?
Furthermore, one does not resort to the future limit, thinking:
"Shall I exist in the future time, or shall I not exist in the future time?
Who indeed shall I become?"
Furthermore, one does not look back to the present, wondering:
"What is this? How is this?
Who are we? Who shall we become?"
It is also said in the *Āryadaśabhūmika*:
"In that regard, ignorance, craving, and grasping constitute the non-interruption of the path of afflictions (*kleśavartman*);
volitional formations and existence constitute the non-interruption of the path of karma (*karmavartman*)."
The remainder is the non-interruption of the path of suffering.
Furthermore, that which is said— “conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces”—
this refers to the perspective concerning the past limit (*pūrvāntika*).
From consciousness up to feeling—
this refers to the present; from craving up to existence— this refers to the future.
This is the "ultimate limit" (aparāntikī) [view], because its occurrence is subsequent to that; ... [etc. ... // pe //
It occurs to him:
"Through conjunction, the conditioned proceeds; through disjunction, it does not proceed."
Conditioned phenomena proceed from a causal complex;
they do not proceed in the absence of a causal complex.
Come now! Having understood that conditioned phenomena are thus corrupted by manifold defects, we shall effect the severance of this conjunction and of this causal complex.
And yet, we shall not attain the ultimate cessation of all conditioned phenomena for the sake of maturing sentient beings. Thus [he said].
This is, in brief, the purification of delusion.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, titled "The Cultivation of the Mind."
[XIII. The Chapter on the Applications of Mindfulness] The thirteenth chapter is the Chapter on the Applications of Mindfulness.
Thus, with a mind made pliant, one should enter into the applications of mindfulness.
In that context, the application of mindfulness to the body was explained by way of the introduction to the foul.
And that very point has been stated with a slight distinction in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:
"Furthermore, noble son, a bodhisattva establishes mindfulness upon the body in this way:
'This body is merely a collection of feet, toes, calves, thighs, hips, belly, navel, spine, heart, ribs, sides, hands, forearms, upper arms, shoulders, neck, jaw, forehead, and skull.'"
Accumulated by the agent of karmic existence, it has become the dwelling place for hundreds of thousands of various afflictions, conceptualizations, and discursive thoughts;
and herein many substances are gathered together, namely:
Hair, body hair, nails, teeth, bones, skin, flesh, fat, sinews, marrow, grease, lymph, liver, urine, feces, the stomach, blood, saliva, bile, pus, snot, brain, and marrow—
such is this collection of many substances. What, then, in this is the "body"?
As he reflects in this way, it occurs to him:
"This body is equal to space.
He establishes mindfulness upon the body as being like space.
He perceives all this as space;
because of his thorough knowledge of the body, his mindfulness no longer extends or disperses anywhere.
"He does not resort [to them]."
It is further said:
This body has not come from the past;

it does not transmigrate to the future; it does not abide in the interval between the past and the future. Rather, it is produced from unreal inversions, devoid of an agent or an experiencer, and its root is not established in the beginning, the end, or the middle.
Without an owner, without "mine-ness," and without possession.

Through adventitious designations, it is conventionally referred to as the "body," the "deha," the "enjoyment," the "basis," the "physical frame," the "corpse," and the "dwelling place. This body is devoid of essence; it is produced from the blood and semen of the mother and father, having a nature that is impure, putrid, and foul-smelling. It is crowded with the thieves of passion, hatred, delusion, fear, and despondency; it is subject by its very nature to constant falling apart, collapsing, breaking, scattering, and destruction;
and it is led away by hundreds of thousands of various diseases.
In the *Āryaratnacūḍa* it is also said:
"Alas, this body is impermanent, short-lived, and ends in death. Knowing this, one does not live for the sake of the body through improper means, but rather takes hold of what is essential.
He takes up three essentials.
Which three?
The essential of the body, the essential of wealth, and the essential of life.
Thinking, "This body is impermanent," he accepts the status of a servant and a disciple toward all sentient beings and becomes eager to perform whatever needs to be done.
Thinking, "The body is impermanent," he does not engage in any bodily faults, crookedness, guile, or hypocrisy.
Thinking, "The body is impermanent," even when finding comfort in life, he does not commit an evil deed even for the sake of his own life.
Thinking "the body is impermanent," one does not form an attachment or craving for enjoyments;
one becomes as if ready to renounce all possessions.
Furthermore, noble son, when a bodhisattva cultivates the application of mindfulness by contemplating the body within the body, he focuses all the bodies of sentient beings upon his own body.
And he thinks:
"I must establish the bodies of all sentient beings so that they are established in the Buddha-body."

And just as there are no outflows (āsrava) in the body of a Tathāgata, so he contemplates the true nature (dharmatā) of his own body; being skilled in the nature of the absence of outflows, he understands that the bodies of all sentient beings also possess that very same characteristic, and so forth.

It is also said in the *Vīradattaparipṛcchā*: "That is to say, this body has arisen gradually and perishes gradually; it is a collection of atoms, porous, subject to rising and falling, exuding from nine wound-like openings and hair-pores, and like an anthill, it is an abode for venomous serpents."
Ajātaśatru is like a monkey in his treachery toward friends; he is like a bad friend in his nature of deception.
It is naturally weak like a mass of foam;
it arises, breaks, and dissolves like a bubble on water;
its nature is deceptive like a mirage.
Like a plantain tree, it is pithless when peeled away; like an illusion, its nature is deceptive;
like a king, it abounds in commands.
Like an enemy, he watches for an opportunity; like a thief, he is not to be trusted; like an executioner, he does not follow [the victim's] will.
Like an enemy, it seeks one's harm;
like an executioner, it creates an obstacle to the life-force of wisdom;
like an empty village, it is devoid of a self.
It ends in destruction like a potter's vessel;
it is filled with various impurities like a leather bag; and it drips with filth like a cauldron of fat. // pe //
It is like a wound, unable to endure being touched;
it is like a thorn, characterized by piercing;
it is like a dilapidated house, requiring constant repair to maintain.
Like an aged ship, it must be kept afloat by means of repairs;
like an unbaked clay jar, it must be guarded with great effort. ... [etc. ...
It is unstable like a tree on a riverbank;
it ends in the ocean of death like the current of a great river;
and it is an abode of all suffering like a guest-house.
Like a shelter for the destitute, he is unclaimed; like a jailer, he is to be won over by bribes. ... [pe] ...
Like a young child, it must be constantly protected.

It is said again: "He who, conceited about his physical form, highly esteems such a body—a mere heap of impurities—is indeed one whose intellect is childish; for though he knows it as such, he wanders about mindlessly, carrying a jar of excrement."
The nose of this creature discharges various kinds of pus, and its mouth always emits a foul odor; likewise,
there is a discharge from the eyes like that of worms.
What passion or high esteem could there be for that?
Just as a fool, taking up a charcoal, might rub it thinking,
"This shall become white," yet it goes only to destruction and never to whiteness— so too is the intellect of the fool characterized by false conceit.

For in this way, even the body of a man of pure mind who thinks, "I shall make this body clean," though well-anointed and consecrated at hundreds of sacred bathing places, becomes impure and goes to its destruction under the power of death.
Likewise, a bodhisattva should contemplate the body as fragile; a bodhisattva should contemplate the body as a flowing stream through the nine openings;
and a bodhisattva should contemplate the body as a dwelling place.
Of the eighty thousand families of worms... [pe] ...
A Bodhisattva should contemplate the body as food for others—
[the food] of wolves, jackals, dogs, and carnivorous beasts.
A Bodhisattva should contemplate the body as being like a machine.

A bodhisattva should contemplate the body as being bound together by a mechanical assembly of bones and sinews, lacking self-mastery, and produced from food and drink; such is the detailed explanation.
In that very regard, it should be understood:
as for the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), it is as stated in the *Āryaratnacūḍasūtra*:

"In this case, noble son, a bodhisattva, while cultivating the application of mindfulness through the contemplation of feelings within feelings, attains great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for those sentient beings who are dependent upon the pleasure of feeling."
And he trains himself thus:

"That is happiness where there is no feeling; for the sake of abandoning the feelings of all sentient beings, he cultivates the application of mindfulness to feelings regarding feelings, and he dons the armor for the sake of the cessation of the feelings of sentient beings."
He does not personally bring about the cessation of feeling;
whatever feeling he experiences, he experiences it all as embraced by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

When he experiences a pleasant feeling, he then arouses great compassion toward sentient beings who are dominated by passion (*rāga*), and he abandons his own underlying tendency toward passion (*rāgānuśaya*).
When one experiences a painful feeling, one then attains great compassion for sentient beings who are dominated by hatred and abandons the latent tendency toward aversion within oneself.

When one experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one attains great compassion for sentient beings who are dominated by delusion and abandons the latent tendency toward delusion within oneself.
He is not attracted to pleasant feeling and achieves the eradication of attraction;
he is not repelled by painful feeling and achieves the eradication of aversion.
Regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he does not fall into ignorance and achieves the total eradication of ignorance.
Whatever feeling he experiences, he experiences it all as impermanent.
He understands all that as the experience of suffering;
he understands it as the experience of non-self.
He regards pleasant feeling as impermanent.
In painful feeling, he experiences it as a thorn;
in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he experiences it as peace. For indeed, that which is pleasant is impermanent, and that which is painful is itself [the nature of] pleasure.
That which is neither painful nor pleasant is non-self, and so forth.

It is also said in the *Āryākṣayamatisūtra*: "When touched by a painful sensation, one generates great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for all sentient beings who have been born in evil states or unfavorable conditions. ... [omission] ...

Furthermore, indeed, feeling is attachment, feeling is grasping, feeling is appropriation, feeling is apprehension, feeling is perversion, feeling is conceptual construction—such is the beginning [of the description].
It is also said in the Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra:
Feeling is said to be experience.
By whom is this experienced?
No experiencer exists as something other than or separate from feeling.
Thus should mindfulness be established by the wise regarding feeling;
for in this way it is awakening—peaceful, pure, and luminous.
This, in brief, is the application of mindfulness to feelings.
As for the application of mindfulness to the mind, it is as stated in the *Āryaratnakūṭa*:
"He thus searches for the mind:
'Which, indeed, is the mind?'"
One either feels attachment, aversion, or delusion, thinking:
"Is it the past, the future, or the present?
In that regard, what is past has perished.
That which is future has not yet arrived;
for the present, there is no duration.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, is formless, invisible, non-obstructive, non-communicative, non-abiding, and homeless.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, has not been seen by all the Buddhas;
they do not see it, and they will not see it—that which has not been seen by all the Buddhas.
They have not seen them, nor will they see them. Of what nature, then, should his activity be regarded? Apart from this, phenomena proceed through perceptions that have fallen into falsehood.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like an illusion; through unreal conceptualization, it grasps at various types of rebirth. ... [as above] ...
For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like the current of a river: it does not remain still; it arises, breaks apart, and dissolves.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like the flame of a lamp: it proceeds by way of causes and conditions.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like a flash of lightning: it perishes in an instant and does not remain.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like space; it is defiled by adventitious afflictions. ... [etc. ...
For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like a bad friend, because it gives rise to all suffering... [and so on] ...
For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like a fishhook, because it perceives suffering as happiness;
likewise, it is like a blue fly, because it perceives the impure as pure.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like an enemy because it inflicts various kinds of harm;
the mind is like a yakṣa that steals vitality because it is always seeking out vulnerabilities;
likewise, it is like a thief because it robs one of all roots of merit.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, delights in forms; it is like the eye of a moth.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, delights in sounds; it is like a battle drum. For the mind, Kāśyapa, delights in odors; it is like a boar in the midst of filth.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, delights in flavors, like a servant-girl who eats the remnants of a meal. For the mind, Kāśyapa, delights in tactile sensations, like a fly in a vessel of oil.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, when thoroughly sought after, is not found.
That which is not obtained is not apprehended;
that which is not apprehended is neither past, nor future, nor present;
that which is neither past, nor future, nor present has transcended the three times.
That which transcends the three times neither exists nor does not exist, and so forth.
It is also said in the *Āryaratnacūḍasūtra*:
"Searching for the mind, he does not perceive the mind internally;
he does not perceive the mind externally."
One does not perceive the mind in the aggregates;
one does not perceive the mind in the elements;
one does not perceive the mind in the sense bases.
Not perceiving the mind, he investigates the stream of the mind, asking:
"From where does the arising of the mind occur? It occurs to him: "When there is an object, the mind arises."
In that case, is the object of cognition different [from the mind],
or is the object of cognition the very same as the mind? If, first of all, the object of cognition is one thing and the mind is another—
Then there would be a duality of mind;
or else, if the object itself were the mind,
how could the mind perceive the mind?
For the mind does not perceive the mind;
just as it is impossible for that very edge of a sword to cut itself,
and impossible for that very tip of a finger to touch itself.
That very mind cannot be seen by that same mind. ... [as before] ...

Furthermore, noble son, the stabilization of the mind—which is like a monkey or the wind, wandering restlessly and rushing about; which ranges far, is bodiless, quick to change, and lusting after sense objects; which has the six sense bases as its domain and is associated with one thing after another—is said to be "mindfulness of the mind," characterized by one-pointedness, taking refuge in that one-pointedness, being undispersed, and the non-distraction of calm abiding (*śamatha*).
It is also said in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*:
"I must apply myself to the creative construction [of phenomena],
yet this true nature of the mind (*cittadharmatā*) must not be abandoned."
In that regard, what is the true nature of the mind (*cittadharmatā*)?
What is its manifestation (*viṭhapanā*)?
The mind that is like an illusion—this is called the true nature of the mind.
Furthermore, that which consists in relinquishing all one's possessions and dedicating them for the purification of all Buddha-fields—this is called "magical creation" (viṭhapanā), and so forth.
But the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) is as follows:
As it is said in this regard:
"A bodhisattva dwelling in the observation of phenomena within phenomena does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever;
for there is no Buddha-qualities, nor is there awakening."
Since there is neither a path nor an escape,
having realized that all phenomena are without escape, he enters the great compassion concentration called "Non-obstruction.
He perceives all phenomena and all afflictions as being merely artificial.
These dharmas are free from afflictions; they are not possessed of afflictions.
For what reason?
For in this way, these converge upon the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*):
there is no accumulation of afflictions (*kleśa*), nor is there any state of being a heap.
There is no state of passion, no state of hatred, and no state of delusion.
Awakening is the thorough understanding of these very afflictions.
One establishes mindfulness in this way: "Whatever is the intrinsic nature of the afflictions, that is the intrinsic nature of awakening."
It is also said in the *Āryaratnacūḍa*:
"In this regard, noble son, for a bodhisattva dwelling in the application of mindfulness through the contemplation of phenomena as phenomena, it occurs thus:
'Only phenomena arise as they arise.'"
Only phenomena, as they are ceasing, cease.

Furthermore, herein within this personal existence, there is no being, nor life-principle, nor creature, nor nourisher, nor person, nor individual, nor human who is born, or grows old, or passes away, or arises;
such is the true nature of phenomena.
If they are fully acquired,
they are fully realized;
if they are not fully acquired, they are not fully realized.
Whatever kind [of factors] are brought together, such they emerge— whether wholesome, unwholesome, or imperturbable.
There is no bringer-together of phenomena,
nor is there any arising of phenomena that are without cause, and so forth.
In that very same place it says:
"Even while contemplating how profound the dharmas may be, he does not abandon that recollection of the mind of awakening directed toward omniscience."
It is also said in the Noble Lalitavistara Sūtra:

"Conditioned phenomena are impermanent and unstable; they are by nature as fragile as an unbaked clay pot. They are like borrowed ornaments for another's play, and as transient as a city made of sand."
Formations are subject to destruction, like plaster washed away by the rainy season;
like a sandy riverbank, they are dependent on conditions and inherently weak.
Formations are like the flame of a lamp, characterized by rapid arising and ceasing;
they are like the wind, unstable, and like a mass of foam, insubstantial and weak.
Formations are inactive and empty; when examined, they are like the trunk of a plantain tree.
Like an illusion, they delude the mind, resembling an empty fist used to deceive a child.
Everything comprised within conditioned phenomena proceeds by means of causes and conditions through mutual dependence; this, foolish people do not understand.

Just as a rope is twisted from muñja grass and balbaja grass through the power of exertion, and the water-wheel with its buckets revolves, yet in each of those individual parts there is no revolving; so it is here.
In the same way, the process of all factors of existence proceeds by mutual reinforcement and dependence;
yet within each of these, no process can be found from the perspective of either the prior or the subsequent limit.
Just as when there is a seed, there is a sprout, yet that which is the seed is not itself the sprout;
it is neither different from it nor is it exactly that—
so too is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) characterized by neither annihilation nor permanence.
Formative forces have ignorance as their condition, yet those formative forces do not exist in reality;
for both formative forces and ignorance are empty, being by nature inactive.
From a seal, an impression is seen, yet no transfer of the seal is perceived; it is not there, nor does it come from elsewhere.
In this same way, conditioned phenomena are neither annihilated nor eternal.
Depending upon the eye and visible forms, visual consciousness arises here;
yet it does not reside in the eye, nor is there any transfer of form into the eye.
These phenomena are selfless and impure, yet they are imagined to be a self and pure;
from this inverted and unreal conceptualization, visual consciousness arises.
The wise one clearly perceives the arising and ceasing of consciousness, its production and its passing away;
the yogi sees it as empty and like an illusion, having gone nowhere and not coming from anywhere.
Just as fire is produced from the lower fire-stick, the upper fire-stick, and the exertion of the hands coming together— thus arising through conditions— it performs its function and quickly ceases.
Then, if some wise person searches for whence this has come or whither it goes—
searching all paths in every direction and intermediate point— not coming nor going is found.

The aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, as well as craving and ignorance, have karma as their condition; yet this collection is merely a designation for a "sentient being," and it is not apprehended in the ultimate sense.
Depending upon the throat, lips, palate, and the movement of the tongue, syllables arise;
yet they do not reside in the throat, nor in the palates, for not even a single syllable is perceived [therein].
And that speech issues forth by the power of cognition, dependent upon a collection of conditions;
this mind and speech, being invisible in form, are not perceived either externally or internally.
For the wise who discern the arising and passing away of vocal sounds, words, and tones,
all such speech is momentary, insubstantial, and like an echo.
Just as, depending on strings and wood, through the conjunction of the three efforts of the hand,
sound issues forth from instruments such as the *tuṇava*, the *vīṇā*, and the *sughoṣaka*, arising from those very causes.
Then, if some wise person searches for where this [sound] has come from or where it goes—
searching through all directions and intermediate points— he finds no sound that has arrived.
In this way, everything comprised of conditioned phenomena proceeds by means of causes and conditions;
yet the yogi, through the vision of reality, perceives that conditioned phenomena are empty and devoid of activity.
The aggregates, sense bases, and elements are empty—internally empty and externally empty;
they are devoid of a sentient being, a self, and a substrate, having the characteristic of the nature of space-like phenomena.
It is also stated in the *Lokanāthavyākaraṇa*:
All phenomena are empty and nameless; why do you ask about names?
Emptiness is not found anywhere—not among gods, nor among nāgas, nor even among rākṣasas.
Whether they be humans or non-humans, all are found to be thus:
for by its very name, "name-ness" is empty; within the name, no name exists.
All phenomena are nameless, yet they are fully elucidated by means of names.
For that which is called "intrinsic nature" is neither seen nor heard;
it has neither arisen nor ceased—of what, then, do you ask the name here?
The name created by conventional usage is a designation shown as a mere name;
for this one is "Variegated with Jewels" (Ratnacitra) by name, while the other is "Supreme Jewel" (Ratnottama).
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, on the Foundations of Mindfulness, in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.
[XIV. Purity of the Physical Body] The fourteenth chapter is the purity of the physical body.
The applications of mindfulness have been explained.

Thus, with a mind thus prepared, one should enter into the emptiness of all phenomena in order to become a means for the perfect awakening that rescues the rest of the world from the ocean of suffering in the ten directions, and furthermore, in order to attain mastery over all phenomena throughout the three times as far as the limits of space.
In this way, the emptiness of the person (pudgala-śūnyatā) is established;
and consequently, because their root has been severed, the afflictions (kleśas) do not manifest.

As it is said in the *Āryatathāgataguhya-sūtra*: "Śāntamati, just as when the root of a tree is cut, all its branches, leaves, and foliage wither; even so, Śāntamati, through the subsiding of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), all afflictions (*kleśa*) subside."
The benefits of cultivating emptiness, however, are limitless.
As it is said in the Candrapradīpa Sūtra:
"Such a person never falters in the training of the Sugatas;
such a person is a hero who never falls under the power of women."
He finds joy in the teaching of the Sugatas,
he who knows the perfectly peaceful intrinsic nature of phenomena.
Before long, he shall become a lord of bipeds here;
he shall become a physician and healer, a bestower of happiness;
he shall completely extract the thorn of suffering for all who are afflicted.
He who knows that very nature of phenomena to be perfectly tranquil.
That moon among men has risen by the power of patience;
though struck by clods of earth and sticks, he does not become angry;
though his limbs are being cut off one by one, he is not disturbed.
He who knows that very nature of phenomena to be perfectly tranquil.
He shall not fall into the miserable states of existence; he will always possess the primary marks and be handsome with the secondary characteristics.
These five superknowledges will be constantly cultivated by him.
"And that hero shall stand before the Sugatas," and so forth.
It is also said in the *Bhagavatī*:

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to bring the Buddha-body to perfection, who wishes to obtain the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics, and who desires to remember his births in every lifetime and never lose the thought of awakening..."
One who desires to attain non-forgetfulness of the bodhisattva conduct; one who desires to avoid all evil friends and evil companions;
one who desires to please all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends; one who desires to conquer all Māras and the deities belonging to the host of Māra;
one who desires to purify all hindrances; and one who desires to attain the state of being unobstructed regarding all phenomena—such a person should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, residing in the ten directions, should speak his praise, must train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, with a single production of thought, desires to transcend world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā—[and so on]—must train in the perfection of wisdom in all directions; such is the detailed exposition.
In this regard, how all phenomena are selfless,
how there is no contradiction between the relationship of action and its fruit and the lack of intrinsic nature, and how there is no contradiction with all phenomena as they are perceived—
this has been demonstrated in the *Pitṛputrasamāgama*.
"Great King, this person consists of six elements, has six bases of contact,
and possesses eighteen mental explorations.
Great King, this person consists of six elements."
Indeed, this is not logical.
Or rather, with what in mind was it said: "Great King, there are these six elements"?
Which six?
They are as follows: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
These, O Great King, are the six elements.
Furthermore, Great King, there are these six spheres of contact.
Which six?
The sphere of visual contact for the seeing of forms.
The ear is the sense base for contact for the hearing of sounds;
the nose is the sense base for contact for the smelling of odors;
the tongue is the sense base for contact for the tasting of flavors.
The body-sphere of contact is for the touching of tangible objects;
the mind-sphere of contact is for the cognizing of mental phenomena.
These, O Great King, are the six spheres of contact... [pe] ...
"O Great King, there are these eighteen mental explorations (*manopavicāra*).
Which eighteen?
Here, a person, having seen forms with the eye..."
One mentally explores those things that are the bases for mental pleasure (*saumanasya*), mental displeasure (*daurmanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The same should be stated for the ear and the other [senses].
Thus, because each of the six faculties is divided into the three types beginning with mental pleasure, there are eighteen mental explorations (*manopavicāra*). ... [etc. ...
And what, O Great King, is the internal earth element? Whatever in this body is internal, characterized by hardness, having the nature of solidity, and appropriated; what, then, is that?
For example:
head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, and so forth;
this is called the internal earth element.
And what, Great King, is the external earth element?
Whatever is external, hard, solid, and not grasped—this is called the external earth element.
In this regard, Great King, the internal earth element, when arising, does not come from anywhere; when ceasing, it does not go to any accumulation.
There comes a time, O Great King, when a woman internally conceives the notion, "I am a woman.
Having internally conceived the notion, "I am a woman," she externally conceives the notion of a man as "a man.
Having externally conceived the notion of a man as "a man," being filled with passion, she desires union with that external man.
As before, the person conceives "I am the person" with respect to the internal self;
through the desire for union between those two, union occurs,
and from the condition of that union, the embryo (kalala) is born.
In this regard, Great King, both that which is the conceptualization and that which is the conceptualizer—
neither of these exists.
Within a woman, "woman" does not exist.
"In a person, no person is found.
Thus, this non-existent, unreal conceptualization has arisen;
even that conceptualization does not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature.
Just as the conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*) does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), so too the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and even the *kalala* do not exist by way of intrinsic nature.
And that which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature—how could it produce solidity (*kakkhaṭatva*)?
Thus, O Great King, having understood conceptualization, one should understand solidity: just as solidity, when arising, does not come from anywhere.
"When it ceases, it does not go to any accumulation.
There comes a time, Great King, when this body ends in the cemetery;
as its solidity dissolves and ceases, it does not go to the eastern direction.
Not the south, not the west, nor the north.
It goes upward, not downward, nor does it go to the intermediate directions.
In this way, Great King, the internal earth element is to be viewed.
There comes a time, Great King, when the world-system has become like space and a Brahmā-palace made of great jewels is established;
that hardness, Great King, as it arises, does not come from anywhere.
The Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains stand firm, solid, compact, and composed of diamond; even their hardness, as it arises, does not come from anywhere.
Sumeru, the king of mountains, Yugandhara, Nimindhara, Īśādhara, and so on up to Kālaparvata, all stand established.
And the entire trichiliocosm, the great trichiliocosm world-system, stands established.
The great earth stands with a depth of eighty-four thousand yojanas and a width of six million eight hundred thousand yojanas in the middle. Furthermore,
Great King, from where does this solidity arise when it comes into being?
There comes a time, Great King, when this world undergoes dissolution;
at that time, this great earth is either consumed by fire, or dissolved by water, or scattered away by wind.
When it is being consumed by fire, not even soot is produced from it, just as there is none from clarified butter or oil.

Just as when something is being burned by fire, neither its soot nor its shadow is perceived, even so, when this triple-thousand great-thousand world-system is being burned by fire, neither soot nor any remaining shadow is perceived.
Likewise, it is taught that just as salt dissolves in water, or as a bird struck by a Vairambha wind leaves nothing behind on the earth, so too nothing whatsoever remains to be perceived.
In this regard, Great King, the arising of the earth element is empty, its passing away is empty, and even the earth element that has arisen is empty of intrinsic nature.
Thus, Great King, the earth element is not apprehended as an earth element, except as a conventional designation (*vyavahāra*). And that conventional designation is neither female nor male.
In this very way, O Great King, this should be seen as it truly is with correct wisdom.
In that regard, what is the water element?
It is that which is internal, within this body, belonging to oneself, and is water.
It has gone into the water; it is the state of being water, its viscidity, its fluidity, having approached and been appropriated.
Furthermore, what is that?
It is as follows:
tears, sweat, saliva, nasal mucus, grease, synovial fluid, marrow, fat, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, milk, urine, and so forth—this is called the internal water element (*abdhātu*).
... [and so forth] ...
It happens, O Great King, that there is a time when tears flow upon seeing what is dear;
or tears flow when one is struck by suffering or by a sense of spiritual urgency (*dharmasaṃvega*); or the eyes well with moisture due to the wind.
To such an extent, Great King, that element of water does not come from anywhere.
There comes a time, Great King, when the internal element of water dries up; as it dries up and ceases, it does not go anywhere. ... [as before] ...
Furthermore, when the world is undergoing dissolution, thirty-two layers of dense clouds gather on all sides; having gathered,
they completely cover the entire trichiliocosm,
so that for five intermediate kalpas the rain falls in torrents as thick as chariot-poles.
In this way, the god rains in five ways: as an elephant's urine,
in five unbroken streams,
and in five large drops.
Then this great earth becomes filled with water as far as the Brahma-world.
Your Majesty, when that vast element of water arises, it does not come from anywhere.
Your Majesty, there comes a time when this world undergoes dissolution.
Furthermore, when the world is undergoing dissolution, a second sun appears.
With the appearance of this second sun in the world, the springs, lakes, and small rivers dry up;
likewise, with the third sun, the great springs and great rivers dry up.
At the appearance of the fourth sun, the great lake Anavatapta completely dries up in its entirety.
Due to the manifestation of the fourth sun, even water of the great ocean measuring one *yojana* goes to total exhaustion and depletion;
likewise, two *yojanas*, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, and even up to forty thousand *yojanas* of water remain.
Until there remains water only as high as a palm tree,
until it is only as high as the neck,
and until it is only as much as the water in a cow's footprint.
There comes a time, O Great King, when only scattered fragments remain in the great ocean... [as before] ...pe... [end].
There comes a time, Great King, when not even a drop of water the size of a finger’s joint remains in the great ocean.
That element of water, Great King, as it ceases, does not go anywhere. ...
Furthermore, Great King, the arising of that element of water is also empty.

Expenditure is also empty; even while it persists, that water-element is empty of intrinsic nature. For indeed, Great King, the water-element is perceived as a water-element only through mere conventional usage.
That conventional usage, too, is neither female nor male, as previously stated.
What is the internal fire element?
Whatever in this body is fire, belonging to the category of fire, characterized by heat, present, and appropriated—
what, then, is that?
It is that by which this body is warmed and thoroughly heated.

What is the external fire element?
It is that which is external, belonging to fire, characterized by heat, approached, and appropriated.
Furthermore, what is that?
Just as when humans seek fire from things associated with the fire-drill or from things associated with the womb, or by means of cow-dung powder or a cotton wick—

once it has arisen, it burns even a village, it burns even a part of a village, and so on, until it reaches an island, a thicket, a field of grass, a forest, or logs of wood, and having burned them, it passes on— and so forth.
In this regard, Great King, the internal fire element arises; it does not come from anywhere, and when it ceases, it does not go to any accumulation.
Thus, having not existed, it comes to be, and having existed, it passes away, because it is devoid of intrinsic nature.

Thus, whatever in this body is wind, or that which belongs to the category of wind—lightness and mobility—what, then, is that? It is as follows: winds moving upward, winds moving downward, those resting in the sides, those resting in the back, those moving through the belly, the "knife-like" winds, the "razor-like" winds, the "needle-like" winds, the "pippalaka" winds, the "stone-tumor" winds (*vātāṣṭhīlā*), the "ball-tumor" winds (*vātagulma*), and inhalation and exhalation.
"Regarding the winds that follow the limbs, and so forth:
there are external winds—winds from the east, south, west, and north; winds with dust and without dust; winds that are limited and winds that are vast.
There comes a time, Great King, when a great mass of wind arises."
It causes even the tops of trees to fall;
it causes even walls and mountain peaks to fall.
Having caused them to fall, it vanishes without any basis for subsistence.
That which beings seek by means of the hem of a robe, a fan, or a wind-vane—
this is called the external wind element;
its arising is as previously described.
What is the internal space element?
Whatever in this body is internal, belonging to the individual, approached, appropriated, and situated in space— counted here as being internal—
which is not pervaded and cannot be pervaded by skin, flesh, and blood.
What, then, is that?
It is whatever in this body is a cavity, such as the eye, up to the mouth or the opening of the mouth, the throat or the gullet, by which one swallows and in which it remains;
and by which what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted flows out from below.
This is called the internal space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
Likewise, externally, that which is unmanifest, non-pervasive, not obscured by form, and consists of a state of voidness or an aperture—
this is called the external space element.

It happens, O Great King, that at a certain time, due to the condition of karma, the sense-bases (āyatana) manifest and they range within the space-element (ākāśadhātu). Therein, it is designated as the "internal space-element. It does not come from anywhere.
There comes a time when all that possesses form becomes like space.
For what reason?
Because the element of space is inexhaustible, stable, and immovable.
Just as, O Great King, the unconditioned realm of nirvāṇa is,
so too should the realm of space be seen as pervading everywhere.
It is just as if, O Great King, a man were to dig a well, a small pit, a deep well, or a lotus pond on dry land.
"What do you think, Great King: as for that space there, from where did it come?
He replied, "From nowhere at all, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"It is just as if, O Great King, that man were once again to fill that well, or even up to that lotus pond.
What do you think, O Great King: has that space gone anywhere?"
He said:
"It has not gone anywhere, Blessed One. For what reason?"
For the element of space is not present in going or in coming;
it is not present as the female state nor as the male state.
The Blessed One said:
For thus, Great King, the external element of space is immovable and unchanging. Why is that?
For the space-element is empty of the nature of the space-element;
the space-element is devoid of the nature of the space-element;
it does not appear as a male state nor as a female state.
In this very way, it should be seen as it truly is with right wisdom.

In this regard, what is the consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*)? It is the discernment of forms conditioned by the visual faculty. Thus, O Great King, whatever discernment there is of color and shape, this is called the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*). ... [as before] ...
Thus, that representation of objects which is governed by the six sense-faculties and has the six objects as its support is called the consciousness-element (*vijñānadhātu*).

Furthermore, O Great King, this consciousness-element does not rely upon the sense-faculties, it does not come from the objects, nor does it abide in between; it is neither internal, nor external, nor in between the two.
Moreover, O Great King, this consciousness-element ceases immediately after having cognized an object.
When it arises, it does not come from anywhere; when it ceases, it does not go anywhere.
Furthermore, the arising of this consciousness-element is empty, and its passing away is also empty.
Even when it has arisen, the element of consciousness is empty of intrinsic nature.
Thus, O Great King, the element of consciousness is empty of the state of being an element of consciousness and is not apprehended, except as a conventional designation.
And even that conventional designation is neither woman nor man.
Thus, this should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
In this regard, Great King, what is the sense-field of the eye? It is the clarity of the four great elements;
namely, of the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element, and so forth.
In that regard, the clarity of the earth element is not the eye base; nor is the clarity of the water element, the fire element, or the wind element the eye base. Why is that?
Because the clarity of the earth element is not the sense base of any dharma, nor does it exist through the acquisition of a sense base.
In this way, up to the clarity of the wind element, it is not the sense-field (āyatana) of any phenomenon, nor is it present through the acquisition of a sense-field.
Why is that?
Because these phenomena are inactive, they are ultimate, beyond the further shore, and equal to nirvāṇa.
Thus, O Great King, when each of the phenomena is investigated individually, the sense-base of the eye is not apprehended, except as a conventional designation.
For what reason?
Because the clarity of the earth-element is empty of the clarity of the earth-element.
To the extent that the clarity of the wind element is empty of the wind element,
and those phenomena which are empty by their own nature— what clarity or agitation could there be for them,
since neither clarity nor agitation is perceived in them?
How will they see form?
For the eye-base is absolutely empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye-base; it is not apprehended from the perspective of the prior limit.
It is not apprehended even from the perspective of the future limit.
Based on the absence of coming and going, its location is also not apprehended because it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
And that which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature—
It is neither woman nor man;
therefore, what conceit could there be? For conceit, O Great King, is the domain of Māra.
Non-conceptualization is the domain of the Buddhas.
Why is that? Because all phenomena are free from conceptualization. ... [as before] ...

In this regard, Great King, what is the sense-field of the ear? It is the clarity of the four great elements. For thus, Great King, all phenomena are oriented toward liberation, fixed within the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), culminating in the realm of space; they are unattainable, beyond conventional expression, inexpressible, and incapable of being spoken.
Great King, those objects in which the sense faculties are obstructed are called "objects" (*viṣaya*).
For the eye is obstructed by forms; therefore, forms are called the "objects of the eye.
Likewise, the ear [is obstructed] by sounds, and so forth.
In this context, "the eye strikes against forms" is a conventional expression;
it indicates their striking against one another,
for the eye thus falls upon forms in three ways.
By means of the perception of the beautiful toward agreeable things, by means of the perception of aversion toward disagreeable things,
and by means of equanimity toward things that are neither agreeable nor disagreeable.
Thus, "the mind [operates] with respect to mental objects," and so forth.
Therefore, these objects are called the domain of the mind,
for it is here that the mind moves.
It ranges over them;
therefore, they are called the domain of the mind.
Great King, when this mind ranges in attachment toward forms that are not disagreeable, [it is said to range].
Because of that, attachment arises in him;
he moves with aversion toward disagreeable forms, and because of that, hatred arises in him;
he moves in delusion toward things that are neither agreeable nor disagreeable.
Consequently, delusion arises in him;
likewise, he experiences the threefold object of perception regarding sounds and so forth, as previously described.
In this regard, Great King, the sense faculties are like an illusion;
the objects of the senses are like a dream.
It is just as if, Great King, a man while asleep were to consort with a woman who is the most beautiful in the land within his dream.
Having woken from sleep, he might recall that woman who was the most beautiful in the land.
What do you think, Great King—is that woman who was the most beautiful in the land actually present within the dream?
He replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Great King? Would that man be considered wise?"
Suppose someone were to recall in a dream a woman who is the most beautiful in the land, or were to become attached to playing with her.
He said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
And why is that?
Because, Blessed One, in an absolute sense, the 'Beauty of the Land' does not exist and is not apprehended within a dream."
How much less, then, could there be any enjoyment with her?
On the contrary, any man who would become attached to her would only be a partaker of frustration and exhaustion.
The Blessed One said:

"In the same way, Great King, an ignorant, unlearned worldling, having seen forms with the eye that are conducive to joy, becomes attached to them. Being attached, he is drawn toward them; being drawn toward them, he becomes impassioned."
Being thoroughly impassioned, one performs karma born of passion:
threefold by way of the body, fourfold by way of speech, and threefold by way of the mind.
And that performed karma, from its very inception, is exhausted, ceased, vanished, and transformed; it does not remain supported by the eastern direction.
Not to the south, nor to the west, nor to the north, nor above, nor below, nor to the intermediate directions;
neither here, nor across, nor in between the two.
Furthermore, at another time, when the moment of death has arrived,

with the cessation of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) due to the exhaustion of the lifespan and the depletion of its corresponding karma, it becomes the object (*ālambana*) for the mind as the final consciousness is ceasing.
It is just as, for example, the "Beauty of the Land" (*janapadakalyāṇī*) becomes an object for the mind of one who has awakened from sleep.

Thus indeed, O Great King, with that final consciousness as the dominant condition and that karma as the objective support, the first consciousness arises, conditioned by two factors pertaining to rebirth—
whether in the hells, or in the animal realm, or in the world of Yama, or among the hosts of asuras, or among humans, or among the gods.
And immediately after that first consciousness pertaining to rebirth has ceased, a continuous stream of similar mental states proceeds.
Where the experience of maturation is discerned,
there the cessation of the final consciousness receives the designation "death," and the manifestation of the first consciousness is "rebirth."
Thus, O Great King, no dharma whatsoever goes from this world to the next world;
yet death and rebirth both occur.
In this regard, O Great King, the final consciousness, as it arises, does not come from anywhere.
As it ceases, it goes nowhere;
and as karma arises, it comes from nowhere;
as it ceases, it goes nowhere.
Even the first consciousness, when arising, does not come from anywhere;
and when ceasing, it does not go anywhere.
For what reason?
Because they are devoid of intrinsic nature,
the final consciousness is empty of the final consciousness;
karma is empty of karma.
The first consciousness is empty of the first consciousness;
death is empty of death;
rebirth is empty of rebirth.
The non-futility of actions arises, as does the experience of their maturation; yet herein there is no agent and no experiencer, except for the conventional designation of a name.
It is just as if, O Great King, a man while asleep were to engage in battle with an enemy in a dream, and upon waking from his sleep, [he were to reflect on it].
One should keep that very thing in mind.
What do you think, O Great King: does an enemy exist within a dream, or a battle with an enemy?
He said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
What do you think, Great King? Would that man be considered wise who,
in the midst of a dream, would become fixated on an enemy or engage in battle with that enemy?
He said,
"Certainly not, Blessed One. And why is that?"

"Indeed, Blessed One, in a dream an enemy does not exist in an ultimate sense; how much less, then, could there be a battle with him? It is only that the person who would become attached to it would partake in frustration and exhaustion. The Blessed One said:

In the same way, Great King, an unlearned, ordinary person, having seen forms with the eye, becomes attached to those that are grounds for dejection; being attached, he is repelled; being repelled, he becomes complacent;
and being corrupted, he performs actions born of hatred, as described before.
It is just as if, O Great King, a man who has fallen asleep were being pursued by a *piśāca* in a dream and, becoming terrified, fell into a state of delusion;
having woken from his sleep, he might then recollect that *piśāca* and that delusion.
What do you think, O Great King? Does the *piśāca* or the delusion exist within the dream?

In the same way, Great King, when an unlearned, ordinary person sees forms with the eye that are objects for equanimity, he becomes attached to them; being attached, he is deluded; being deluded, he performs karma born of delusion—and so on as before.
It is just as if, Great King, a man were asleep and in a dream heard the sweet sound of singing and the sweet sound of lute strings from a woman who is the most beautiful in the land.
She would entertain him with that singing and instrumental music.
Having woken up from sleep, he would recollect that very same singing and instrumental music.
What do you think, Great King? Would that man, being of a wise nature, become attached to the singing and instrumental music of a "Beauty of the Land" within a dream?
He said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, in an ultimate sense, a woman who is the most beautiful in the land does not exist and is not apprehended even within a dream;
how much less, then, her singing and instrumental music?
"Otherwise, that person would only be a partaker of frustration and exhaustion who would become attached to it. The Blessed One said:
In the same way, Great King, the foolish, unlearned worldling, having heard sounds with the ear, becomes attached to those that are conducive to mental pleasure;
as before. In this manner, it should be understood in three ways for each of the [objects] beginning with odors. ... [as above] ...
In this regard, O Great King, you should fix your mind thus:
"How may I become the eye for the world including its gods; how may I be a torch, a lamp, and a source of light?"
The shore is the boat, the crossing;
the leader is the guide, the instructor, the caravan leader;
may I go before them.
"Once liberated, may I liberate others; once comforted, may I comfort others; once attained to final nirvana, may I lead others to final nirvana.
For, Great King, the prior limit of the experience of sovereign power and lordship is not known. Thus, Great King, the sense-faculties are like an illusion—insatiable and incapable of being quenched.
Sense objects are like dreams; they do not satisfy and bring no fulfillment.
In this regard, the story of the Cakravartin Anantayaśas is recounted as follows by the citizens together with the king when he had fallen from heaven:
"Great King, it is just as if a film of clarified butter or a film of fresh butter were placed upon hot sand; it sinks down and does not remain."
In the same way, Great King, Anantayaśas was sinking and could not remain steady. Then King Priyaṃkara approached King Anantayaśas, who was thus sinking, and said this to him:
"Great King, what should we explain to the world?
What is the well-spoken word of King Anantayaśas?
He replied:
It should be said: Great King Anantayaśas, having exercised sovereign power over the four continents and experienced the fulfillment of his desires,
[witnessed] the simultaneous fruiting of all trees out of season, the subsiding of all calamities, the fulfillment of the desires of all sentient beings, and a rain of fragrant water.

"Having experienced a rain of gold, a rain of precious gems, and a rain of all kinds of requisites, and having dwelt upon the four great continents, he even ascended to half the throne of Śakra; yet, because he was not released from excessive desire, he passed away while still unsatiated with sensual pleasures.
"In this way, Great King, you should explain it. Having spoken thus, King Anantayaśas passed away. ...pe...
Therefore, O Great King, in a mirage there was no intrinsic nature of water, there will be none, and it does not exist now either.
In the very same way, O Great King, the intrinsic nature of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness did not exist, will not exist, and does not exist now either—and so forth.
Furthermore, it has been said:
"The knowable is just this much:
namely, the conventional and the ultimate."
And that has been well-seen, well-known, and well-realized by the Blessed One through emptiness;
therefore, he is called "the Omniscient One.
In this regard, conventional reality was seen by the Tathāgata according to worldly usage.
Furthermore, that which is the ultimate truth is inexpressible;
it is unknowable, indiscernible, untaught, and unrevealed; it is, moreover, without action, and neither gain nor loss, neither pleasure nor pain, neither fame nor infamy;
it is neither form nor formless, and so forth.
Therein, for the sake of the world and for the benefit of the world, the Jina taught the conventional truth,
so that the world might here generate serene confidence toward the Sugata for the sake of happiness.
The Lion among Men, consisting of conventional wisdom, spoke of the six destinies for the multitudes of sentient beings:
the hells, animals, and likewise the hungry ghosts, the hosts of asuras, humans, and gods.
Those from low-born families as well as those from high-born families, those from wealthy families and those from poor families, and so forth.
Furthermore, it was said:
"Which is this dharma that has been predicted by the Blessed One for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
Is it form, or feeling, or perhaps perception, or perhaps mental formations, or is it consciousness that has been predicted by the Blessed One for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?"
This thought occurred to them:
"Neither form, nor even consciousness, has been predicted by the Blessed One for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. For what reason is that?"
For non-arising is form, and non-arising is awakening.
How, then, does non-arising fully awaken to non-arising?
The same applies up to consciousness. ... [as before] ...
Thus, when all phenomena are not being perceived, who here is the Buddha?
What is awakening?
Who is the bodhisattva?
What is the prophecy?
Form is empty of form, and so on up to consciousness. ... [as before] ...
This is merely conventional usage;
it is a mere name, a mere convention, a mere worldly reality, a mere designation.
In this regard, the wise should not give rise to any attachment.
Likewise, they said right here: "O Blessed One, as we understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, we are the gods who Delight in Emanations."
All phenomena are the limit of reality, the infinite limit, the unobstructed limit, the non-abiding limit, and so forth.
"Blessed One, all phenomena are awakening;
they should be understood as being devoid of intrinsic nature.
Even the immediate transgressions, in the final analysis, are awakening."
For what reason?
Because, O Blessed One, awakening is without intrinsic nature, and the five acts of immediate retribution are also without intrinsic nature;
therefore it is said that the acts of immediate retribution are awakening.
In that way, Blessed One, those who desire to attain parinirvāṇa are laughed at.
Why is that?
Because if anyone were actually engaged in saṃsāra, [they would not be so ridiculed].
"He seeks nirvāṇa."
It was said again:
"O Blessed One, regarding that which was called 'the limit of reality' (bhūtakoṭi) by the gods who delight in emanations (nirmāṇarati), we do not perceive even 'reality' (bhūta) there;
how much less its limit?"
For what reason?
Blessed One, whoever perceives a real entity,
he perceives its limit as well, and he courses in duality.
Likewise, right here, the Teacher was praised by Brahmā Sahāmpati.
Just as a man overcome by hunger might eat food of a hundred flavors and yet remain unsatisfied,
and wherein there is neither hunger, nor food, nor a person— just so have all phenomena been seen in a dream.
When a person speaks pleasant words while reciting, they become dear, yet there is no transition of those words [to another].
His speech does not cling to words, nor do you perceive any acquisition of words; there is no doubt in this matter.

Just as one hears the charming and sweet sound of a lute, yet that sound has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), so too the wise and sagacious person, when examining these aggregates (*skandha*), does not find any entity existing by way of intrinsic nature. ... [etc. ...
Just as a wise man here, having heard the sound of a conch shell, reflects, "From where has this arisen?
and does not find its intrinsic nature because it is empty of being, so too, O Lord of Men, are all phenomena seen.

Just as a person here examines exquisite food that has been prepared from various ingredients and is devoid of intrinsic nature—just as its flavor is, so too are those ingredients of that same nature; in this way, O Great Seer, you have seen all phenomena.
Just as a person here, having seen a sacrificial pole, reflects that its parts are devoid of intrinsic nature and empty;
just as you reflect that the parts of the pole are empty, so too, O Great Seer, have you seen all phenomena.
Just as when this excellent city is analyzed part by part, neither the city nor its own nature is found by name;
and just as the city and its parts are entirely empty, so too, O Lord of Men, have all phenomena been seen by you.

Just as a drum, though empty by nature, produces a sound that brings joy to people when struck, so too, O Great Seer, have you seen all phenomena to be of that very same nature. Their intrinsic nature is just like that sound.

... may it destroy [the afflictions] just as a man strikes that drum; for in the drum there is no element of resistance, nor is there an element of cohesion. Reflect upon your own limbs as being like the drum, having such a nature; O Lord of Men, all phenomena are seen to be thus.

Just as a man might strike that drum, yet he does not think, "I am delighting the world"; O King, just as it is with the sound, so too are all these phenomena of yours by their very nature; thus have all dharmas been seen, O Lord of Men.
Just as when a man strikes a drum, there is no sound in the individual parts, nor is it independent;
just as the sound is, so too are those parts of that nature—thus, O Great Seer, have all phenomena been seen by you.
And it is further said:
"The Leader has taught that loving-kindness is the cultivation of purity with sentient beings as its object;
yet for him, sentient beings have been deconstructed, and he thoroughly understands that the entire world is devoid of sentient beings."
In this regard, O supreme among bipeds, you are stainless and possess a mind free from doubt;
therefore, let us worship you, the Sugata of perfected intellect, who are worthy of honor.
Suffering, O Sugata, is not seen thus as pervading the ten directions;
yet you, God among Gods, have spoken of what is called compassion for sentient beings.
Thus, O Bull among Jinas, the doctrine of the Jina has not been understood by us according to its true nature.
Therefore, O best of bipeds, we, the foremost of men, shall worship you who are worthy of worship.
Those for whom suffering has been removed by Śākyamuni do not experience suffering at all;
they are born joyful and delighted in heart, and they are no longer moved by discontent.
Thus, for one who knows the Buddha’s method, that inconceivable method, as it truly is, we therefore worship you, the most excellent among men, and may we attain the fruit that has been reached.
The Sage, who is devoid of a body, has not attained the state of being a path by means of that which is devoid of a body;
thus, your guides of mindfulness have not been spoken of as such, nor has mindfulness been lost.
And it was said by the Sugata: "These meditations, which follow the path of cultivation, have entered into the body.
Having thus understood the way of the Buddhas, the Sugatas have performed worship for the Protector.
Cultivate calm abiding and insight; this is the path for the peace of suffering.
O Blessed One, those who have pacified the stains along with their latent tendencies are the ones by whom the world is afflicted.
"O Sage, both calm abiding and insight are entirely empty of all stains;
O Leader, let the hosts of gods have no doubt anywhere as they worship you. And so forth.
It is further stated:
"The eye is indeed empty of the intrinsic nature of an eye;
and that dharma which lacks an intrinsic nature is without substantial reality."
That which is without substance is unperfected; that which is unperfected neither arises nor ceases... [and so forth].
That which is not apprehended in any of the three times is neither the eye nor a sense faculty; how, then, can its conventional usage be known?
It is just like, for example, an empty fist, which is false. It is merely a name, and in the ultimate sense, neither the "empty" nor the "fist" is apprehended.
Thus, the eye and the faculty are like an empty fist—false, unreal, hollow, deceptive by nature, a mere delusion for the childish, a bewilderment for the foolish, being nothing more than a mere name.
Furthermore, it says in this very same place: "In a dream, O Great Hero, you have shown a great rain— the flowing forth of the outflows— to those who are wise regarding the arising of the outflows."
Just as the cutting off of your head was seen in a dream, so has the destruction of the outflows been demonstrated to all who possess wisdom; O All-Seeing One, homage be to you!
And on this very point, the Blessed One replied when he was questioned by Druma, the king of the kinnaras:
"As for what you say regarding emptiness and the prophecy,
I do not know them either."
If there were anything non-empty, there would be no prophecy concerning it by the Jina.
For what reason?
Because it would remain established in its own state of being.
It is immutably stable and changeless;
it has neither increase nor decrease,
neither action nor cause.
Just as a reflection, which is empty of intrinsic nature, appears in a perfectly pure mirror-disk,
even so, O Tree, should you understand these phenomena. You should analyze this offering limb by limb, [seeing it as] the unchanging realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Having examined the worship limb by limb,
which are the limbs that are unchanging?
Furthermore, you do not understand what I have taught regarding the absence of agency and action;
observe the assembly of the parts of a cart and the very activity of the cart itself.
And although karma has been explained to me, no agent is found in the ten directions; for just as fire ceases when the wind-stirred tree [is consumed], so too does it cease.
Neither the wind nor the tree intends for the fire to arise during the sacrifice; yet the fire does not fail to proceed.
In the same way, the agents of karma do not intend it, yet it proceeds.
Furthermore, as for what you say— that there is no accumulation of merit nor the full realization of good conduct—
listen now to the sequence regarding that awakening.
Just as you say that the measure of human life is a hundred years,
yet there is no such thing as a "pile of years," so too is this [attainment] likewise.
It is also said in the Bhagavatī:
"Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, does a dharma that has already arisen arise, or one that has not yet arisen?
Subhūti replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra, I do not desire the arising of a dharma that has already arisen, nor of one that has not yet arisen."
It is also said in the *Dharmasaṃgīti*:
"O son of good family, 'suchness, suchness' is a designation for emptiness;
and that emptiness neither arises nor ceases."
He said:
"If it is thus that the Blessed One has taught that all phenomena are empty, then all phenomena will neither arise nor cease;
the bodhisattva would be without any undertaking."
He said:
"It is just so, noble son; it is exactly as you have realized: all phenomena are neither produced nor extinguished.
He said:
Regarding that which was said by the Blessed One—
"conditioned phenomena arise and cease"— what is the intended meaning of this speech of the Tathāgata?
He replied:
Noble son, the world is attached to arising and ceasing.
In that regard, the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, for the sake of removing the world's ground for fear, has spoken according to conventional usage that "things arise and cease.
Yet, herein there is no arising and no ceasing of any dharma whatsoever.
Furthermore, it is said in this very same [text]:
"In that regard, Blessed One, the eye does not clash with forms, nor does the ear with sounds."
As long as one does not clash with mental objects,
that is the Dharma.
In that regard, how does one not clash with the eye and forms?
Because there is no contact;
for the eye does not come into contact with form, nor indeed does it come into contact with anything up to the mind with mental phenomena.
That which does not come into contact does not clash.
Blessed One, for a non-dual dharma there is no conflict.
And, Blessed One, all dharmas are non-dual; they do not know one another, nor do they cognize one another.
They do not conceptualize nor do they discriminate; they neither come into being nor pass away; they neither diminish nor increase.
They do not become attached, they do not become dispassionate;
they do not transmigrate, nor do they enter final nirvana; these belong to no one.
"There is none among them;
these phenomena, Blessed One, neither tremble, nor are they defiled, nor are they purified.
Thus, Blessed One, do I know; thus do I understand."
Furthermore, Blessed One, when I say,
"Thus I know," or "Thus I understand," [it is not out of my own power].
This is a transformation of the sense bases;
yet, Blessed One, it does not occur to the sense bases themselves,
"This is our transformation."
For whoever understands in this way does not dispute with anyone;
that which is non-disputing follows the dharma of a śramaṇa.

Thus, the vision of the Dharma is the vision of the Buddha, the vision of all sentient beings, the vision of the causes and conditions of all sentient beings, the vision of emptiness; and the vision of emptiness is non-vision.
"O Blessed One, the non-perception of all phenomena is the perception that constitutes right view."
How is it logical for conventional reality to have no objective basis?
And how, then, is it illogical? It is like the delusion of a person where there is no post.
Furthermore, for one who propounds emptiness, what "post" is established in ultimate reality such that it could serve as the basis for the delusion of a "person"?
Indeed, all phenomena are rootless in reality, because a root is logically untenable.
And so it is said in the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa*:
"What is the root of unreal imagination?
He replied:
Perverted perception is the root.
He asked:
"What is the root of perverted perception?"
Non-abiding is the root. He asked:
"What is the root of non-abiding?"
He said:
"Mañjuśrī, that which is non-abiding has no root whatsoever; for all phenomena are established upon the root of non-abiding."
This perfection of wisdom should, in brief, be cultivated by one who desires the purification of the mind;
and having cultivated it, one should become skilled in slaying the enemy of the afflictions, not a hero only within one's own home.
As it is said in the *Āryadharmasaṃgītisūtra*:
"The proponent of emptiness is not drawn away by worldly conditions because of being non-reliant;
he does not rejoice in gain."
He does not become despondent through lack of gain;
he is not elated by fame, nor does he shrink from ill repute;
he is not cowed by blame.
One is not led astray by praise;
one is not attached to pleasure, nor does one become disenchanted by suffering.
For he who is not carried away by such worldly conditions (lokadharma) knows emptiness (śūnyatā).
Likewise, for one who proclaims emptiness, there is neither attachment nor aversion toward anything whatsoever.
One knows that whatever one might be attached to is indeed empty;
one sees only emptiness.

He who is attached to or repelled by any phenomenon does not know emptiness; likewise, he who would engage in conflict or dispute with anyone does not know emptiness. He knows only emptiness and sees only emptiness, and so forth.
This is the purification of the mind in brief.

Now, even when there is such supreme purity in the vision of the Dharma, for one who is defiled by the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*) in this world, or one who has been brought low by a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), where should one briefly apply effort so that mental purification occurs quickly?
