It is in the abandonment of self-conceit and contempt for others; the root of these two is the view of a self and a sentient being (*ātma-sattva-dṛṣṭi*).
And since that [defilement] is easily abandoned through such practice, one should cultivate reverence for others and self-depreciation in this way.

Whether it be a sentient being or the aggregates, if forbearance is established in every respect, how could the state of being both self and other possibly exist for a single entity? It would be a contradiction.
Embodied beings indeed perform this even without an objective basis;
for those accustomed to wholesome practices such as [giving] food, what is difficult for habituation?
Since the capacity for mastery through practice is equal in both cases, why is it that people desire their own happiness by abandoning respect for others?
The wish-fulfilling gem and the aforementioned causes for respect do exist;
yet, because of my lack of respect, there is no happiness for me here either, due to the misfortune of the people.
Therefore, just as the conduct of those who possess harshness, envy, and pride toward another being is that of one who has self-love, one should cultivate the opposite of that.
This self-conceit increases through the sprinkling of praise, blame, and the like,
just as the fire of hell increases from the sprinkling [of fuel] under the power of hell-beings.
First of all, since sound is insentient, it is impossible that it praises me;
the thought that "another person is indeed pleased with me" is merely a delusion of my own mind.
My pleasure arises solely from his satisfaction; let that not always be directed toward common people.
If I have no concern for his happiness, what do I care about him being satisfied?
What indeed is the use of affection for another directed toward me?
For even if another is pleased, there is not the slightest bit of physical pleasure here for me.
Knowing this, one should abandon all conceptual constructions that create obstacles;
likewise, ill-repute, censure, and honors should be understood as being fruitless.
Neither dharma, nor longevity, nor health, nor strength is gained through prostrations and the like,
just as there is none for one who is being mocked by physical contortions of another's body.
Whether joyful or dejected, gain and loss have an equal outcome;
therefore, having abandoned that which is fruitless, I shall be one whose mind is like a mountain.
And through the relinquishing of familiarity, the purification of the mind occurs swiftly. Thus it is said.
In this regard, it is further considered:
Recognition, which arises from the grasping of signs, repeatedly produces attachment;
from that, aversion also arises.
For one who possesses aversion and attachment, evil is unrestrained;
there are various kinds of false accusations, along with stinginess and envy.
The desire for gain and such things recurs frequently;
therefore, with every effort, the sage should abandon intimacy.

Due to similarity, even this other [moment] is perceived like a stream of water through the delusion that "this is that very same thing"; therefore, I remain firmly established in reality by force of logic.
This similarity is a non-entity and will give rise to suffering;
both I and all this shall cease to exist before long. Thus [he thought].
The fourteenth chapter: Purification of the Personal Existence.
[XV. Purity of Enjoyment and Merit] The fifteenth chapter: Purity of Enjoyment and Merit.

In the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, following the purification of oneself (*ātmaśuddhi*), comes the purification of enjoyments (*bhogaśuddhi*); since there is no accumulation [of wealth], this is written here separately. And one should understand the purification of enjoyments through the thorough purification of right livelihood (*samyagājīva*).
As it is said in the *Āryograparipṛcchā*:
"In this regard, householder, a lay bodhisattva seeks wealth through righteous means and not through unrighteous means; through impartiality and not through partiality."
One's livelihood is right, not wrong.
It is also said in the *Āryaratnamegha*:
"A bodhisattva does not arrange his deportment upon seeing a donor or a master of generosity. How does he not arrange his deportment?"
He does not lift or set down his steps slowly or very gradually; rather, he looks only a yoke’s length ahead, looking with confidence and looking without effortful exertion.
In this way, he does not practice deception of the body. How does he not practice deception of speech?
A bodhisattva, for the sake of gain or on account of gain, does not become one who speaks sparingly, who speaks softly, or who speaks agreeably; nor does he utter words of compliance. ... [etc. ...
How does he not practice mental hypocrisy?
When a bodhisattva is being offered gain by a donor or a patron, he does not display a lack of desire,
nor does he give rise to longing in his mind.
“Son of good family, this is an internal burning: that while one is verbally modest, the mind desires gain.
For in this way, son of good family, a bodhisattva becomes free from hypocrisy, flattery, and gain. ... A bodhisattva does not make a sign upon seeing a donor.”
I have need for robes; I have need for a bowl; I have need for medicine for the sick.
Nor does he request anything from that donor or benefactor,
nor does he utter a word;
for in this way, the bodhisattva has become free from the acquisition of signs.
As long as a bodhisattva, upon seeing a donor or benefactor, does not utter such speech as:
"This or that object was bestowed upon me by this or that benefactor, and I performed such and such a service for him;
because he thought, 'This one is virtuous,' he gave me this and that; because he thought, 'He is learned'..."
Thinking, "He has few desires," I established a mind of compassion toward him and accepted him. ... [as before] ...
In this context, injury to the body refers to running hither and thither for the sake of gain, on account of gain, as well as the practice of immoral conduct;
injury to the mind refers to longing,
and an abundance of malice toward fellow celibates who possess gains.
In this way, the bodhisattva becomes one who has abandoned gains obtained through improper seeking... [and so forth].
In this regard, a bodhisattva does not acquire gain through fraudulent scales, fraudulent measures, betrayal of trust, or deceit.
In this way, a bodhisattva becomes one who has abandoned unrighteous gain. ...

Furthermore, those gains which are mixed with what belongs to a stupa, or mixed with what belongs to the Dharma, or mixed with what belongs to the Saṅgha, or which are not given, or which have not been authorized—[he does not take these].
He does not accept them nor does he appropriate them;
for in this way, the bodhisattva becomes free from impure gains. Thus, whatever gain he has obtained, he does not treat it as "mine."
He does not crave wealth; he does not make a hoard;
and from time to time, he gives to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
From time to time, he enjoys [food] himself from his mother, father, friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations; and while enjoying it, he does so without attachment.
He is not obsessed with it, nor does he produce a mind of distress when gain is not obtained;
he does not suffer, nor does he produce a mind of ill-will toward donors and benefactors, and so forth.
In this regard, this purity of enjoyments of the bodhisattva, like the purity of his physical form, shall serve for the benefit of others.
As it is said in the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa*:

"Furthermore, Reverend Śāriputra, for those who enter this house, as soon as they have entered, all afflictions (*kleśa*) no longer trouble them; this is the second marvelous and extraordinary quality.
Furthermore, it is said in that very same text:
Then, from that food, the entire assembly became satisfied,
yet that food was not exhausted; and by whichever bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, Śakras, Brahmās, world-protectors, and other beings it was consumed, [they were all satisfied].
When they had eaten that food, such happiness entered their bodies as is the happiness of the bodhisattvas in the world-system Sarvasukhamanditā;
and from all their pores, such a fragrance wafted forth.
It is just like the fragrance of the trees in that very world-system called Sarvagandhasugandhā.
And it was further said:
"Venerable Ānanda, for those monks who have not yet entered the fixed course of certainty (niyāma) to eat this food, it will be digested only when they have entered that fixed course...
[and so on] ...for those beings who have not yet generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) to consume it, it will be digested only when they have generated the mind of awakening."
"For those by whom the thought of awakening has been generated, food that is eaten will not be digested until they have attained patient acceptance (kṣānti)," so it is said at length.
The purification of merit arises from activity whose essence is emptiness and compassion.
For it is said in the noble Gaganagañja Sūtra:
"That is, one gives that gift purified of the notion of 'I';
one gives that gift purified of the notion of 'mine'."
He gives that gift with purity of cause; he gives that gift with purity of view;
he gives that gift with purity of signs.
He gives that gift purified of diversity;
he gives that gift purified of expectation for karmic fruition;
he gives that gift as purely equal as space.
...as space is limitless, so he gives that gift with a mind made limitless;
as space is vast and unobstructed, so he gives that gift dedicated to awakening;
as space is formless, so he gives that gift without relying on any form.
Just as space is without a knower, so he gives a gift in which all sensation has been stilled;
thus he gives that gift which is without perception, unconditioned, characterized by non-informativeness, and without assertion.
Just as space pervades all buddha-fields, so does he give that gift which pervades loving-kindness toward all sentient beings...
[as before] ...Just as space is eternally luminous, so does he give that gift whose nature of mind is pure.
Just as space provides room for all sentient beings, so does he give that gift which sustains the livelihood of all sentient beings.

Just as one who is magically created gives to another who is magically created— being free from conceptual construction, effortless, devoid of mind, mentation, and consciousness, and having no expectations regarding any phenomena—
in the same way, through the departure from duality, the Bodhisattva gives that gift which is pure by nature, having the characteristic of an illusion.
One who possesses such renunciation of giving, who through the wisdom of insight abandons all the afflictions of sentient beings,
and who through the wisdom of skillful means does not abandon sentient beings—
such a Bodhisattva, O son of good family, whose mind is thus characterized by relinquishment, becomes one whose generosity is equal to space.
It is also said in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*:
"There is no taking [of gifts] by oppressing sentient beings;
furthermore, there is no giving less than what was promised."

As long as there is no gift involving contempt for those worthy of offerings among all sentient beings... [and so on] ...there is no gift given with lamentation; as long as there is no gift given with distress toward supplicants, no gift given with derision or mockery, no gift given with averted face, no gift given by casting away, and no gift not given with one's own hand...
[and so on].
There is no gift that is improper;
there is no gift at an improper time; there is no gift of poison or weapons; and there is no gift that involves the harming of sentient beings.
As for what was said in the *Ugraparipṛcchā*:
"This is the time for the perfection of generosity; it is the time to give to each person whatever they require. Nevertheless, I shall act in this way."
"I shall give the drinking of liquor only to those who drink liquor;
I shall cause them to undertake mindfulness and clear comprehension."

Even regarding the drinking of intoxicants, resentment toward a bodhisattva who has rendered one hopeless is more serious; furthermore, there is the loss of the means for gathering sentient beings. Therefore, the intention is that if no other means of inspiring confidence is possible, intoxicants may be given.
This applies even to weapons and the like, provided that the gift does not result from a failure to consider the gravity of the consequences or similar factors.
It is understood from this very point that there is no offense at all;
however, in the sūtras, there is a general prohibition. Thus has been explained the direction for the purification of giving.
The purity of ethical discipline (*śīlaviśuddhi*) is explained in the *Āryagaganagañjasūtra* itself:

"Not being separated from the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is for the sake of purity of mind; being free from the thoughts of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* is for the sake of purity of authoritative means," and so forth.
Furthermore, there is another purity of ethical discipline:
as the sky is pure, so is that ethical discipline; as the sky is stainless, so is that ethical discipline.
The sky is peaceful; that ethical discipline is peaceful.
The sky is not elevated; that ethical discipline is not elevated. The sky is unattached; that ethical discipline is unattached.
As far as the sky is indestructible and indivisible, so too is that ethical discipline (śīla) indestructible and indivisible, and so forth.
The unimpeded sky is the purification of patience for one whose mind is free from aversion toward all sentient beings;
the sky of equal application is the purification of patience for one whose mind is equal toward all sentient beings, and so forth.
It is just as if there were a great grove of *śāla* trees, and someone were to come and cut down one *śāla* tree therein;
the remaining ones would not think: [“He has cut us down”].
"This one is cut off, but we are not cut off"—
for them there is no attachment and no aversion; there is no conceptualization, no discursive thought, and no mental construction.
This patience which is thus [described] is the supreme patience of a bodhisattva, equal to space. Thus it is said.
Having explained it in detail in the *Āryaratnacūḍasūtra*, it says:
"This is called vigor;
its purification is the purification of the body."
It is the knowledge that the body is like a reflection or an image, the knowledge that speech is inexpressible,
and the knowledge that the mind is utterly stilled;
likewise, it is being armored with the mail of loving-kindness and established in the empowerment of great compassion.
He practices the meditative absorption that is endowed with the excellence of all aspects and brought forth through the aspect of emptiness.
In this regard, what is emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects?
It is that which is not deficient in generosity.
As long as it is not devoid of skillful means;
not devoid of great loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
and not devoid of entry into the knowledge of the truths.
It is not lacking in the aspiration for awakening and regard for sentient beings; it is not lacking in intention, resolute intention, and application;
and it is not lacking in generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful action, and consistency between words and deeds.
It is not deficient in mindfulness and clear comprehension;

it is not deficient in the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold path; it is not deficient in calm abiding and insight; and so forth...
it is by its very nature utterly tranquil.
She is not pacified regarding karma and afflictions;
she is equanimous toward all phenomena,
yet she regards the qualities of a Buddha.
And just as it is by way of its own characteristic,
it is active through the performance of its empowerment,
yet it is effortless by its own nature.
She is ever engaged in the activities of a Buddha,
cooled by tranquility,
and yet always ablaze in the ripening of sentient beings.
This is called emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects.
"O son of good family, this is the perfection of meditative concentration, which is the purification of conduct."
By this, the purification of wisdom is to be understood;
thus it is with all merits.
Likewise, it is also said in the *Ārya-vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*:

"The sphere of manifesting the turning of the wheel of the true Dharma and the great parinirvāṇa, as well as the sphere of not abandoning the conduct of a bodhisattva—this too is the sphere of a bodhisattva."
The fifteenth chapter: The Purification of Enjoyments and Merit.
[XVI. The Procedure for the Bhadracaryā] The sixteenth chapter: The Procedure for the Bhadracaryā.
Now, the increase of all three must also be stated.
For what purpose? There are very many recipients, yet this [teaching] is so small; what can be achieved by it? Furthermore, it does not produce complete satisfaction; therefore, it must be increased.
Supreme satisfaction is Buddhahood;

the meaning is that this is not produced in sentient beings by mere purity shared with the Śrāvakas. What is the increase of the personal existence? It is the strengthening of the powers and the absence of indolence.
In that regard, the *Āryaratnamegha* speaks of power:
"No such being is found within the assembly of beings who could crush the power of a bodhisattva with his own power," and so forth.
How is its increase brought about?
As stated in the *Āryatathāgataguhya-sūtra*, the Blessed One, when questioned by King Ajātaśatru—who was struck with wonder at the sight of the power of the noble Vajrapāṇi—said:
"Great King, a bodhisattva endowed with ten qualities attains such strength as this."
By which ten?
Here, O Great King, a bodhisattva relinquishes both body and life,
yet he does not relinquish the true Dharma.
He bows down before all sentient beings and does not further increase his pride;
he is patient toward weak beings and does not harbor resentment.
He gives the finest and most excellent food to beings who are hungry;
he grants fearlessness to beings who are afraid;
and he is intent upon providing genuine medical treatment for beings who are ill.
He satisfies poor beings with enjoyments,
applies a coating of lime plaster to the reliquaries of the Tathāgata,
and causes beings to hear the words of Ānanda.
And he shares his wealth with sentient beings who are poor and suffering;
and he carries the burden of sentient beings who are weary and exhausted.
It is by these ten, O Great King.
What is the increase of non-laziness?
It is the increase of vigor,
as it is said in the *Sāgaramati-sūtra*:
Sāgaramati, a bodhisattva must be one who has initiated vigor and is always firm in prowess;
a bodhisattva must have intense aspiration and not cast off the burden.
For, Sāgaramati, for bodhisattvas who have initiated vigor, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is not difficult to attain.
For what reason?
Sāgaramati, where there is vigor, there is awakening;
but for those who are indolent, awakening is very far, indeed exceedingly remote.
For one who is lazy, there is no giving, and so on, up to: there is no wisdom; for one who is lazy, there is no benefit for others.
It is also said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
"Like a blue lotus in the midst of water, it grows gradually," and so forth.
This, in brief, is the increase of the personal existence.
From generosity whose essence is emptiness and compassion, there is the increase of enjoyments.
As it is said in the *Vajracchedikā*:
"The Bodhisattva who gives a gift without abiding—
it is not easy to grasp the measure of his mass of merit."
Furthermore, it is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*:

"Moreover, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives even a small gift, he should desire to make it immeasurable and incalculable by dedicating it toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) through skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) for the sake of all sentient beings."
One should train in the perfection of wisdom;
likewise, one who desires to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings—
even by means of such requisites as gold, silver, gardens, and kingdoms— should train in the perfection of wisdom.
And we shall explain that without compassion, there is no activity whatsoever on the part of Bodhisattvas;
thus concludes, in brief, the increase of wealth.
Since the increase of merit is the root of all increases, the preparation for its sake is now described.
Having first made both resolve and hope firm through effort,
and having placed compassion at the forefront, one should strive for the increase of virtue.

This verse is intended to bring about firmness by once again bringing to mind resolve and the other qualities—which were cultivated at the time of purifying the mind—at the commencement of the actual practice;
it begins with the words "having performed," and so forth.

The inclusion of the word "beginning" (ādi) is for the purpose of preventing laxity, so that one might strengthen [the resolve] at the very moment of application out of respect for skill in weapons when the time of battle is near.
In that regard, how does one strengthen one's determination?
Just as the noble Sudhana approached the noble Maitreya, being incapable of perfect conduct;
bowing his body with a body reaching back to the limits of the past, strengthening his physical strength through mental attention to the body;
and restraining his mental application by attending to the purification of the body and mind throughout the limits of the past, while reflecting upon the causeless activity of the mundane mind.
Reflecting upon the great efficacy of present purposes through the contemplation of the fruitless exertion applied to worldly tasks and unwholesome actions throughout the limits of the past;

generating the power of the correct mental formation of all bodhisattva practices through the contemplation of mental attention manifested by false conceptualizations arising from unreal imaginings in the past;

and strengthening the power of his resolute intention through the superiority of his undertakings for the sake of all sentient beings, by contemplating the unevenness of his own past applications toward personal goals.
By reflecting on the lack of relish for the conduct of past bodies;

by increasing the force of his faculties through the attainment of great confidence in the application toward the acquisition of all Buddha-dharmas; and by purifying his mental continuum through the undertaking of the bodhisattva vow, which is associated with the non-erroneous right view of the present time and dissociated from the application of false intentions associated with the errors of the past time.

By reflecting upon the non-attainment of the undertaking of the noble path and the failure to initiate the vigor of yoga throughout the past; by manifesting the present realization of the Buddha-dharmas through the exertion and prowess of great vigor, generating a firm grasp of body and mind;

and by reflecting upon the acquisition of physical aggregates throughout the limits of the past across the five destinies and the miserable states—aggregates that were cast away and lacked both self and others, as well as the means of subsistence and the basis for livelihood.

Increasing the force of vast joy and gladness by assuming a physical existence capable of giving rise to all the qualities of a Buddha, sustaining the entire world, and pleasing all spiritual friends, he [regarded] this present life— which has been brought forth as a mine of old age, sickness, death, and sorrow, and as a repository of union and separation.

He was devoted to practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva throughout tens of millions of kalpas extending to the furthest limit; he was dedicated to maturing sentient beings and embracing the qualities of a Buddha;
he was intent upon beholding the Tathāgatas, traveling through all buddha-fields, attending upon all Dharma-preachers, and upholding the teachings of all Tathāgatas;
he had become a companion in the search for all dharmas; and he was devoted to seeing all spiritual friends and accomplishing all the qualities of a Buddha.
Having observed that it serves as the cause and condition for the body of the bodhisattva’s vow and wisdom, he increases the force of his faculties through inconceivable roots of merit.
Thus it is also said in the *Āryākṣayamatinirdeśa*, a Mahāyāna sūtra:
A single bodhisattva, without a second and without a companion, dons the armor for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
With a resolute intention sustained by the power of vigor, he acts independently without leaving room for others;
he has emerged through the power of his own strength.
Having thus donned this firm armor, he thinks:
"Whatever there may be that must be fully accomplished for all sentient beings, that I shall fully accomplish;
whatever all the noble ones and all bodhisattvas who have newly set out in the vehicle will not fully accomplish, that I shall fully accomplish."
Giving is not my companion;
rather, I am the companion of giving.
Morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom are not my companions.
I, moreover, am the companion of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
I am not to be served by the perfections, but rather the perfections are to be served by me.
In this same way, I should proceed with regard to the articles of attraction and all roots of virtue.

"Until I, alone, without a second, and without a companion, standing upon the adamantine mandala of the earth, having subdued Māra together with his army and his mounts, shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through wisdom conjoined with a single moment of mind."
The Noble Vajradhvaja Sūtra also says:
"It is just as, for example, when the divine son Sūrya rises, he does not remain [hidden] because of the defect of those born blind."
It does not abide due to the defect of a city of the Gandharvas;
it does not abide due to the defect of the dust of the earth of the world-system of four continents;
it does not abide due to the defect of Rāhu, the lord of the asuras.
It does not remain due to the defect of a circle of smoke; it does not remain due to the defect of the afflictions of Jambudvīpa;
it does not remain due to the defect of various shadows.
He does not stop because of the defect of uneven mountains;

in the very same way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva— whose mind is vast and deep with mindfulness and clear comprehension, and whose being is undaunted— does not turn back until he reaches the end of the practice of qualities and the practice of knowledge, nor does he depart from the defects of beings' hostility, nor does he stray from the dedications of his roots of virtue.
He does not turn back because of the defects of the turbidity of views regarding sentient beings;
he does not distance himself from them because of the agitated minds of sentient beings;
and he does not let the armor of awakening be obstructed by the ruined continuums of sentient beings.
One who has made the vow to protect the entire world does not allow that vow to falter because of the defilements of the degenerate age, even through association with foolish people;
nor does one become weary of the faults of other beings.
Why is that?
This mandala of the removal of obscurations arises, namely, for the sake of purifying and disciplining the entire world; and so forth.

And whatever mass of suffering belongs to all those sentient beings, and whatever various obstructive karma has arisen by which, through that obstructive karma, they do not see the Buddhas, do not hear the Dharma, and do not know the Saṅgha— [may all that be extinguished].
Therefore, I take upon my own body the threefold obstructive karma accumulated by them as a mass of suffering within those various rebirths in hells, states of woe, and dwellings;
and may all those sentient beings pass away from there.
I undertake this taking up of suffering; I resolve and I exert myself.
I do not turn back, I do not flee, I am not startled, I am not terrified, I do not fear, I do not retreat, and I do not despair.
For what reason?
Because I must necessarily carry the burden of all sentient beings.
This is not a matter of my own desire;
it is my vow to deliver all sentient beings.
I must liberate all sentient beings.
I must deliver the entire world from the wilderness of birth, the wilderness of old age, the wilderness of sickness, the wilderness of death and rebirth, the wilderness of all transgressions,
the wilderness of all miserable realms, the wilderness of all saṃsāra, the wilderness of the thicket of all views, and the wilderness that destroys wholesome dharmas.
From this wilderness arisen from ignorance, I must deliver all these sentient beings from all such wildernesses.
They are caught in the net of craving, shrouded by the veil of ignorance, conjoined with the thirst for existence, ending in destruction, cast into the cage of suffering, and dependent upon prison.
They are unawakened, contradictory in their assertions, full of doubt, always possessed of uncertainty, and seeing no security.
Unskilled in the means of escape, they move with but a single foot within the whirlpools and circles of the ocean of existence... [etc.]
I practice for the sake of establishing all sentient beings in the sovereignty of unsurpassed knowledge;
I am not merely intent upon my own liberation.
For all these sentient beings must be rescued by me from the miserable swamp of saṃsāra by means of the raft of the mind of omniscience.
They must be lifted up from the great precipice;
they must be liberated from all calamities; they must be ferried across the stream of saṃsāra. By myself, the entire mass of suffering of all sentient beings has been taken upon me.
To the extent that I am able, I shall endure dwelling in all sufferings within all the states of woe included in all world-systems;
yet I must not deprive all sentient beings of their roots of virtue.
I resolve to dwell in each and every state of woe for as many eons as reach to the furthest limit of the future.
And just as it is for a single evil destiny, so too is it the cause for the complete liberation of all sentient beings included within all world-systems across all evil destinies without exception.
Why is that?
Because it would indeed be better for me alone to suffer than for all these sentient beings to fall into the realms of the evil destinies.
I must give myself there as a pledge;

the entire world must be ransomed from the wilderness of hell, the animal realm, and the world of Yama. For the sake of all sentient beings, I shall experience the entire mass of painful sensations with this body of mine, for the sake of all sentient beings.
And I am willing to stand as a surety for all sentient beings—I who am a speaker of truth, trustworthy, and non-deceptive.
And I have not abandoned all sentient beings.
For what reason?
Because my production of the mind set on omniscience has arisen with all sentient beings as its objective support, namely, for the sake of liberating the entire world.

Nor have I set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening out of a desire for pleasure; nor for the sake of experiencing delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure, nor for the sake of indulging in the objects of desire.
Nor do I practice the conduct of a bodhisattva for the sake of bringing about an array of delights included within the various realms of desire.
Why is that?
For these are indeed non-delights, whereas all worldly delights belong to the realm of Māra; namely, the indulgence in the objects of desire.
For this path is frequented by those of corrupt intellect.
For this instruction, namely the indulgence in sensual desires, is indeed censured by all the Buddhas.
Therefore, this very indulgence is the production of the entire mass of suffering; for this very reason, it is the production of the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama.
And from this very source, quarrels, strife, disputes, and disturbances among sentient beings arise.
And these beings, by indulging in sensual desires, become distant from the presence of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Even for rebirth in heaven, these desires lead to an obstacle;
how much more so for the unsurpassed king of knowledge, which provides security and well-being for all sentient beings?
Thus, seeing these immeasurable faults of sensual desires—as limited and as ablaze—I shall therefore practice the non-pursuit of this cause. ... [as before] ...

In that very same way, I must dedicate my roots of merit so that all sentient beings may attain ultimate happiness, the happiness of felt bliss, up to the happiness of omniscience; [I must do so] as their charioteer, as their leader, as their bearer of the torch, as the one who shows the path to safety, as the one who has attained the favorable moment, as the one who knows skillful means, as the one who understands the goal, and as the one established upon the great vessel of the ship of omniscient wisdom in the ocean of saṃsāra.
By me, who am skilled in dedication; by me, who am one who sees the further shore... [etc. // pe //

Furthermore, it is not the case that as many suns rise in this world-system of four great continents as there are sentient beings therein for the purpose of illuminating the world-system of four continents;
rather, only a single sun rises for the illumination of the four continents.
And yet, for those sentient beings born in the four continents, no light appears from their own respective bodies.
By means of which they might know the number of days,
or accomplish their own tasks,
or bring the crops to maturity.
Day after day, they might experience the enjoyment of pleasure and play in gardens and cities; or they might look toward the various directions;
or they might travel back and forth among villages, towns, market towns, kingdoms, and royal capitals.
They should be employed in judicial matters...
And yet, when the divine son Sūrya rises, the light of a single, peerless solar orb appears for all sentient beings throughout the world-system of four continents.
In the very same way, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva accumulates roots of virtue and dedicates those roots of virtue, this thought arises:
These beings do not possess that root of virtue by which they might protect themselves,
let alone others.
I, however, for the sake of all sentient beings, accumulate roots of virtue and dedicate those roots of virtue.
That is to say: for the sake of liberating all sentient beings;

for the illumination of all sentient beings; for the making known of all sentient beings; for the introduction of all sentient beings [to the path]; for the gathering of all sentient beings; for the perfection of all sentient beings; for the gladdening of all sentient beings; for all sentient beings...
For the sake of gladdening all sentient beings and for the sake of cutting through their doubts, we must become like the orb of the sun; we should not look for anything else,
nor should we cast off our armor toward sentient beings by making room for another.
One must not turn back from the resolve to protect all sentient beings for the sake of any sentient being; one must not turn away from the dedication that destroys all suffering;
and one must not grasp at limited roots of virtue.
"One should not consider oneself satisfied with a limited dedication," and so forth.
It is also said in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*:
"He does not seek awakening by calculating eons,
thinking, 'I shall arm myself for this many eons.'"
"I shall don the armor for this many eons"—
indeed, he dons an armor that is truly inconceivable;
even if the entire prior limit of saṃsāra were to constitute a single day and night.

By means of days and nights of such a nature— by a fortnight consisting of fifteen days, by a month consisting of thirty days, by a year consisting of twelve months, and by this calculation of years up to a hundred thousand years— may I generate a single thought of awakening (bodhicitta) and behold a single Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

By this entrance and by this calculation, through as many productions of the thought of awakening and visions of the Tathāgata as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, may I know the mental conduct of even a single sentient being; and by this very entrance and by this calculation, through that same number of productions of the thought of awakening and visions of the Tathāgata, may I fully understand the mental conducts of all sentient beings— this armor, being undaunted, is the inexhaustible armor of a bodhisattva.
Such is the method regarding generosity and the other perfections, as well as the factors conducive to enlightenment and the marks of a great person.
It is also said in the *Āryaratnamegha*:
A bodhisattva, having recognized the stubbornness and the unruliness of sentient beings, does not think,
"Enough with these sentient beings who are so stubborn and so unruly," and thereby become weary on that account or turn his back upon them.
He makes a vow for a completely pure world-system,
one in which he would not even hear the names of such beings;
for a bodhisattva who is averse to the welfare of sentient beings does not attain rebirth in a completely pure world-system.
In that regard, the wise bodhisattva generates this thought:
"Therefore, among those beings in the realm of sentient beings who may be inferior—those born dull-witted, stupid, or mute;
those whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa; those who are entirely uncared for within the realm of sentient beings and rejected by all Buddhas and all bodhisattvas—"
May there be a gathering of them in my buddha-field;
having seated them all upon the seat of enlightenment, may I cause them to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.
For when a bodhisattva reflects in this way, at every single arising of the thought of enlightenment, all the abodes of Māra tremble,
and all the Buddhas become speakers in praise of him.
Thus, first of all, one who desires the increase of merit must strengthen their intention (*āśaya*).
Now, for the purpose of strengthening that intention, it is asked:
"But what is the use of this being strengthened?"
To dispel such doubt, it is stated in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:
"O Blessed One, right intention is the root of the Buddha-dharmas;
for one who lacks right intention, all the Buddha-dharmas are far away."
Furthermore, Blessed One, for one who is endowed with pure intention, even if Buddhas do not exist, the sound of the Dharma issues forth from the expanse of the sky and from budding trees.

For a Bodhisattva whose intention is purified, all instructions and admonitions issue forth from the very mental discourse of his own mind. Therefore, Blessed One, a Bodhisattva should be endowed with pure intention.
Just as, Blessed One, one who has feet has the ability to walk, so too, Blessed One, one who has the resolute intention (āśaya) possesses the qualities of a Buddha.
Just as, Blessed One, one who has a head has life, even so, Blessed One, one who has the resolute intention possesses the awakening of a Buddha.
Just as, Blessed One, one who has life possesses gain.

In the same way, Blessed One, for one who possesses the right intention, there is the attainment of Buddhahood. Just as, Blessed One, fire blazes when there is fuel, but does not blaze when there is no fuel.
In the same way, Blessed One, when the bodhisattva’s intention is present, all the qualities of a Buddha blaze forth;
when the intention is absent, they do not blaze forth.
Just as, Blessed One, when clouds of rain exist, it rains, but when they do not exist, it does not rain.
In the same way, Blessed One, when the intention (āśaya) exists, the Buddha-qualities (buddhadharma) arise.
Just as, Blessed One, for a tree whose root is decayed, its flowers and fruits no longer grow,
even so, Blessed One, for one whose intention is decayed, all wholesome qualities (kuśaladharma) no longer come into being.
Therefore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva who seeks the awakening of a Buddha should well-grasp, well-guard, well-purify, and well-sustain his own intention.
What is this so-called intention (*āśaya*)? It is stated in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*:
"Furthermore, that intention is indeed uncontrived, because it is uncreated."
It is unconditioned because it is beyond being accomplished;
it is beyond being accomplished because it is well-known;
it is well-known because it is free from deceit.
It is uncreated because of its purity;
it is pure because of its straightforwardness;
it is straightforward because of its lack of crookedness.
It is not crooked because it is clear;
it is clear because it is even;
it is even because it is solid.
It is "essence" because it is indivisible;
it is "indivisible" because it is firm;
it is "firm" because it is immovable.
"Unshakable because of being non-dependent," and so forth.
This very state, which proceeds toward the attainment of ever-increasing qualities, is called the "resolute intention" (*adhyāśaya*).
As it is said in this very same [text]:
"The resolute intention for crossing over is due to proceeding with distinction," and so forth.
Moreover, high resolve is said to be gentleness toward living beings and friendliness toward sentient beings.
A mind of benevolence toward the noble ones,
compassion for the ignoble,
and reverence for one's teachers.
Being a protection for those without protection;
being a refuge for those without refuge;
being an island for those without an island.
Being a refuge for those without refuge;
being a companion for those without companions;
and being straightforward toward those who are crooked.
Clarity toward the unruly; honesty toward the deceitful; and freedom from guile toward those whose conduct is profound and obscure.
Gratitude toward those who are ungrateful;
thankfulness toward those who do harm; and helpfulness toward those who do not help.
Truthfulness toward those who have fallen into untruth; freedom from pride toward those who are arrogant; and blamelessness through not censuring those who have committed faults.
Not pointing out the transgressions of others;
protecting those who have fallen into wrong conduct;
and seeing no fault in any practice of skillful means.
It is the state of desiring to hear [the teachings] from all those worthy of offerings,
and the state of receiving instructions with respectful compliance, and so forth.
Thus, having thus strengthened both resolve and intention, and placing compassion at the forefront, one should strive for the increase of virtue.
As it is said in the *Āryadharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:
"Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Blessed One as follows:
'Blessed One, a bodhisattva should not train in too many dharmas.'"
“Blessed One, there is one dharma that a bodhisattva must thoroughly master and fully penetrate;
for him, all the qualities of a buddha will be as if held in the palm of his hand. What is this one dharma?”
Namely, great compassion.
Blessed One, through great compassion, all the qualities of a Buddha come to be held in the palms of the hands of bodhisattvas.
Just as, Blessed One, wherever the wheel-treasure of a universal monarch proceeds, [the entire army follows].
Just as the entire army follows where its commander goes,
even so, Blessed One, all the qualities of a Buddha follow wherever the great compassion of a bodhisattva goes.
"Just as, Blessed One, when the sun has risen, sentient beings become abundant in their various activities,
even so, Blessed One, wherever great compassion has arisen, there the other factors that bring about enlightenment become abundant in their activities.
Just as, Blessed One, when all the sense-faculties are presided over by the mind, there is an abundance in their grasping of their respective objects."
In the same way, Blessed One, for other qualities that bring about awakening which are sustained by great compassion, there is abundance in each of their respective functions.
Just as, Blessed One, when the life-faculty exists, the other faculties function, even so, Blessed One, when great compassion exists, the other qualities that bring about awakening function.
It is also said in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*:

Just as, Reverend Śāradvatīputra, for a person the inhalations and exhalations are the precursors to the life-faculty, even so, Reverend Śāradvatīputra, for a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna, great compassion is the precursor. ... [as above] ...
It is just as if, for example, a merchant or a householder had marrow-deep affection for an only son endowed with virtuous qualities;
in the very same way, a bodhisattva who has attained great compassion has marrow-deep affection for all sentient beings.
How is this to be cultivated?

One should cultivate loving-kindness toward those who are dear and so forth—whether they are currently suffering from illness or are led away by the calamities of the long, boundless cycle of existence within the great ocean of suffering—by first cultivating within oneself the realization that one's own various kinds of past or present suffering and fear are absolutely undesirable. Thus should loving-kindness be cultivated by one who possesses loving-kindness.
As it is said in the *Āryadaśabhūmikasūtra*:
"It occurs to him: 'How marvelous! These foolish ordinary people are indeed deluded by ignorance, for whom incalculable personal existences have ceased, are ceasing, and will cease.'"
And thus, even as their bodies waste away, they do not give rise to world-weariness;
rather, they increase the machinery of suffering to a greater degree and do not turn back from the great terrors of the stream of saṃsāra.
They do not relinquish their abode in the aggregates; they do not become weary of the serpents of the elements;
and, blinded by the passion for delight, they do not awaken.
They do not perceive the village of the six sense-bases as empty;
they do not abandon the underlying tendencies of attachment to the notions of "I" and "mine";
and they do not extract the thorn of pride and false views.
They do not pacify the net of passion, hatred, and delusion;
they do not dispel the darkness of ignorance and confusion;
and they do not dry up the ocean of craving.
They do not seek out the Caravan Leader endowed with the ten powers;
instead, following the dense thickets of Māra’s intent, they drift about in the ocean of saṃsāra, which is turbulent with the crocodiles of various unwholesome thoughts.
Having no refuge, they fall into such a state of agitation as they experience manifold sufferings.
Namely, birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair. Come now,

for the sake of these beings who are afflicted by suffering, who are without a protector, without a refuge, without a shelter, without a dwelling, without a resort, blind, and overwhelmed by darkness— being shrouded by the film of the eggshell of ignorance— I shall act alone and without a second.
Having become thus, I maintain the accumulation of the equipment of merit and wisdom in such a manner that,
through the accumulation of the equipment of merit and wisdom thus gathered, all these sentient beings may attain inner purity.
Likewise, it says in this very same place:

"Alas, these beings have entered the path of the wilderness and forest of saṃsāra; they are facing downward toward the precipices of the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama; they have fallen into the treacherous net of wrong views; they are shrouded by the thicket of delusion; they have set out upon false paths and erroneous courses;
they have become blind and are destitute of a guide. ... [pe] ...

Carried along by the current of saṃsāra, they have entered the river of craving; seized by its great force, they are unable to look back, following after the precipices of sensual desire, ill-will, doubt, and harmful intent.
They are seized by the water-demon of the view of their own body; they have entered the whirlpools of the deep forest of sensual desires; they are stuck in the midst of delight and craving;
and they are submerged in the mud of the conceit "I am."
They have no other refuge;
they have not emerged from the village of the sense-bases;
they are devoid of the accumulation of wholesome qualities.
Having rescued them by the power of our great roots of merit, we must establish them on the jewel-island of peaceful omniscience, which is free from affliction and free from dust.

Alas, these beings are imprisoned in the dungeon of the three realms, which is filled with much suffering, dejection, and despair; which is bound by the shackles of craving and fettered by attachment and aversion toward the pleasant and unpleasant; which is haunted by sorrow and lamentation; and which is shrouded in the thicket of illusion, deceit, and ignorance.
"We must establish them in the city of fearlessness, which is the seclusion from the entire triple world, the pacification of all suffering, and the unobstructed nirvāṇa," and so forth.
Thus, by means of these—resolute effort, intention, and compassion—which mutually reinforce one another, one should undertake the increase of merit.
In that regard, first of all, the ritual of the Bhadracaryā should be performed, including prostrations and so forth, with constant devotion.

For in the *Āryogradattaparipṛcchā*, it is stated that one who is pure and dressed in clean garments should perform the "Three-Sectioned Recitation" (triskandhaka) three times during the night and three times during the day.

In this context, there are three aggregates known as the confession of misdeeds (*pāpadeśanā*), the rejoicing in merit (*puṇyānumodanā*), and the entreaty to the Buddhas (*buddhādhyeṣaṇā*), because they constitute accumulations of merit. Among these, the act of homage (*vandanā*) is included within the confession of misdeeds,
since in the *Upāliparipṛcchā* it is stated that one performs the confession after having paid homage to the Buddhas.
Solicitation is not mentioned because it has the same meaning as entreaty;
worship is not mentioned because it is impermanent due to the lack of material resources;
and mental and verbal [worship] are not mentioned because they are well-known from other sūtras.
However, from the statement of the three, their preeminence is understood;
therein, salutation is expressed as "I pay homage to all Buddhas."
In the *Āryākṣayamatisūtra*, however, the confession of one's own and others' misdeeds is recited as part of the accumulation of merit.
And worship is performed with the four verses and with hymns as they have been sung,
or with the verses beginning with the *Ārya-bhadracaryā*.
As it is said in the *Āryaratnamegha*:

"In this case, whatever kinds of flowers or fruits there may be that are without 'mine-ness' and without possession, the bodhisattva offers them to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas three times by night and three times by day. ... [etc. ...

Just as these incense trees, or fragrance trees, or jewel trees, or wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa) are without "mine-ness" and without possession, so too, three times by night and three times by day, he offers them to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
In the *Āryatrisamayarāja* as well, it is stated that the land-born jewel-mountains,
the water-born jewel-mountains, and the jewels born of both land and water situated in the ten directions—
being without "mine-ness" and without possession— are to be given as gifts.
And by this same method, all medicinal herbs, all elixirs, all waters— blameless and free from impurities—
as well as all golden grounds,
or whatever patches of earth in manifest world-systems are endowed with the most excellent taste and touch; [all these should be understood].
The nectar-creeper;
or rice that grows without being sown or ploughed,
found throughout all the continents of Uttarakuru.
And in those completely pure world-systems, whatever enjoyments are most delightful;
And as it is said in the *Āryaratnamegha*:
"Whatever most sublime services and offerings to the Tathāgata he hears described in the sūtras,
he dedicates them to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with an intense disposition and a resolute superior intention."
Likewise:
"He reflects upon various forms of worship and service."
The confession is as previously described;
however, in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*, the confession of one’s own and others’ misdeeds is recited within the accumulation of merit.
The rejoicing is performed with the verses of the *Bhadracaryā*.
Alternatively, the request [for teaching] is made by means of the *Candrapradīpa-anumodanā-parivarta*,
while the dedication is performed by means of the complete and perfected *Āryabhadracaryā*.
Or one may see the dedication of merit known as the Vajradhvaja.
Alternatively, there are the great vows as taught in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*,
as it says: "That is to say, for the purpose of performing worship and service for all Buddhas, without exception, without remainder, and without residue."

He brings forth the first great vow: to perform great worship and service that is endowed with the excellence of all modes, purified by sublime resolve, as vast as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), extending to the limits of the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), reaching to the furthest reaches of the future, and continuing unceasingly through the number of all eons and the number of the arising of Buddhas.
Namely, for the sake of upholding the way of the Dharma spoken by all Tathāgatas, for the sake of being sustained by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
and for the sake of protecting the teaching of all Perfectly Enlightened Ones—
[a resolve] as vast as the realm of phenomena, reaching the limit of the realm of space, and extending to the furthest reaches of the future.
He brings forth the second great vow: to never cease the arising of Buddhas throughout the number of all conceptual constructions, for the sake of upholding the true Dharma.
That is to say, for the purpose of approaching— in every single instance throughout the entire expanse of all world-systems where Buddhas arise—
the dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, beginning with that,

and proceeding through the descent from there, the entry into the womb, birth, childhood, play, residence in the inner palace, renunciation, the practice of austerities, the approach to the seat of awakening, the subduing of Māra, the manifest perfect awakening, the request to teach, the turning of the great wheel of Dharma, and the great final nirvāṇa.

Having made the practice of gathering the Dharma of worship the precursor, he formulates the third great vow for the sake of turning back [the cycle of existence] everywhere at all times: vast as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), reaching the limit of the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), extending to the furthest reaches of the future, continuing uninterrupted through the number of all eons and the number of the appearances of Buddhas, until the attainment of the Great Parinirvāṇa.

That is to say: for the sake of accomplishing the arousal of the thought of enlightenment, which is supported by the granting of instructions and advice, the cultivation of the perfections, and the teaching on the path of the stages exactly as they are—the true nature of all bodhisattva conduct, including its characteristics and lack of characteristics, its dissolution and evolution, up to the purification of all stages together with their primary and secondary branches; and which is well-comprised within all the perfections that are vast, magnanimous, immeasurable, and undifferentiated.

He brings forth the fourth great vow: for the production of the thought of enlightenment that is as vast as the realm of phenomena, reaches the limits of the realm of space, extends to the furthest reaches of the future, and continues without interruption through the enumeration of all eons and the enumeration of all practices.

That is to say, for the sake of maturing the entire realm of sentient beings without exception—whether with form or formless, with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception; whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by spontaneous generation; included within the three realms and encompassed by all states of existence within the six destinies; and comprised of all name-and-form—for the purpose of causing them to enter into all the qualities of a Buddha.
For the sake of cutting off the enumeration of all states of existence;
for the sake of establishing the wisdom of the omniscient one;

vast as the realm of phenomena, reaching the limit of the realm of space, extending to the furthest end of the future, and continuing unceasingly through the number of all eons and the number of all realms of sentient beings.
He brings forth the fifth great vow for the sake of maturing the realm of all sentient beings.

That is to say, he brings forth the sixth great vow for the sake of attaining direct perception through the pursuit of the knowledge that discerns the entry into and the differentiation of the entire variety of world-systems throughout the ten directions— without exception, including those that are vast, condensed, expansive, immeasurable, subtle, gross, inverted, upright, and level— as well as the entry into Indra’s net-like array; a vow that is vast as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), reaching the limits of space, extending to the furthest reaches of the future, and continuing uninterrupted through the number of all eons and world-systems, in order to lead beings into the understanding of the diverse natures of world-systems.
That is to say: the purification of all fields as a single field, and the single field as the convergence of all fields;
adorned with the array of immeasurable Buddha-fields’ splendors, and endowed with the path of purity that removes all afflictions.
It is filled with immeasurable forms of knowledge and sentient beings; it converges upon the vast domain of the Buddhas; it manifests to satisfy all sentient beings according to their inclinations;
it is as expansive as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), reaches the limits of the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and extends to the furthest reaches of the future.
He brings forth the seventh great vow: to never cease throughout the number of all eons and the number of all buddha-fields, for the sake of purifying all buddha-fields.
That is to say: for the sake of the application of a single intention toward all bodhisattvas;
for the accumulation of roots of virtue that are without rival;
and for the equality of all bodhisattvas through a single object of focus.
For the sake of never being separated from constant and perpetual association with Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
for the sake of manifesting the appearance of Buddhas according to one’s wish; and for the sake of following the knowledge of the power of the Tathāgata arising from the production of one's own mind.
For the attainment of the superknowledges that follow the Unfallen One;
for wandering through all world-systems; for achieving the manifestation within all circles of assemblies;
and for following one's own body into all modes of rebirth.
For the sake of being endowed with the inconceivable Mahāyāna;
for the non-interruption of the practice of the bodhisattva conduct;
[a state] vast as the realm of phenomena, reaching the limit of the realm of space, and extending to the furthest reaches of the future.
He brings forth the eighth great vow, which is never interrupted throughout the enumeration of all eons and the enumeration of practices, for the purpose of causing others to enter the Mahāyāna.
That is to say: for the practice of the conduct of Bodhisattvas mounted upon the irreversible wheel; by means of making body, speech, and mind fruitful;
and for the certain attainment of all Buddha-dharmas at the very moment of seeing [the Buddhas].
For the sake of following the knowledge that arises simultaneously with the utterance of sounds;
for the sake of turning away from both faith and afflictions simultaneously;
and for the sake of attaining a physical basis comparable to the Great King of Medicines.
Like a wish-fulfilling gem, for the attainment of the body,
for the practice of all the conduct of bodhisattvas,
vast as the realm of phenomena, reaching the limit of the realm of space, and extending to the furthest reaches of the future.
He brings forth the ninth great vow: that his conduct throughout the count of all eons shall never cease, so that his voice may never be in vain.
That is to say: for the sake of manifesting unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in all world-systems;

for the sake of demonstrating—in a manner that does not exceed the path of a single hair—the birth, rebirth, renunciation, miraculous transformations, sitting at the seat of enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, and the great final nirvana of all ordinary, foolish worldlings;
and for the sake of following after the knowledge of the power and majesty of the great domain of the Buddhas.
To manifest the attainment of peace through the moment-to-moment awakening to the arising of Buddhas according to the inclinations of the realms of all sentient beings;
to pervade the entire realm of phenomena with emanations from a single perfect enlightenment;
and to satisfy the mental dispositions and intentions of all sentient beings by uttering a single sound.
To ensure the non-interruption of the power of the conduct that demonstrates the great parinirvāṇa;
to demonstrate the emergence of all phenomena upon the stage of great gnosis;
and to pervade all world-systems with the supernatural powers of the illusion of the knowledge of phenomena.

Vast as the realm of phenomena, extending to the limits of the realm of space, reaching to the furthest reaches of the future, and continuing unceasingly through the number of all eons until the number of perfect awakenings— this is for the accomplishment of the Mahāyāna.
He brings forth the tenth great vow.
And while contemplating this, one should apply the thought: "I dedicate [the merit] everywhere."
And that which is said in the *Āryāvalokiteśvaravimokṣa* should also be applied in this way:
"I dedicate this root of merit for the sake of removing the fear of falling into the abyss for all sentient beings;
for the sake of pacifying the fears pertaining to the mental continuums of all sentient beings."
I dedicate this for the sake of turning back the fear of delusion for all sentient beings;
for the sake of utterly severing the fear of bondage for all sentient beings;
and for the sake of averting the fear of threats to the lives of all sentient beings.

I dedicate [this merit] for the sake of removing the fear of all sentient beings regarding a deficiency of necessities, for the sake of pacifying the fear concerning the livelihood of all sentient beings,
and for the sake of transcending the fear of ill repute for all sentient beings.
For the sake of pacifying the fears of cyclic existence for all sentient beings;
for the sake of removing the fear of timidity in the assemblies of all sentient beings;
and for the sake of transcending the fear of death for all sentient beings.

I dedicate [this merit] for the sake of turning back all sentient beings from the fear of miserable rebirths; for the sake of producing illumination so that all sentient beings do not turn back from the uneven paths of the blinding darkness of ignorance; and for the sake of the complete disappearance of the fear of encountering discordant circumstances among all sentient beings.
For the cessation of the fear of separation from all beloved beings;
for the removal of the fear of dwelling with all unloved beings;
for the dissociation from the fear of physical affliction for all beings.
"I dedicate [this merit] for the sake of liberating all sentient beings from the fear of mental affliction,
and for the sake of transcending all suffering, dejection, and despair of all sentient beings."
In brief, moreover, this is the unsurpassed dedication which is found in the *Ārya-bhadracaryā-gāthā*:
"Just as the heroic Mañjuśrī knows, and as Samantabhadra likewise knows,
following their example, I dedicate all this merit."

Whatever supreme dedication has been praised by all the Victors who have gone throughout the three times, with that I dedicate all this merit toward the practice of the Excellent Bhadra. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the Procedure for the Bhadracaryā, in the Śikṣāsamuccaya.
[Chapter XVII: The Benefits of Prostration and Other Acts] Chapter Seventeen: The Benefits of Prostration.
The procedure for prostration and so forth has been explained. From what is it known that through this there is an increase of merit?
From the Āryāvalokana-sūtra; for it is said there:
"One avoids the eight inopportune births (akṣaṇa) which have been taught by me."
And for a moment, one encounters a single, most auspicious appearance of a Buddha.
Possessed of a fine complexion, endowed with beauty, adorned with the primary marks, and gifted with steadfastness and strength, he does not fall into indolence.
He was wealthy and possessed great riches; he was invincible and meritorious as well.
Having pleased the Light of the World, he honored him again and again.
He is reborn into prosperous and wealthy merchant families;
he becomes a heroic master of generosity, truly free from stinginess and capable of renunciation.
He shall become a righteous king, a lord and sovereign of the four continents;
he shall rule the entire earth, which is adorned with oceans and mountains as its earrings.
Possessing great supernatural power, the universal monarch, endowed with the seven jewels,
established in his kingdom, repeatedly pays honor to the Buddhas.
Having passed away from here and gone to heaven, being well-pleased with the teaching of the Jina,
he becomes Śakra, the lord of gods, a sovereign upon the summit of Mount Meru.
It would not be possible, even in tens of millions of eons,
to exhaust the description of the merit of that person who performs a circumambulation of a stūpa of the Lord of the World.
Having generated the thought of awakening, he who bows before a stūpa of the Teacher shall never be blind or lame, even for tens of millions of eons.
Possessing firm vigor, firm strength, and heroic, steadfast prowess,
one quickly attains skillfulness by performing the circumambulation of a stūpa.
If one were to weigh and honor hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas for millions of eons,
and another were to worship a stūpa here in this final, terrible age, the latter’s merit would be far greater.
For the Buddha is the foremost field, incomparable and worthy of offerings; having practiced the supreme conduct, he has attained the excellence of practice.
By performing worship here to him, the bull among men, the maturation that results is most excellent and of incomparable form.
Having passed away from among humans here, he goes to the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
there he obtains a celestial palace adorned with various jewels.
Having personally given a gabled chamber, served by hosts of apsarases,
and having offered a garland at a stūpa, one is born among the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
He shall obtain a divine lotus pond, filled with water possessing the eight qualities, its bed strewn with golden sand, and adorned with beryl and crystal.
Having enjoyed that divine pleasure and completed his lifespan, the wise one,
passing away from the world of the gods, becomes a human being possessed of wealth.
For hundreds, thousands, and millions of births,
one will be honored everywhere by offering a garland at a shrine.
By offering a garland at this shrine, one becomes a universal monarch, a lord such as Śakra, and even Brahmā in the world of Brahmā.
But having offered a silk cloth to the Protector of the World, the Savior,
all his goals— both divine and human— will flourish.
One should abandon those who are dull-witted and unskilled; he will not be reborn there.
And having constructed a flower-garland monastery for the relics of the Lord of the World, one shall become a king of great supernatural power, accompanied by an invincible retinue.
He was beloved and dearly cherished, honored and praised by the gods,
the nāgas, and those who are wise in this world.
Wherever that hero is born, brilliantly illuminated by the splendor of his merit,
those families, as well as the kingdoms and cities, become honored.

Listen as I speak of the benefits for one who, having taken incense even finer than a mustard seed, offers it as incense at the shrines of the Blessed One; with a clear mind, abandon all obstructions and impurities.
That meritorious one wanders in all directions, having attained health, firm in mind, and vigilant;
he dispels sorrow as he travels on his journey, becoming dear and pleasing to the great multitude of people.
Having obtained the kingdom, that wise and majestic universal monarch, O Best of Victors, honors [the Buddha];
golden-hued and endowed with diverse marks, he obtains delightful fragrances throughout the entire world.
As soon as he is born, he obtains the finest garments— divine, exquisite, and beautiful Kāśika silks—
and his body becomes exceedingly pleasant to touch, having wrapped the stūpa of the Protector with robes.
Whoever performs incomparable worship of the Leaders at the shrines with robes [attains this].
In this world, his physical form becomes peerless, armored with the thirty-two marks;
upon the palms of his hands appear various and infinite kinds of beautiful pearl necklaces,
and lion-tail fans of exquisite color and thread, having wound them around the stupa of the Blessed One with his robes.

Having offered a banner at the shrines of the Blessed One and having generated the aspiration, "May I likewise be in the world of the Buddhas," he becomes worthy of worship by the great multitude as he practices the supreme conduct of the Conqueror.
His physical form becomes golden in color, and he obtains most beautiful robes:
those made of cotton, well-woven woolens, fine linen, and likewise excellent silks.
Having offered the banner to the Essence of Beings who has destroyed all dust, one obtains abundant wealth before long.
One possesses a vast treasury and infinite wisdom; one's retinue becomes numerous, and one’s mind is never dejected.
Such a person, with a mind of serene faith and always heedful, does not cause mental anguish to others.
Fire does not overcome him, nor do poison or weapons; he becomes one who is to be gazed upon by the great multitude.
From the depths below up to the peak of existence, a buddha-field would become like Jāmbūnada gold;
yet such a lifespan and glory could be exhausted, but not a single lamp offered at a stupa of a Buddha.
His body is never without its limbs; he becomes firm, with arms like iron bars, and fearless.
Having attained light, he wanders through all the world after having given a lamp at the shrines of the Blessed One.

Even if hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddha-fields were filled with mustard seeds upon the tips of their awns, it would be possible to count, weigh, or describe them; yet it is not possible to maintain even a single lamp among the Tathāgatas.
Whoever, having adorned it so that it is most beautiful and lovely to behold, gives a parasol at the shrines of the Blessed One,
for him there arises here an incomparable physical form, armored with the thirty-two marks.
By these [qualities], the body of the Victor blazes with a form as distinguished as refined gold,
or like the Jāmbūnada gold, beautiful and lovely to behold, strewn over with blossoming marks.
He becomes one who has attained the superknowledges, renowned for great fame, and he conducts himself in the supreme and excellent course of conduct.
There is never any loss of his enjoyments; among the gods, he is held in high esteem and honored.
The wise one, possessing pure virtue and practicing the wholesome holy life, never delights in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures;
having gone forth and dwelling in the forest grove, he becomes devoted to meditation and attains distinction.
There is never any loss of knowledge for him, nor does he ever abandon the thought of awakening in any way;
he dwells in loving-kindness with a heart undepressed, having given a parasol here at the shrines of the Blessed One.
Having performed worship with musical instruments for the Bull among Men, one never comes under the power of the thorn of sorrow;
one becomes possessed of a pleasing voice in the world of men, and the components of one's speech become complete and pure.
He becomes one with pure vision and possesses clear comprehension; he becomes one with pure hearing and an uplifted mind.
His faculty of smell becomes supremely refined by having played musical instruments at the shrines of the Blessed One.
His tongue becomes exceedingly beautiful and lovely to behold, very fine and soft, with a voice that is radiant and pleasing;
like the coral-red tongues of the deities, it emits immeasurable millions of excellent vocal qualities.

One never becomes serpent-like or tongueless, nor lame, hunchbacked, or with deformed limbs; rather, one possesses a distinguished and most beautiful physical form after playing music at the shrines of the Blessed One.
Never shall any god, nāga, human, or mahoraga give rise to faith;
yet, having played musical instruments at the shrines of the Blessed One, one wanders through the entire world having attained consolation.
For hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, he possesses a distinguished body with faultless limbs;
having purified a stūpa of the Blessed One who has entered parinirvāṇa, he becomes gracious and armored with the primary marks.
He obtains a supreme celestial mansion, divine and distinguished with the exquisite fragrance of beautiful sandalwood;
having purified a stupa of the Blessed One who has entered parinirvana, he never at any time gives rise to craving.
During the time of destruction of the teaching of the Supreme Victor, he never comes to Jambudvīpa;
at that time, he remains established in heaven because he offered fragrant ointments to the stupa of the Victor.
Firmly established in the aggregate of ethical discipline, he constantly avoids desires that are foul-smelling and loathsome as impure;
having applied fragrant ointments to the stūpa of the Jina, he always practices this supreme holy life.

Passing away from here, he shall become a lord of the gods in the heavenly world; before long, he will weigh out wealth by the thousands, and he will provide vast benefit for the deities by applying fragrant ointments to the stupa of the Jina.
One becomes distinguished in speech, possessing a pleasing voice, dear and beloved, and honored by many people;
and for one who applies fragrant ointments upon a stūpa of the Jina, there is always constant happiness and clarity.
One abandons the realms of misery without exception and becomes near to the Tathāgatas;
having attained serene faith, one is always happy and beloved for having applied fragrant ointments to the stūpa of the Victor.
He indeed abandons all unfavorable conditions, and his eight favorable conditions become preeminent;
he performs incomparable worship of the Buddhas by removing the net from the shrines of the Blessed One.
He becomes a hero of firm mind and heedfulness; he finds no delight in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.
Having cast off the net, his mind is undaunted in the attainment of renunciation as he makes offerings at the shrines of the Blessed One.
His bodhicitta is never lost; he possesses unbroken morality and is well-restrained. Having offered a net to the shrines of the Blessed One, he attains the pure Dharma of dispassion.
He abandons harsh speech at all times and relinquishes ignorance entirely;
possessing vast wisdom, he dwells in his conduct after having removed the net [of defilements] from the shrines of the Blessed One.
And he becomes a recipient of pure foods and obtains distinguished garments of fine gold,
endowed with pleasant textures and beautiful to behold, by having offered a net to the shrines of the Jinas.
Having joyfully and with great fervor removed the dried floral offerings from the shrines of the Jinas,
one should abandon desires— which are as terrible as the forest fires of suffering— and please the Caravan-leaders endowed with the ten powers.
He becomes gracious, with a purified body, worthy of being looked upon and honored by many people;
even a king will not harbor a malicious mind toward him who removes withered flowers from a shrine.
The Bodhisattva, established in the aggregate of ethical discipline, has closed off all evil paths and the realms of misery;
having removed flowers previously offered by other men from the shrines of the Jinas, he offers them himself.
The heedful person abandons sorrows and faults; they abandon manifold diseases without exception.
Having attained consolation for infinite eons, they remove withered flowers from a shrine.
And he becomes a Buddha, an incomparable recipient of offerings, one who has attained the peerless state, worthy of worship by humans and gods;
his body is adorned and purified, he who removes withered flowers from a shrine.
And whoever should offer beautiful, divine flowers— whether *māndārava*, *pāṭala*, or even a faded garland from a shrine— the maturation of that merit for him would be supreme and incomparable.

Whoever, having generated a resolute desire for the world of the Buddhas, bows with palms joined before the stupa of the Protector, becomes one who is honored and revered in the world; he is serene and beautiful to behold.

His sovereignty here prevails; the entire world—including gods, asuras, nāgas, and humans—as well as all thousands of blossoming world-systems, and even the lords and masters, are under the king's command.
Whatever beings reside in his realm, he shall establish them all in the stainless wisdom of a Buddha;
the grounds of the lower realms are abandoned for them, and he accomplishes for them the most supreme benefit.
His attendant possesses a pleasing voice; endowed with merit, he is honored for his mindfulness and wisdom.
Having attained consolation, he moves through the world of living beings, always generating noble joy according to their intentions.

His attendants possess pure qualities of voice; he is known by beings for his sweet and peaceful speech. No one treats him with arrogance, and he becomes worthy of being looked upon by the great multitude.
He inspires in the great multitude the joy of giving, the practice of kind deeds, and the spirit of common purpose.
He who, even when reviled, does not give rise to anger, but bows with palms joined toward a stūpa of the Buddha;
He becomes a lord of gods in the world of heaven, or he becomes a king of men among humans;
there is never any decline for him who here bows with palms joined to a stūpa.
Such a person shall never fall into an evil rebirth and will avoid base desires in this world;
he becomes wealthy, affluent, and possessed of abundant treasuries—he who bows with palms joined before a stupa of the Buddha.
In this world of men, the practice of the sūtras never provokes his anger toward those who do not take refuge;
and beings become satisfied and joyful toward him who releases even a single word of virtue.
