Whoever, with an uplifted mind and out of faith, takes a handful of flowers and scatters them over the Lord of the World, that person becomes meritorious in the world of humans; and remaining in heaven, they honor the Jina.

Sorrow is no longer a fault; for him there are no barren stains or impurities. Having attained the incomparable, his limbs are well-proportioned; he is worthy of being beheld by the great multitude. Thus, one should abandon desires, which are terrifying, full of enmity, and dreadful.
It is also said in the *Āryamahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "Let alone, Ānanda, one who would honor me face to face;
let alone the worship of my physical remains contained within relics the size of mustard seeds."
"Let alone the honor shown toward stupas built for my sake;
Ānanda, as for those who, taking the Buddha as their object, should throw even a single flower into the air—
even if the ripening of that mass of merit were equal to the extent of saṃsāra, including food and so forth, whose prior limit is not known."

As they wander through that many eons, their attainments of the state of Śakra, the state of Brahmā, and the state of a universal monarch (cakravartin)—it is impossible to reach the limit of those. Let alone the state of taking the Buddha as one's object of focus; even the act of casting a single flower into space [for his sake] is beyond measure.
"If even those beings who, while in the midst of a dream, take the Buddha as their object and throw even a single flower into the sky, I declare that root of merit of theirs to culminate in nirvāṇa.
And it is said in the *Ārya-bṛhatsāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā*:
"O Lord of Nagas, bodhisattvas endowed with eight qualities constantly and perpetually obtain association with the Buddhas."
By which eight? By causing beings to see the image of the Buddha and by performing service to the Tathāgata.
By frequently speaking the praises of the Tathāgata; by having images of the Tathāgata made; and by encouraging all sentient beings to behold the Tathāgata.
And in whichever Buddha-field they hear the name of the Tathāgata, there they form a vow; their mental continuums do not become dejected,
and possessing noble continuums, they long for the wisdom of a Buddha.
How much more so, then, for one who desires the increase of merit— what need could there be for meeting with a Buddha,
the limit of whose qualities even an omniscient being would not reach?
As it is described in the *Āryagaṇḍavyūha*:
"The sound of 'Buddha' is extremely difficult to encounter even in hundreds of millions of eons;
how much more so is the sight of him, which cuts through all doubts and is supreme?"
The Lamp of the World has been clearly beheld; he has reached the ultimate state of all phenomena. He is the merit-field of the three worlds, the purifier of all sentient beings.
This great merit-field, the joyful mandala of wisdom,
illuminates the world on all sides and increases the mass of merit.
It cuts through the web of suffering and purifies the aggregate of knowledge;
there is no fear of miserable rebirths for those by whom the Jina has been propitiated here.
As they behold the Supreme among Men, a vast mind arises;
and an incalculable, radiant power of wisdom is born.
Furthermore, it says in this very same place:
"For the sake of all sentient beings, the Tathāgatas arise—
those who possess great compassion, who are heroes, and who turn the wheel of Dharma."
How could all embodied beings ever be able to repay the Buddhas,
who are dedicated to the welfare of sentient beings, even in hundreds of millions of eons?
It would be better to suffer for ten million eons in the most terrible three lower realms than never again to behold the Teacher, who brings an end to all rebirth.
Whatever various states of miserable rebirth exist throughout the entire world, it is better to dwell there for a long time than to never hear the name of the Buddhas.
For what reason is dwelling for a long time in the states of woe desired?
Because the vision of the Lord of Jinas increases one's wisdom.
All sufferings are severed upon seeing the Victorious One, the Lord of the World;
and entry arises into the wisdom that is the domain of the Perfectly Awakened Ones.
"Having seen the Buddha, the supreme among men, one exhausts all obscurations and increases immeasurable merit by which awakening is attained. Thus it is said.
Thus, in this way, there is a purpose in meeting a Buddha for the increase of merit.
Moreover, even the mere sight of an image of the Tathāgatas yields immeasurable fruit; how much more so, then, the sight of his actual form?
For it is said in the *Ārya-śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*:

"Mañjuśrī, if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to give, day after day, food of a hundred flavors and divine garments to as many Pratyekabuddhas as there are atoms in all world-systems, and were to continue giving in this manner for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges; [compared to that,]"
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, any other son of good family or daughter of good family who should see a Buddha depicted in a painting or fashioned as a book-image produces incalculably more merit than that;
how much more so for one who should join their palms in reverence, or offer flowers, or offer incense, fragrance, or a lamp?
This very person generates merit even more incalculable than that.
In the *Āryabodhisattvapiṭaka* as well, the means for increasing merit is taught:
"Whoever cleanses a *caitya* of the Tathāgata attains four supreme purities of aspiration. What are the four?"
The supreme purity of the vow for physical form; the supreme purity of the vow for firm undertaking;
the supreme purity of the vow for beholding the Tathāgata.
The supreme purity of the vow for the perfection of the primary marks.
Furthermore, it is stated in this very same place:
by offering flowers and applying fragrant ointments at the reliquaries (caityas) of the Tathāgata, one attains eight forms of non-deficiency.
What are these eight?
He does not become deficient in physical form,
nor deficient in wealth,
nor deficient in retinue.
He is not deficient in ethical discipline, not deficient in meditative concentration,
not deficient in learning, not deficient in wisdom, and not deficient in his aspiration.
And it is said in the *Āryaratnarāśisūtra*:
"Suppose all those beings included within the three realms of existence were each to construct stūpas for the Tathāgata of such a form in height,
namely, like Sumeru, the king of mountains."
And suppose they were to honor each of them with every form of respect for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges;
yet a bodhisattva who, never being separated from the mind of omniscience, should offer even a single flower—
this latter person would generate far more merit than that previous mass of merit.
It is said in this very context:

"Furthermore, suppose all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were to set out upon the Mahāyāna, and each were endowed with the sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); and suppose each universal monarch were to fashion a lamp-vessel the size of the great ocean."
Having lit a wick the size of Mount Sumeru, one should perform such an offering of lamps individually at the reliquaries (caityas) of the Tathāgatas.
And if a bodhisattva who has gone forth from the household life were to prepare a wick soaked in oil, light it, and maintain it at a reliquary of the Tathāgata,
the former gift of lamps does not approach even a hundredth part of this wick soaked in oil.
"Even a mere fraction [of it] is not possible," and so forth.

Furthermore, if those universal monarchs were to honor the community of monks headed by the Buddha with all the requisites for comfort, and if a bodhisattva who has gone forth from the household life, having wandered for alms, were to eat after sharing what has been placed in his bowl with others; [the latter would be superior].
This is far more abundant and far more precious than if those universal monarchs were to give a heap of robes as large as Mount Sumeru to the community of monks headed by the Buddha;

and it is even more so than if a bodhisattva who has gone forth from the household life were to give his three robes externally to the community of monks headed by the Buddha, or to a stūpa of the Tathāgata, having set out in the Mahāyāna.
Monk, this gift of a robe to a monk surpasses that previous heap of robes;
it surpasses what those kings, each having covered the entirety of Jambudvīpa with flowers, might offer at a Tathāgata’s stūpa;
and it surpasses what a Bodhisattva who has gone forth from the household life might place upon a Tathāgata’s stūpa, even if it be but a single flower.
This former gift does not approach even a hundredth part of this gift;
indeed, it does not even approach its infinitesimal fraction.
It is also taught in the *Āryānupūrvasamudgata-parivarta*:
"Perceiving these four auspicious benefits, a bodhisattva becomes eager for the worship of the Tathāgata. What are the four?"
The foremost among those worthy of offerings will have been honored by me; and upon seeing me, others too will train accordingly.
By honoring the Tathāgata, the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) will become firm;
and through the direct vision of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the root of virtue will be accumulated.
"These four."
And this is the unsurpassed service and worship of the Tathāgata,
as it has been declared in the *Āryasāgaramatiparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
"Sāgaramati, these three are the unsurpassed services and worship of the Tathāgata."
Which three?
That which generates the mind of awakening,
and that which upholds the true Dharma.
And that which gives rise to a mind of great compassion toward sentient beings.
It is also taught in the *Āryaratnamegha*:
"Noble son, endowed with ten qualities, bodhisattvas are born unstained by the impurity of the womb.
What are these ten?"
Namely:
by having images of the Tathāgata made, and by restoring ruined stūpas.
By the offering of fragrant ointments at the reliquaries of the Tathāgata;
by the offering of bathing with scented water for the images of the Tathāgata;
and by the offering of sweeping and smearing at the reliquaries of the Tathāgata.
By performing physical service for one's mother and father; by performing physical service for one's teachers and preceptors;
and by performing physical service for one's fellow practitioners of the holy life—and that with a mind free from worldly desire, not one possessed by worldly desire.
And they dedicate that very merit in this way:
"By this root of virtue, may all sentient beings be born unstained by the impurity of the womb.
And they contemplate this with an intense resolve.
"By these ten qualities, noble son."
The benefits of rejoicing (*anumodanā*) have been taught in the *Āryaprajñāpāramitā*:
whoever rejoices in those productions of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*) of bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, who have newly set out in the vehicle;
and whoever also rejoices in those productions of the thought of awakening of those who are practicing the bodhisattva conduct.
He also rejoices in the non-retrogressive nature of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, which is itself non-retrogressive.
Blessed One, how much greater a mass of merit does that son of good family or daughter of good family produce?

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: “...Furthermore, Kauśika, it might indeed be possible to grasp the measure of the great trichiliocosm world-system by weighing it on the tip of a balance; but it is not at all possible, Kauśika, to grasp the measure of the merit of those mental productions of a bodhisattva mahāsattva that are accompanied by sympathetic joy.”
When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, those beings should be known as being under the influence of Māra, who—

beginning from the first production of the thought of awakening by the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, up until their full realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening— do not thus rejoice with immeasurable rejoicing."
They do not hear that it is merit, they do not know it,
and they do not attend to that rejoicing;
O Blessed One, those beings will belong to the faction of Māra.
The Blessed One said: ...

"Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the vehicle of the śrāvakas, by whom these productions of the thought [of awakening] are rejoiced in, will quickly please the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas."
The Blessed One said:
Thus, by means of those roots of merit consisting of the production of the thought of awakening accompanied by rejoicing, wherever they may be reborn,
there they will be honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, adored, and venerated;
and they shall not behold unpleasant forms.
And they shall not hear unpleasant sounds;
likewise, they shall not encounter unpleasant odors, tastes, or tangibles, nor should their rebirth in the states of woe be expected, for their rebirth in heaven should be expected.
Why is that?

For by those beings, the roots of merit of incalculable beings— which bring happiness to all beings— have been rejoiced in, up until the point that they will realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and lead immeasurable and incalculable beings to final nirvana.
Furthermore, it says in this very same passage:

"Subhūti, suppose all the sentient beings in as many triple-thousand great thousandfold world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges were to all establish themselves in unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment; having established themselves in unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment..."
Suppose there were beings who, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, were to enter the four dhyānas while perceiving them as objective entities (*upalambhasaṃjñin*).

Yet, compared to a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who— sustained by this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*)— [dedicates] the aggregate of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, past, future, and present,
as well as the aggregate of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas...

Having gathered all this together from one side, having condensed it, having weighed it, and having taken it up without remainder, one should rejoice with the foremost rejoicing— the highest, best, excellent, most eminent, sublime, unsurpassed, peerless, ever-surpassing, incomparable, unequaled, and matchless rejoicing— and, having so rejoiced, one should [dedicate] the basis of meritorious action associated with that rejoicing.
He dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Subhūti, compared to this basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing, that previous accumulation of merit consisting of the four dhyānas of the bodhisattvas who perceive objects does not approach even a hundredth part, and so on.
"It does not even tolerate the Upaniṣad," so it is said.
This very same method has been stated regarding the dedication [of merit].
Alternatively, because all merits have been dedicated by means of the supreme dedication, for one whose aspiration for Buddhahood has been honored, there will indeed be Buddhahood itself;
therefore, what further increase of merit could there be?
For that is endowed with the merit and wisdom acquired through the liberation of all sentient beings without exception, and it is free from conceptual construction.

However, the benefits of making a formal request (adhyeṣaṇā) are stated in the *Āryograparipṛcchā*: by virtue of being receptive to the Dharma, one's lifespan is preserved in immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-fields.
The seventeenth chapter, on the Benefits of Veneration and so forth, in the *Ārya-Śikṣāsamuccaya*, is completed.
[XVIII Recollection of the Three Jewels] The eighteenth chapter, titled "Recollection of the Three Jewels."
The increase of merit has been explained according to the procedure of the *Bhadracaryā*;
and this is another cause for it:
namely, the constant practice of faith and the other [virtuous qualities].
As it is said in the *Āryatathāgataguhyasūtra*:
"O Great King, these four qualities lead those who have set out in the Mahāyāna toward excellence and prevent their decline. What are the four?"
"Great King, faith leads to progress toward excellence and to non-retrogression.
In this regard, what is faith?
It is that faith by which one approaches the Noble Ones."
And he does not do what should not be done.
Great King, reverence leads to progress toward excellence;
through that reverence, one listens to well-spoken words, desires to hear them, and listens to the Dharma with undistracted ears.
"O Great King, freedom from pride leads to the attainment of distinction;
by means of that freedom from pride, one bows down, prostrates, and pays homage to the Noble Ones."
Great King, vigor leads to progress toward distinction and to non-decline.
By means of that vigor, one attains lightness of body and lightness of mind, and carries all tasks to completion.
"These four, O Great King," [are they].
One should constantly practice these [faculties] beginning with faith; or else, one should practice other [faculties] beginning with faith.
As it is said in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*: "There are these five faculties.
Which five?
The faculty of faith, the faculty of vigor, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom."
In that regard, what is faith? It is that by which one has deep conviction in four things through faith. Which four?
He places faith in the mundane right view pertaining to the realm of saṃsāra. He takes refuge in the ripening of karma, thinking:
"Whatever karma I shall perform, I will experience the fruit and ripening of each and every such karma."
Even for the sake of his life, he does not commit an evil deed;
he has deep faith in the conduct of a bodhisattva,
and having entered upon that practice, he does not give rise to a longing for any other vehicle.

Having heard all phenomena— which are of ultimate meaning and definitive meaning, and which are characterized by profound dependent origination, selflessness, the absence of sentient beings, the absence of living souls, the absence of persons, conventional emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— he places his faith in them.
He does not adhere to any views that have been constructed, and he places his faith in all the qualities of a Buddha, such as the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and so forth.
Having faith and being free from doubt, one fully realizes those qualities of a Buddha;
this is called the faculty of faith.
In that regard, what is the faculty of energy?
Those phenomena which one has faith in by means of the faculty of faith, those very phenomena one brings to fulfillment by means of the faculty of energy; this is called the faculty of energy.
In that regard, what is the faculty of mindfulness?
Those phenomena which one brings to fulfillment by means of the faculty of energy, those very phenomena one does not allow to be lost by means of the faculty of mindfulness;
this is called the faculty of mindfulness.
In that regard, what is the faculty of concentration?

Those phenomena which one does not cause to be lost through the faculty of mindfulness, one brings to a state of one-pointedness by means of the faculty of concentration; this is called the faculty of concentration.
In that regard, what is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)?
Those phenomena which one makes one-pointed by means of the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), those one examines and penetrates by means of the faculty of wisdom.
That which is personal knowledge regarding these phenomena, a knowledge not dependent on others—this is called the faculty of wisdom.
Thus, these five faculties, when conjoined and interconnected, bring all the qualities of a Buddha to fulfillment and cause one to reach the stage of receiving the prophecy.
One should always practice the powers, such as faith and the rest.
As it is said in the *Āryaratnacūḍasūtra*:
"In that regard, noble son, what is the purification of the bodhisattva’s practice of the powers?"
When one is supported by these very faculties, one becomes invincible to all Māras;
one becomes irreducible by the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
and one becomes irreversible from the Mahāyāna.
He becomes invincible to all afflictions;
he becomes firm in his former vows;
and he becomes satisfied in his mind.
He becomes strong in body;
he is guarded by his sense faculties;
he becomes difficult for heretics to defeat, and so forth.
Thus, first of all, the constant practice of faith and the other [faculties] leads to the increase of merit.
What is loving-kindness?

As it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*: "Whatever immeasurable and manifold offerings there may be throughout tens of millions of billions of fields, even if one were to constantly perform those offerings to the Best of Men, they would not equal even a fraction of the merit of a mind of loving-kindness."
What is the recollection of the Buddha and so forth?
In that regard, it is described in the *Rāṣṭrapāla Sūtra*:

"I pay homage to you, who resemble the color of gold, endowed with excellent marks, and whose face is like the stainless moon. I pay homage to you, supreme in peerless wisdom; there is no one equal to you, free from dust, within the three worlds."
Your hair and nails are soft, beautiful, lustrous, and auspicious; your crown-protrusion (uṣṇīṣa) here is like the king of mountains.
There is no one equal to you in possessing this uṣṇīṣa; O Sage, the ūrṇā between your eyebrows shines brilliantly.

Resembling jasmine, the moon, a conch, and snow in its pure whiteness, with beautiful eyes as lovely as blue lotuses, you gaze upon this world with compassion; therefore, O Victor of stainless eyes, I pay homage to you.
Your tongue is long, slender, and resembles copper; with it you cover your own face.
Speaking the Dharma, you discipline the world; I pay homage to you, whose speech is sweet and gentle.
Your teeth are beautiful, very firm, and like diamonds; thirty in number, they are even and closely set.
Smiling, you discipline the world; I pay homage to you, whose speech is sweet and true.
O Jina, you are peerless in form, and with your radiance you illuminate hundreds of fields;
O Blessed One, the Brahmās, Indras, and World-Protectors are eclipsed by your splendor.
O Blessed One, with thighs like those of the eneya antelope, you possess a gait equal to that of the king of elephants, the peacock, and the king of beasts;
even while walking, O Blessed One, you look ahead only the distance of a yoke, causing the earth, its mountains, and its slopes to tremble.
O Blessed One, your body is adorned with the marks; your skin is subtle and resembles the color of gold.
O you who possess incomparable form, the world never reaches satiety when beholding this beauty of yours.

You have practiced austerities for hundreds of previous eons; you delight in universal renunciation, self-control, and generosity; your mind is filled with compassion and loving-kindness for all sentient beings; I pay homage to you, the supremely compassionate one.
You are constantly devoted to generosity and ethical discipline; you are firmly established in patience and diligence.
You possess the radiant splendor of meditative concentration and wisdom; I pay homage to you, the bearer of peerless knowledge.
You are a hero among speakers, a crusher of evil factions; you roar like a lion in the assembly.
You are the King of Physicians, the ender of the three stains; I pay homage to you, the one who brings supreme joy.
O Sage, pure in speech, body, and mind, unstained by the three worlds like a lotus in water;
you possess the voice of Brahmā and the song of the kalaviṅka bird—I pay homage to you who have gone beyond the three worlds.
This world has been understood by you to be like an illusion, resembling a theatrical stage or a dream;
there is no self, no sentient being, and no life-principle, for all phenomena are like a mirage or the moon reflected in water.
The world wanders in delusion, not understanding the principle of emptiness, peace, and non-arising;
out of your great compassion, you lead them across by means of hundreds of skillful methods, reasonings, and logical arguments.
Beholding the world constantly bewildered by passion and hundreds of other defilements,
O Sugata, you wander like an incomparable physician, liberating hundreds of beings.

O Sage, beholding the world constantly afflicted— stricken by birth, old age, death, and sorrow, and by hundreds of lamentations due to separation from the beloved— you wander about out of compassion, liberating it.
The entire world revolves like a chariot wheel among animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, and those in happy realms;
to those who are deluded, directionless, and without a protector, you reveal the supreme path.
Those Victors who existed in the past, the lords of Dharma who brought benefit to the world—
they too proclaimed this very same noble path which you, O peerless Lord, now teach.

For you utter that speech which is smooth, not harsh, charming, excellent, superior even to Brahma, and supremely pleasing— surpassing the voices of the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and the finest Apsarases.
For having heard that speech of infinite qualities— which is purified by truth, uprightness, and the methods of skillful means—
hundreds of millions of beings produce peace through the three vehicles.
Through worship of you, they obtain manifold kinds of divine happiness among humans;
likewise, one becomes a king who brings benefit to the world, wealthy, possessing great riches and great majesty.
Moreover, as a powerful universal monarch and lord of the continents, he covers the world with the ten wholesome actions;
he obtains the seven most auspicious jewels, for you are incomparable in generating serene faith.
Through your worship, one becomes Brahmā, Śakra, and the Lord of the World; one becomes the contented lord of the gods, Paranirmita, and the lord of the Yāmas; and one even becomes a Jina.
For thus, O Amogha, your worship performed—even the sight of you or hearing your name—is incomparable;
it removes the manifold sufferings of the world and leads one to touch the supreme, stainless state.
O Knower of the Path, O Skillful in the Path, Blessed One, you turn this world away from evil paths;
O Blessed One, you establish the world upon the Noble Path—secure, auspicious, and stainless.
For you, who seek merit and are a treasury of merit, meritorious action becomes eternally inexhaustible;
it does not reach exhaustion for many millions of eons until you indeed touch supreme enlightenment.
He obtains a beautiful, completely pure field, always radiant like that of the Paranirmita gods and ever-joyful;
moreover, in that excellent field, sentient beings become pure in body, speech, and mind.
Thus, by performing worship of the Victors, a person obtains manifold virtues such as these;
he attains heaven, liberation, and happiness among men, becoming a treasury of merit for the entire world.
Your vast fame and renown have spread throughout hundreds of many fields in all directions;
the Sugatas, the Jinas, constantly proclaim the garland of your praises within their assemblies.
Free from the fever of passion, you bring liberation to the world; you are lovely to behold and possess peerless compassion.
Your senses are stilled and you delight in tranquility; O Blessed One, supreme among the best of men, I pay homage to you.
O Victor, having heard your words while standing in the sky, I have attained the five superknowledges;
O Hero, I shall become equal to the Sugatas and shall distribute the stainless Dharma to the world.
Having today praised the Sugata, who has reached the further shore of all virtues and is honored by men, gods, and nāgas—
may the world obtain this vast merit that has been acquired, as well as the state of Buddhahood.
Alternatively, as it is said in the *Āryadharmasaṃgītisūtra*:
"Furthermore, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess the great accumulation of merit and wisdom; they range within great loving-kindness and great compassion;

they have become a refuge for the great multitude of sentient beings; they are the great physicians who extract the thorns [of suffering]; they possess minds of equanimity toward all sentient beings; and they range within the samādhi of impermanence."
They are liberated from both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; they are like parents to all sentient beings, possessing a mind of equal loving-kindness. ... [and so forth] ...

They are unconquered by all the worlds, having become the light of all the world; they are practitioners of great yoga, great-souled ones with vast retinues of eminent people, whose audiences, teachings, and services cannot be obstructed; they are indifferent to their own happiness and devoted to the alleviation of the suffering of others;
they love the Dharma, uphold the Dharma, take the Dharma as their sustenance, are physicians of the Dharma, lords of the Dharma, masters of the Dharma, and patrons of the gift of the Dharma.

The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are ever-delighted in renunciation, ever-vigilant, and ever-delighted in solitude; they serve everywhere as bridges and embankments, resembling great royal highways, and their appearance is such that one can never look upon them enough.
Thus he recollects them.
And having thus recollected them, one establishes mindfulness for the sake of perfecting those qualities.
That is called the recollection of the Buddha.
In this very context, he speaks of the recollection of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*).
Here, it occurs to the bodhisattva:

"These Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who possess infinite and boundless qualities, are born of the Dharma, have the Dharma as their foundation, are emanated from the Dharma, have the Dharma as their sovereign, have the Dharma as their radiance, have the Dharma as their sphere of activity, and have the Dharma as their refuge."
They are established in the Dharma... [and so on].
Whatever worldly and supramundane happinesses there may be, they too are born of the Dharma and perfected by the Dharma;
therefore, one who seeks awakening must regard the Dharma as the highest priority.

Through reverence for the Dharma, taking refuge in the Dharma, being devoted to the Dharma, having the Dharma as one's essence, pursuing the Dharma, and practicing in accordance with the Dharma— this is called a bodhisattva’s recollection of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*).
Furthermore, it occurs to the bodhisattva:
"The Dharma is indeed equal; it proceeds equally toward all sentient beings. The Dharma proceeds without regard for whether beings are inferior, middling, or superior."
In that way, I must possess a mind that accords with the Dharma;
for the Dharma does not function out of a desire for pleasure,
since the Dharma is indeed impartial.
In the same way, I must possess a mind that accords with the Dharma;
for the Dharma does not function by waiting for time,
as the Dharma is indeed timeless.
It is to be seen here and now;
it is to be personally realized.
In that same way, I must possess a mind that accords with the Dharma.
The Dharma does not operate in the sublime, nor does it fail to operate among the lowly; for the Dharma is neither elevated nor depressed. Thus, I should maintain a mind that accords with the Dharma.
The Dharma does not operate upon the pure, nor does it fail to operate upon the wounded;

for the Dharma is free from both elevation and depreciation. Thus, I should possess a mind that accords with the Dharma. The Dharma does not operate among the noble ones, nor does it fail to operate among ordinary beings.
For the Dharma is free from the perception of a field;
likewise, I should possess a mind that accords with the Dharma.
The Dharma does not function by day, nor does it fail to function by night.
Whether it proceeds at night or does not proceed by day,
the Dharma is indeed eternally established;
likewise, I must possess a mind that accords with the Dharma.
The Dharma does not transgress the proper time for discipline;
there is no delay whatsoever in the Dharma.
In this same way, I must possess a mind that accords with the Dharma.
There is neither decrease nor increase in the Dharma, for the Dharma is immeasurable and incalculable; like space, it neither diminishes nor increases.
Thus, I should maintain a mind that accords with the Dharma.
The Dharma is not protected by sentient beings.
Dharma protects sentient beings;
likewise, I must possess a mind that accords with Dharma.
Dharma does not seek out a refuge.
Dharma is the refuge of the entire world;
likewise, I must possess a mind that accords with Dharma,
for there is no resistance anywhere toward Dharma.
For the Dharma has the characteristic of being unimpeded;
likewise, I should possess a mind that accords with the Dharma.
The Dharma does not carry latent tendencies.
For the Dharma is free from latent tendencies;
likewise, I must possess a mind that accords with the Dharma. The Dharma is neither terrified by the fear of saṃsāra nor attached to nirvāṇa.
For phenomena are always free from conceptual construction;
likewise, I should maintain a mind that accords with phenomena.
In this way, the bodhisattva establishes mindfulness upon phenomena in accordance with phenomena.
That is called the recollection of the Dharma.

Regarding this very point, it is said: "The Saṅgha indeed speaks according to the Dharma, practices the Dharma, contemplates the Dharma, is a field of the Dharma, upholds the Dharma, takes refuge in the Dharma, honors the Dharma, performs the duties of the Dharma, has the Dharma as its sphere of activity, and is perfected in the conduct of the Dharma.
It is upright by nature, pure by nature, compassionate, sympathetic toward the Dharma, and always dwells in seclusion."
"Always devoted to the Dharma, always performing pure deeds," and so forth.
In that regard, as the bodhisattva recollects the Saṅgha, it occurs to him:
"These actual qualities of the Saṅgha are those which I must bring to fulfillment for myself and for all sentient beings."
Just as the qualities of a bodhisattva are described in the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa*, so should the recollection of the Saṅgha be cultivated:
"In a single instant, the confident bodhisattvas manifest all the forms, sounds, and utterances of all sentient beings."
Those bodhisattvas appear as aged and diseased, even manifesting themselves as dead;
for the sake of maturing sentient beings, they sport with the nature of illusion.
They display the conflagration at the end of an eon, burning the earth,
in order to show the impermanence to beings who perceive things as permanent.
Invited by hundreds of thousands of beings within a single kingdom,
they eat in the homes of all and dedicate them all to awakening.
Whatever mantra-sciences or various fields of craftsmanship there may be,
they have attained perfection in all of them, bringing happiness to all sentient beings.
However many heretics there are in the world who go forth everywhere,
he ripens those beings who have fallen into various types of views.
They become moons or suns, Śakra, Brahmā, or lords of progeny;
they likewise become water, fire, earth, and wind.
During the intermediate eons of disease, they become supreme medicines, by which those beings are liberated, become happy, and free from illness.
During the intermediate kalpas of famine, they become food and drink;
having removed hunger and thirst, they teach the Dharma to living beings.
During the intermediate kalpas of weapons, they become meditators on loving-kindness;
they establish many hundreds of millions of beings in non-malice.
And in the midst of a great battle, those Bodhisattvas of great power remain impartial toward both sides; they delight in reconciliation and harmony.
And whatever hells there may be in inconceivable Buddha-fields,
they intentionally go there for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
In as many realms of existence as are revealed within the animal womb, they teach the Dharma everywhere; therefore, they are called Leaders.
They display the enjoyment of sensual pleasures as well as meditative absorption for those who practice meditation;
they utterly destroy Māra and allow him no opportunity to gain entry.
Just as one would point out a lotus in the midst of fire as something that has not come to be,
so too did he show you that sensual pleasures and meditative absorption are both unreal.
Intentionally becoming courtesans, they attract men; having enticed them with the hook of passion, they establish them in the wisdom of a Buddha.
And for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they always become village headmen, caravan leaders, family priests, chief ministers, and ministers.
And for sentient beings who are impoverished, they become inexhaustible treasuries;
and having given gifts to them, they cause them to generate the mind of awakening.
Among sentient beings stiffened by pride, they become great champions;
they seek supreme enlightenment, which uproots all pride.
They always stand before sentient beings who are afflicted by fear;
having granted them fearlessness, they bring them to maturity for enlightenment.
Having become seers endowed with the five superknowledges and living as celibate practitioners,
they establish sentient beings in ethical discipline, patience, gentleness, and self-restraint.
Seeing beings here who are venerable because they provide service, those who are confident become their servants or slaves, or they enter into the state of being their disciples.
By whatever means a sentient being might come to delight in the Dharma,
they— well-trained in great skillful means— demonstrate all those very actions.
For those whose training is indeed infinite and whose sphere of activity is also infinite,
who are endowed with infinite wisdom and are liberators of infinite living beings.
"Even by Buddhas speaking for ten million eons, or even for a hundred times ten million eons, the end of their virtues could not easily be told. Thus it is said.
Just as the qualities of a bodhisattva are described in the *Ārya-ratnolkā-dhāraṇī*, so should they be cultivated.
Emitting rays of light that display arrays of garlands— garland-ornaments, garland-canopies,
and garlands scattered and strewn everywhere— those great-souled ones perform worship to the Victors.
Emitting rays of light, those great-souled ones perform worship to the Jinas by scattering powders in magnificent arrays, powder-ornaments, powder-canopies, and various powders strewn everywhere.
Emitting rays of light adorned with lotuses— lotus-crests, lotus-canopies,
and lotuses strewn in various ways all around— those great-souled ones perform worship to the Jinas.
Emitting rays of light adorned with necklaces, with necklaces as crests and necklaces as canopies,
those great-souled ones perform worship of the Jinas, scattering various necklaces all around.
He emits rays from the array at the tip of his banner; those banners are white, red, and yellow, with many variegated blue streamers.
The fields of the Jinas are adorned with banners, featuring variegated arrays of jewel nets;
they are hung with garlands of silk streamers and pennants, and possess the resonance of the Jina’s voice through networks of tinkling bells.
They hold parasols over the head of the Tathāgata, just as they would for a single Jina;
from the palm of their hand, they perform inconceivable worship in this way for all the Jinas without exception.
This is the miraculous transformation of the sages' meditative absorption; it is their miraculous display of the wisdom that gathers in the world.
By accomplishing this supreme meditative absorption, they perform all activities through the ease of skillful means.

They discipline sentient beings through thousands of skillful means: some by way of worshiping the Tathāgatas; some by way of inconceivable giving and renunciation; and some by way of all the ascetic qualities and moral discipline.
Some [attain] inexhaustible patience through the gateway of imperturbability; some [attain] the vow through the gateway of ascetic vigor;
[some attain] meditative absorption through the gateway of dwelling in tranquility; and [some attain] wisdom that ascertains its own object through the gateway of discernment.
By means of the thousand doors of all skillful methods, by means of the doors of the divine abodes and the superknowledges,
by means of the doors of the articles of attraction and the desire for the welfare of others, and by means of the door of the accumulation of merit and wisdom.

Some [attain it] by way of the liberation door of truth and dependent origination; some by way of the doors of the powers, the faculties, and the path; some by way of the liberation door of the Śrāvaka vehicle; and some by way of the purification door of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
Some [were taught] by way of the miraculous display of the supreme vehicle; some by way of impermanence and suffering;
some by way of selflessness and the absence of a living soul; and some by way of the perception of impurity and dispassion.

Whatever gateways of conduct there are in the world, and whatever gateways of phenomena are being realized, they are all encompassed by the gateway of universal liberation through the gateway of the meditative absorption of peaceful cessation.

Those who discipline sentient beings in the world according to their inclinations through the gateway of universal liberation— those who discipline sentient beings in the world according to their inclinations— it is impossible to grasp any sign of them.

By means of this, one performs the miraculous transformations of meditative concentration; by that, the supreme concentration is arrayed, which is in accordance with the ripening of all worlds and brings joy, delight, and exhilaration through the gateway of all delights.

Having reflected, they manifest everything to discipline those beings where famine prevails and all things are very difficult to obtain; and whatever requisites bring happiness in the world, they provide them there through the fulfillment of every desire.
Those who give for the sake of the world’s welfare bestow excellent food, drink, and the finest flavors;
they give through the renunciation of various garments, ornaments, and jewels, as well as kingdoms, wealth, themselves, and their own dear ones.

Those whose bodies are adorned with excellent marks, who possess supreme ornaments and noble steadfastness, and who are decorated with garlands and anointed with perfumes, discipline the world through their devotion to generosity.

Having manifested forms, they discipline sentient beings who delight in the joy and rapture of seeing them; those of excellent form, beautiful appearance, and great wisdom display their supreme beauty.

They discipline the world through devotion to form with the sweet songs of the kalaviṅka bird, with the cries of the cuckoo, the swan, and the kuṇāla, and with the sounds of the drum, the kinnara, and the voice of Brahmā; they teach the Dharma within all forms of devotion.

Those eighty-four thousand gateways for the differentiation of the Dharma, by which the Victors accomplish the welfare of the world— through these, they discipline sentient beings in the world according to their inclinations.
They act as companions in both happiness and suffering; they become companions in both profit and loss.
Having become companions in all activities, they discipline sentient beings through the means of companionship.
But they endure those faults brought about by suffering and calamity, taking their companions as the cause;
together with those companions, they endure the pain for the sake of the welfare and happiness of the entire world.

Where there is no renunciation, nor is dharma known, nor liberation found even when gone to the forest— there, with the prosperity of a kingdom as their companion, they are homeless, having set their minds on renunciation and peace.

For the sake of liberating the entire world from the dwelling of thirst that binds one to the home, they abandon all delights of sensual desire, remaining homeless as they manifest the power of renunciation and liberation.
Cultivating those ten practices, they practiced the Dharma of the Great Beings;
cultivating every practice of the Sages without exception, they act for the benefit of the world.
Where there are beings with immeasurable lifespans, endowed with happiness and possessing only mild afflictions,
there he— himself powerless— shows himself afflicted by old age, struck down by disease, and subject to death.
Seeing the world inflamed by passion, ablaze with hatred, and set on fire by the great fire of delusion— a world burning with old age, sickness, and death— they lead sentient beings to discipline.

Indicating the great-souled Buddha by means of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they accomplish the welfare of the world through the Buddha's virtues.

And by means of the power of the foundation of form, those Tathāgatas display miracles and supernatural transformations throughout all directions; teaching through these miraculous powers, they discipline sentient beings.
They wander through the world for the sake of living beings by means of various skillful methods;
unstained by the world like a lotus in water, they move about, inspiring joy and serene confidence.
O King of Poets, those who compose poetry become like actors, dancers, cymbal players,
wrestlers, acrobats, fortune-tellers, jewelers, performers, magicians, and those who display various forms.
They become village headmen, leaders, charioteers, caravan guides, guild masters, and householders;
they become kings, ministers, chaplains, and messengers, as well as physicians who are expert and learned in the sciences and ritual procedures.

In the forests, O great tree, they become medicinal herbs and inexhaustible treasuries of jewels; they are wish-fulfilling gems and trees that grant all desires, acting as guides for those who have strayed onto wrong paths.
Having understood the world, let them be honored; for sentient beings are ignorant regarding the methods of action.
They shall cause agriculture, the application of labor, trade, and various crafts to flourish in the world.
Those practices of non-violence and non-harming, which bring about all happiness and are praised by the wise;
those various sciences, spells, medicinal herbs, and treatises—all these were brought forth by those sages.
Those supreme and foremost practices of the sages, in which the world including the gods has placed its faith;
those difficult vows and those most excellent austerities—all have been manifested by those wise ones.

Those wandering mendicants, renunciants, and heretics are indeed the teachers of the ascetics, followers of Gautama, and forest-dwellers; they are the teachers of the naked ones, the unclothed ones, and the śramaṇas.

They indeed become teachers even among those Ajivikas who practice the Dharma, those who seek what is higher and unsurpassed, those with long matted hair, and those observing the vow of perpetual celibacy.
The five-fold heat-practitioners who follow the sun, those who observe the dog-vow and the cow-vow,
the deer-like ascetics, the wanderers, and the ten types of heretics— among these three groups as well, they indeed become teachers.
For those who delight in entering the knowledge of the deities and who travel through the lands to point out the sacred sites,
even though they subsist on roots, fruits, and water, their inconceivable Dharma is supreme and most excellent.
Even among those who remain in a squatting posture, who wander alone, who sleep on thorns, ashes, or grass,
and who dwell in disciplined practice while lying upon a pestle— even among them, these indeed become teachers.
Having observed the inclinations and the faith of as many outsiders and various heretics as there may be,
he disciplines those heretics— who are fierce, difficult to approach, and fierce in their asceticism— so that they may abandon suffering.
Having perceived that the world is agitated by views and that the non-Buddhists rely upon all manner of false views,
they reveal the truth to them through subtle words and skillful means.
To some he taught the truth through Dravidian mantra-words and well-guarded phrases;
to some through clear and distinct words, and to some indeed through secret words.
By means of certain words distinguished by syllables, by vajra-words for the definitive determination of meaning,
by words of knowledge for crushing opponents, and by words concerning the teacher, the Dharma, and liberation;
In some [teachings], it was by means of human mantra-words and all words of linguistic expression;
in some, by means of divine words of expression, and by means of the words of nagas and yakshas.
Through the stations of the rākṣasas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, and through those of the bhūtas, kumbhāṇḍas, and mahoragas,
as well as the stations of the kiṃnaras, apsarases, and garuḍas, they lead beings to liberation by means of the illumination of truth.

Those who know the rules of etymology according to reality, who thus [know] the qualities of the Victors in their entirety, and who know the path of speech regarding the inconceivable Dharma—they teach it; this is the miraculous power of this samādhi.

Bringing forth the supreme samādhis for the sake of the world’s happiness throughout the entire universe, they emit inconceivable rays of light; having released these rays, they discipline sentient beings.
Emitting rays of light that reveal themselves to as many beings as can perceive those rays,
they become a beautiful sight for them— an unfailing cause for the supreme, excellent knowledge.
He reveals the Buddha, reveals the Dharma, and reveals the Saṅgha as the path for humanity;
he reveals the reliquaries containing the images of the Jinas—thereby the Sudarśana ray is produced.
The light-ray named Prabhaṃkara was emitted, which eclipses the splendor of the gods;
having destroyed all dust and darkness, that radiance shines for the benefit of the world.
Urged on by that radiance, those beings hold lamps for the worship of the Jinas;
having held those lamps for the worship of the Jinas, they become Jinas who act as lamps for the world.

O Light-Maker, by giving lamps of oil, lamps of ghee, and lamps of wood, grass, reeds, and bamboo, as well as lamps of perfumes, elixirs, and jewels to the Jinas, these [splendors] have been obtained.
He emitted a ray named "The Ferrying Across" (*pratāraṇī*); by its light, sentient beings were impelled.
[They were] on the paths of rivers where there was no ferryboat;
they had reviled the conditioned and praised peace. By that, the ray "The Ferrying Across" was brought to completion.

Sentient beings, impelled by that light of the ray named "Dispeller of Thirst," abandon their craving for the qualities of sensual pleasure and become seekers of the essence of liberation through the Dharma.
Having abandoned craving for the qualities of sensual desire and having become seekers of the essence of liberation through the Dharma,
they become Buddhas who rain down the water of the Deathless, dispelling the thirst and parching of the world.
Lotus ponds, rivers, wells, tanks, and springs were caused to be made as the cause for awakening;
sensual desires were disparaged and meditative absorptions were praised, and by that, the quenching of thirst was accomplished.

When he emits the light-ray called "Gladdening," sentient beings impelled by its radiance, their hearts suffused with joy, conceive the thought of supreme enlightenment, thinking: "May we ourselves become self-arisen Buddhas."
Because the compassionate ones have fashioned their forms seated upon lotuses adorned with the [thirty-two] marks,
and because they always speak of the qualities of a Buddha, a light has arisen that brings joy.

He emits a ray of light named Ratiṃkarā; by its radiance, sentient beings are awakened, and they always become those who delight in the joy of the Buddha, delight in the joy of the Dharma, and delight in the joy of the Saṅgha.
Having always delighted in the three jewels— the Buddha, the Dharma, and the noble Saṅgha—
those many beings who have been exhorted and reminded attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena.
Having revealed the qualities of the mind regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and the Noble Bodhi,
by that [revelation] the ray called "Producer of Delight" was manifested.
They emit the ray called "Accumulation of Merit"; incited by that light, sentient beings give various and manifold gifts, aspiring for unsurpassed awakening.
The light called "Accumulation of Merit" arises when those sacrificers fulfill the intentions of supplicants with unobstructed sacrifices, bestowing gifts according to every desire.
When she emits the light-ray called "Possessing Wisdom," sentient beings impelled by its radiance awaken in a single instant to many gateways of the Dharma from within a single gateway of the Dharma.
Having caused sentient beings to grasp the distinctions of phenomena through the analysis of knowledge that determines their meaning,
and having performed an exposition of the categories and meanings of the Dharma, the radiance called Jñānavatī was produced by him.
A ray of light was emitted from the lamp of wisdom; by its radiance, sentient beings were exhorted.

They entered into the dharmas that are empty, devoid of self, unborn, and non-perishing, having the nature of non-existence—like an illusion or a mirage, like the moon in water, a dream, or a reflection.
He teaches that phenomena are ownerless, empty, and effortless, through the cessation of the lamp of wisdom.

He emits the light-ray called "Transformation of Dharma"; incited by that radiance, sentient beings, having obtained the *dhāraṇīs* of inexhaustible treasuries, obtain the treasuries of all the Tathāgatas.
Having undertaken the preservation of the holders of the Dharma, having provided righteous protection for the sages,
and having bestowed the favor of the Dharma upon the world, the light of the miraculous transformation of the Dharma has arisen.
When those possessed of renunciation emit a ray of light, by that [light] sentient beings incited by stinginess,
having realized that enjoyments are impermanent and non-eternal, always become devoted to the delight of renunciation.

Having understood that beings are difficult to tame due to their stinginess and are unsubdued, and that wealth has the nature of a dream or a cloud, she increased her generosity with clarity; by means of this, she became known as Tyāgavatīprabhā.
The ray called "Free from Fever" is emitted; by it, beings who are ill-behaved are exhorted.
Having become established in the purity of ethical conduct, they generate the thought: "May I myself become a Self-Existent One."

When he has caused many beings to undertake pure ethical discipline within the wholesome paths of action, by means of inspiring them toward the mind of awakening, that light ray is produced as one free from feverish affliction.
When the ray called "Array of Forbearance" is emitted,
those beings who were incited to intolerance abandon the thicket of anger and arrogance, and they always become those who delight in the joy of forbearance.
For those whose minds are undisturbed even when subjected to ill-treatment and who possess the intent not to fall into the lower realms, patience is the cause of awakening;
since he has praised the qualities of patience at all times, he has thus attained the array of patience.
When the ray named Utaptavatī is emitted, sentient beings are exhorted by it;
they apply themselves with diligence to the Three Jewels and perform worship with tireless application.
Those who are properly engaged with the three jewels, performing worship with tireless application,
have transcended the four paths of Māra and will swiftly touch unsurpassed awakening.
Because she incited many beings to diligence by making offerings to the Three Jewels and upheld the Dharma during the time of its decline, she has obtained this blazing radiance.
When he emits the light-ray called "Peace-Maker," those beings who were driven by confusion are awakened;
in them there is no longer passion, hatred, or delusion, and their minds become concentrated in meditative absorption.
Having turned away from association with evil friends and those of defiled conduct,
and having praised the tranquil meditation in the forest which brings peace, light was produced by him.
When the light rays of the Array of Wisdom are emitted, sentient beings who were of poor wisdom are stirred;
through this method of truth and dependent liberation, they come to reach the course of knowledge regarding the faculties.
Having attained mastery over the range of sensory cognition,
and having obtained the "Sun-Lamp" samādhi, they become Victors who radiate the light of wisdom.
Through the renunciation of kingdom, wealth, and one's own dear self, you sought the Dharma as the cause of awakening;
by honoring that and proclaiming the Dharma, this ray of light called "the Array of Wisdom" has emerged.
When the Buddha emits the ray called "Possessing Buddhas," sentient beings, impelled by its light,
behold many thousands of inconceivable Buddhas seated within groves of lotuses.
The greatness of the Buddha, the liberations of the Buddha, and the infinite miraculous transformations of the Buddha have been proclaimed;
having manifested the powers of the Buddha, the light called "Possessing the Buddha" has arisen from that.

The Giver of Fearlessness emits that ray; touched by it, sentient beings who are afflicted by fear are liberated from all calamities and fears, such as being harmed or beaten by spirits and demons, or being bound.
Those beings who have been invited by fearlessness are turned away from the killing of living creatures;
those who were terrified and have come for refuge are protected—by that, the ray named "Giver of Fearlessness" is perfected.

The ray that brings all happiness was emitted; those who were sick and afflicted were touched by it, and being completely liberated from the suffering of disease, they obtained the bliss of meditative absorption and concentration.
By giving roots, fruits, medicinal herbs, gems, elixirs, perfumes, and ointments;
and by giving molasses, milk, honey, ghee, oil, food, and drink, you have attained this.

The Buddha emits a light ray called "Manifestation of the Buddhas"; impelled by that ray at the end of their lifespan, they remember the Buddha and behold the Buddha; having passed away, they go to the realm of the Buddhas.
And as they were passing away, they were reminded of the Buddhas who display joy through the forms of the Victors;
having taken refuge in the Buddhas at the end of life, they obtained the vision of the Buddhas as it was proclaimed.
He emits the ray called "Illumination of the Dharma"; sentient beings inspired by that light recite, hear, and write the Dharma, and they always remain delighted in the joy of the Dharma.
In this famine of the Dharma, the Dharma has been illuminated; the hopes of those seeking the Dharma have been fulfilled.
Having generated aspiration, apply yourselves to the Dharma; I have attained the power of the Dharma as it is being spoken.
When the Buddha-son emits the light called "Possessing Sound" for the purpose of exhortation,
they hear every sound circulating in the three worlds as the voice of the Tathāgata.
With loud voices they praise the great seers through the offering of musical instruments, great bells, and gongs;
for the sake of the sound and meaning of the Conqueror’s voice throughout the entire world, she has obtained the radiance of the "Resounding Voice."
They emit the ray called "Bestower of Immortality"; incited by its light, sentient beings abandon all negligence for a long time and apply themselves to the practice of all virtuous qualities.
You have declared that the conditioned is always full of manifold sufferings and calamities, and is inherently insecure;
yet, by teaching the peace of cessation which is eternally secure, O Giver of the Deathless, you have attained it.

When he emits the special ray called Viśeṣavatī, sentient beings impelled by its light hear of the excellence of morality, the excellence of concentration, and the excellence of wisdom belonging to the Victors.
The Great Sage-King is supreme in virtue, supreme in concentration, and supreme in wisdom;
he who has praised and extolled the cause of enlightenment has thereby obtained this distinguished radiance.
When the ray called Jewel Array is emitted, sentient beings who are stirred by its light obtain a treasure-store of syllables and worship the Great Sages with the most excellent jewels.
By relinquishing jewels before the Victors and at the stupas of the Victors, and by gathering all people with jewels,
and by making offerings of jewels to the Victors— the ray named Jewel Array is produced.
When the light-ray called Gandhaprabhāsa is emitted,
the beings stirred by that radiance smell divine and delightful fragrances and become intent upon the millions of qualities of a Buddha.
Having performed worship for the lords of men with human and divine perfumes and ointments,
and having fashioned stupas containing the forms of the Jinas made of incense, he has now returned as Sugandhaprabhāsa.
He emits rays of light with manifold arrays, as variegated as the tops of Indra’s banners and flags;
they are beautified by the sounding of musical instruments, perfumed with incense, and strewn with the finest flowers of the gods.
They went forth to meet the Victors with music, honoring them with flowers, ointments, incense, and powders;
with parasols, banners, crest-flags, and canopies, they brought about various wonderful arrays.
When he emitted the light that brings forth serene faith, the earth became as level as the palm of a hand;
because the Sage purified the hermitages and the stūpas, he obtained this radiance that inspires serene faith.
When Meghavatī emits her ray, a cloud of exquisite fragrance gathers and rains down;
having sprinkled the courtyard of the stūpa with fragrant water, Meghavatī attains radiance.
The Array of Ornaments emits rays: those who are naked and without clothing become beautifully adorned.
Having given various ornaments such as garments, girdles, and necklaces, the ray "Ornament" is manifested.
When she emits the ray called Rasāgravatī, those who are hungry obtain the finest flavors of food;
by giving various foods and drinks of the finest flavors, she has attained the radiance known as Rasāgravatī.
The Arthanidarśanī ray emits light rays so that the poor obtain treasures of jewels;
through the gift of the Three Jewels, the Arthanidarśanī is obtained as an inexhaustible treasury of jewels.
The ray called "Purifier of the Eye" is emitted; then the blind see various forms.
This Purifier of the Eye ray is produced by the gift of lamps to the Jina or to a stupa of the Jina.
He emits light rays that purify the ear; those deprived of hearing hear vast sounds.
These light rays that purify the ear arise from having offered musical instruments to the Victorious One and to the stūpas of the Victorious One.
He emits light rays that purify the sense of smell, whereby one smells fragrances never smelled before;
this "Purifier of the Sense of Smell" ray is produced by the gift of fragrance to the Jina or to a stūpa of the Jina.
The tongue-purifying ray is emitted, praising the Buddhas with smooth and charming sounds;
having abandoned harsh speech and uttered words that are gentle, this ray is brought forth.
The Bodhisattva emits rays called "Purifier of the Body"; those who lack sense faculties become possessed of them.
By prostrating the body before the Victorious One or at a stupa of the Victorious One, one obtains the Purifier of the Body.
The ray called "Purifier of Mind" is emitted; all sentient beings become insane.
Having brought the mind under the control of meditative concentration, the ray "Purifier of Mind" returns.
He emits light rays that purify form; having seen and contemplated the lords of men in their forms, he attains the purification of form, which is everywhere variegated, and adorns the stūpas.
The light-ray called "Purifier of Sound" is emitted; it causes one to understand that sound is non-sound and empty.
Arisen from conditions and equal to an echo, the manifestation of sound ceases through this light-ray.
The Gandhaviśodhani ray emits beams such that all foul odors become fragrant;
this is the radiance of the Bodhi-tree, which bathes the stūpas of the Jinas with the most excellent and supreme perfumes.
They emit light rays called "Purifier of Tastes," by which excellent flavors that contain poison become free of poison;
this is their radiance resulting from the gift of the finest flavors to Buddhas, Śrāvakas, mothers, and fathers.
The Purifier of Touch emits rays so that harsh touch becomes soft and pleasant;
showers of spears, tridents, swords, and lances become soft garlands of lotuses and water-lilies.
On the path where the Jinas travel, many soft cloths, pleasant to the touch, are spread out;
this is the manifestation of their gift of flowers, ointments, fine robes, garlands, and canopies.
The Purifier of Dharma emits rays from every pore;
as they issue forth, one hears them proclaiming the teachings for the benefit of the world, thereby satisfying all the Victors according to their various inclinations.

Arising from conditions yet unborn by nature, the body of Dharma is the unborn body; eternally abiding in the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) like space, it indicates that the purification of phenomena has been attained.

With the light-ray "Sukha" as the foremost, from a single pore of the sages there issued forth rays of light equal in number to the sands of the Ganges, each engaged in various distinct types of activity.
Just as they emit rays of light like the sands of the Ganges from a single pore,
so do the sages display the miraculous transformations of their meditative concentrations from every single pore without exception.
By whichever quality a particular ray was produced, and by whom that quality was previously assisted, to those very persons he emits that same ray; such is the manifestation of wisdom of these sages.
Those who were their former companions in merit, by whom it was rejoiced in and requested,
and by whom it was seen or accumulated as wholesome— they recognize this ray for them.
And for those who have accumulated merit, performed virtuous deeds, and have repeatedly honored the Buddhas—
those who long for and desire the qualities of a Buddha— this ray of light provides them with exhortation.
Just as one born blind does not see the sun, yet it is not that the sun does not rise in the world;
so too, having realized the emergence of the Eye, all those who apply themselves to their respective duties [attain it].
Such is the radiance of the Great Beings; others do not see it.
Those who are destroyed by falsehood and devoid of resolute faith find it difficult to perceive the light of those with noble minds.
Ornaments, palatial dwellings, jewels, elixirs, perfumes, and ointments—
these indeed belong to those of noble soul, yet they are very difficult to obtain for those who have fallen into hardship.
Such is the radiance of the Great Beings; others do not see it.
Those who are destroyed by falsehood and devoid of resolute faith find it difficult to encounter those of noble intelligence.

Whoever, having heard this classification of rays, shall develop faith and serene confidence, by them no doubt or uncertainty should be entertained; they shall indeed become a banner of great qualities.
Manifesting the miraculous transformations of their retinues through the realization of the supreme samādhis,
these sons of the Buddha, peerless throughout the ten directions, display their entourages.
They empower a lotus of variegated dimensions equal to three thousandfold worlds with an array of light rays;
this display of the power of samādhi shows the lotus clearly manifesting the cross-legged body.
Others, numbering as many as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, presided over lotuses together with their retinues—
all surrounded by sons of the Buddha who dwell in various meditative concentrations.
Those beings whom he had matured and established in the qualities of a Buddha surrounded that great lotus, and they all gazed up at it with palms joined in reverence.
And they, being concentrated, emerged from the bodies of children and stood amidst those possessed by the force of youth.
Those established in the force of youth, being concentrated, emerge from it;
those with bodies worn out by age and old age, being concentrated, emerge from the body of a faithful female lay follower.
Absorbed in the body of a faithful female lay disciple, he emerged from the body of a nun;
absorbed in the body of a nun, he emerged from the bodies of many learned monks.
The many learned monks who were concentrated emerged from the bodies of those in training and those beyond training;
those concentrated in the bodies of those in training and those beyond training emerged from the bodies of the pratyekabuddhas.
Absorbed in meditative concentration within the body of a Pratyekabuddha, they emerge from the body of the supreme and foremost Buddha;
absorbed in meditative concentration within the body of the supreme and foremost Buddha, they emerge from the body of a celestial being.
Absorbed in the bodies of the devas, they emerge from the bodies of nāgas of great supernatural power;
absorbed in the bodies of nāgas of great supernatural power, they emerge from the bodies of yakṣas of great supernatural power.
Those who have attained meditative absorption within bodies of great supernatural power as yakṣas emerge from all such elemental bodies;
those who have attained meditative absorption within all elemental bodies emerge from a single pore.
Concentrated within a single pore, he emerges from all pores;
concentrated within all pores, he emerges from the path of a single hair.
Concentrated within the path of a single hair, he emerges from all paths of hair;
concentrated within all paths of hair, he emerges from those atoms of dust.
Having entered meditative absorption upon a single atom, he emerges from all atoms without exception; having entered meditative absorption upon all atoms, he emerges from the vajra-base of the ocean.
Absorbed in meditative concentration upon the vajra-base of the ocean, they emerge from the fruits of jewel-trees;
having become absorbed in concentration within the fruits of the trees, they emerge through the gateways of the rays of light of the Victors.
Concentrated within the rays of light from the Victors, the Great Being emerges from the waters of the oceans and rivers;
concentrated within the waters of the oceans and rivers, he emerges from the path of fire.
Having become concentrated in the path of fire, the Great-souled One emerged mindful of the path of wind;
having become concentrated in the path of wind, he emerged mindful of the surface of the earth.
Having become composed upon the surface of the earth, he emerges from all the celestial palaces of the gods;
all those who were composed within the divine hosts emerge from the sky, possessing mindfulness.
The concentrations and liberations of those who have accumulated inconceivable qualities are themselves inconceivable;
even if all the Victors were to speak of them for inconceivable eons, it would not be possible to exhaust them.
All the Victors have declared that this ripening of karma for the world is inconceivable;
it is the miraculous transformation of a nāga, the miraculous transformation of a Buddha, and the inconceivable miraculous transformations of one who meditates in dhyāna.
Established in mastery over the eight liberations, they become many from being one, and having become many, they become one again; thus they meditate and blaze forth in the sky.
For they are devoid of great compassion, indifferent to the world, and have no desire for enlightenment;
yet, who would not behold the inconceivable transformations of the body displayed by him who seeks the welfare of the world?
The moon and the sun, moving through the sky, display their reflection in every direction—
in springs, lakes, ponds, wells, and pools, as well as in vessels, jewels, oceans, and rivers.
In this way, those heroes among men display inconceivable forms throughout all ten directions;
they are masters of the methods of all samādhis and liberations, wherein the Tathāgata, the Self-Existent One, is his own witness.
Sāgaradeva was known by the name Rutāvatī; as many beings as were born in the ocean, he, knowing the methods of their various vocal qualities and sounds, satisfied them all with his own voice.
For she understands passion, hatred, and delusion, and knows the resonance within every sound;
having attained mastery through the power of the dhāraṇīs and the Dharma, who in the world of gods and men would not be pleased by her?
Just as a magician, skilled in the methods of spells, displays various and infinite forms—
whether for a day and night, a single moment, months, or even a hundred years, all appearing vast and radiant.
For a magician, though full of passion and hatred, delights the world with his illusory transformations;
how much more so one who is well-trained in meditative absorption, supernormal powers, and liberation, and who knows the proper method of conduct? Who would he not delight?
Just as Rāhu creates an emanated body that forms a vajra-step with the soles of his feet pressed together,
his vision becomes as vast as the ocean and his head is level with the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Even Rāhu, possessed of passion, hatred, and delusion, displayed such supernatural power;
O crusher of Māra, lamp of the world, whose infinite powers would you not display?
Behold the inconceivable miraculous transformations of Śakra when the battle between the lord of the gods and the asuras has begun;
for as many as the bodies of all the asuras are, so many bodies does Śakra emanate from his own.
All the lords of the gods and the gods themselves recognized Śakra... as he went before Svāyu;
"This one shall be seized," they thought, and all the lords of the gods were struck with agitation toward the wielders of the thunderbolt.
Beholding Śakra with his thousand eyes terrifying to behold, emitting flames and grasping a vajra, his body armored and his splendor unassailable, the lords of the asuras fled.
O Śakra, if even he performs such transformations through the power of limited merit while desiring victory over the gods,
why would he who is the protector of the entire world without exception— not possessing inexhaustible merit— not perform transformations?
... by wind clouds are produced and rain falls; by wind clouds are again pacified. By wind grain grows in the world; wind brings happiness to the entire universe.
For he has not trained in the perfections, nor has he trained in the qualities of a Buddha;
he displays the inconceivable ripening of the world—whose [fault] would that not be, since you have obtained such excellence?
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "Recollection of the Three Jewels," in the Śikṣāsamuccaya.
[Chapter XIX: (The Increase of Merit)] The Nineteenth Chapter.
Furthermore, another cause for the increase of merit should be practiced:
this service to sentient beings in all circumstances.
As it is said in the *Āryaratnamegha*:

"When he offers flowers, incense, or perfumes at a shrine of the Tathāgata or to an image of the Tathāgata, he dedicates [the merit] for the removal of the stains of immorality and foul odors from all sentient beings, and for their attainment of the ethical discipline of the Tathāgata."

While performing the sweeping and smearing [of the ground], he dedicates it so that all sentient beings may be free from ungraceful modes of conduct and may achieve perfection in graceful modes of conduct.
While placing a flower canopy, he dedicates it so that all sentient beings may be free from the burning heat of all afflictions.
Upon entering the monastery, he generates this thought:
"May I cause all sentient beings to enter the city of Nirvana. Upon departing, he generates this thought: [May I likewise lead them forth]."
"I shall cause all sentient beings, who are imprisoned within the jail of saṃsāra, to emerge from it. Opening the door of liberation, he generates this thought:
"May I open for all sentient beings the door to nirvāṇa and the happy realms through supramundane wisdom."
When closing [the door], he generates this thought:
"May I close all the doors to the lower realms for all sentient beings.
When sitting down, he generates this thought:
"May I seat all sentient beings upon the terrace of enlightenment.
As he prepares his bed on his right side, he generates this thought:
"May I lead all sentient beings indeed to final nirvāṇa."
As he is rising from that state, he generates this thought:
"May I cause all sentient beings to rise from the obsession of all afflictions.
As he walks with the movement of his body, he generates this thought:
"May all sentient beings proceed by way of the path of the Great Person.
Seated there, he generates this thought:
"May all sentient beings be made free from thorns, namely, from passion, hatred, and delusion."
While performing purification, he generates this thought:
"May I wash away the stains of the afflictions of all sentient beings. While washing his hands, he generates this thought:
"May I remove all the latencies of the afflictions of all sentient beings.
While washing his feet, he generates this thought: "May I remove the dust of the afflictions of many kinds from all sentient beings.
While washing his face, he generates this thought:
"May I purify all the gateways of all dharmas for all sentient beings.
While chewing his tooth-stick, he generates this thought:
"May I remove the various stains of the afflictions of all sentient beings."
He dedicates every state of his body for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
While bowing to a stūpa of the Tathāgata, he generates this thought:
"May all sentient beings become worthy of veneration by the world, including its gods."
Alternatively, as it is said in the *Āryaprajñāpāramitā*:

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has entered the midst of a wilderness infested with wild beasts should not be afraid, should not be terrified, and should not fall into a state of terror. Why is that?"
For he has renounced everything for the sake of all sentient beings;
therefore, he should generate this thought:
"If predatory beasts should devour me, let that be a gift given to them."
My perfection of the perfection of giving will be fulfilled and brought near;
and I shall act in such a way that when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there will be no beings at all belonging to the animal realm in that buddhafield.
They will not be discerned.
