Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has entered the midst of a wilderness infested by robbers should not be terrified, should not be frightened, and should not fall into fear.
Why is that?

Because those bodhisattva mahāsattvas are skilled in relinquishing all possessions; indeed, a bodhisattva must be one who has surrendered even his own body and has renounced all personal requisites and belongings.
He should therefore generate this thought:
"If those beings take away my necessities and requisites, let this be considered a gift given to them.
If anyone should deprive me of life, I must not give rise to hatred or anger toward them."

I must not commit any offense against them in body, speech, or mind; and in this way, at that time, my perfection of generosity, my perfection of ethical discipline, and my perfection of patience will reach fulfillment,
and my unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening will draw near.

And I shall act and practice in such a way that, when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, all these and other faults will, in every respect, entirely and in every way, neither exist nor be perceived in that Buddha-field.
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has entered the midst of a waterless wilderness should not be terrified, should not be frightened, and should not fall into a state of panic.
Why is that?
Because bodhisattva mahāsattvas are indeed those whose nature is free from fear.
And he should generate this thought:
"I must train for the sake of cutting off all craving in all sentient beings;
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not fall into terror."
If I should die of thirst, nevertheless I shall give rise to a mind of great compassion toward sentient beings:
"Alas! These beings have little merit, since such waterless deserts are known in their world."

Furthermore, I shall act and practice in such a way that when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, in that buddha-field there will not be found anywhere, in any way, or at all, any waterless deserts;
and I shall endow all sentient beings with merits such that they shall become recipients of water endowed with the eight qualities.
In that way, I shall undertake firm vigor for the sake of all sentient beings, so that at that time the perfection of vigor will reach fulfillment.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has entered the midst of a wilderness of hunger should not be afraid, should not be terrified, and should not fall into a state of panic.
Moreover, he should arm himself with this armor:
"I shall exert such firm vigor and purify my own buddha-field in such a way that..."

When he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, in that buddha-field there shall be, in every way and in all respects, no such wildernesses of hunger at all, nor shall they even be known;
those beings shall be happy indeed, possessed of happiness.
Provided with every happiness, I shall act in such a way that whatever intention those beings may have, and whatever they may desire in their minds, that very thing shall manifest;

just as, for example, among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, everything manifests by mind and everything arises by mind. I shall undertake such firm vigor that the righteous aspirations of those beings will reach fulfillment.
And there will be no deficiency in the requisites for life for all sentient beings, for everyone, everywhere, and at all times.
Thus, this benefit for sentient beings in all circumstances is a cause for the increase of merit;
it should be seen in detail, however, in the *Āryagocarapariśuddhisūtra*.
Furthermore, ... the gift of Dharma that is free from worldly motives becomes the cause for the increase of merit.
As it is said in the *Āryādhyāśayasaṃcodanasūtra*:
"Maitreya, there are these twenty benefits in the gift that is free from worldly motives,
for one who gives the gift of Dharma without longing for gain or honor."
Which twenty? Namely:
he is possessed of mindfulness, he is possessed of intelligence, he is possessed of understanding, he is possessed of insight, he is possessed of steadfastness, and he is possessed of wisdom.
And he penetrates supramundane wisdom;
he becomes one with little passion,
little hatred, and little delusion.
Māra finds no opportunity to gain entry into him;
he is sustained by the mindful attention of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; and non-human beings protect him.
The gods infuse vigor into his body;
enemies find no opportunity to harm him;
and his friends become unbreakable.
His speech becomes authoritative;
he attains the grounds of self-confidence;
he becomes abundant in mental joy and is praised by the wise.
And that gift of Dharma becomes something to be remembered by him;
Maitreya, these are the twenty benefits.
But in the Noble *Prajñāpāramitā*, it says: "Ānanda, if you were to teach the Dharma on the level of the Śrāvakas to persons belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle,

and if through that teaching of the Dharma all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were to realize arhatship, even then, as my disciple, you would not have fulfilled your duty as a disciple."
It would not have been done.
But if, Ānanda, you were to teach or explain even a single word connected with the perfection of wisdom to a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by that I would be truly served by you as a disciple.

And if all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system were to attain arhatship through that previous teaching of the Dharma, and if one were to consider the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving, the basis of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline, and the basis of meritorious action consisting of cultivation belonging to those arhats—
"What do you think, Ānanda? Is that mass of merit not great? He replied, "Great, Blessed One; great, Sugata."
The Blessed One said:

"Therefore, Ānanda, that person belonging to the vehicle of the disciples generates a much greater mass of merit who teaches the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom to bodhisattva mahāsattvas;
even more than that, Ānanda, does that bodhisattva mahāsattva generate a mass of merit who teaches the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom to another bodhisattva."
Even for a single day;
let alone a single day, Ānanda,
even for as little as before a meal.
Let it be, Ānanda, regarding the morning meal; even for as little as a single *nālikā*,
or even for as little as a single moment of conjunction— [the rest is as before].

Ānanda, this Dharma-gift of that bodhisattva mahāsattva surpasses the roots of merit of all persons belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas and all persons belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is thus endowed with such roots of merit,
and who maintains such roots of merit, Ānanda, it is impossible and there is no occasion for that bodhisattva mahāsattva to turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"This possibility does not exist."
How should the gift of Dharma be given?
As it is stated in the *Ārya-saddharmapuṇḍarīka*:
"The wise one, reflecting at the proper time, enters his dwelling and closes the door."
Having contemplated all these phenomena thoroughly and properly, one should rise and teach them with an undaunted mind.
The wise one always remains at ease; likewise, seated comfortably, he preaches the Dharma after having prepared a magnificent seat upon a clean and pleasant spot of earth.
Having put on a clean robe, well-dyed with pleasing colors, and having likewise donned a black upper garment and a lower robe of great dimensions, he—
Having sat upon a seat provided with a footstool, which was well-spread with various fine cloths,
he ascended it with his feet well-washed and his head and face anointed with oil.
Seated there upon the Dharma-throne, observing all beings with one-pointed attention and equanimity,
he should offer many diverse discourses to the monks as well as to the nuns.
One should avoid weariness and must not give rise to the perception of fatigue;
the wise one should abandon all discontent and cultivate the power of loving-kindness within the assembly.
And that wise one should speak of the supreme dharmas day and night with millions of billions of parables;
he should gladden them and likewise satisfy them, yet he should never seek anything at all therein.
He should not think about food, soft fare, as well as drinks, clothing, beds, seats, or robes; nor should he request anything else from the assembly, even for medicine when ill.
The wise one should always think otherwise: "May I become a Buddha, and may these sentient beings do so as well;
and this teaching of the Dharma for the benefit of the world is my provision of all happiness."
Regarding this very point, it says:
He does not bestow upon anyone a greater favor, even out of love for the Dharma, to such an extent.
The *Āryacandrapradīpasūtra* also says: "If they should entreat you for the sake of the gift of Dharma, you should first say these words: 'I am not trained in the Vaitulya [Mahāyāna].'"
Thus you should speak these words, or you who are wise and learned:
"How could it be possible for me to speak in the presence of such great beings?"
One should not speak to them hastily, but rather after having examined whether they are a worthy vessel;
if you recognize them to be a worthy vessel, you should teach even if you have not been requested to do so.
If you see many who are of immoral conduct present in the assembly, do not speak of ascetic austerity; rather, you should proclaim the praise of giving.
If they should be few in desire, pure, and established in ethical discipline,
you should generate a mind of loving-kindness and deliver a discourse conducive to ascetic refinement.
"If those with evil desires are few and those who possess virtue are numerous there, then, having gained a following, you should proclaim the praise of ethical discipline. Thus it is said.
And it is said in the *Āryasāgaramati-sūtra*: "That is to say:
same."
Samavati! Śamitaśatru! Aṅkure!
Maṅkure / Mārajite / Karāḍe /
Keyūre / Oghavati / Ohokayati.
O you who are free from all defilement and pure; O you who remove all impurities;
O Okhare!
O fierce one!
O devourer!
O Hemukhī!
Averted; brought face-to-face;
all bonds of seizing spirits have been pacified.
All rival proponents have been subdued;
the snares of Māra have been severed;
the seals of the Buddha have been established, and all Māras have been utterly destroyed.
Through the purity of the unshakable state, all the activities of Māra vanish.

Sāgaramati, these mantra-words should be well-recited by the Dharma-preacher; having recited them well while seated upon the Dharma-seat, he should pervade the entire assembly with a loving-kindness produced through the aspect of awakening. He should conceive of himself as a physician, of the Dharma as medicine, and of those who listen to the Dharma as patients.

Having conceived the notion of the Tathāgata as a true person (satpuruṣa) and the notion that the guidance of the Dharma (dharmanetrī) will endure for a long time, one should bring these mantra-words to mind and engage in discourse on the Dharma.
Within a hundred leagues around him, neither Māra nor the deities belonging to Māra’s host shall approach to cause him to lose his vision.
And even those who approach him will not be able to create an obstacle for him.
Regarding this very point, it is said: "The Dharma-preacher must be clean, pure in conduct, well-bathed, and dressed in clean garments."
Thus is the gift of Dharma.
And, in brief, the thought of awakening is the cause for the increase of merit.
As it is said in the *Āryaratnakaraṇḍaka-sūtra*:
"Mañjuśrī, just as various fragrant trees grow while being sustained by the four elements,
even so, Mañjuśrī, the roots of merit of a bodhisattva are accumulated through various provisions."
"Comprehended by the thought of awakening and dedicated toward omniscience, it increases. Thus it is said.
This brief summary of the training for Bodhisattvas has been presented for the sake of recollection by beginners;
however, in detail, it is the domain of the Buddhas alone.
And herein lies the accomplishment of this aforementioned training:
through the right exertions, by not being separated from heedfulness,
and by means of mindfulness, clear comprehension, and thorough reflection.
In that regard, for the sake of the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states, one generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, uplifts the mind, and applies right effort;
by this, there is protection.
By the statement, "he generates desire for the abandoning of arisen [unwholesome states]," purity is indicated;
likewise, "he generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states," up to "he generates desire for the maintenance and further increase of those that have arisen," and so forth.
By this, there is growth;
and these tasks must always be performed with vigilance, for they are the root of all roots of wholesome merit.
As it is said in the noble *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:

"However many wholesome qualities have been proclaimed—ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and likewise patience—the root of them all is this heedfulness; it is taught by the Sugata as the attainment of a treasure."
What is this so-called heedfulness (*apramāda*)?
It is the application of effort toward a remedy preceded by the apprehension of the destruction of what is desired and the arrival of what is undesired.
For example, it is like that of a servant walking along a slippery path while carrying a vessel filled with medicinal oil for a king whose anger and favor are both intense.
For it is said in the Noble Tathāgataguhya Sūtra:
"In that regard, what is heedfulness?
It is the restraint of the sense faculties."
Having seen forms with the eye, he does not grasp at their signs, nor does he grasp at their secondary characteristics.
Likewise, up to the point of cognizing mental phenomena with the mind, he does not grasp at their signs.
He does not grasp at secondary characteristics;
he understands, as they truly are, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding all phenomena.
This is called heedfulness.

Furthermore, vigilance (*apramāda*) is the taming of one’s own mind, the protection of the minds of others, the non-cultivation of delight in the afflictions (*kleśa*), and the pursuit of delight in the Dharma; this is called vigilance. Lord of Guhyakas, one who possesses both faith and vigilance must apply effort that is concordant with them, by which one fully accomplishes those qualities that are the causes of vigilance and the causes of faith.
O Lord of Guhyakas, whoever possesses faith, heedfulness, and vigor should apply themselves to mindfulness and clear comprehension;
by means of that mindfulness and clear comprehension, they do not lose any of the factors conducive to awakening.
O Lord of Guhyakas, whoever possesses faith, heedfulness, vigor, mindfulness, and clear comprehension should apply themselves to appropriate practice.
For a bodhisattva who is correctly applied, O Lord of Guhyakas, understands that which exists as "it exists," and understands that which does not exist as "it does not exist"— namely,
that the eye and so forth exist conventionally.
Likewise, it says in this very same place:
"For constant heedfulness is the root of immortality, and the thought of awakening belongs to one intent on the welfare of sentient beings;
moreover, proper mental application and a mind of solitude are the root of all happiness, being free from grasping."
And it is said: Through the practice of equanimity between self and others, the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) becomes firm;
for the status of "self" and "other" is relative, just as the terms "this shore" and "the far shore" are unreal.
That shore is not "this side" by itself; in relation to what, then, could there be "the other side"?
Selfhood is not established by itself; in relation to what, then, could there be "the other"?
If you do not protect yourself because you think, "I am not afflicted by that suffering," then since you are not afflicted by the suffering of future bodies, why do you protect against it?
The conceptual construction that "I myself am that even then" is false,
because one who has died is indeed other, and another is born there.
If another [self] is born there, what is the use of merit?
What is the use of the accumulation of wealth for the happiness of a youth who has an old body?
When one in the womb dies, another child is born;
when childhood dies, youth arises; and upon the destruction of that, the young man arrives.
And because that [body] has perished, how can it be considered that "the old man has come"? For in this way, the body is different at every moment, just like hair, nails, and so forth.
Now, if through not abandoning childhood a child attains the state of youth,
then the intrinsic nature of the body must be declared as that which remains even when devoid of its states.
If the body were of the form of a statue, it would not exist in the embryonic mass or in ashes.
If, by way of its subtle state, it remains there having abandoned grossness,
it is inherently unindicatable;
it is not called "body."
In this regard, I have no concern at all; for the visible body is subject to destruction, and its connection with various states is perceived only through conventional reality.
And its existence, though claimed on the basis of scripture, is refuted by both reasoning and scripture;
for there exists no primal matter (pradhāna) apart from its constituent qualities (guṇas).
Nor are the three primary principles (pradhāna) such that existence (sattā) and the qualities (guṇas) are likewise;
each of those is also tripartite in nature, and thus the remainder of the world is not of a single kind.
And how could insentient things such as cloth be of the nature of pleasure and so forth?

Pleasure and the like do not arise from cloth; nor do pleasure and the like arise from cloth and such, because cloth and the like lack causality [for them]. Since they would be non-existent, whence could that pleasure come?
Therefore, through both scripture and reasoning, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
their causal relationship is not something to be proven, because it is directly perceived.

And since this [momentariness] is observed within one's own continuum, how could it apply to eternal things? Furthermore, a single atom does not exist, because the distinction of spatial directions would otherwise be impossible.
The oil of a lamp goes toward exhaustion, yet its diminishing is not perceived;
in this same way, phenomena are not perceived as they diminish moment by moment.
The continuum and the aggregate are false, like a row or an army;
why then does the sense of "I" not arise with respect to another [being] through habituation to them?
Therefore, this world should be understood in this way as a mere collection of sense-bases;
that suffering, which has not yet arrived, must be countered by both oneself and others.
Even if this [argument] is improper, it exists in itself but not in another;
that which is improper must be removed, whether it be one's own or another's, according to one's power.
If compassion is so very painful, why is it produced by force?
Having examined the suffering of the world, how could this suffering of compassion be considered great?
Thus those whose mental continuums have been cultivated, for whom the suffering of others is as dear as their own,
plunge into the Avīci hell as swans enter a lotus grove.
When sentient beings are being liberated, there arise those oceans of joy; surely that alone is sufficient—what need is there for a liberation that is devoid of flavor?
Thus, even after performing deeds for the sake of others, there is neither pride nor astonishment;
nor is there any longing for the fruit of maturation, due to a singular thirst for the welfare of others.
The excellence of sentient beings in the ten directions will undoubtedly become his own;
even regarding the happiness of others, there is no room for envy, as he perceives it as his own.
The confession of sins is common to both others and oneself;
likewise are the rejoicing in merit, the entreaty of the Buddhas, and the request for their teaching.
In this way, even dedication proceeds without distinction;
therefore, merit proceeds as infinitely as the realm of sentient beings.
This is that supreme path, a festival of security and infinite bliss,
which increases the joy of the great caravan of Bodhisattvas.
And he was constantly protected by the attendants of the Buddha, who were like the servants of Vajrapāṇi, exceedingly vigilant, and capable of striking terror into the outposts of Māra.
The sons of the King of Perfectly Awakened Ones, seated upon the chariot of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta),
travel along that path while being praised by the gods and other beings.
Therefore, having superimposed the nature of self upon sentient beings through the practice of cultivation,
one should relinquish oneself and all else in every way for the sake of pacifying the suffering of others and oneself.
For one who has craving as their grasping, suffering does not cease;
because it is subject to transformation and destruction, it gives rise to further suffering.
When the world is scorched by the fire of suffering, what delight could there be even in supreme happiness?
For one who is burning on all sides, what pleasure can there be even if the nails are not burning?
And craving for self is the supreme root of all sufferings; therefore, renouncing my own interest for the sake of sentient beings, I shall destroy that very craving.

Therefore, that messenger of the foremost [desire], which is the longing for the known, must be conquered with every effort by maintaining mindfulness of the reality of the self through reflection on dependent origination.
The very thing that I do not cast away out of fear is itself the source of fear for one who clings to it;
for both my body and my mind are indeed passing away at every moment.
If even eternal awakening could be attained through an impermanent body that carries impurities, then surely it has already been attained by me!
Thus, having renounced oneself, one should act for the sake of all sentient beings,
like a vessel of medicine, unconcerned with worldly dharmas.
One should apply one's own wisdom to the role of a counselor for the sake of all sentient beings;
having protected one's wealth through proper means, one should employ it for the benefit of sentient beings.
Whether in one's own body or in another's, that which is suffering does not cause pain here; rather,
because they obstruct the enjoyments of sentient beings, the afflictions must be purified with effort,
like snakes or corpses from a sacred bathing place that the world depends upon for livelihood.
This pure field of merit, which yields the great fruit of the harvest of prosperity,
will satisfy the world tormented by the famine of suffering.
I have renounced gain, honor, body, and so forth for the sake of all people;
for whose sake, then, do I still harbor anger? Or was that which I spoke previously false?
If there is hatred toward those who destroy their own welfare, where will compassion arise?
And if the welfare of others is destroyed, what anger can there be even for one who is merciless?

Those who endure abuse and the like, as well as sugarcanes, saffron, and so forth, though they possess reality, do not become fit for enjoyment when placed in a bad position due to the master's misfortune.
He thinks of a remedy, yet not out of a desire for his master's welfare;
nor does he urge him on, nor does he approach him for the sake of wealth.
By recollecting and being mindful of these, the sons of the Victors, though not sown or plowed,
[cure] the great maladies of all the sense faculties within the various realms of objects.
Having informed and reminded these benefactors even when they are angry,
those whose natural sweetness is never abandoned surely bring happiness to the suffering.
The five elements, known as earth, water, fire, wind, and space,
perform the welfare of all beings for as long as sentient beings remain.
I shall turn them away from all misconduct for the sake of sentient beings;
in this way, I shall make even these six elements free from affliction.
As long as the existence of the world may endure, reaching its limit in space,
so long shall I remain for the sake of the world, preceded by primordial wisdom.
For one should always instruct oneself like a good disciple;
yet, without questioning oneself by oneself, one's actions remain unprotected through sheer force.
Who indeed would become sorrowful through my sorrow, or fearful through my fear?
Or who, knowing the latent tendencies of those faults, would be like a teacher to himself for his own sake?
How could there be a disciple who is not devoid of passion, who does not flee, who is an object of compassion, and who is always present, being equal to oneself?
Intoxicated by the afflictions and blinded by delusion on a path full of precipices,
stumbling at every step, both others and oneself are always to be pitied.
Therefore, it is not fitting to seek out the faults of people who share one's own misfortunes; rather, it is appropriate here to perceive their great and wonderful virtues.
This great ocean of faults cannot be taken up by me alone;
my task here is with others, so why should I look at the faults of another?
I receive upon my head the words of those skilled in exhorting others and who assist by providing food; I become a disciple to all.
For my battle is indeed with many enemies that are the afflictions;
therein, while I am occupied in combat with one, others easily strike me down.
In that regard, he who causes one to hear of danger from behind or from any other direction—
whether he be hostile or well-disposed— is a friend who bestows life in times of equal peril.
He wore a mass of matted hair that was dark blue and unshakable,
and he was adorned with a captivating crest of various fragrant and abundant flowers.
Moving simultaneously through oceans of Buddha-fields in all directions,
he is powerful, capable of counteracting [all adversaries], and the remover of all Māras.
With water released for the pacification of the torments of hell-beings and hungry ghosts,
it flows for the benefit of fortunate beings situated within the thicket of saṃsāra.
By that wise one, who possessed a youthful body, who wore ornaments that produced a festival for the eyes of the world, and who caused wonder among the people.
To that which is named Mañjuśrī, who is the embodiment of the welfare of the world,
I pay homage again and again with my entire being.
A great lake that refreshes those tormented by manifold sufferings;
a great cloud that fills the abyss of thirst within the three worlds.
He is the wish-fulfilling tree for the ten directions, abundant with the fruits desired by the world; he is honored by the lotus-eyes of the world, which rejoice at the attainment of their prayers.
I pay homage with ever-deepening prostrations to Mañjuśrī, who is praised by hundreds of bodhisattvas whose hair stands on end with wonder.
Homage to you, Mañjughoṣa, the physician for all suffering without exception, the bestower of the sacrificial feast of happiness, and the one who is to be relied upon in every way.
By whatever merit I have acquired through composing this account of the deeds of the sons of the Conquerors, who are in every way most wonderful,
may there be infinite happiness for all embodied beings, until they reach the state of the Sugata, the sovereignty over the boundless limits of space.
The Increase of Merit is completed.
And thus concludes this *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, an extraction from many sūtras, which constitutes the Vinaya of the Bodhisattvas.
